title: Spider-Man >>
review:
I walked into Spider-Man: Brand New Day expecting another fun MCU movie, but I left feeling like I'd just watched one of the best Spider-Man films ever made. It finally feels like Peter Parker has earned the title of Spider-Man. He's alone, nobody remembers who he is after No Way Home, and you can feel the weight of that in every decision he makes.

What makes it so good is that it goes back to the character's roots. Peter isn't relying on Avengers or high-tech gadgets-he's just a trying to protect New York while dealing with grief, loneliness, and impossible choices. It feels grounded in a way the previous films sometimes didn't and has a darkness to it and you sympathise with it.

Spider-Man movies never fail to miss.
author: khuraym

title: Without needing to be bigger in scale, the movie finds the Spider-Man that Tom Holland was missing.
review:
Who would have thought that, after No Way Home, the best course of action would be to scale things back? Brand New Day works precisely because it understands that this Peter Parker didn't need another multiverse, but rather time to exist on his own.

It's great to finally see Tom Holland as a more urban, independent Spider-Man who's truly connected to New York. The film makes better use of his powers, delivers great action scenes, and finds plenty of emotion in the loneliness of someone who's lost everything but still chooses to help people.

Not everything works. There are too many characters, some ideas are left half-baked, and the third act drags on longer than it should. Still, it's been a long time since a Marvel movie seemed so interested in its own protagonist. For the first time, I felt that this version wasn't living in the shadow of Tony Stark, the Avengers, or the multiverse. It was just Peter Parker trying to figure out how to move forward. And that was exactly what he needed.
author: oNerdcall

title: The Spider-Man I've Always Wanted!
review:
"Spider-Man: Brand New Day" is absolutely phenomenal and might just be one of the greatest live-action Spider-Man movies ever made...if not the greatest.

The cinematography is on a completely different level compared to the previous films. Every frame is bursting with beautiful, vibrant colors that constantly stand out, making the movie a visual treat from start to finish. Some shots are direct recreations of iconic comic book panels, and seeing those moments brought to life on the big screen made the experience even more special.

The practical stunt work deserves a lot of praise. It gives the action a sense of weight and realism that's often missing in modern superhero films, making every fight and swing through the city feel authentic.

Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal have incredible chemistry together. Every scene they share is engaging, and I honestly can't wait to see them interact again in future projects. Sadie Sink makes a fantastic MCU debut, and Mark Ruffalo's Hulk hasn't looked this good in years. Both performances add a lot to the movie and fit naturally into the story.

Speaking of the story, it's emotional, compelling, and feels like the perfect progression after the events of "No Way Home". It balances heartfelt character moments with spectacular action, and the pacing never lets up. The fight sequences are outstanding, and the stunt work throughout the movie is simply incredible.

Jackie Chan's stunt team clearly poured their hearts into this film because the choreography is among the best the MCU has ever delivered. The only Marvel movie I can really compare it to in terms of action is "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings". Considering they're directed by the same filmmaker, I'm not surprised by the final result at all.

Destin Daniel Cretton has crafted a Spider-Man movie that presents the character in a way fans have dreamed of seeing for years. It truly feels like the comic books have come to life right before our eyes.

Overall, "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" exceeded every expectation I had. It's emotional, visually stunning, packed with incredible action, and understands exactly what makes Spider-Man such a beloved character. For me, it's not just another great MCU movie - it's one of the finest Spider-Man films ever made!

title: The Most Vulnerable, Heartfelt, and Emotionally Mature Spider-Man Film to Date
review:
Brand New Day offers a look at the most vulnerable Spider-Man we've ever seen on screen, the film explores Peter rebuilding his life and figuring out who he wants to be, taking him on a journey of self-discovery after the world forgets who he is, i think the film succeeds in capturing that emotional journey from start to finish, and that's easily what i loved most about it.

The action is exciting and incredibly well done, but somehow it feels different this time, even the action sequence carries its own meaning, Peter wasn't only fighting villains and trying to save the city, he was also fighting his own doubts, grief, and loneliness.

It's deeper than just another Marvel flick, at least in my opinion, it probably won't have the same impact on people who aren't really connected to Peter's story or the larger lore, and they might not enjoy it as much, but for me, this felt like something genuinely different, a literal brand new chapter for Spider-Man, and i absolutely loved it.

The cast also delivers some great performances, Jon Bernthal returns as Frank Castle, and i really enjoyed seeing him again, his role never feels distracting and fits naturally into the story, the same goes for Mark Ruffalo, who returns not only as Bruce Banner, but the Hulk himself, and if you've missed the old, angry Hulk, i don't think you'll be disappointed, and last but not least, Sadie Sink is simply a nice addition to the franchise, that's all i can tell.

Overall, Brand New Day isn't just another Spider-Man adventure, it's a heartfelt story about loss, identity, and finding the strength to move forward, it's one of the most emotionally mature Spider-Man films to date, it shows that Peter's hardest fight isn't always against villains, but sometimes against himself, and that's what makes this film stand out to me.

author: ahmadfcb

title: A more mature, emotional, and grounded Spider-Man
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day feels like a refreshing new direction for Tom Holland's Peter Parker. The film brings Spider-Man back to a more personal, street-level story, focusing on Peter's emotional weight while still delivering the humor, energy, and action that make the character so enjoyable to watch.

Tom Holland gives one of his strongest performances as Peter, now more vulnerable, more mature, and much more human. The chemistry between the cast remains a major strength, and Destin Daniel Cretton's direction gives the action a lively, physical feel that really works.

What I appreciated most is that the film doesn't rely too heavily on multiverse spectacle or oversized MCU setup. It has heart, real emotion, and a clear sense that Spider-Man is once again the center of his own story.

The only small downside is that the film feels a bit overstuffed at times, with a few ideas and characters not always getting enough breathing room. Still, that doesn't take away from how satisfying, entertaining, and emotionally effective the movie is overall.
author: ivan_lilo

title: Spider Man Brand New Day Great Visuals & Cast, But Lacks a Real Spidey Villain (7/10)
review:
After a 5 year wait and two amazing trailers, Brand New Day delivers a fun watch, but it falls short of the classic Spider Man story hardcore comic fans were hoping for.

The biggest issue is the script ignoring Peters ground level life post No Way Home. Key questions are left unanswered. What has he been doing for 4 years? Did he go to college or work to pay rent and bills? Where did he get his expensive tech, and how did he not make a single new friend like Gwen Stacy in all that time?

Pacing wise, the opening montage is weak, Act 1 is okay, Act 2 is fantastic, but Act 3 falls into the classic rushed MCU formula similar to Thunderbolts. Having Jean Grey and the DODC as main antagonists feels like Kevin Feige using Spidey popularity just to force long awaited mutants into the MCU, rather than giving Spider Man the rogue he deserves.

Regarding what works, Tom Holland gives his absolute best performance yet as both Peter and Spidey. Sadie Sink is a brilliant casting choice and very excited for her future in the MCU. The Punisher is a surprisingly great addition, handled very well despite the PG 13 rating. The Yelena Belova cameo is a fantastic surprise and a total highlight that completely stole the scene. The technical quality, visuals, and audio presentation are top tier throughout.

Regarding what does not work, the film is missing a classic Spidey supervillain. Spider Man has arguably the best rogues gallery in comics, so not having a proper Spidey villain in the main plot is a huge letdown. I honestly expected street level heavyweights like Tombstone or Scorpion to take center stage instead of mutant setups. Also, Ned and MJ feel completely unnecessary for a Brand New Day. MJ feels like a totally different character compared to the first trilogy, and Ned only works because his screen time is short.

Overall, it is a solid 7 out of 10, visually impressive and wonderfully acted, but held back by MCU universe building over a focused Spider Man story with a proper villain.
author: Jopeta_Castiglione

title: A fresh, emotional and grounded rebirth for Peter Parker, stepping into a brand new era...
review:
The first thing that comes to my mind is how remarkably authentic and emotionally raw this new direction feels. It's masterfully crafted, layered with profound humanity and, above all, deeply touching. Peter Parker faces the painful aftermath of his ultimate sacrifice, carrying the unbearable weight of a world where he has become a complete stranger... Living like a lone wolf (pretty much in isolation) after losing everything that once defined him (deeply missing MJ as well as Ned, and still very much grieving Aunt May), he once again chooses to put his heart on the front line for people who don't even know his name... Watching him navigate that overwhelming loneliness while continuing to protect New York is both heartbreaking and inspiring.

And what makes this movie so compelling is that, despite its emotional heaviness, it never loses sight of hope. At its core, this isn't simply another battle between good and evil. It's a story about resilience, identity, forgiveness and the courage to rebuild your entire life from scratch after losing everything that mattered. Every major decision Peter makes carries genuine emotional weight, making his journey feel more human than ever before.

The return of some familiar as well as new faces naturally reinforces that emotional core, as Peter tentatively seeks to rebuild fragile bridges with MJ and Ned through instinctual beats of connection rather than forced exposition. Meanwhile, the newcomers fit seamlessly into this new chapter. Jon Bernthal's brutal yet nuanced Frank Castle/Punisher creates a fascinating ideological contrast with Spider-Man ; Mark Ruffalo brings warmth and wisdom as Bruce Banner (the same can't exactly be said about Hulk) ; and Sadie Sink immediately establishes herself as a captivating addition to the MCU, delivering a deeply tragic performance that explores the heavy burden of telepathy, mutant identity, and the profound bond of shared isolation she forms with Peter. The chemistry across the entire ensemble feels effortless and deeply authentic.

From a technical standpoint, this may very well be the most visually accomplished Spider-Man movie ever made. Modern filmmaking technology has reached an astonishing level, but what truly impresses is how creatively it's used here to serve the narrative. The swinging mechanics genuinely feel alive, fluid, and believable, constantly placing you alongside Spider-Man rather than simply watching him from afar. The action is phenomenal throughout-culminating in an endgame combat sequence against The Hand's red ninjas in the Damage Control facility that feels like a living painting you could witness in the Louvre. Every frame balances spectacle with clarity, constantly serving the story rather than overwhelming it.

Yet for all its visual brilliance, it's the emotional dimension that truly elevates the experience. Several beautifully crafted scenes explore grief, empathy, sacrifice and second chances with remarkable restraint, proving that some of the movie's most powerful moments rely on quiet human connection. There are also a handful of unforgettable sequences that comic-book fans have dreamed of seeing adapted for years (Punisher carrying an injured Spider-Man is a comic-book frame that's as iconic as it can be), all handled with tremendous care and genuine emotional impact.

On a lighter note, the subtle comic-book references, clever callbacks and unexpected surprises naturally flow with the story, maintaining a wonderful balance between melancholy and humor, strength and vulnerability. Long-time fans will constantly find rewarding details, while the film quietly plants intriguing seeds for the future-opening exciting possibilities without allowing them to overshadow the story being told today.

What's certain is that you'll experience an wide range of emotions from beginning to end... The movie delivers thrilling action and breathtaking visuals, but what truly stays with you is the human emotions, with Peter's deeply personal journey in its core...

By the time the credits roll, you're left thinking less about the spectacular battles than about the humanity behind the mask. Important to point out how Tom Holland fully embodies both Peter Parker and Spider-Man with extraordinary dedication, with all of his heart 'n soul. He has always been a gifted actor with impressive emotional range and undeniable physical commitment, but his growth over the years has been remarkable, reaching new and greater levels as an actor. Watching him evolve from the hyperactive kid under Iron Man's wing to this mature, battle-tested, yet deeply vulnerable hero carrying the heavy weight of isolation is pretty mesmerizing, to be honest. Much like Peter himself, Tom Holland continues to evolve, embracing new challenges to offer newly delightful flavors to the audience... Quite admirable, if you ask me.

And of course, how can you not applaud what director Destin Daniel Cretton accomplishes here ? From the vibrant color palette to the score's memorable new themes, every aspect reflects an obvious passion... He understands exactly when to let spectacular sequences breathe and when to slow everything down for quiet conversations that carry just as much impact (if not more)... His vision balances high-octane action with intimate, deeply heartfelt character moments, building toward a magnificent final act where the connections between the different characters reaches its peak ! Above all, the raw chemistry shared by the cast-especially between Tom Holland & Zendaya (for obvious reason) works nicely ; and the tasty on-screen connection with Jon Bernthal, whose real-life friendship dating back to 2015 and the filming of the independent movie "Pilgrimage" adds incredible weight to their scenes (the hospital bedroom moment near the end is particularly touching and genuinely cute)-makes this an feel so nice and real...

"Spider-Man : Brand New Day" isn't just one of the best superhero movies ever made ; it is -because of its emotional and psychological layers- a pretty memorable film in its own right-one that reminds us why Peter Parker remains one of the most relatable and inspiring heroes for generations.
author: valmont1702

title: Woah guys, easy now.
review:
Very, very competent, and there are some exciting highs here, but I'm not really feeling the same level of excitement as some other people. There is a real tension here between keeping things from getting too crazy, but then having some reveals and moments that could be considered spoilers. It makes it a hard movie to review, because things can be given away, and then you can also talk about other parts where not enough happens, and then that gives things away in a different way. I don't know.

I felt some fatigue here. The excitement of thinking about where this could go, in the first half, beat the experience of finding out where it did go. Revelations lay good groundwork for movies to come, but also had me feeling a bit like "I guess that's it."

My biggest disappointment is with the action. Destin Daniel Cretton directed Shang-Chi, and that movie had some great martial arts-influenced action. They keep teasing the idea of doing a big hand-to-hand sequence in Brand New Day, but that action never really explodes as it should. There are action scenes that start well but then don't really last long enough. It's less about wishing the action scenes were bigger (we don't need a Thanos-level threat every movie), and more about wishing those grittier and more grounded fight scenes just went on for a bit longer. Most fights get wrapped up too cleanly and quickly.

There are dramatic things that happen, with Peter losing control of his powers, and The Punisher going too far, but little by way of significant consequences get explored regarding those two moments, and some other ones. Everything felt a bit too neat here, and something that felt like it was supposed to be a twist felt too obvious when it was revealed.

This film was lacking in a lot of ways, but there were ways it worked for sure. Tom Holland is really good here, and the story here is compelling when it focuses on the aftermath of No Way Home. That's a bigger part of the movie than I was anticipating, dominating at least the first half or so, and maybe contributes further to this feeling better in its first half. For all my gripes, I also generally liked how other characters were worked into this, be they cameos or supporting roles. It was the first time in a while that the MCU felt like a proper shared universe again, and there is fun to be had in seeing established characters cross over. I think the MCU forgot the value in doing that throughout much of Phases 4 and 5, even though it seems so obvious (I'm thinking about how little time the Guardians were in Thor 4... Brand New Day at least sits with the ending of No Way Home and its consequences for quite a bit longer).

In terms of balancing a large number of characters while keeping most of the drama about Peter, Brand New Day works. I wish I could be a bit more excited about where it did go in its final act, and I really didn't like how neatly so many things were wrapped up (even by MCU standards). But this was an enjoyable movie. I just think it had a lot of flaws holding it back from being more than just pretty enjoyable.
author: Jeremy_Urquhart

title: Tom Holland delivers his best performance to date, excellent movie.
review:
Following the reality-altering events of Doctor Strange making the world forget Peter Parker, the young hero must navigate a life of complete isolation while facing a deep and dangerous new mystery involving unfamiliar threats, comic book adversaries and unexpected crossovers that pull him into a much larger universe.

If I were reviewing this movie based solely on its special effects, I'd be discussing greatness. Honestly, if dazzling visuals, breathtaking fight sequences and sheer spectacle are your thing, this movie is sensational. The production values are exceptional, the opening absolutely hooked me, and the ending delivered the emotional rollercoaster I'd been hoping for. The middle perhaps doesn't quite hit those same dizzying heights, but that's only because the beginning and end are so incredibly strong. It still moves along at a cracking pace, with more than enough action and intrigue to keep you invested.

Tom Holland has grown on me more and more with every passing outing. Here he very much feels like Spider-Man, and it's easily his most assured performance yet. While much of his personal journey is engaging, parts of it felt as though Christopher Nolan had wandered into the writers' room, giving us yet another central character weighed down by heavy trauma. It works, but it is a direction modern blockbusters seem increasingly fond of taking. You definitely get to see some classic comic book adversaries, and you can decide for yourself just how effective they are.

The production values extend wonderfully to the sound design, which is sharp and powerful without becoming overwhelming, something I appreciated after my recent experience with *The Odyssey*. Watching the film for a second time allowed me to appreciate many of the subtleties I'd missed on first viewing. I caught an early ten o'clock screening and the cinema was absolutely packed, so I have a strong feeling this is going to do exceptionally well, and it deserves to.

One thing that did make me chuckle, however, was the absurd number of themed commercial tie-ins before the film started, featuring everything from superhero car insurance to tactical toothbrushes. Not that I'm cynical at all-now hand me my Spidey black coffee.

8/10.
author: Sleepin_Dragon

title: The MCU Finally Gives Peter Parker Room to Hurt
review:
I went into Spider-Man: Brand New Day with very low expectations. As a longtime comic-book reader, I'm often skeptical of live-action adaptations when the source material is so carefully written, and the previous MCU Spider-Man film left me feeling that a lot of the storytelling had been sacrificed for spectacle. I was actually planning to skip this movie, but I ended up catching it on opening day-and I'm glad I did.

This is easily the darkest and most mature Spider-Man film in the MCU. After the reality-altering ending of No Way Home, Peter Parker is completely anonymous. No friends, no family, no one who remembers him. The movie follows him during that lonely period as he throws himself entirely into being Spider-Man while dealing with mysterious incidents across Manhattan and an unsettling evolution of his powers.

What surprised me most was how much the film focuses on Peter's emotional state rather than on multiverse spectacle. Themes of anonymity, grief, identity, and rebuilding your life after a devastating loss are front and center. Tom Holland gives one of his best performances as Peter, and the supporting cast is excellent. Sadie Sink is especially impressive, and Tramell Tillman brings real weight to his scenes.

If acting is the standard, the movie is very strong. The storytelling is also polished if you don't compare it directly to specific comic-book runs. My ongoing issue with the MCU Spider-Man films is that they rarely feel like truly solo Spider-Man stories. There are always characters from other corners of the Marvel universe, and I still wish Marvel would make a film focused almost entirely on Spider-Man, his supporting cast, and his villains without the need for outside collaborations.

The first act is definitely too long. The film spends a great deal of time emphasizing that Peter is lonely, anonymous, and miserable, and after a while the point becomes obvious. The Punisher subplot, which is meant to show Peter that he doesn't have to carry everything alone, feels stretched out. On the other hand, I really liked the decision to make Detective Jean DeWolff Peter's confidant.

The narrative involving Bill Metzger, Damage Control, Jean and Sara Gray is less successful and sometimes feels forced. The screenplay introduces a lot of interesting ideas-Peter's unstable powers, his unresolved feelings for MJ, the new characters-but not all of them receive enough development. At times the movie feels overstuffed, and its 145-minute runtime is longer than it needs to be.

Still, once the main plot kicks in, the pacing improves significantly, and several emotional scenes genuinely work. The audience reaction in my screening was intense; people were openly crying during multiple moments. The film is uneven, but it is also ambitious, and after years of multiverse-heavy MCU storytelling, this feels like a sincere attempt to reset Peter Parker and push him into a more grounded, character-driven era.

It's not the perfect Spider-Man movie I'm still hoping for, but it's a solid and surprisingly affecting step in the right direction.
author: karlandrewcruz

title: When You See Yourself Behind the Mask
review:
!!! SPOILERS !!!

It's hard to put into words what this movie truly means to me. I know some people might brush it off as "just another average Spider-Man movie" or "another Marvel slop that somehow pulled a billion dollars in a single day." But to me, it means everything. Sitting in that theater, I genuinely saw myself behind the mask, minus the superpowers and, you know, actually fighting the Hulk.

Peter Parker's MCU journey peaks here. No Way Home set up a perfect clean slate with Aunt May's tragic death and Doctor Strange's memory-erasing spell, and Brand New Day utilized it masterfully. It doesn't shy away from the raw isolation of Peter's new life, his struggle with evolving powers like organic webbing, and the slow, painful work of healing. More importantly, the movie understands that Peter's biggest enemy isn't necessarily the person standing across from him. Damage Control may be the movie's external antagonist, but the story's real conflict is much more personal. It's the shared struggle of Peter, Jean, and the people around them with loneliness, grief, and learning how to live with the losses that shaped them.

Jean Grey fits into that theme beautifully. Rather than simply being another powerful character thrown into the MCU, she is someone dealing with her own loss and psychic trauma. Her connection with Peter feels natural because, despite being completely different people, they understand what it means to carry something painful that nobody else can truly see. The emotional bond between them builds to one of the most powerful climaxes in the franchise. When Jean spends hours and days keeping a fatally wounded Peter breathing after he throws himself in front of Frank Castle's bullet, it says more about their bond than any line of dialogue could.

Bringing in Frank Castle was brilliant. Frank serves a much greater purpose than simply being another fan-favorite character. His tragic history gives him a unique understanding of Peter's isolation, and having Frank show Peter that he doesn't have to completely shut everyone out because, at the end of the day, everyone needs someone in their life, gave the story genuine emotional weight. Peter doesn't need to forget his losses. He needs to learn how to live with them without letting them completely consume him.

Tom Holland delivers his most grounded performance yet, showcasing the sad grind of Peter's daily life. Jon Bernthal stole every single scene he was in. Despite the PG-13 rating, Castle never felt out of character. Sadie Sink was fantastic in her MCU debut, while Zendaya and Jacob Batalon showed visible growth in their performances.

Destin Daniel Cretton also deserves a huge amount of credit. His strengths were already obvious in Shang-Chi, so I was genuinely curious to see what he could bring to Spider-Man, and he more than delivered. The action has an incredible sense of movement and spatial awareness. One of my favorite examples is Peter's fight with the Hand, when he jumps onto the ceiling and the entire camera rotates with him. It's such a simple directorial choice, but it completely changes our perception of the space and makes Peter's movement feel genuinely three-dimensional. Cretton understands that Spider-Man shouldn't just fight in a room. He should use the entire room.

The action sequences and web-swinging were absolutely top-notch, easily the best we've seen in any Spider-Man movie. The swinging in particular doesn't just look incredible, it actually feels like Spider-Man. There's a sense of freedom and momentum to it that perfectly contrasts Peter's miserable everyday life. If they released a three-hour cut of pure swinging and fights, I'd sit through it without blinking.

The soundtrack was impeccable as well. Hearing Tame Impala's "Loser" perfectly matched Peter's mental state and gave me instant chills. And yes, I absolutely love that song, so maybe I'm biased.

If I had to nitpick, I felt Scorpion was underused. I understand why he was given a slightly larger role than some of the other street-level villains, especially since Homecoming has been teasing his return for years, but even then, his presence felt more like someone higher up told them to include him more than something the story genuinely needed. I really wanted to see more of him in action and, more importantly, I wanted the story to give him a stronger reason to be there. I also wished we got a bit more of Frank Castle's backstory through flashbacks, similar to Peter's memories. It would have helped casual audiences understand his motivations and made his connection with Peter even more impactful. The post-credit scene felt slightly underwhelming after the emotional weight of the ending.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a great example of Marvel Studios still being capable of making genuinely impactful movies. It proves that not every chapter needs a traditional happy ending. Sometimes the most important part of a new beginning is accepting what you've lost and learning how to keep moving forward.

I've already seen it twice in theaters and could watch it 10 times back-to-back. Tom Holland has officially solidified his place as my favorite Spider-Man, and this is now my favorite live action Spider-Man movie of all time.

The extra bonus is that you don't need extensive prior MCU knowledge to enjoy this. It stands strong on its own, while still rewarding longtime fans who understand where these characters came from.

Rating: 9.5/10.
author: benedekdavid-42715

title: I'm Sorry, I Just Don't See What Others Clearly Do In This.
review:
I struggled through the bloated runtime of Brand New Day and after feeling initially underwhelmed coming out of the cinema, having a few days to ruminate on the film has made me think that it's actually not very good at all.

The film seems well made but the writing, pacing and plotting just don't work for me for the most part. I'll list my main issues with the film in no particular thematic or chronological order.

Jean's plan makes no sense and borders on the ridiculous; there are far more obvious, efficient and effective ways for somebody with her abilities to find out what happened to her sister.

She is also an outright evil villain before the film needs her not to be one. She walks innocent people in front of cars and tortures Peter before even learning of what happened to her sister. Then she is jarringly absolved of it all with zero accountability at the end of the film.

The conversation with May that begins Jean's 'redemption' at the end is so trite and cliche that it might as well have been written by AI.

Rather than move him on as a character, the film spends a good third of its runtime trying to get Peter back to exactly the same dynamic with MJ and Ned that the last film conclusively ended.

The inability to use mechanical and genetic webshooters is nonsensical.

As is some magic universal inhibitor that stops all mutant abilities somehow being manufactured in an attic room.

MJ being offered and then turning down a job with a 'soulless corporation' was eyerollingly cliche. Then why apply for one then, genius?

The action scenes, while well done, took obvious cues from the Insomniac games and pale somewhat by comparison.

The whole thing has pacing issues and many of the interpersonal relationship scenes were just flat out poor, dull and shallow. It doesn't have the sophistication or performances for a compelling drama while the action sequences are too interspersed for it to be a straight up superhero film. The comedy, while not overdone is very hit and miss with one or two sequences like the pre-fight stretching just being flat out annoying and out of place to me.

It just seemed nowhere near the crowd pleaser that No Way Home was, and is somehow being held up as the far superior film. I'm not really the target audience for either film but I know which one I had a better time with.

author: Slightgamer_0

title: Finally Street-Level Spidy We've Been Waiting For
review:
BND is a strong, emotionally grounded reset for Tom Holland's Spider-Man and one of the more satisfying MCU movies in recent years. Holland gives his best performance yet as both the earnest, burdened Peter and the wisecracking web-slinger. The film leans into the classic Spider-Man themes of loneliness, responsibility, and the cost of heroism more directly than the earlier trilogy entries, and it actually feels like it means it.

Jon Bernthal's Punisher is a real standout. The odd-couple dynamic with Spider-Man gives the movie some of its funniest and most grounded moments. Sadie Sink is fantastic. One of the best MCU debuts in a long time. Can't wait to see her in future projects.

The story is actually pretty basic, but the whole thing still feels like a genuine step forward rather than just another interchangeable MCU installment. The action set pieces are spectacular and often inventive

Highly recommended, especially if you're a fan of the character. It's incredibly entertaining and completely worth every penny.

title: A Brand New Day, the Same Old Formula
review:
I didn't think this was a bad movie from a technical standpoint. The production values are solid, the action is constant, and longtime Marvel fans will probably enjoy the references, cameos, and the connections that seem to pave the way for the X-Men's future in the MCU.

My problem is that fan service becomes the movie's main identity.

The story tries to juggle too many plotlines at once: Peter's mutation, his emotional struggles, Damage Control, The Hand, Punisher, Jean Grey, the never-ending MJ subplot, and the setup for future MCU projects. Instead of building one compelling central conflict, the film spreads its attention across so many ideas that none of them reaches its full potential.

It also falls into one of the most overused crossover formulas: heroes fighting each other over misunderstandings until they realize someone else is the real villain. Rather than creating meaningful ideological conflict, the movie manufactures fights simply because the plot demands them.

The biggest issue, however, is Spider-Man's inconsistent power scaling. This is the same character who casually stopped the Winter Soldier's metal arm in Captain America: Civil War, yet here he struggles against ordinary members of The Hand. The film explains this with a device that suppresses his mutation, but it feels less like a believable limitation and more like a convenient excuse to weaken him whenever the script needs artificial tension.

The movie also spends far too much time revisiting Peter's relationship with MJ, a storyline that, in my opinion, has long since run out of fresh ideas.

Ironically, many of these story beats reminded me of the 1994 animated Spider-Man series, where a similar mutation arc worked much better because it had time to develop Peter's struggle over multiple episodes. Here, it feels compressed into a film already overloaded with characters and franchise setup.

If you're looking for spectacle, fan service, and MCU connections, you'll probably have a good time. If you're looking for a focused story with strong dramatic substance, Spider-Man: Brand New Day feels more like a bridge to future movies than a satisfying film on its own.

title: Unexpectedly Profound: A Masterclass in Emotion, PTSD, and Character Study
review:
In a remarkably sophisticated way, this film manages to tackle heavy themes like PTSD and the overwhelming weight of guilt without ever feeling bogged down. It caught me completely off guard. The movie captures the silent struggle of fighting your demons alone - trying to suppress your inner pain out of fear that you are flawed, hiding it from the world, and unintentionally hurting those around you in the process.

To be honest, I was never a big fan of Tom Holland's Spider-Man films - until now. This easily ranks among my favorite Spider-Man movies of all time. The brilliance lies in the direction and writing: it successfully places us right inside Peter's suit, letting us feel his emotional state organically without relying on cheap inner-monologue narration.

The thematic core is incredibly strong. Peter's desperate grip on the past and his struggle to let go - especially while those he loved no longer remember him - delivers a heartbreakingly powerful message about the vital need for an anchor in this world and the realization that no one can survive completely alone.

I was particularly moved by the symbolism surrounding the technology used to control the "monstrous" side. It serves as a brilliant allegory for modern medication, where so many people attempt to simply suppress their internal darkness. The film reminds us that trying to force the beast into submission only guarantees a more volatile explosion later; quick technological or biological fixes aren't the answer. Sometimes, you have to allow that side of yourself to be expressed and processed.

With phenomenal acting, sharp editing, and stunning cinematography, nothing about this felt like a glorified two-hour trailer for the next Marvel phase. It was a genuine, soul-stirring story that brought me to tears long after the credits rolled. I truly hope Marvel continues to make films with this level of maturity and sophistication.

author: boydmatta

title: Marvel Pulled a Wanda 2.0
review:
The biggest issue isn't just that the villain is an unseen telepath-it's that the villain is Jean Grey, and the movie completely fumbles her character. For two hours, she acts like a sadistic psychopath. She hijacks the minds of innocent people, forces civilians into traffic, drives a rigged tank through New York, and literally possesses Bruce Banner just to unleash the Hulk on the city.

Then, out of nowhere in the third act, the writers expect the audience to feel sorry for her because the Department of Damage Control wronged her sister. It is the exact same frustrating trope Marvel used with Wanda Maximoff: having a highly powerful character do unspeakably evil things to innocent bystanders, only to hand-wave the accountability away with a tragic backstory.

If you are going to strip away the classic superhero formula for a grounded psychological thriller, the payoff needs to make sense. Instead, after Jean spends the entire movie terrorizing the city-and even violating Peter's life by manipulating MJ into kissing him while she has no memory of it-what happens?

Spider-Man literally takes a bullet for her and lets her skip town. She shows absolutely zero remorse for the random families she endangered, yet the film treats her as a misunderstood victim who deserves to be saved. It is baffling that Peter would lay down his life for an unrepentant telepath who just ruined countless lives for her own revenge.

title: A Fresh Take on Spider-Man.

The film isn't without its flaws. Some of the visual effects look surprisingly inconsistent for a blockbuster of this scale, and the runtime occasionally feels overlong. A tighter edit would have improved the pacing.

What truly stood out to me, however, were the supporting characters. Hulk, Jean Gray, and especially Frank Castle completely stole the show whenever they appeared. Their presence added energy, charisma, and a darker edge that made the film even more enjoyable.

Overall, this is a solid superhero movie that offers a fresh perspective on one of Marvel's most iconic heroes. Despite a few technical shortcomings, it's an entertaining, well-written adaptation that both comic book fans and casual audiences can appreciate.

author: smartbaast

title: An Unexpected Masterpiece
review:
When I walked into the theater to watch Spider-Man: Brand New Day, settling into our three adjacent seats at the very back of the auditorium with my friends, I honestly didn't have high expectations. It wasn't that I had absolutely zero expectations, but I was definitely highly skeptical. Spider-Man: No Way Home was such an absolute masterpiece and a massive cinematic event that I genuinely thought it was technically unnecessary to bring a new episode into the picture. To me, they had already reached the absolute peak with that previous installment, and they could have perfectly closed the story right there and just left it alone. I was convinced they wouldn't be able to hit that exact same level again, and that whatever came next would just feel like a forced attempt to ride the wave of the previous movie's phenomenal success.

Honestly, I mostly sat down in the cinema just thinking that it would be nice to see them all again. I figured it would be fun to reunite with the whole team, see the familiar characters back in action, and just enjoy a fun ride with the cast. I expected a decent superhero flick, but I certainly did not expect it to be this incredibly good, nor did I anticipate that it would hit me so profoundly hard.

I am incredibly happy to admit that I was completely wrong. Exactly because of my initial skepticism and my firm belief that making this movie was completely unnecessary, I was blown away far more than I ever could have imagined. Brand New Day doesn't just survive on the legacy of its predecessor; it confidently carves out its own spectacularly unique path, delivering a phenomenal experience from beginning to end. I genuinely loved every single minute of it.

What surprised me the most was the fresh, much more grounded direction they decided to take with the narrative. Instead of desperately trying to replicate the massive, multiverse-breaking scale of the last film, Brand New Day strips everything back down to its roots. It focuses on the absolute core of what makes Peter Parker such an amazing, universally relatable, and deeply human character. The emotional depth presented here is absolutely staggering. It strikes a flawless balance between the classic, lighthearted, friendly neighborhood superhero action and some truly heavy, character-defining moments. The villains written for this installment are incredibly fleshed out, posing a genuine threat that feels intensely personal rather than just another generic, world-ending CGI catastrophe. You can truly feel the immense weight and high stakes in every single punch thrown and every web slung across the skyline.

The action sequences are breathtaking, the cinematography is consistently stunning, and the pacing keeps you completely hooked for the entire runtime without a single dull moment. The acting performances are top-tier across the board, and the musical score beautifully elevates the incredible visuals on screen. Overall, this was a fantastic cinematic experience. It is a brilliant new chapter for the web-slinger that definitively proves there are still plenty of amazing, gripping stories left to tell. title: A Good Spider-Man Movie, Just Not the One I Expected
review:
A fun watch and a solid pick if you're an action lover.

After the ending of No Way Home, where everyone forgets Peter Parker, I was expecting either soft reboot with totally new characters or serious, grounded street-level Spider-Man story. That's how it was marketed too. But simply adding Punisher doesn't make it a street-level movie. What we actually got is a stylish action flick.

Story-wise, it's good. It introduces the new characters well without losing the main plot. But for a standalone Spider-Man film, it relies way too much on cameos and that hurts both the movie and the continuity of the universe. C'mon yaar... let Spider-Man take down a villain on his own for once.

This is where the Home trilogy did a better job. It balanced cameos and the larger MCU while still letting Peter struggle and grow. Here, because of all the cameos, things become too easy for him. I never got the same feeling of struggle that Homecoming and Far From Home gave me.

The emotional moments work, but they could've hit much harder. The twist is decent and the action is easily the biggest highlight. Every action sequence is worth watching on the big screen.

My only other complaint is that some character arcs feel incomplete. Their endings leave so many questions that it's hard to guess where they're heading next. The post-credit scene is decent too, but it could've set up the future in a much stronger way.

If you're planning to watch it, I'd definitely recommend the theatre. The action deserves the big screen. Just don't spend extra for 3D, it barely adds anything. The movie feels like it was made with 2D in mind.

title: A good movie, but nowhere near the best of the Spider-Man films.
review: *Spider-Man: A New Day* is a film that seeks to return to a more intimate and darker perspective of the masked hero. First and foremost, the cinematography deserves praise; it is impeccable, capturing New York in exemplary fashion. The film succeeds in its portrayal of Peter Parker-his internal conflicts are well-developed-and Tom Holland's performance effectively conveys Spider-Man's emotions to the audience. Zendaya-who had limited screen time in previous films-shows growth here, though, in my view, she still lacks the spark expected of an MJ. Jean Grey (Sadie Sink) is a highlight-despite her somewhat questionable methods-and the character holds great potential within the MCU. The Punisher's appearance works well and is engaging, though it serves primarily as comic relief. The film's flaws must also be noted. The Hulk's inclusion is very weak; one of Marvel's greatest heroes is made to look ridiculous. Scorpion is introduced in a terrible, confusing manner. Furthermore, the movie ends abruptly and anticlimactically-lacking an epic, cathartic conclusion-and, once again, without a major villain worthy of Spider-Man. Rating: 7.5/10.
author: GabrielS-282

title: Some Great Ventillation (If You Know, You Know)
review:
The summer has been hot from where I'm sitting, and everyone is using fans to ease the effects of the constant heat. In some ways, you could say that this movie was some much needed ventillation against the heat of the MCU dumpster fire since Endgame (I'm also winking at those of you who have seen the movie - you'll know what I'm talking about, hahaha).

Many other commentators and critics are saying it, so I do not think it's far fetched to argue that this is by far the best Spider-Man film since the original Spider-Man 2 by Sam Raimi. It is also easily the best MCU movie since Endgame, although in some ways perhaps it's not accurate to categorise it this way, since these movies are technically made on the Sony side. While No Way Home was an epic journey and grander in scale in many ways, I believe this film is better written and has more fleshed out character arcs that return Spider-Man to the feel of the original movies.

You have to give credit to Cretton for an amazingly well directed film, the sequences in New York are very well done. McKenna and Sommers also do an awesome job in giving this reset story an emotional core. Every character has a role to play, and none of them are just there for fan service - they fit organically into the plot. The film does a great job of handling the past of this Spider-Man, while also moving the story forward in a balanced way.

Finally, without giving any spoilers, the villain and their backstory was set up flawlessly in paralell with what Peter Parker goes through in this movie.

Bring on the fifth film!

title: Once You Understand Jean Grey's Powers, the Movie Falls Apart
review:
I guess I'm in the minority on this movie. I just didn't think it was good at all.

Jean Grey makes no sense. Once you actually understand how her powers work, a lot of what she does falls apart. If she can possess people and read their minds, why does she need to break into a building with a tank and send supervillains after Spider-Man? Why not just possess the bad guy or someone close to him and find out everything she needs to know?

It's even more confusing when Jean possesses MJ and tries to kill her. So she clearly has no problem invading someone's mind and controlling them when it benefits her, but somehow doesn't use the same ability to get the information she needs? The rules around her powers feel completely inconsistent.

I'm also getting tired of superhero movies turning their third acts into therapy sessions. It's lame. They did the exact same thing in Thunderbolts, and it's becoming a trend I really don't like.

And why is Spider-Man suddenly okay with Jean Grey doing horrible things just because she lost her sister? Since when does personal tragedy excuse evil? It's another example of flawed morals being treated as if they're noble or compassionate. I just can't get behind that.

title: "One of the Best Spider-Man Films Yet"
review:

author: KAIGAI-KASENIOR

title: A Refreshing Return to the Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man
review:
After everything Peter Parker went through in Spider-Man: No Way Home, I was hoping this movie would slow things down and focus on the character rather than trying to top the multiverse spectacle. Thankfully, Spider-Man: Brand New Day does exactly that.

This feels like the most grounded MCU Spider-Man film to date. Instead of another world-ending threat, the story brings Peter back to the streets of New York where he truly belongs. The smaller scale allows the film to focus on what has always made Spider-Man special: an ordinary young man carrying extraordinary responsibility while dealing with loneliness, loss, and the weight of doing the right thing.

Tom Holland delivers what I believe is his strongest performance as Peter Parker. He perfectly captures a version of Peter who has matured through hardship but still refuses to lose his compassion and hope. The emotional moments are handled with sincerity and never feel forced. Some of the conversations in this film are among the best written in the MCU Spider-Man series, adding real emotional depth without becoming overly dramatic.

The action is another major highlight. The street-level combat feels fast, creative, and grounded, making every fight engaging. The web-swinging sequences are absolutely breathtaking and, in my opinion, the best the Spider-Man franchise has ever delivered. The sense of speed, freedom, and momentum is incredible, and every swing through New York reminded me why Spider-Man is such an iconic hero.

The supporting cast also deserves praise. Jon Bernthal brings a fantastic presence whenever he's on screen, balancing intensity with perfectly timed humor. Sadie Sink also gives a strong performance and fits naturally into the story without feeling like she's there simply to set up future films.

The final act delivers exciting action while staying true to the movie's grounded tone. Rather than relying on nonstop visual effects, it emphasizes choreography, tension, and Spider-Man's agility, making the climax genuinely satisfying.

The movie isn't perfect. There are a few moments where the pacing slows down, and I would have liked a little more development for certain characters. However, those issues never take away from the overall experience.

Most importantly, Spider-Man: Brand New Day understands who Spider-Man is. It reminds us that Peter Parker doesn't need multiverse chaos or universe-ending stakes to tell a compelling story. Sometimes, all he needs is New York City, a web-shooter, and the determination to keep doing the right thing even when no one knows who he is.

If you've been waiting for a true friendly neighborhood Spider-Man movie, this is exactly that.

title: Good film but could've been more

Once the hulk was fallen off the building all we hear is that banner has been sent off to hospital and that's all we see of him for the rest of the movie. Again so much potential was wasted here as it seems they just wanted to include hulk as a cameo and then move on to the next part of the film.

My final point is the main villain. There is a lot of villains or enemy that Spider-man has to fight but there isn't necessarily a clear one. As mentioned earlier Scorpion was brought into this film as a villain but was hardly used to what he could've been. Then next villain in the film was Jean Grey who was a good villain played by Sadie Sink. Jean was given a proper backstory in this film however by the end of the film we are left wondering if she was the main villain or if it was William Metzger. As many people have already stated in their reviews there is just a lack of a clear villain.

Overall Spider-man Brand New Day was a decent movie and was fun to watch. The cast provided amazing performances, the cinematography was impeccable and same with the costume designs. However they introduced a lot of plots but then made sure to get them over with quickly. I just wish the film had been longer to give them more time to go deeper into these plots instead of cramming them all in and making a mess of how to end them. title: Refreshing Return to the Heart of Spider-Man
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day doesn't try to outdo No Way Home in terms of spectacle, and that's exactly why it works.

This is a more grounded, character-driven story that feels true to the spirit of Spider-Man. Tom Holland delivers one of his strongest performances, portraying a Peter Parker who has clearly matured while still retaining the humour, compassion, and relatability that define the character.

The action sequences are exceptionally well choreographed, balancing excitement with genuine stakes. The trademark Spider-Man humour is present throughout, providing plenty of laughs without undermining the emotional weight of the story.

One of the biggest highlights for me was Sadie Sink. As a new addition to the cast, she delivers a standout performance with a compelling backstory and an emotional depth that makes her character instantly engaging. She genuinely steals many of the scenes she's in.

The supporting cast remain excellent, with familiar characters staying true to themselves, and the interactions between Spider-Man and other Marvel characters add both entertainment and heart.

Most importantly, the film understands that Spider-Man has always been at his best when the focus is on Peter Parker as much as the superhero. It explores growth, responsibility, and resilience in a way that feels earned, while still delivering thrilling action and memorable moments.

This isn't another No Way Home-nor does it try to be. Instead, it confidently tells its own story, and because of that, it stands as one of the strongest Spider-Man films in recent years.
author: Shahzone

title: A Well-Executed Return and Brand New Day for the MCU!
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is one of the best films Marvel has put out in recent years!

The pacing is perfect and intense enough to pull at the audience's hearts. Both the action and emotional scenes are well executed, and the actors all deliver amazing performances (well except for a certain scene). Although the film still carries some clichés from old superhero tropes (which is why I can't give it a higher score, but 7.5 out of 10 should be valid), I love how Peter Parker and his opposite are contrasted: they are both without families or anyone to rely on, both possess remarkable abilities, and both have broken hearts, yet they handle themselves and the ordinaries differently-one chooses to control (just as their kind was controlled by authorities) and the other chooses to help (by following instinct simply as a "nice kid"). This makes the endgame solution make so much sense (happy to see logical plots!).

What's more is that as an audience, I am so proud to see Peter grow as a person throughout all these years. In this film, the winding path where he grew on his own, how he becomes a stronger Spider-Man who masters his abilities and understands himself, and eventually opens up on his own, was truly moving.
author: Carol_Zzz

title: More than saving the day.
review:
Every hero wears a mask. Few manage to hide behind it the weight of simply continuing to exist. Spider-Man: Brand New Day understands that Peter Parker has never been compelling merely because he fights villains, but because he must live with the consequences of being who he is. A sense of melancholy runs through nearly the entire film, making it perhaps the darkest portrayal of the character since Spider-Man 3, directed by Sam Raimi. Rather than pursuing grandeur at any cost, the narrative chooses to follow a hero who no longer sees the world with the same innocence he once had.

This shift is also reflected in the film's aesthetic. The cinematography abandons much of the exaggerated brightness of recent productions and finds an identity defined by cool tones and an uneasy atmosphere, as though New York carries the same emotional exhaustion as its protagonist. It is a choice that reinforces the feeling of isolation accompanying Peter throughout his journey. There are a few visual missteps here and there, but nothing that undermines a direction that, for the most part, knows exactly what kind of feeling it wants to convey.

Curiously, that visual confidence is not mirrored in the screenplay. The film constantly seems to distrust the audience's ability to interpret what it is seeing. Instead of allowing emotions to mature through silence and uncertainty, or letting certain images speak for themselves, almost everything receives an additional explanation. The ideas are there, many of them genuinely compelling, but they rarely have the chance to breathe on their own. The impression is that the narrative is afraid to leave any empty space, as though every second needed to come with an invisible subtitle. Spider-Man swings between buildings with remarkable freedom; the script, not so much.

Peter Parker, on the other hand, is the film's greatest strength. His growth unfolds without erasing the qualities that have always made him such a beloved character. The humor is still present, but now it emerges less as a parade of jokes and more as a way of coping with the weight of his own life. For the film, growing up does not mean abandoning lightness, but learning how to carry it when it feels more necessary than ever. It is precisely this transformation that makes the final act work so convincingly.

And that is exactly where the film's greatest surprise lies. At a time when blockbusters seem determined to outdo one another with the loudest explosion or the most apocalyptic villain, Spider-Man: Brand New Day chooses a different path. The resolution of the central conflict does not seek to impress through scale, but through meaning. Instead of turning everything into a spectacle of destruction, the film focuses its energy on what truly matters; Peter's choices. That emotional simplicity is far more powerful than any CGI skyscraper collapsing. It is a rare moment in superhero cinema that reminds us a character can carry an entire scene without needing half the city flying through the air. The visual effects are grateful... and so is the heart of the story!

That decision connects directly with the film's ending, which finds a sensitivity remarkably close to that of the comics. There is an honesty there that reaffirms the very essence of Spider-Man; a hero who has never been defined by the grandeur of his victories, but by his willingness to keep moving forward even when everything feels unbearably heavy. The film understands that Peter does not need to save the universe to be extraordinary; he simply needs to keep being Peter Parker.

It is understandable that Spider-Man: Brand New Day embodies a curious contrast. Visually, it finds a striking identity; emotionally, it understands its protagonist remarkably well; narratively, however, it insists on explaining what was already perfectly clear. Even so, its greatest strengths speak louder. Whenever it abandons the anxiety of trying to impress and instead trusts the power of small decisions, the film reminds us why Spider-Man remains one of the most deeply human heroes in cinema. Sometimes, saving the day is far less interesting than figuring out how to live the next one.

title: Brand New Reboot
review:
From comic book pages to Tobey Maguire, Andrew Garfield, and now Tom Holland, one consistent bell that never goes unrung remains the same regardless of who's playing or writing the iconic character: you can't have both.

Due to the events of the last two Spider-Man films, it's a brand-new day for the hero-or, in other words, a reboot. Now free from the burden of juggling two lives and being completely anonymous, he should be able to operate as both Spider-Man and Peter Parker without the worry of a threat in the corner waiting for the right opportunity but that's not, nor will it ever be, the case. I don't know if there's another character on page or the screen who gets it worse than the Queens native, yet continues to fight against villainy mostly to protect those closest to him-even if they don't remember him.

Even with a new threat in New York puppeteering the citizens, the biggest conflict for Peter is within himself and the mutation he's undergoing. Yeah, it's lonely at the top of the Empire State Building, but he often chooses to carry this weight as if it's a punishment. Repressing the truth about his life and friends, he buries himself in the job-and now that he's hit this late stage of radioactive puberty, things are looking messed up, even by Spider-Man standards.

Desperate to keep at least one hand on the wheel and control this change from within, elements are introduced that will undoubtedly return in the MCU's future. There are also a few surprise cameos that don't just exist to remind viewers of the characters, but feel entirely natural and actually help drive the plot forward-rather than just being a quick 'hi and bye.

To better understand these changes on a cellular level, Parker seeks help from Bruce Banner-though surprisingly, the somebody who you can lean on (if you can call him that) throughout most of this turns out to be Jon Bernthal's Punisher. I personally prefer the murderous psychopath, but when both heroes have lost everything and are married to the vigilante life, someone needs to bring a little light, even if it's the guy wielding an assault rifle as an equalizer. Some aspects of their partnership give off comedy-duo vibes, which works for a quick laugh, but it's still not quite the Frank I'm familiar with.

Unsurprisingly, this film is visually stunning. Captivating scenes are shot like they're ripped straight off a comic book page, and I have zero complaints. When it comes to the action, that POV shot of Peter swinging through New York City is always jaw-dropping, but it's the small details in the fight choreography that truly kept my full, undivided attention. Bring all these different forces together into a single setting, and you get one of the best MCU scenes in years.

Though the film itself and the cast worked like a charm, I feel some parts could've used a bit more focus in the third act. Despite the solid pacing throughout its 145-minute runtime, the conclusion felt slightly anticlimactic. Still, this is definitely a fun addition to what I already consider a great run for the character on the big screen. It offers a nice balance of heartbreak and heartfelt moments that will leave a lasting impression on hardcore fans and casual moviegoers alike.

title: Half of a Spider-Man movie, and half something else...
review:
I'll just say it: I didn't enjoy "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." Is Tom Holland still a good Spider-Man? He is. Is Zendaya's chemistry with Tom Holland off the charts (and off the screen)? Of course. Is there plenty of crowd-pleasing and genuinely funny comedy? You bet! But is this an exciting, satisfying, and action-packed super hero movie? It's really not.

It's easy to say that the recent Tom Holland Spider-Man films are more corporate products than creative outlets, but never has that felt more apparent to me than in "Brand New Day." Flat, dull, and uninspired are all ways to describe the visual style of this movie. It's easy to be tricked into thinking it looks naturalistic or documentary-esque, but it's all a cover to have virtually every scene in this film be set in constant bleak, grey locations. And none of these locations are ever interesting or visually pleasing - grey city streets, grey office buildings, grey college dorms - everything is colorless and lifeless.

Going hand-in-hand with this low-budget feel is the fact that "Brand New Day" doesn't feel like it has a real villain, at least to me. "Brand New Day" seeks to shorten the scope and scale, which is fine with me - after "No Way Home" and before "Doomsday," it's admittedly hard to up the stakes, but I had faith that they'd pull out one of Spider-Man's many villains, perhaps even one that the audience has never seen on screen before. Instead, the main antagonist is... a villain from the X-Men? What a disappointment. It feels lazy and uninspired, like they just grabbed someone from another franchise instead of giving Spider-Man a real threat of his own. The conflict never feels personal or exciting because of it, especially because, if you're a comic book fan, you know that Jean Grey is a hero for longer than she is a villain.

The action is another weak point. There are a few decent sequences, but nothing that feels particularly creative or memorable. Most of the fights are short, straightforward, and lack the inventive web-slinging set pieces that made earlier films more fun. There's one really good fight with Scorpion, a fun team-up with Punisher against Hulk, and of course some fun little slow-motion montages, but beyond those highlights, the action never really takes off. Because the movie doesn't have a strong, central villain, there's no real sense of escalation. You're left waiting for a big, jaw-dropping climax that never fully arrives, and so the final confrontation ends up feeling more like just another set piece instead of a proper payoff, which is pretty disappointing for a Spider-Man movie.

All in all, I wanted to like this more than I did. Holland and Zendaya are still great together, and the humor lands more often than not, but the dull visuals, underwhelming villain, and general lack of energy make "Brand New Day" feel like a step down. It's not a terrible movie, but it's a surprisingly lifeless one, and for a Spider-Man film, that's kind of a problem.

title: A notable refresh for Spidey
review:
Spider-Man was given a notable refresh. Jon Watts did a decent job with Homecoming and Far From Home-and excelled with No Way Home-but that last entry felt more like the product of studio and production company mandates than a film with a distinct directorial signature.

Now, Destin D. Cretton has been given some creative freedom-partly due to the success of Shang-Chi and Wonder Man-and the result is unexpectedly good. His touch is most evident in the sequences where Spider-Man swings through the buildings of New York and in the fight against The Hand.

In this story, Spidey appears mature and evolved as a character, yet he somehow retains his agile, lighthearted, and humorous essence. There is a highly entertaining interaction with Frank Castle and a great depiction of the origin story of a major mutant.

There is also strong interaction and a solid confrontation with the Hulk, who looks better here than he has in a long time.

The fan service here goes hand-in-hand with scenes that look like iconic comic book covers brought to life-brief, fleeting moments lasting just a couple of seconds.

The performances don't particularly stand out, unlike the direction, screenplay, and cinematography. The latter highlights the vibrant colors of a city that never sleeps while also playing skillfully with shadows and chiaroscuro effects.

Finally, the visual effects team delivers a strong performance, making a healthy recovery after several previous missteps.

In short, the film successfully takes a risk by introducing a major character to kickstart a new saga within the superhero subgenre. I appreciate that the script isn't overcrowded with heroes; instead, the plot develops, twists, and resolves around just a couple of them, making the most of their presence.

Highly recommended for fans of superhero cinema.

title: The MCU finally understood Spidey.
review:
This is the defining Spider-Man movie from the MCU, with a beautiful story about grief, acceptance, and learning to move forward after losing everything you've had, from your Aunt to your own identity.

I was blown-away by the direction of this movie after three bland movies from Jon Watts, the work of Daniel Cretton is so fresh and interesting compared to the former. Visually, the movie is packed with references to Spider-Man's history in both cinema and comic-book, but never feeling like forced moments just for the fans to look at and say they recognized. Whether through the framing of certain shots, the staging of the action, or recreations of iconic comic covers, the film constantly pays homage to what came before while telling its own story. Borrowing even the fight choreography and even general movements from the Insomniac games, incorporating all of this in such a creative manner that it fits seemingly in the narrative.

Tom Holland is at his best here since entering the MCU. This version of Peter Parker is more mature, carrying the emotional scars of the previous films without ever losing the kindness and optimism of the character. Holland sells both the quieter dramatic moments and the lighter humor effortlessly, and for the first time it truly feels like we're watching Peter become the Spider-Man he was always meant to be, without some mentor to tell him what and how to do things.

Still the movie can hit emotionally with a surprisingly mature story about living with grief instead of trying to erase it. Peter cannot undo his past or recover everything he has lost, but he can choose not to let those losses define the rest of his life. It is a simple message, yet one that the movie communicates with sincerity, so when the emotional beats come, they land without becoming overly sentimental.

But the film occasionally loses focus because it is so busy setting up the future of the MCU. New characters and side plots constantly interrupt what is otherwise a very personal story. None of these additions are necessarily bad on their own, but together they create the feeling that the movie is being pulled in several different directions. Whenever the screenplay returns its attention to Peter, it becomes immediately more engaging.

But even with those diversions, Spider-Man: Brand New Day works because it never loses sight of what the message is. We get exciting action, beautiful visuals, heartfelt emotion, and the best characterization Tom Holland's Spider-Man has received so far. It is a movie that respects both the comics and the previous films while confidently taking its own step forward.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day - One of My Favourite Spider-Man Movies
review:
I watched Spider-Man: Brand New Day during its first weekend of release, and honestly, this has become one of my favourite Spider-Man movies.

The action scenes were really good, but what made the movie especially enjoyable for me was the appearance of Hulk and the Punisher. Their scenes with Spider-Man were some of the most entertaining moments in the movie and made the film feel much bigger than a typical Spider-Man story.

What I especially liked was the more mature version of Peter Parker. After the events of No Way Home, Peter is essentially living alone, with the world having forgotten who he is. The movie does a good job showing how lonely his life has become and how he struggles to deal with everything without the support of his friends. Tom Holland also gave a really strong performance as Peter Parker.

I also really liked Sadie Sink as Jean Grey. Her character is dealing with the loss of her sister Sara and is desperately trying to understand what happened to her. I thought Sadie gave a really strong and emotional performance, and honestly, I think she fits the role of Jean Grey extremely well. Her portrayal makes Jean feel vulnerable and conflicted rather than simply being another superhero character.

I particularly liked the relationship between Peter and Jean. Peter understands her loneliness and the pain of losing someone important, because he has experienced that kind of loss himself. Their conversations and the way Peter tries to support her added a surprisingly emotional layer to the movie.

The movie isn't just about Spider-Man fighting villains - it's also about loss, loneliness, and finding someone who understands what you're going through. That's probably what made it stand out to me.

Overall, I had a great time watching it. The action, Hulk and Punisher appearances, Peter's character development, Tom Holland's strong performance, and Sadie Sink's performance as Jean Grey made this one of my favourite Spider-Man movies.

My rating: ⭐ 10/10.

title: One of My Favourite Spider-Man Films
review:
Spider-Man is my favourite superhero of all time. I grew up watching his movies, and to be honest, I've loved-or at the very least enjoyed-every single one of them. From the animated series to the live-action films, he's always been one of my favourite fictional characters. Yes, that definitely gives me a bit of a bias whenever a new Spider-Man movie hits theatres, but I still try to be critical whenever I feel something deserves to be pointed out. That really wasn't the case with Spider-Man: Brand New Day, though. This is easily one of my favourite Spider-Man movies ever made. While I have a couple of minor nitpicks here and there, I honestly don't have much to complain about. I had a huge smile on my face from beginning to end, and I found myself tearing up on multiple occasions. If a movie can make me laugh, smile, and get emotional all in one sitting-especially when it's a Spider-Man movie-then it's done something very special for me.

Picking up four years after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the world has completely forgotten that Peter Parker is Spider-Man, leaving him to live a lonely life while continuing to protect New York in secret. This feels like the first true street-level version of Spider-Man we've seen in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and it's something I've wanted for a long time. Seeing Peter simply trying to help everyday people instead of constantly dealing with universe-ending threats was incredibly refreshing. The action is some of the best we've seen from Spider-Man in live action in years, with several sequences that perfectly capture how agile, creative, and exciting the character can be. However, the biggest surprise for me was the film's villain. Without spoiling anything, I'll just say this is a character who could have easily felt forced into the story, but instead became one of my favourite parts of the movie. Their presence feels completely natural, and the final act delivers some incredibly intense and emotional moments that had me fully invested.

Jon Bernthal returns as the Punisher, while Mark Ruffalo reprises his role as Bruce Banner, and both are excellent additions to the story. They each bring some well-timed humour while also contributing to dramatic scenes. Tom Holland, however, is the standout. I truly believe this is the best performance he's ever given as Peter Parker and Spider-Man. He brings so much maturity, vulnerability, and heart to the role that I found myself getting emotional multiple times throughout the film. His relationship with MJ, played by Zendaya, is handled with a lot of care and complexity, and I really appreciated the direction they took. Likewise, Peter's friendship with Ned, played by Jacob Batalon, is explored in a way that feels honest and surprisingly touching. Whether you look at this as a standalone Spider-Man movie, a sequel to No Way Home, or another chapter in the MCU, I think it succeeds on every level.

One of the things that surprised me most was how great the movie looked. Many recent Marvel films-including the previous Spider-Man movies-have often felt visually flat, with muted colours and fairly standard cinematography. Brand New Day is a huge step up in that department. The colours are vibrant, the contrast is much stronger, the shadows are used beautifully, and the cinematography gives the film a much more cinematic feel. Every frame looked like genuine care had gone into how it was composed, and that alone made me appreciate the movie even more. I had such a great time with this film and walked out of the theatre as one very happy Spider-Man fan. Whether you've followed every MCU movie or you're simply someone who enjoys Spider-Man as a character, this movie does a fantastic job of welcoming you in. It feels like a true fresh start for Peter Parker, and I think they absolutely knocked it out of the park. I can't wait to watch it again.
author: kjproulx

title: "A new day. A new threat. A hero reborn."
review: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he's devoted himself entirely to protecting his city - a full-time Spider-Man - but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced. Tom Holland as Peter Parker/Spider-Man, Zendaya as MJ, Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Jacob Batalon as Ned Leeds, Jon Bernthal as Frank Castle/Punisher, Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner/Hulk, Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova/Black Widow and Olivia Booth-Ford as Sara Grey were amazing. From the very first second, Spider-Man: Brand New Day reminded me why I love this character. The Marvel Studios intro was nothing short of brilliant. Watching moments from previous MCU films featuring Peter Parker, only for him to gradually disappear from them, perfectly reflected the ending of No Way Home, where the entire world forgot he ever existed. It wasn't just a logo sequence-it was storytelling. It was creative, emotional, and one of the best Marvel intros I've ever seen. From there, the movie does an incredible job of showing Peter embracing the role of the friendly neighborhood Spider-Man. His conversations with Bruce Banner, where he still doesn't fully understand his own potential, were some of my favorite moments. His reunion with MJ was emotional and reminded me why their relationship has always been so compelling. The biggest surprise for me was the Jean Grey twist. Knowing who Jean Grey eventually becomes made seeing this version of her even more fascinating. Finally, that post-credit scene..I genuinely have no idea where Marvel is heading next, and I love that. It leaves you excited without giving too much away. Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is emotional, thrilling, surprising, and everything I wanted from a Spider-Man film. It honors Peter's journey, delivers unforgettable moments, and proves that even after No Way Home, there's still plenty of magic left in this story.
