author: Matthenry129

title: Most Underwhelming Spider-Man Movie of All Time
review:
If not for the vfx and cinematography in this one, it would have been a complete disaster. Spider-Man is one franchise where you can't screw up with the plot. This felt more of an MCU filler movie for set-up of next flims than the core standalone spiderman drama that every fan expects out of this franchise.

Few very problematic things with the movie: (spoiler alert)

1) It JUST DOESN'T MAKE SENSE as to why JEAN GREY would kiss Peter Parker while possessing MJ. A character who is struggling with corrupt DDC and finding her sister, trying to threaten spiderman pulls of a romance pretending to be his ex-gf? And then she clarifies MJ had no memory of Peter in there which makes it lot more absurd. That was a lazy attempt at fulfilling a pure fan fantasy.

2) The final scene with Aunt May inside Peter's head, where an attempt to give closure to both Spiderman and Jean is shown. This was the weakest part when it could've been very impactful. Aunt May is inside Peter's head and probably this is a conversation which has happened with Peter in past. She says "You're beautiful and people don't love you because you are special but because you are you" A. Why would she call Peter beautiful in the original conversation. And B. It is the most generic thing ever said. Expected little more from a movie that carries a great legacy at these things specially. It makes fan feeling nothing after all the anticipation and call-back. I understand it doesn't have to be extremely moving but it should give the logical closure to characters, where both the conflict and closure seems more like trying to make a story around the forced characters than having something organic.

3) Spiderman has plenty of villains from his own comic books and we are yet to see so many of them in their full glory. Instead of that we get Jean Grey to build up on X-Men. This is unfair to what this movie could have been. In name of exploring inner world of Spider-Man they have failed to do both, having a gripping story and exploring the stakes well.

For instance take Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2. We see a Peter who is under immense stress, job is lost, college performance suffers, gf is no longer available, is under debt. And then loses self belief and powers under that. Under this all Doc Ock captures his gf and he has to let go of all things holding him back get the confidence and self belief and fight. Just like how it is in life, when stakes are so high you have no option but to show up for the right thing regardless of how you feel. That's Spiderman.

Here we are told he is lonely and overworked but little is built around that, told how he is suffering while denying and accepting that he actually is. Again nothing expect for mutation to show that. It doesn't have to be same but still lot is left on table to explore.

4) Most of the movie plot was leaked in the trailer itself. Hulk's clip in the entire duration of movie is same is that shown in trailer, you literally get around a minute more of it here. That happens when you know you have shot limited good things and have to bank on them to get the audience to turn up. While leaving you don't feel like there was story worth 2hrs.

Now few things they did get right:

5. The way Spider-Man is shown in new light by Dustin was refreshing to see. The cinematography here is evidently different than the usual MCU Spiderman movies you see. It has a dark undertone to it and it's genuinely immersive. You can feel things like you are Peter. That's genuinely difficult to get right.

6. MJ's offical closure to Peter. The way she acknowledged that they both might have had something in past but as the memories are erased she doesn't love him. This was very logical and doesn't magically just undo all that has happened and the struggle of Peter and this was way better as closure because from this point the very thing eating up Peter on inside was that what if he had told MJ everything, they might have been together but knowing this he understands that all that they have had exists only in his head right now. You can see him getting that closure but much better than being eaten up everyday from the dilemma and choosing it over and over again. They have not closed the romantic doors completely but if they decide to rebuild something from here it is a very good foundation to start from.

7. The scene with Scorpio (Jean controlled) where Peter actually unleashes his raw growing mutation and shows glimpse of his true strength, this showed that if spiderman actually doesn't hold back how dangerous he could be. What makes him great are his intentions.

8. The hand scene where finally embraces his mutation and accepts it all, and answers the question by "I'm both" was PEAK CINEMA. The scene following it was peak action and you see Spiderman at his fullest expression and this is probably the best written action sequence in any Spider-Man movie, although short but the way Peter webbs them making sure they are not killed and doing it just like a spider would. Beautiful.

9. Last but the most impressive, Sadie Sink. She did immense justice to whatever screen time she had. Her presence is magnetic and you can't take your eyes off her. She perfectly balances her character and beautifully brings it to life. Such a wonderful casting. She will not feature in Spider-Man movies anytime soon but whenever they meet again, I'm really looking forward to their dialogue then.

Finally, nothing to hurt anyone's effort or anything critical, purely a fan opinion who has grown up watching Spider-Man and is a die hard fan. Hope people notice this review and consider it for next installments. (Which is an extremely remote possibility but we can always try :p)

author: RebeccaW-2016

title: Tom Holland's Best Spider-Man Yet
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is, in my opinion, one of the best Spider-Man movies ever made and easily Tom Holland's strongest solo film. It may even rival No Way Home. While No Way Home will always be a special event because it brought together three generations of Spider-Man, I think Brand New Day tells the stronger and more focused story.

The story is easily the movie's greatest strength. Rather than relying only on action and nostalgia, it explores loneliness, isolation, and the darker instincts that can take over someone who has no one left to lean on. Those themes felt surprisingly relatable and gave Peter Parker more emotional depth than we've seen in a long time.

Tom Holland delivers his best performance as Spider-Man. He feels older, more mature, and carries the emotional weight of the film exceptionally well. This is exactly the direction I hoped Marvel would take after No Way Home.

The villains aren't necessarily the most memorable on their own, but they don't need to be. Much of the movie keeps you guessing about who the real threat is, and the morally gray characters and anti-heroes make the story much more interesting than a simple hero-versus-villain plot.

The action is fantastic. The fight choreography is some of the best in the MCU, and the web-swinging looks incredible. I'd only rank it behind the first-person swinging sequences from The Amazing Spider-Man films.

One thing I also loved was the cameos. Both Hulk and Punisher are used well, but Punisher especially steals every scene he's in. His appearance never feels forced or like simple fan service-it genuinely adds to the story and was one of the highlights of the movie for me.

The supporting cast is excellent as well. Sadie Sink does a great job, Jacob Batalon is once again very enjoyable as Ned Leeds, and Tom Holland carries the film from beginning to end. I've always thought Zendaya was a little overrated, but she gives a very strong performance here too.

The humor is used much more sparingly than in some previous MCU films, and I actually preferred that. When the jokes happen, they land naturally without taking away from the emotional moments.

My biggest criticism would be the pacing. The beginning is slower than it probably needed to be, while parts later in the movie move a little too quickly. It's never enough to hurt the overall experience, but it is noticeable.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an emotional, mature, and action-packed Spider-Man film that understands what makes Peter Parker such a compelling character. It balances heartfelt storytelling with fantastic action and delivers one of the strongest entries in the character's cinematic history.

I would recommend this movie to everyone-not just Spider-Man fans, but anyone looking for a genuinely great superhero film.

title: A Classic Spider Man Story
review:
Brand New Day ends up feeling at its core like a quintessential Spider Man adventure. It doesn't necessarily use its trope in the most revolutionary way but in a way that's exciting and so energetic. It feels like it takes the best aspects of the Holland era, the Raimi movies and even the Insomniac video games to create something that clearly comes from a place of love and reverence for the character.

Destin Daniel Cretton is clearly one of the MCU's best assets right now and this movie just makes me so sad that we never got to see his take on Avengers. I like 2/3 of Jon Watts' movies but from a visual perspective this is a massive step up in every regard. Just like Shang-Chi he manages to create some truly breathtaking and epic fight scenes that merge CGI and practical elements seamlessly. The swinging scenes are beautiful in large part because it always feels like there's an effort to continually capture them in new ways visually. It's also really well paced from the outset even with lot of exposition being given out but it never felt like empty set up.

I've had my reservations about Tom Holland's interpretation of Spider Man in the past but this movie is the best he's ever been. By this point the character feels so lived in and I thought this film built of the ending of No Way Home in a really satisfying way. This movie feels like it's earned the right to use the classic Spider Man tropes by this point and I really loved that it took a more grounded approach to the character and its story. The inclusion of Zendaya and Jacob Batalon were done perfectly and in a way that did not take away from the consequences of the last film at all. I've been critical of the previous movies for their need to constantly include wider MCU characters but Jon Bernthal's appearance in this movie was something I didn't know I needed. The Punisher doesn't feel diluted at all and not only are the scenes between him and Holland frequently hilarious but moments towards the end were a lot more wholesome than I expected.

My hang ups with the movie aren't major but only that it does collapse occasionally under gen weight of how much it's trying to balance. There are so many characters and moving pieces and I couldn't help but feel like the narrative just forgets about some of them at certain points. As a massive Better Call Saul fan I was so excited to see Michael Mando come back for this movie but I just didn't feel like the film gave him much to do and I feel very much the same about Mark Ruffalo's appearance. It feels like he's there as a plot device more than anything and given some of the events that transpire I felt there was the potential for more worth exploring. I also found myself underwhelmed by the villain aspect of this movie. Maybe because it's shrouded in so much mystery for so long but I just thought there was potential for something much more interesting. The motivations ended up being very generic and set the climax down a very expected and familiar path that went on to feeling very preachy at times.

Brand New Day is a classic Spider Man story and I think the movie is all the better for it. Even with its familiar aspects the film just feels so passion filled and energetic and I love that it feels like a Spider Man movie first rather than an MCU entry. I wish it was tighter and I wish the third act surprised me more but I was always totally and completed entertained. I think Spider Man as a character is in very good hands and I really hope to see more entries from these writers and this director.

title: Exceptional! One of a kind!
review: Spider-Man: Brand New Day follows a lonely Peter Parker (Tom Holland) lives in isolation after Dr. Strange erased his identity from the world. author: makatron

title: A Mature and Stunning New Chapter
review:
The latest installment in the cinematic franchise delivers a remarkably mature, emotionally grounded, and visually stunning fresh start for the iconic hero. Following the tragic events that left Peter Parker completely isolated from everyone he loves, the story explores his psychological toll as he navigates life in a world where nobody remembers his name. Director Destin Daniel Cretton brings a gritty dramatic sensibility that transforms the tone into something far more personal and deep, making it one of the most compelling entries in the entire superhero genre.

Tom Holland delivers easily his best and most nuanced performance yet as an older, grief stricken Peter trying to find his footing. The supporting cast provides excellent backing throughout the narrative, with Zendaya and Sadie Sink bringing impressive emotional weight to their scenes. While there are a few minor visual effects issues during a couple of the heavier CGI sequences, the striking cinematography, atmospheric score, and powerful character focus far outweigh those small flaws, resulting in an unforgettable cinematic experience.
author: harishnj

title: Now we're getting somewhere
review:
Wow! I felt like a kid again watching Spider-Man fly on my screen saving people. Whoever is writing the character has changed direction for Tom Holland's Peter Parker. There were so many little delicious moments in this film, and big plot choices even, that alluded to Tobey Maguire's Spider-Man, the OG movies. It was as if for the first time ever Marvel's spidey was coming home. These moments ranged from character traits, scenes with Peter hurting his back, struggles that affected his powers, the soundtrack, to even the choice of cinematography that showed Spider-Man's inspiring flying moments through NYC. I got chills again! This is who Spider-Man really is, the Spider-Man that raised so many kids to love superhero films, like me.

While there were some parts that I loved beyond anything else in Tom Holland Spider-Man films, the movie as a whole posed some issues with me as well. Tom Holland is the heart of the film, the same as Milly Alcock was the heart of Supergirl. Similarly to Supergirl, there were some plot choices that didn't make the movie fly as high as it should. What makes a Spider-Man film work is him fighting his enemies mostly by his own strength. This time Peter Parker had to share the spotlight AGAIN with other major characters such as the Hulk and Frank Castle. While it was nice to see them again, it felt a bit crowded.

Furthermore, the movie didn't feel very well put together. It was as if they had to put some scenes in there to easily remedy the previous movie's conflicts without organically matching this "brand new day". Script-wise this movie is not as satisfying as it could have been, as it does not show us anything refreshing or different than an average Marvel story.

Ultimately, what I truly loved about it (again, very similar to Supergirl) was that Tom Holland's character is finally developing, he has struggles and conflicts in him that are equal to one and only, Peter Parker.

title: Superhero fatigue
review:
For the majority of my nearly three decade long life, superhero movies have been a constant. Every. Single. Year. Since 2019, I like many others feel DONE with it all. I thought Spider-Man was the exception. I have always loved Spider-Man, and really enjoyed the third film 'no way home'. title: Finally got the stand alone spider
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day feels fresh and different. Peter Parker finally feels older and more mature, and you can really tell that time has passed since his last appearance. Tom Holland delivers one of his best performances as Spider-Man, taking Peter Parker to another level emotionally and making him feel more experienced and grounded.

One of my favorite things about this movie is that it's finally a true Spider-Man story. Unlike some previous MCU Spider-Man films, this one doesn't rely on other heroes to carry the narrative. Yes, characters like Hulk and the Punisher appear, but they don't act as mentors or overshadow Peter. Instead, they simply cross paths with him because of the situation he's in-more like colleagues meeting while doing their jobs. The focus always stays on Spider-Man.

The biggest surprise for me was the duo of Spider-Man and the Punisher. Their chemistry was incredible. Their relationship feels completely different from the Daredevil and Punisher dynamic. It's more like a big brother-little brother relationship, filled with funny moments, disagreements, and fantastic action scenes. I honestly think they're one of the best MCU duos we've had.

My biggest criticism is that I wanted the movie to go further. The story felt a bit too straightforward, and I was hoping for more emotional depth and a darker tone. Maybe my expectations were just too high, but I felt there was room to push the story further.

I also wish Hulk had a larger role. I was expecting him to become even more furious and eventually kill Peter, only for Peter to later be revived or influenced by the symbiote. I think that direction would have made the story much darker and even more compelling.

I really liked the mutation aspect of the movie because it brought out a darker side of the characters. I just wish the film explored that darkness more. At times, it almost felt like Peter already had the symbiote because of how intense and emotionally conflicted he became. I think the movie was subtly showing us what Peter could become once he finally bonds with the symbiote. If that's the case, then his future black-suit Spider-Man is going to be terrifying.

Overall, I really enjoyed the movie. It gave us a mature, grounded Spider-Man, an outstanding performance from Tom Holland, and one of the most entertaining partnerships in the MCU with the Punisher. Even though I wanted a darker story with more depth, it has me incredibly excited for Peter's next appearance in Secret Wars, especially if the symbiote storyline is where they're heading.

10/10.

title: Visually appealing but shallow
review:
This movie is a mess that a child tries to hide under the bed. On the surface, it incorporates elements from all Spider-Man media, but it is shallow at its core.

First off, Daniel Crestton is to Spider-Man what Zack Snyder is to Superman. Both only looked at the panels and never read what was written in the speech bubbles. There's an interview where he hems and haws about his favorite Spidey comic, which turns out to be Amazing Fantasy #15 (truly amazing, uh?).

Don't get me wrong: the suit looks great, and the direction of the fight scenes and web-swinging meets the standard I expected from a Spider-Man movie, but I don't see the point of this film's existence (except for the 💰).

A reboot? They missed that chance.

A new future for Spider-Man? Who knows, the movie offers any hints.

An advertisement for the X-Men? That seems more likely.

Speaking of the X-Men, I don't understand why they needed to include that element in this movie. Her storyline goes nowhere and really wastes opportunities to delve deeper into Peter's internal conflicts. Because this movie actually contains at least three stories: the mutation plot, Peter trying to win back his friends, and the Jean Grey origin story.

I was really disappointed that they brought back that tedious "MJ" and Ned storyline. The previous movie gave Peter an ultimatum, which would have been perfect for a reboot and the introduction of new characters. Here, not only do they repeat information we already know, but they also erase the entire plot of the previous film.

On top of that, I constantly felt like I was watching an extended version of the trailer scenes (which, obviously, they are duh), but my point is: I didn't feel surprised or connected to the movie.

As for the mutation plot: I actually like the idea and had been the main plot of comics and cartoon shows. The problem is that there are no real stakes. Peter isn't going to turn into a monster; he has practically no social or personal life, so his powers won't affect anyone close to him. The only decision, then, is to accept these stronger abilities and learn to control them, which he kinda does. And, honestly, the movie doesn't seem to have a main villain. I guess Spidey has already locked up all the good ones.

Peter's personal drama: I hate comparing movies but I gotta bring Spider-Man 2. In the Sam Raimi movies, we see the impact that Spider-Man is having on Peter's life, because we actually see him with a job, as a student and interacting with his friends. Here, this Peter Parker is isolated and so little is done to show how his life is now. We know he's struggling but doesn't have consequences in other aspects of his life. Again, shallow, despite having good elements.

Regarding other MCU characters included here: I actually appreciate the inclusion of other characters when they serve the story's purpose, like Dr. Banner (not the Hulk) and Peter interacting with a purpose and sharing their perspectives on mutation. But in a few cases, not only some of them could easily been cut from the film entirely, but others (like the Punisher) are completely out of character. Why does the Punisher want to kill Jean Grey? The Punisher only kills people who have committed heinous acts. She hasn't even killed anyone in this movie, and the threat of her controlling part of New York felt superficial for that very reason.

Oh, and the fact that The Hand is portrayed as a group of Chinese kids is a total disservice to what the Netflix series did previously (they are the same group btw).

I'd say that if you're a fan of the previous movies, this one won't disappoint. On the other hand, it feels like an evolution when you don't overthink about what you're watching. And that's fine.

It just doesn't work for Spider-Man.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is everything a great Spider-Man movie should be. NO SPOILERS. NO REVEALS ABOUT CERTAIN CHARACTERS
review:
If you're wondering whether Spider-Man: Brand New Day is worth watching with your teenager, my answer is an easy yes.

The movie reminded me why Spider-Man has remained one of the most beloved superheroes for generations. While the movie delivers everything fans expect, spectacular action sequences, emotional moments, humor, and several surprising twists, it also tells a deeply human story that stayed with me long after the credits rolled.

Many people will understandably focus on the action and the excitement, but what impressed me most was something much quieter. Spider-Man: Brand New Day doesn't just show us Spider-Man saving the world. It shows us a much deeper Peter Parker trying to navigate life, loneliness, and finding his place in the world, even when he doesn't feel like a hero himself.

That emotional journey is what makes this movie so special. Beneath the superhero suit is a young man trying to understand who he is, how to live with loss, and how to keep moving forward when life doesn't unfold the way he imagined. Those are experiences that many teenagers know all too well, which is why I believe this is one of the best Spider-Man movies to watch together as a family.

At its heart, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a story about family, friendship, love, grief, identity, resilience, and hope. While it delivers breathtaking action and unforgettable set pieces, its greatest strength lies in the emotions driving every decision Peter makes. The movie reminds us that even superheroes experience doubt, loneliness, and uncertainty, and sometimes the hardest battles are the ones nobody else can see.

Peter isn't only facing dangerous enemies. He's trying to find his place in a world that suddenly feels unfamiliar. He's learning to keep moving forward after loss, making impossible choices, and trying to do the right thing even when he doesn't feel like a hero himself. Those internal struggles are incredibly relatable for teenagers, who are often navigating similar emotions while trying to discover who they are becoming.

That is what elevates Spider-Man: Brand New Day beyond another entertaining superhero adventure. It tells a story that feels personal, honest, and surprisingly universal.

Without revealing any spoilers, Spider-Man: Brand New Day follows Peter Parker as he continues rebuilding his life after everything he has experienced. He finds himself standing at a crossroads, trying to move forward while carrying the weight of everything that has shaped him. As new challenges emerge, Peter is forced to make difficult decisions that test not only his abilities as Spider-Man but also his character as a young man.

The movie does an excellent job of balancing large-scale action with intimate character moments. One minute you're watching thrilling sequences that remind you why Spider-Man is one of the most exciting heroes in cinema, and the next you're sitting quietly with Peter as he wrestles with loneliness, responsibility, and the desire to belong. Those quieter moments give the story its emotional depth and allow audiences to connect with Peter on a much more personal level.

Along the way, the story explores friendship, family, sacrifice, grief, forgiveness, hope, and the courage to keep choosing kindness even when life feels unfair. Rather than relying only on spectacle, the movie continually returns to the emotional questions at its core: Who are we when life changes us? How do we move forward after loss? And how do we continue believing in ourselves when we no longer feel strong?

The result is a movie that is exciting, emotional, funny, heartfelt, and surprisingly reflective. It entertains from beginning to end while also giving audiences plenty to think about once they leave the theater.

The Parental Lens This is where I believe Spider-Man: Brand New Day truly shines.

One of the most powerful lessons in the movie is that grief comes in many different forms. We often associate grief with losing someone we love, but teens experience many other kinds of loss that adults sometimes overlook. They grieve friendships that quietly fade away, dreams that no longer seem possible, relationships that end, opportunities they never had, and even the version of themselves they thought they were going to become.

Those feelings can be confusing because they don't always look like grief. They often appear as anger, withdrawal, frustration, or self-doubt. That's one reason I appreciate the way this movie approaches Peter's emotional journey. It reminds us that healing isn't about pretending everything is fine. It's about learning to keep moving forward while carrying experiences that have changed us.

The movie also explores another lesson that many parents know well: sometimes loving someone means allowing them to grow, even when that growth creates distance. As parents, we naturally want to protect our teens from disappointment and pain. Yet growing up requires them to make mistakes, develop independence, and slowly build lives that become uniquely their own.

Watching Peter navigate that journey can open meaningful conversations about what growing up actually feels like. Teenagers often experience tremendous pressure to know exactly who they are, where they're going, and what their future should look like. This movie gently reminds us that identity isn't something we discover overnight. It's something we build through experiences, relationships, setbacks, and resilience.

Another message I loved is that our identity should never be defined by what we've lost. We all experience disappointment, failure, rejection, and heartbreak. Those moments shape us, but they don't have to define us. Peter's journey shows that while loss may change us, it doesn't have to take away our hope or our purpose.

After watching the movie together, I encourage parents to ask their teen one simple question: "What do you think Peter was really fighting?"

There isn't a right or wrong answer. Some teens will talk about the villain, while others may focus on Peter's loneliness, fear, grief, or search for identity. Whatever answer they give, listen carefully. Sometimes the way our teenagers understand a character reveals something about how they're experiencing their own world.

Movies often become a safe way to talk about difficult emotions because the conversation starts with someone else. Before long, it becomes a conversation about ourselves. That is the real power of watching the right movie together.

My Final Take Spider-Man: Brand New Day is everything a great Spider-Man movie should be. It's exciting, emotional, funny, hopeful, and full of heart. It delivers spectacular action for longtime fans while also telling a story that feels deeply personal and emotionally honest.

What makes it truly memorable, however, is its ability to connect generations. Teenagers will see themselves in Peter's search for identity, belonging, and hope. Parents will recognize the emotional challenges that often remain hidden beneath the surface of adolescence. Watching those perspectives come together is what makes this movie such a rewarding family experience.

If you're looking for one of the best movies to watch with your teen this year, I wholeheartedly recommend Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Not simply because it's entertaining, but because it has the power to spark meaningful conversations about family, friendship, grief, identity, resilience, and hope long after the credits roll. Those are exactly the conversations worth having.

title: The best since Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2
review:
"Spider-Man: Brand New Day" is a delight of Marvel charm and is honestly the second best Spider-Man film of all time. This film makes the Spider-Man character very grounded and is true first time seeing the MCU make Spider-Man a Friendly Neighborhood Hero. The film takes place four years after the events of "Spider-Man: No Way Home" and follows Peter Parker (Tom Holland) becomes self-absorbed into the Spider-Man role after everyone including his love MJ (Zendaya Holland) and best friend Ned (Jacob Batalon) all forget that he exists. As he begins facing an unknown enemy that has the ability to switch bodies of every one around him. Peter goes through an accelerated mutation caused by traumatic experiences attached to his past. Peter must use his new found abilities and team up with Frank Castle (Jon Bernthal) to stop this unknown enemy (Sadie Sink) from getting what she seeks from the Department of Damage Control and its leader William Metzger (Tramell Tillman). So I'll first start with the positives: * The chemistry between Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal was fantastic and hilarious, they work will as a buddy comedy action duo who both completely work off of each other and every scene with them both in it are very entertaining and enjoyable.

* Sadie Sink's role is an absolute standout in this film,I won't go into details who she plays even though I'm sure everyone already knows. But she really plays off of Tom Holland as well and their hatred and misunderstandings with each other are some of the best tension pieces in the film.

* The web swinging in this film is some of the best of the franchise since "The Amazing Spider-Man 2". I love the settings and background of the New York Skyline and how Destin Daniel Cretton used the background to make the web swinging seem more artistic and lively just like it was in TASM 2. I hope Spider-Man 5 maintains this same style for the web swinging in that film as well.

* This story is very grounded and well balanced and we finally get a Spider-Man adventure that feels like Peter is actually Spider-Man and that previous three films are like a origin story for the character and this is the first main story for the character. Fans will be happy to see that Spider-Man is really on his own in this one. While Frank Castle and Bruce Banner are in the film, they more like guides for Peter to find the missing pieces to defeat the film's enemy and unlike the previous films were he is having to be taught what is right and wrong from mentors, Peter finally becomes the hero that he needs to be in this one.

For the Negatives, I honestly only have two critiques: * I feel like the Hand honestly had no proper reason to be in the film and they were literally throw away characters for Peter to fight. I feel like if they used the DODC's agents or if they hired mercenaries that would feel more better as enlistment of soldiers for Spider-Man to fight.

* The similarities between the villain of this film and The Leader seemed a little familiar and I feel like at times, we were watching carbon copy of "Captain America: Brave New World" but with Spider-Man in it instead of Sam Wilson.

Overall "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" is a delight of a film and fantastic inclusion for the MCU and by the end of the film, audiences will understand why the subtitle is called Brand New Day cause it is a truly new restart for Peter in the end. I highly recommend you check this one out ASAP.

title: Absolute Banger with an Grounded story
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day feels like a true return to what makes Spider-Man special. Instead of relying on massive multiverse events, it brings the focus back to Peter Parker-the ordinary guy trying to do the right thing while carrying extraordinary responsibilities. The story has heart, emotion, humor, and that classic "friendly neighborhood Spider-Man" vibe fans have been waiting for.

Tom Holland delivers a more mature and grounded Peter Parker, showing how every choice comes with a cost. The supporting characters each have meaningful roles that help shape Peter's journey without taking the spotlight away from him. The chemistry between the cast feels natural, and every major character adds something important to the story.

The action is exciting and creative, but the emotional moments are what truly stand out. It reminds fans that Spider-Man isn't defined by his powers-he's defined by his compassion, determination, and willingness to keep going no matter how difficult life becomes.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a heartfelt chapter that respects Spider-Man's legacy while opening the door to a fresh future. Whether you've followed every Spider-Man movie or are just jumping in, this film captures the spirit of the character in the best way.

author: RuneD-85

title: Definitely NOT a New Day - 7/10
review:
Let's start with the positives. Hands down, the absolute highlight of the film is the new suit. For the first time since Tobey Maguire's era, it truly feels like Spider-Man has stepped right off the pages of a comic book onto the screen. It looks absolute perfection: the fluid movement, the screen presence, and the subtle nods to iconic comic book covers. It was also refreshing to see Tom Holland's Spidey actually keep his mask on instead of unmasking in front of everyone. Unfortunately, that's where the major wins end.

Main issues and critiques: 1. Unresolved arc: The storyline involving the surge in spider-hormones was left completely underdeveloped. I highly doubt they'll return to it in future installments, especially with Doomsday and Secret Wars on the horizon.

2. Wasted X-Men debut: Jean Grey makes her first appearance in this franchise, yet her character is barely explored and feels entirely superficial-almost like a quick checkbox exercise.

3. Undermining No Way Home: Why did the writers feel the need to let Ned and MJ remember Peter again? It completely undercuts the emotional weight and lessons of the previous movie. What was the point of that sacrifice if it's so easily undone?

I was really hoping to see a fresh, independent Spider-Man who lets go of the past and finally becomes that iconic hero we all know. Instead, we got more of the same...

title: The Ultimate Spider-Man Experience
review:
This is, without a doubt, the best Spider-Man movie ever made. From the opening scene to the ending, I was completely hooked. It had everything I wanted: action, emotion, humor, incredible visuals, and an amazing soundtrack. Every big moment felt huge, and the movie constantly kept me invested.

The audience absolutely loved it. You could tell everyone was having a great time. People laughed during the funny moments, reacted to the biggest scenes, and stayed invested from beginning to end. It felt like a true event movie.

The music deserves a special mention because it was incredible. Every track fit the scenes perfectly and made the emotional and action moments even more memorable. It's easily one of my favorite Spider-Man soundtracks.

There is some Stranger Things references. Since Sadie Sink, who plays Jean Grey, is also known for playing Max in Stranger Things, those references got some laughs and were a fun little bonus for fans.

I'm also really happy that Mark Ruffalo returned as the Hulk because he's the GOAT. Every time he appears, he brings so much personality to the character, and I can't imagine anyone else playing Bruce Banner as well as he does.

One thing I love about Spider-Man is that every actor has brought something special to the role. Tobey Maguire will always be the OG and the one who introduced so many people to Spider-Man. Andrew Garfield is still underrated and deserves far more appreciation for his performance. Tom Holland continues to prove why he's an excellent Spider-Man, bringing his own energy and personality to the character.

The action scenes are spectacular, the visuals look amazing, and the movie balances humor and emotion really well. It never felt slow, and there was always something happening to keep me interested.

If you're a Spider-Man fan, this is a movie you absolutely need to see. It celebrates everything that makes Spider-Man such an iconic superhero while delivering an unforgettable adventure.

author: kamalload

title: SUCH A MASTERPIECE
review:
Spider-Man is one of the best superhero movies I have ever watched, and I would give it a perfect 10/10. It is a movie that delivers everything you could ask for: exciting action, memorable characters, emotional moments, and a meaningful story. Even if you are not a huge fan of superhero films, Spider-Man is still incredibly enjoyable because of how well it is made.

One of the movie's greatest strengths is its storytelling. The plot is engaging from beginning to end and keeps viewers interested without feeling confusing or overly complicated. The movie does an excellent job of balancing superhero action with the personal life of Peter Parker, making him feel like a real person rather than just a hero in a costume. His struggles, decisions, and growth throughout the film make him a character that many people can relate to.

The action sequences are another major highlight. They are fast-paced, creative, and visually impressive. Spider-Man's unique abilities are used in exciting ways that make every scene entertaining to watch. The special effects are outstanding and help create an immersive experience that keeps the audience invested throughout the movie.

The characters are also fantastic. Each character has a distinct personality and contributes something meaningful to the story. The interactions between the characters feel natural and often bring both humor and heart to the film. The movie knows exactly when to be funny and when to be serious, creating a perfect balance that never feels forced.

Another reason why I love this movie is the emotional depth it brings. It is more than just action and spectacle. The film explores themes such as responsibility, perseverance, friendship, and personal growth in a way that feels genuine and inspiring. These themes give the movie lasting impact and make it memorable long after it ends.

Overall, Spider-Man is a true masterpiece and one of the strongest superhero movies ever made. It combines great storytelling, amazing action, strong characters, and emotional depth into an unforgettable experience. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an entertaining and meaningful movie. Without a doubt, it deserves a 10/10 rating.
author: AriangR

title: "Friendly Neighbor."
review:
After No Way Home, I honestly didn't expect Marvel to fully commit to the direction they had set up. That is exactly why Spider-Man: Brand New Day surprised me. Instead of rushing into another massive spectacle, the film takes its time with Peter Parker and shows that the consequences of No Way Home are still shaping every part of his life.

That is what worked best for me. Peter is not just fighting new villains. He is living with the weight of the choices he has already made. That internal conflict stays with him throughout the entire film and gives the story an emotional maturity I had not seen in any of Tom Holland's previous Spider-Man films. Watching both Peter Parker and Spider-Man grow from those experiences made this feel like the most mature chapter of his journey so far.

I was also surprised by how well the supporting cast was handled. At first, I was worried that so many recognizable Marvel characters would make the film feel overcrowded. Thankfully, that never happened. Everyone has a purpose within the story and none of the appearances feel like they exist simply for fan service.

The biggest highlight was the chemistry between Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal. Every scene they share feels completely natural and you can tell how well they play off each other. That said, I still prefer the raw, uncompromising R-rated version of the Punisher. Even so, Bernthal is fantastic here and their dynamic became one of my favorite parts of the film.

I was also genuinely happy to see the old rage-driven Hulk again. Just seeing that version of the character brought back memories of earlier MCU films and reminded me how intimidating he can be. "No Banner. Just Hulk." was one of those moments that instantly stuck with me.

The action delivers exactly what I want from a Spider-Man film. The web-swinging sequences through New York are some of the strongest in the series and there were several moments where I genuinely felt like I was swinging alongside Peter. That sense of freedom has always been one of the character's biggest strengths and Brand New Day captures it beautifully.

What impressed me most, though, was the film's confidence. It never feels the need to become louder or bigger just because it is part of the MCU. Instead, it trusts its characters, lets its emotional moments breathe and tells its story at a pace that allows everything to land naturally. That slower, more grounded approach was something I appreciated far more than I expected.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day does not feel like a simple fresh start. It feels like the moment Peter Parker truly grows up. That alone makes it my favorite Tom Holland Spider-Man film after No Way Home and one of the biggest surprises I have had with the MCU in quite some time.
author: FilmNotesByDen

title: Spider-Man saves the day
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a great movie, not perfect, but definitely great than it's recent predecessors. It is a welcome return to a more grounded, street-level Spider-Man story. While the pacing slows down in places, it does give the characters and story room to breathe and build.

The story is fantastic, sadly because of a leak I knew who the villain was, so some of it was predictable, but the movie fooled me at times. The characters are very relatable and likeable. This installment had more emotional depth and Tom Holland gave his best performance as the superhero character. The mysterious antagonist character had a good writing and backstory.

The directing is fantastic, there's vision in this film, both in terms of visuals and themes. The cinematography is vivid and cheerful, with its dark shadows and the strong colors. The editing is done well. Even with a runtime of almost 2Hr 30mins, the movie didn't felt boring or overstretched, except at certain moments where the dialogues became a little cheesy.

The recent MCU movies haven't fared well with it's story and narrative. However, this franchise is one of the highlights of a successful longevity and love of the audience. From the action to the drama to the superhero cameos, this is a more mature Spider-Man with smarter storytelling and a more satisfying payoff.

Overall, Brand New Day is dark, grounded, vulnerable, and unexpectedly moving and finds the heart and soul of Peter Parker, with Tom delivering his personal best performance as the superhero.

My Rating : 4.5/5.

author: PenguinK-28

title: Padded, but a great Spider-Man adventure and tear jerker.
review:
Spider-Man must stop a mysterious villain who, unlike everyone else, cannot enter his mind-while he undergoes profound changes of his own.

Tom Holland once again proves why he is one of the finest live-action Spider-Man since Nicholas Hammond first donned the mask in the 1970s. Carrying the emotional weight of Peter Parker with warmth, vulnerability and quiet determination, Holland delivers his strongest performance yet.

Director Destin Daniel Cretton brings genuine heart to the FX spectacle, packed with nods and also some more obscure comic callbacks. Writers Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers craft a story that embraces Spider-Man's comic-book roots, with the welcome inclusion of several beloved Marvel characters including Hulk and Punisher, to name a few. They have purpose and are not just slotted in. That said, there are many villain cameos thrown in for good measure from the get go, to show how hard Spider-man has been working.

Sadie Sink is excellent throughout, with her seemingly effortless screen presence. Zendaya and Jacob Batalon continue to shine as MJ and Ned, their chemistry with Holland remaining one of the franchise's greatest strengths, while Florence Pugh steals every moment with her extended cameo.

The action scenes feel few and far between, playing out with dot-to-dot, The Fallen, The Hidden and Jason Goes to Hell type vibes. And the bigger set-ups, including the Hulk and Scorpion have very little pay off. The stakes feel all left for the final act.

That said, Brand New Day is an emotional, often heartbreaking chapter that earns more than a few tears. Yet, at two hours and twenty-five minutes, it occasionally overstays its welcome. As with many Marvel productions, it suffers from a little too much padding between its strongest moments. But what about an adaptation of Spider-Man and His Amazing Friends next?

Overall, it's an entertaining, heartfelt adventure. Recommended.

title: Spiider man Brand new nothing
review:
A film that gives us nothing. No compelling villain, no engaging plot, and boring CGI. There are no believable stakes for Spider-Man. It's just a bland, soulless, and meaningless movie.

The story raises several mysteries, but most of their resolutions are either weak or deeply unsatisfying. Jean's search for V-Max ultimately leads to a reveal that feels contrived rather than clever. Sara's final message contradicts her earlier goal of protecting her sister, and the movie never explains that change in motivation. Spider-Man's mutation is treated as a major conflict until it suddenly isn't, with little explanation of how he ultimately gains control.

The biggest problem is the complete lack of tension. Once it's revealed that Jean Grey is not the real villain, the movie never replaces her with a compelling antagonist. Damage Control is presented as the true force behind everything, yet it never becomes a satisfying enemy for Spider-Man, nor does the film provide meaningful consequences for its actions.

This movie feels more like a setup for future sequels than a complete story. Even the Spider-Man video games have delivered stronger villains, better character arcs, and far more satisfying narratives. Don't waste your time watching this ode to nothingness.plete waste of time. I honestly don't understand what people see in it. Even the Spider-Man video games have better stories-even the first Miles Morales game that was the worst one of the 3 games.

Don't waste your time watching this ode to nothingness.

title: Greatest live action spiderman movie
review:
As someone who's been obsessed with Spider-Man for years, this was everything I wanted it to be.

Brand New Day doesn't try to be bigger than every Spider-Man movie that came before it. Instead, it remembers what makes Spider-Man special in the first place: Peter Parker. It's a return to the heart of the character, and I honestly couldn't stop smiling through most of the movie.

Tom Holland gives what is easily his best performance as Spider-Man. This version of Peter feels older, more experienced, and more independent, but he never loses that awkward charm and relentless optimism that make him so lovable. He finally feels like Spider-Man, not just a kid caught up in someone else's story.

The action is incredible. The web-swinging is the best it's ever looked, the fights are fast, creative, and packed with personality, and New York actually feels alive again. Every action scene had me grinning like an idiot.

But what surprised me most was how much heart the movie has. It slows down when it needs to, lets its characters breathe, and actually gives emotional moments time to land. I cared about Peter throughout the entire film, and that's something I haven't felt this strongly in a long time.

The humor is also spot-on. It's funny without trying too hard, and it never undercuts the emotional scenes. The balance between comedy, action, and drama is honestly one of the best in any Spider-Man movie.

Is it perfect? No. There are a couple of moments where I wished certain ideas had been explored a little more. But those are tiny complaints in a movie that absolutely nails what Spider-Man is supposed to be.

Walking out of the theater, I had that same feeling I had after watching the best Spider-Man movies growing up: I just wanted to go back in and watch it again.

If you're a Spider-Man fan, this movie understands why you fell in love with the character in the first place.

⭐ 10/10 - A heartfelt, exciting, and genuinely refreshing Spider-Man movie that reminds you why Peter Parker is one of the greatest superheroes ever created.

title: Not 'No Way Home', But a Strong Foundation for Peter's Future
review:
After the insane hype of No Way Home, director Destin Daniel Cretton definitely had a massive weight on his shoulders. Fortunately, Brand New Home succeeds in bringing Peter Parker back to his street-level superhero roots, while still delivering some pretty massive surprises.

Tom Holland proves once again that he was born to play Peter Parker. His character growth in this one is super palpable. New faces like Sadie Sink bring a much-needed breath of fresh air, and let's be real, seeing Jon Bernthal back as The Punisher is absolute chef's kiss. The dynamic between Punisher and Spidey successfully gives the film a much darker and grittier tone compared to previous MCU Spidey outings.

Unfortunately, not everything is executed perfectly. Throwing Mark Ruffalo's Hulk into the mix honestly feels a bit cramped and slightly distracts from Peter's personal storyline. Some plotlines also feel a bit rushed just to keep up with the pacing.

Overall, it's a solid transitional era for the next chapter of Spider-Man. Sure, it doesn't break the internet with fan service quite like No Way Home, but it successfully lays a strong foundation for Peter's future. The fight choreography and web-swinging action are absolutely top-tier, and Holland and Zendaya's chemistry remains undefeated.

Catch it on the biggest screen you can find, it's still a massively fun ride!

title: The Definitive Spiderman
review:
This movie is a thrill ride from start to finish with a lot of Spider-Man, and I really think they went for that comic booky feel with the large array of villains and "things" happening in New York that don't just revolve around our main villain. I'm not going to style this review as some nonsense of trying to figure out how accurate the movie is to the comic Spider-Man and quantifying its worth based on that, but rather observe it as a standalone movie and examine how good it is for being a film. However, it must be stated, it is the definitive Spider-Man movie.

The swinging, fights, and effects were out of this world, and I liked the inclusion of the Punisher because Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal had excellent chemistry; seeing them onscreen was very entertaining. Performances were great all around, but Sadie Sink did a phenomenal job as Jean Grey. The expressions displayed at the end when she's sitting after sending the shockwave were very good, and she spoke a lot through that gaze without even a word being actually spoken. I do think there were issues regarding her character, especially her moral compass and the way the story tries to portray her by the end; however, as a performance and a character, for the most part, I think it's really good.

The first half, or two-thirds, of the film is just Spiderman going from place to place in the city, figuring things out. He goes on a tank chase, talks to people at the damage control facility, and discusses things with Yelena, and then we get the big reveal that Ned and MJ are back, and that whole sequence is satisfying as well. The arachnid problems segwaying into that encounter with the scorpion is well executed, and then we get the exhilarating chase of him trying to beat Jean to MJ, which leads to one of the coolest scenes in the entire movie. He also visits Bruce Banner somewhere in there, but all in all the culmination of the first half of the film, being at damage control with the Hulk fight, was really good, and I really liked that entire sequence. I just wish it could have been a bit longer; it did unfortunately feel cut short.

At this point the momentum in the story is high but kind of ends with the Hulk fight concluding, but then we instantly get into the gut-wrenching scene of MJ finding the letter and telling Peter she does not love him due to her not even knowing him. The way they handled this in the film was perfect, and then the interaction following this with Ned and MJ was wholesome, and at this point the movie really had only minor issues like the Hulk fight being cut short. I really do have to emphasize how smart it was putting the MJ scene right after the Hulk fight and being the connecting factor that pushes the movie from act two to act three.

The problems with the movie come after. After my second re-watch in theaters, I concluded they didn't really spend too much time on Jean Grey, and the people saying that are missing the mark completely. The Jean Grey stuff was good and I would even say a highlight of the movie; however, the issue arises in where they chose to have the final conflict of the film.

The setting being constrained to that island and the experiment facility for basically the last 45 minutes of the film was infuriating, to be frank. I mean, the rest of the film is Spider-Man going from place to place, dealing with issues going on multiple chases, but then in the end we are constrained to a few rooms and Jeans cell. I hate it when movies do this in general because I believe the setting needs to be dynamic to some degree so that it feels good because the enjoyment of most stories especially in the action genre are derived in large part from the adventure aspect of it, and when they decide to spend the last half of the film in these constrained environments, it completely kills the momentum of the story, and it's very noticeable in the movie. For a character like Spider-Man, I think the setting is even more vital because the swinging through the city, especially in chase sequences or fights that span multiple parts of the city or a building, gives the viewer so much more to enjoy and look at versus being in a grey building for 50 minutes and briefly cutting to the city. This last half isn't bad by any means, but it just streamlines into this villain and situation that, in my eyes, does not have that much gravity to begin with. I mean, she has been set free, and the villains Peter is fighting in the end aren't even Jean; it's yet again just another group of bad guys she controls, and these villains have already been defeated by Spider-Man.

The story also attempts to treat her as a misunderstood person who can get away with her bad deeds just because she was trying to find her sister. She causes a man to be run over and possibly die or, at the very least, suffer catastrophic injuries; she causes psychological harm to Bruce and Spider-Man; however, in the end, it feels like Spider-Man forgives her way too quickly, and the story treats her like it's all right she caused all that mayhem and destruction with the tank and the other things she did. It's definitely something I noticed more in my second watch, but I did feel there was a bit of a discrepancy in how the story treated her, and it felt like the plot and moral compasses of Frank and Peter just bended to serve the plot. I understand that neither Peter nor Frank were in positions where they could have apprehended her; however, the story still strongly implies that what she did was not necessarily okay but justified, which it just wasn't. The character who killed Sarah Grey is also overlooked, completely following the shot Frank takes, and I think they should have wrapped that up a little bit better.

It's still a great and entertaining movie even with a weaker second half, which is still good. Apart from the issue regarding the setting, I didn't really think there were many big issues in the film that really meaningfully dropped my rating to an eight. Regardless of the errors and. Things overlooked, I still think the movie was great and the best Spider-Man movie we have ever gotten.

title: Holland's best outing as Spider-Man.
review:
It's a BRAND NEW DAY for Spider-Man. Of course, the film only borrows the comic title rather than adapting the actual storyline, but still I overall enjoyed it. It was also never going to top the epic scale of NO WAY HOME, with its three legacy Spider-Men and an all-star lineup of iconic villains. So where do you go after that? You don't have to raise the stakes by making everything bigger. You raise them by making the story more personal and emotionally resonant.

The narrative's focus on Peter Parker was one of the movie's biggest strengths. On the other hand, I really wish Tombstone and Scorpion had been given more to do. Understanding that Zendaya's MJ and Jacob Batalon's Ned is the what makes Peter's story in this film go, still if it were up to me though, I would've cut the MJ and Ned subplot entirely and devoted that screen time to developing those villains more properly, even if they were just mind controlled pawns to Sadie Sink's Jean Grey. NO WAY HOME already gave Peter the bittersweet ending that felt right, accepting the burden of being Spider-Man and letting MJ and Ned move on with their lives. I was ready for this movie to fully commit to that new chapter. Of course easier said than done, but I would have just zoned in on Peter and Jean's isolation without them.

The backdoor pilot for the X-Men was clever, but at the same time, a little distracting because like I mentioned prior it undercuts The Hand, Scorpion and Tombstone. My biggest issue isn't Sadie Sink's performance, she does a good job with what she's given, but rather the direction. Personally, I don't want the X-Men starting out in their early twenties again. Physically, Sadie also doesn't evoke Jean Grey for me the way Famke Janssen did in the original X-Men films. When you looked at Famke, she felt like Jean Grey had stepped right off the comic page. I understand Marvel's reasoning, though. Casting younger actors allows them to grow into these roles over the next decade or more, and that's clearly the long-term plan.

I wasn't a fan of the PG-13 version of Punisher. Seeing Frank Castle interact with Spider-Man was fun, but I don't like Punisher cracking jokes. Frank should be a man consumed by death, guns, and his war on crime. Thomas Jane's portrayal from 2004's THE PUNISHER is still my benchmark for the character. I do like Bernthal in the role and again, I like seeing the larger universe at play too.

Mark Ruffalo's Hulk finally returns in a more familiar form, although he's mostly used as a spectacle piece. Still, I'm just happy to see the end of Professor Hulk. Give me the 2012 Avengers Savage Hulk every time. I did appreciate that we briefly see Professor Hulk before he fully transforms back into the classic rage monster.

The fanboy in me still can't help but wonder what could have been. I would've loved to see Harry Osborn, Gwen Stacy, a proper comic-accurate Mary Jane Watson, a stronger version of Liz Allan, and a more faithful Flash Thompson introduced from the very beginning of the HOMECOMING trilogy. It is what it is though.

I also wish the movie had leaned into Peter's photography skills. Having him sell Spider-Man photos to make rent is such a classic part of the character, and the film mostly ignores that angle. It would've been a natural way to show Peter struggling financially while also giving us another excuse to see J. K. Simmons return as J. Jonah Jameson.

Director Destin Daniel Cretton does a solid job making the film feel grounded and street-level while still giving it a larger sandbox to play in through the inclusion of multiple villains, Jean Grey, Punisher, and Hulk even if the other villains don't get nearly enough screen time. I'd say this is a stronger outing than SHANG-CHI. Part of that comes from Spider-Man already having years of groundwork laid before this film, whereas the character of Shang-Chi had to build its world from scratch, but Cretton still proves he's more than capable of carrying the torch.

Outside of the excellent Damage Control action sequence against The Hand and the exciting Hulk set piece, most of the action is fairly standard Marvel fare. Where the movie really succeeds is in Peter's character development as he struggles to balance life as an ordinary young man with the responsibility of being Spider-Man, taking a page off of Raimi's SPIDER-MAN 2.

So with all that being said, this is Tom Holland's strongest performance yet with top of the line growth exploring his grief, longing and maturation. The HOMECOMING trilogy ended by laying the foundation for the Spider-Man many fans had always wanted, and BRAND NEW DAY at least delivers on that promise.

7/10.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Review!
review:
🏆98%

I was already going into this film with very high expectations, but somehow, it still went way past them. This is easily one of the best MCU movies and one of the best Spider-Man movies in general. Actually, it is probably my favorite live-action Spider-Man movie. The film is definitely significantly more profound than the average MCU movie. Peter is at this point more Spider-Man than just Peter. He's losing himself in the process of being Spider-Man and not being honest with the people who used to love him but no longer remember him. Instead of introducing himself to them, he instead keeps his distance while constantly looking at their social media accounts. Eventually, Peter starts to gain organic webs, probably due to being bitten by a radioactive spider. Though, instead of trying to embrace his newfound powers, he tries to take control of them and tone them down just as Spider-Man. When finally finishing his device that tones down his powers, Peter heads out to finally stop Jean. Though, she ends up possessing Banner, and it eventually leads to Banner's device breaking and him fully becoming the original Hulk. Peter eventually is able to get him to calm down, and he turns into Banner again. After that, Peter takes care of Jean, only to hear her mutter the name Sarah, which the movie gets back to sometime later. When Peter returns to Frank's place where MJ is currently protected, it turns out that MJ found the note Peter had about what happened in No Way Home. Peter finally takes off his mask and they have a talk. Peter says he loves her, but MJ says she doesn't love him. It's tragic, but also very realistic. Peter loves her because he knows her, but MJ can't love Peter because she technically now doesn't know him. It's just another tragic blow towards everything Peter is currently going through. Eventually, Peter figures out the truth that he was lied to by the people he was working with, which leads to him heading to their location to find Jean. Once Jean finds out the truth that her sister Sarah is dead, she begins to lose herself even further. While Peter goes into fight the Hand which Jean is currently possessing, Peter comes to this realization that wraps up his arc in the film perfectly. He's not just Spider-Man, he's Peter Parker, which makes him both. He removes the device that's toning down his powers, and he fully embraces his true self instead of letting his past losses change him, making it to Jean in the process. Peter tells Jean she isn't a killer, then Peter lets her into his mind, where she finds Aunt May, where they have a heartfelt talk, and the whole sequence ends with Peter showing up and telling Jean that he's here for her, and that she isn't alone. Though, Frank ends up firing his sniper from afar, aiming exactly for Jean. Which ends with Peter taking the bullet for Jean. This nearly kills Peter, though Jean keeps his body alive by possessing him, and once his body finally begins to heal properly, she gives him control of his body again. Peter wakes up to finding Frank right next to him in the hospital, and Frank instantly apologizing for what he did. Frank admits his wrongdoing, and seems to hopefully be going down a better path now due to this incident. The meaning behind the movie is; just because you lost someone, it doesn't mean you should lose yourself on the way. Peter was losing himself by being only Spider-Man, he thought that he was protecting the people he cared about by not confronting them, but in reality, he was only hurting himself. When it comes to Frank, he lost himself after the deaths of his family, but after nearly killing an actual not bad girl, and also nearly killing a friend of his, he realizes that maybe killing isn't the right thing to do, and that maybe he shouldn't let his past losses change him into this killing machine. When it comes to Jean, she loses her sister, but after going into Peter's mind, she realizes just like him how just because things will be hard at times, she was still loved, and she shouldn't become a monster just because of things getting hard, like her losing a loved one for example. All three characters go through the same arc of learning to not lose themselves on the way after losing someone, and that's the main message behind the movie. This movie wraps up Peter and Frank's arc beautifully while also making an amazing origin story for Jean Grey. This is definitely one of my personal favorite Marvel movies of all time, and I'm honestly very excited for when I get the chance to give it a rewatch!

title: The Biggest Villain of Brand New Day? The Missing 35 Minutes
review:
The most important issue has to be the fact that around 35 minutes of footage was reportedly cut from the final film. Unfortunately, Sony has built quite a reputation for removing some of the best scenes from its movies. Just think about the touching sandcastle scene with Sandman and his daughter in Spider-Man 3, or the restaurant sequence from Spider-Man: Far From Home where Iron Spider stops the Manfredi crime family a scene that almost felt like it came straight out of the PS4 game.

Another frustrating decision is the way the studio handled the test screenings. The film was screened, feedback was collected, and changes were made accordingly. Then, according to reports, the executives decided those changes "weren't working," reverted many of them, and ultimately went with their own vision anyway.

There are other examples as well. Hulk was originally turned gray, and the film even contained dialogue acknowledging this change, only for the gray Hulk storyline to be removed later while traces of it reportedly remained. Likewise, several scenes shown in the marketing that perfectly captured Spider-Man's spirit never made it into the final cut.

Hopefully, we'll eventually get answers when an Extended Edition or a "More Fun Stuff" version is released. Until then, it's hard not to wonder how much better the movie could have been if those deleted scenes had been left intact. Now, let's talk about the movie as it currently stands.

To summarize its biggest problems, the story feels unfocused. Despite its lengthy runtime, the film somehow feels like it either didn't have enough time or simply didn't use that time effectively.

I've been following Destin Daniel Cretton's work since Short Term 12, and I genuinely think he's an excellent director. Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings is one of my favorite MCU projects, and I'm also excited about Wonder Man. In that sense, I was happy to see Jon Watts leave the Spider-Man franchise, since I wasn't a fan of most of his work (with Homecoming being the exception).

However, even though Watts left behind a strong foundation and a clean slate with the ending of No Way Home, this movie doesn't make the most of that opportunity. Considering the title is "Brand New Day," it should have truly felt like a fresh start-but it rarely does.

Instead of exploring long-awaited storylines like Scorpion, who has been obsessed with Peter since Homecoming, or the newly emerging criminal factions in New York we get brief montage sequences and a forgettable villain who never feels like more than a temporary obstacle.

The film's biggest weakness is that, unlike Spider-Man 2 (2004), which stayed focused on telling one compelling story, this movie tries too hard to set up the future of the Marvel universe. It attempts to function as an X-Men origin story, plants seeds for multiple future projects, and constantly references the past. As a result, it ends up weighed down by all that baggage instead of standing confidently on its own.

In fact, if you took the ending of Spider-Man: No Way Home and immediately played Brand New Day afterward, the transition wouldn't feel nearly as significant as it should. A film called "Brand New Day" is supposed to feel like the beginning of a new era, but this one never fully delivers that feeling. But that's enough about the negatives-let's talk about what the movie gets right.

Destin Daniel Cretton has easily delivered the most visually stylish Spider-Man film of Tom Holland's era. The web-swinging through New York feels dynamic and exhilarating, the stunt work is excellent, and the action choreography is some of the best we've seen in these movies. Even the Spider-Man suit deserves praise-it finally has visible texture and wrinkles, making it look far more practical and believable than before.

Sadie Sink also gives a strong performance. She doesn't come across as someone who was simply cast because Cretton had worked with her before on The Glass Castle; she fully commits to the role and makes a genuine impression.

The color palette, cinematography, and overall shot composition are fantastic throughout the film. Michael Giacchino's score takes on a darker and more epic tone while still feeling unmistakably Spider-Man, and it elevates many of the movie's strongest moments.

Although the Hulk storyline suffers from the script revisions and obvious cuts, the character's design and action scenes are exactly the kind of Hulk moments many fans have been asking for. Punisher is also handled surprisingly well. Instead of overwhelming the movie with his darker tone, he's integrated naturally into the story, and his chemistry with Spider-Man is one of the film's highlights. On top of that, Frank Castle receives meaningful character development that moves him forward instead of simply repeating what we've already seen.

Overall, considering Cretton was clearly trying not to disrupt the existing cast and continuity, Marvel's insistence on setting up future stories and referencing multiple corners of its universe, and Sony's well-known habit of interfering with the story and cutting significant scenes, I think the film turned out better than I expected.

My ranking of the live-action Spider-Man films is now:

Spider-Man 2 (2004) > Spider-Man (2002) > Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026).

That makes this, in my opinion, Tom Holland's best Spider-Man movie and the third-best live-action Spider-Man film overall (excluding the animated movies).

It's darker, feels much more like a friendly neighborhood Spider-Man story, and generally heads in the right direction. Its biggest flaw is that it's too afraid to fully embrace the fresh start promised by its own title.

If a Director's Cut or Extended Edition is eventually released and restores the missing material, I could easily see myself raising my score.

Review Score: 86/100.

title: The Bold, Grounded Reset the Franchise Needed
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day" isn't just another chapter in the web-slinger's cinematic saga, it's the bold, refreshing reset the franchise desperately needed. Goodbye to the tech-heavy, mentor-dependent era of Tom Holland's previous films; this installment strips Spidey back down to his core, delivering a grounded, emotionally resonant story.

Where the film truly shines is in its breathtaking action sequences and flawless combat choreography, every punch carries weight, and Spider-Man's agility is captured with a dynamic, fluid camera style that makes you feel every swing and dodge. Also the return to the swinging through New York was amazing, giving us some feelings of the good old Spidey.

The inclusion of The Punisher and Hulk isn't just fan service-they act as dark mirrors to Peter's new isolation. Frank Castle brings a raw, lethal edge that pushes Spidey's moral boundaries, while Bruce injects sheer, jaw-dropping scale into the narrative. The contrast between Spider-Man's agile acrobactics, Castle's grounded violence, and Hulk's raw power creates an incredible dynamic that makes every team-up and clash unforgettable. Another standout aspect of the film is Sadie Sink's magnetic performance. She brings an incredible screen presence, perfectly balancing emotional depth with a sharp, mysterious edge. Her dynamic with Tom Holland's Peter Parker is electric-there's an instant, natural chemistry between them that grounds the movie's quieter, more character-driven moments.

However, beyond its inmediate story, 'Brand New Day', leaves behind some loose ends without a clear and specified ending, like the mysterious disappearance of the Damage Control director leaves a lingering sense of threat surrounding the DODC's true agenda. Even more intriguing is Peter's discarded power inhibitor left behind in the facility, a piece of tech designed to suppress genetic mutations that is practically screaming to be weaponized by anti-mutant factions in future X-Men storylines. So we can suppose how all of this could clearly lay the groundwork for the MCU's upcoming Mutant Saga.

Without spoiling what actually unfolds, the closing moment with Ned is easily one of the film's most memorable beats. It's a beautifully crafted interaction that balances a heavy sense of nostalgia with a subtle glimmer of hope for Peter's future. It leaves you with that perfect mix of warmth, heartbreak, and endless questions about where their dynamic goes from here. As for the post-credits scene, make sure you stay in your seat until the very end. Without dropping any spoilers, it delivers a massive tease that could completely redefines the trajectory of the MCU moving forward. It's not just a throwaway gag, it's a high-stakes reveal that will have fans theorizing for months.

title: Let's call it what it is, shall we?
review:
Let's be brutally honest about what this movie is, it's a backdoor pilot to set-up the X-Men and to give Jean Grey her origin story. It's a cameo infested backdoor to the next, big team movies that aren't the Avengers, and to be perfectly honest, that's okay. Did Hulk, Punisher, and dollar store Black Widow actually move the movie along and would the movie still happen without them? Absolutely it would. Was there any point for Spider-Man to be involved in this at all? Not even remotely. Literally any other character could have been copied and pasted into his place and it wouldn't have changed a single thing.

So what did we get in the 4th Spider-Man movie?

Mopey Peter who accepts who he is by the third act(Thought Peter already accepted who he was considering that was the point of the final scene in No Way Home) and basically powers up to Tobey Macguire's Spidey level.

A Bruce Banner D plot that still makes no sense whatsoever as Banner and the Hulk finally settled their issues and became one at the beginning of Endgame, but apparently that's not the case anymore and Hulk is once again a menace to the world.

A Frank Castle C plot where Frank does, something, I guess, then gets turned into a clown.

A Yelena Belova D plot that's entirely pointless.

A B plot with Ned and MJ that legitimately goes no where and does nothing but remind the audience that they were friends before Dr. Strange's spell.

A series of cameo by Spider-Man B & C villains that are nothing more than glorified cameos.

And a main plot that's nothing more than the origin story of the first MCU member of the X-Men, complete with an ending shot of her travelling to upstate New York(Gee, I wonder where she's going).

Again, there's nothing wrong with all of this, but this was supposed to be a Spider-Man movie. Does that mean the movie was bad? No, it's an actual good movie, but it's a Jean Grey origin story, not a Spider-Man story. Like I said, Spider-Man could have been swapped out for literally anyone else and it would be the exact same movie.

And don't be fooled by what the hack Kevin Feige is on social media saying, this movie in no way, shape, or form, leads into Avengers: Doomsday. It's a standalone movie that doesn't even hint at the next movie, and again, that's perfectly okay. In fact, it's actually preferable, there's nothing wrong with having the other MCU characters in it, but Feige is lying through his fake teeth when he says that it leads into and helps setup Doomsday, it doesn't.

TL:DR This is an X-Men origin story masquerading as a Spider-Man movie.
