title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day - A Grounded, Masterful New Beginning
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day - A Bold, Grounded Resets for Peter Parker Spider-Man: Brand New Day succeeds by taking Tom Holland's Peter Parker into darker, more mature, and emotionally isolated territory. Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton (Shang-Chi), the film trades floaty CGI for heavy, practical stunt work and inventive martial-arts fight choreography that gives every swing and blow actual weight.

The Highlights: The electric screen presence and gritty dynamic between Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal's Punisher steals the show, while Sadie Sink delivers a standout, mysterious MCU debut. Visuals are vibrant and comic-accurate, framing Spider-Man in classic panel-like arrangements.

The Drawbacks: While Peter's emotional isolation and mutating powers add genuine psychological weight, some middle-act pacing stumbles under the burden of setting up broader MCU Phase 6 plotlines.

The Verdict: A visceral, visually vibrant street-level thriller that successfully matures Peter Parker while delivering some of the best live-action action sequences in the character's history.

I also really like how Spider-Man gets alot of love, it feels earned and think it can compare to Raimi's Spiderman films, although not on the same level as their impact wasn't as strong in terms of the bad guys. But having differences and someone trying to evolve them for evil purposes is well-explored.

It's well explored with Jean Gray's past and how she feels disconnected from everyone else, it's used in a good way because the story develops her character where we see her past, her feelings for her sister and how she feels betrayed. All good things to raise the stakes. The Pov's are well done, the story shows Spider-man flying in such a good way, you get to see the emotional background he also faces and the trauma it comes with being different.

It's not the strongest message, but when you have great action, acting and some heartfelt moments between the ensembled cast, it feels worthy enough to call it a strong message. I think the Punisher's story was under-developed, but his relationship with the vigilanty creates for some nicer moments that feel fresh because they have some of their moments of humour and bond together.

The Ending is also such a great an interesting way to wrap up the story, and the credit scene whilst not much could be something and mean something bigger. So the real questions you're asking. Is it the best Spider-man movie? Honestly, no. Is Spider-man 2 the best still? Yes. The only reason I say that is because they added characters from other series that doesn't fully connect with the Spider-Man universe, and that lessers some of the movies moments. But overall a good movie, would recommend, it's a 9 Out of 10.

title: Holland's definitive leap
review:
The film Tom Holland deserved in his Spider-Man run. That sums up the excellent new installment of the web-slinging hero, played by Holland, who achieves a perfect transition into the character's maturity, guided by the actor himself. An exciting, harmonious, well-executed, well-written, and powerfully acted film.

This is perhaps the best film of the Holland era as Peter Parker, and they achieve it intelligently. They understood that their previous installment had been overly fan-serviced, but that they needed to evolve into a new stage, and they captured that message perfectly. Their screenwriters, like Peter himself, evolve toward an intensity that goes beyond mere pandering; they dare to fill the Spider-Man universe with nuance and don't hesitate to offer us horror, terror, drama, comedy, and love all in one film, without ever forgetting that we are watching a superhero movie.

Tom Holland is given free rein to shine. The actor delivers a compelling performance, moving the audience and showcasing his talent as the lead. His evolution as Peter is also a testament to a great actor who moves with natural ease on every level. Zendaya, for her part, follows the same path. We feel at home, part of a reunion, and witnesses to everyone's new life, which proves to be a captivating experience. The first part of the film feels entirely like a comic book, and that's a huge plus.

When the film decides to forge a new path, that's when Sadie Sink shines. Welcome to the MCU, dear redhead. The actress becomes the second great pillar of the equation and, at times, she's frightening; at others, unsettling; and, in her development, dazzling. A marvelous Jane Grey. The film's main villain is pure ease and power.

Destin Cretton manages to convey the ideas and make the most of a good script with great precision. He's a reliable director who successfully completes the task, knowing how to fit together all the necessary elements to drive the evolution in quality towards the new world they're building. He blends comedy well with Frank and Spider-Man, but also manages to deliver drama and horror at just the right moments. A director at the studio's service, with a completely dependable style.

In short, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is one of the best films in the Spider-Man saga. It carefully portrays Peter's development and precisely lays the groundwork for the next big era of the MCU. While it does have some less inspired moments, these don't detract from the overall satisfying result for both fans and casual or neutral viewers. It's an entertaining, satisfying, and genuinely enjoyable film. It proves that we can still enjoy great superhero movies if the filmmakers are truly committed.

title: Review Spider-Man
review:
Spider-Man (2026) Movie Review Overview An overall enjoyable cinematic experience that delivers a good mix of action and excitement while exploring new relationships and challenges for Peter Parker. While it isn't the best entry in the franchise, it still delivers some solid moments.

Performances & Characters * **Peter Parker (Spider-Man):** A fantastic and thoroughly convincing performance across all his scenes. The actor brilliantly captured the depth and emotional struggles of the character.

* **Gwen / Jean:** The actress delivered a great performance despite notably weak character writing and development, which made it difficult to connect or empathize with her for most of the film.

* **The Punisher:** A strong and welcome addition to the story; his presence added a unique dynamic and a grounded intensity to the movie.

Pros & Cons * **Pros:** * Beautiful and powerful acting performance for Peter Parker across various scenes.

* **Portrayal of Suffering:** The film successfully conveys the intense struggle and psychological pressure Peter endures, giving the character real depth and relatability.

* The final scene was exceptional, bringing together Peter, Gwen/Jean, and The Punisher in a memorable and impactful way.

* Overall entertaining experience.

* **Cons:** * **Average Plot & Lack of Thrill:** The events felt somewhat ordinary and failed to build the level of excitement or anticipation expected.

* **Ranking in the Series:** The movie falls short of being the best in the Spider-Man franchise.

* **Runtime:** The film suffers from pacing bloat; trimming down certain scenes would have made the story tighter and more impactful.

* **Character Development:** Weak writing for Gwen/Jean's character hindered her impact on the plot and made her hard to engage with.

Conclusion An enjoyable movie that is worth watching, shining through impressive acting in Peter's scenes, a brilliant ending, and a powerful depiction of his struggles. Although the plot feels somewhat average without reaching high levels of excitement, and the movie suffers from extra length and weak writing for certain supporting roles-keeping it from being the best in the series-it ultimately delivers a fun experience.

title: A really REFRESHING Spider Man Movie!
review:
Spider Man Brand New Day is a FUN and ENJOYABLE movie that has many standout moments.

Its one of those films which will give you a really good time in the theatres.

This is a CLASSIC Spider Man film, not the traditional MCU type, this feels more like the classic Tobey Maguire trilogy.

I craved for a FRESH and a comic book type of a spider man film and this is just like it.

The visuals of this film are AWESOME, you almost cannot believe that these are the visuals of a Marvel film, the colors and the lighting of the world and the scenes are just TOP NOTCH!

The film also takes a really unconventional approach with its climax which is really something new and I love that.

Let's talk about the performances, Tom Holland has been playing this character for 10 years now, he has LIVED it and for me this is his MOST MATURE performance in that character, loved him in it, the loneliness of Peter Parker, the problems he was facing, his grief, I felt that pain, Zendaya was brilliant too, specifically the chemistry between Tom and her is just SPECTACULAR in every film(ofcourse because they are married), the confrontation scenes between them plays out well, the way in which Peter just wants to tell to Zendaya about his feelings but couldn't is so realistic, Zendaya really did a great job, Sadie Sink was good as the main villain, her back story and powers were explored and we connected with her, not in a SPECTACULAR way but it was good, Jacob Batalon doesn't have that MUCH screen time but he is good too, Jon Bernthal is AMAZING as the Punisher, his character is not a CAMEO, he has a lot of scenes in this film, and his arc is also explored which makes it GREAT and he delivers a BRILLIANT performance, Mark Ruffalo was there for very few acting scenes, the directing, the set design, the story progression were all done fantastic. The fight scenes were very fun to watch, specially the sequence including the Hulk, that was AWESOME, the climax was great too.

The setting of this movie is just like a comic book coming to life.

A hyper stylized Spider Man film which makes the experience really cool.

For me the film reaches its peak just at the time of entering the third act, after that it couldn't reach that level of brilliancy.

Also for me the 1st half was a bit SLOW paced and I didn't like it as much as the second half, which I thought was INCREDIBLE, the emotional arcs of all the characters was brilliantly portrayed, not a lot of twists but when they did occur, they were really shocking.

The background score fit in with the tone of the film pretty well, the mind control aspects were really FASCINATING for me, the scenes between Peter and MJ and the the climax had a lot of emotional DEPTH. I can't put in the perfection category because of the first half being a bit slow and average for me, also some scenes were a bit dragged, but its still a really good film. The psychological elements were also MIND BLOWING.

Overall if u want to watch a very refreshing and engaging movie, this is it, it does all the things you want a good film to do, it makes you laugh, it makes you emotional/sad, it makes you shocked, it makes you happy, all of that, you will get in the film and that's why I loved it so much.

Overall, I liked it!

Rating- 9/10.

title: Less Than I Expected
review:
Unfortunately, the movie fell below my expectations. It had several strong elements, but it also suffered from some major weaknesses that made it lose much of the usual Spider-Man magic.

From a visual and technical perspective, the movie was excellent. The cinematography, action sequences, and overall direction were all handled very well. However, the story lacked the element of surprise, especially considering how many major twists and unexpected appearances I was expecting.

My biggest issue was the absence of a strong main villain. For me, the villain has always been one of the most important elements of any Spider-Man movie. This might be the first Spider-Man film I have watched without a clear, memorable, or truly threatening main enemy. Even when villains appeared, none of them felt important or powerful enough to carry the story.

Some of the confrontations and fights that I expected never happened. The movie still included several enjoyable action scenes, but they were fewer and less impactful than I had hoped.

On the positive side, Frank Castle, also known as The Punisher, significantly improved the movie. His presence added a lot in terms of action, comedy, and entertainment. He also proved that the character has a strong place in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and he was easily one of the best parts of the film.

The movie may also work as a good introduction to Avengers: Doomsday. It feels like Marvel is finally closing the chapter on the old Avengers era and beginning to build a new storyline with different characters, conflicts, and connections. From that perspective, the movie does a reasonably good job of preparing the audience for what comes next.

Overall, it is a good and visually entertaining movie, but it lacks the surprises, major confrontations, and powerful villain that I expected from a Spider-Man film

A decent beginning for Marvel's next chapter, but not the Spider-Man movie I was hoping for.

title: A Refreshing Return To Spider-Man
review:
After the emotional ending of No Way Home, Spider-Man: Brand New Day takes Peter Parker back to his roots. Instead of relying on multiverse spectacle, the film delivers a more personal, grounded story that explores what it truly means to be Spider-Man.

The biggest strength of the film is its performances. Tom Holland gives what may be his most mature performance as Peter Parker, portraying a young man carrying the weight of loneliness while refusing to give up on doing the right thing. Sadie Sink is a welcome addition to the cast, bringing charisma and emotional depth to her role of Jean Grey while Zendaya once again proves why she remains one of the franchise's strongest supporting characters. The chemistry between the cast feels natural, making the emotional moments hit just as hard as the action.

Speaking of action, the movie delivers some of the best Spider-Man set pieces in years. The web-swinging sequences are thrilling, the fight choreography is creative, and the grounded scale makes every battle feel more personal. Beyond the spectacle, the film explores themes of responsibility, identity, sacrifice, and finding hope after loss which are core ideas that have always defined Spider-Man.

The movie isn't without flaws. The second act occasionally struggles with pacing, slowing the momentum. A few supporting characters could have benefited from more screen time, and some story beats feel slightly rushed as the film approaches its conclusion. None of these issues are major, but they keep the movie from reaching absolute greatness.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a confident and emotionally satisfying new chapter for Spidey. It successfully balances heart, humor, and action while staying true to the spirit of Spider-Man. It's a film that understands its hero and leaves audiences excited to see where Peter Parker's journey goes next.

Spider-Man brand new day doesn't just raise the bar for superhero films-it completely redefines what the genre can be. From its opening scene to its emotional finale, the movie delivers a rare combination of breathtaking action, genuine heart, and unforgettable storytelling.

What makes it stand above every other superhero film is its understanding of Peter Parker. Rather than relying solely on spectacle, the movie focuses on the difficult balance between being an ordinary person and carrying extraordinary responsibility. Every victory comes with a cost, making the action feel meaningful instead of just exciting.

Visually, the film is stunning. The web-swinging sequences are exhilarating, creating a true sense of speed and freedom that makes the audience feel like they're soaring through the city alongside Spider-Man. The cinematography and visual effects blend seamlessly, making every set piece feel both grand and grounded.

The supporting cast elevates the story even further. Every major character has a purpose, and the relationships feel authentic rather than existing simply to move the plot forward. The villain is compelling, with believable motivations that make the conflict more than just a battle between good and evil.

Perhaps the movie's greatest achievement is its emotional impact. It reminds audiences why Spider-Man has remained one of the world's most beloved heroes for decades-not because he's the strongest, but because he never stops trying to do the right thing, even when it costs him everything.

The score perfectly complements every emotional beat, the pacing never drags, and the balance between humor and drama feels effortless. By the time the credits roll, it leaves viewers with the feeling that they've witnessed not just an outstanding comic book movie, but a truly great film.

If there's a new gold standard for superhero cinema, Spider-Man (2026) is it. It's thrilling, heartfelt, visually spectacular, and emotionally resonant-a movie that captures everything fans love about Spider-Man while pushing the genre to new heights. It isn't just the best Spider-Man movie ever made; it's the greatest superhero movie of all time.

title: An emotional journey with Peter after almost 5 years!
review:
Mild spoilers ahead.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an excellent, emotionally grounded return for Peter Parker after a five-year gap, even though it fumbles the one decision that would have made it great.

Peter is now older and more guarded, trying to do his duty while keeping distance from the people closest to him, MJ and his best friend included. The film front-loads its trailer-featured action into the first thirty minutes, which briefly makes the remaining runtime feel uncertain - but it resolves that uncertainty fast once Sadie Sink shows up as Jean Grey.

Sink's performance is the film's clearest strength. Her chemistry with Peter gives the story its emotional center, and it directly serves the film's actual subject: a hero who's spent years isolating himself learning to let someone back in. The action is Marvel's usual high bar - the organic web ability makes Peter feel physically stronger and more evolved, and the Hulk fight sequences work well on their own terms, even with minimal Avengers tie-in.

The film's real weakness is its ending. After building two hours toward Peter choosing not to be alone anymore, the story pushes him back toward his old connections instead of letting him move forward with Jean Grey - a character the film had just spent an hour establishing as a major, powerful new piece of the Marvel puzzle. That choice costs the film its cleanest possible landing: it sets up a fresh start and then declines to take it, leaving Sink's future in the franchise genuinely uncertain.

Viewers expecting heavy Avengers connectivity should adjust expectations - this is a Peter Parker character study, not a team-up film. But taken on those terms, it's one of the more sincere, mature entries the character has had: a story about loneliness and the fear of moving on, told with real craft, undercut only by an ending that hesitates right when it should commit.

Rating: 9/10 - Excellent.

title: Tom Holland's Spider-Man at its peak
review: Spider-Man brand New Day abandons the grand and lavish spectacle and plot of the previous three films, instead focusing on Peter Parker's psychological journey. This is an interesting approach. In this installment, we see Peter Parker constantly trying to suppress his emotions. The director doesn't rely solely on Tom Holland's acting to portray this; the first half of the film is set in rainy New York City at night, a landscape that perfectly reflects the character's emotions. Even the villain's problems seem familiar to Peter. Nearly every narrative choice in the film exists to deepen our understanding of Peter Parker's emotional struggles. Some might consider this too narrow in scope, but I believe that after the plots of the previous three films, Spider-Man truly deserves a more profound exploration. Overall, this is an excellent Spider-Man movie, perfectly continuing the No Way Home storyline. However, it might disappoint some fans expecting spectacular action sequences. But if you adjust your expectations accordingly, it's definitely a masterpiece.

Plot-wise, it hits all the right classic Marvel beats and delivers a solid story.

To be completely honest, I haven't really been following most of Marvel's recent output, just like a lot of people. But I've watched Tom's entire Spider-Man run, and seeing a 4th installment in this franchise is genuinely inspiring-I'd happily watch four more.

What I loved most is how Peter goes back to his roots. I'm talking about the Tobey Maguire era where the webs were organic-that's always been the true canon for me. Seeing this version of Peter finally get that proper upgrade is a massive plus.

It's also great that we're seeing fewer crossovers taking the spotlight away from him. Going back to the classics-and this applies to both Tobey and Andrew Garfield-Spider-Man should fight the main villain on his own strength. title: This movie deserves every dollar it's making this opening weekend.
review:
From the very first second, Spider-Man: Brand New Day reminded me why I love this character. The Marvel Studios intro was nothing short of brilliant. Watching moments from previous MCU films featuring Peter Parker, only for him to gradually disappear from them, perfectly reflected the ending of No Way Home, where the entire world forgot he ever existed. It wasn't just a logo sequence-it was storytelling. It was creative, emotional, and one of the best Marvel intros I've ever seen.

From there, the movie does an incredible job of showing Peter embracing the role of the friendly neighborhood Spider-Man. His conversations with Bruce Banner, where he still doesn't fully understand his own potential, were some of my favorite moments. His reunion with MJ was emotional and reminded me why their relationship has always been so compelling.

The biggest surprise for me was the Jean Grey twist. Knowing who Jean Grey eventually becomes made seeing this version of her even more fascinating. Maybe I was naïve for not expecting it since we already knew she'd be in the movie, but it completely caught me off guard, and I loved it. The reveal involving her sister was a little easier to predict, but it was still executed incredibly well.

Then came the moment that gave me literal goosebumps: seeing Bruce Banner and Jean Grey controlling Professor Hulk, followed by the appearance of the Incredible Hulk. As someone whose favorite superheroes have always been Batman, Spider-Man, and Hulk, seeing the Incredible Hulk back on the big screen was unforgettable.

And I can't forget to mention The Punisher. He absolutely stole every scene he was in.

Ned and MJ were fantastic as well. My only thing that I would change personally was MJ's ending. When she reunited with Peter while under Jean Grey's control, I genuinely believed it was real, and I was so happy. I was hoping the movie would end with her truly remembering him and choosing to return to Peter. The painting she left for him in the hospital gave me hope, but I wanted just a little more closure.

If I had one criticism, it's that Jean Grey's arc never reached its full potential. She was excellent throughout the film, but it felt like there was still much more that could have been explored.

Finally, that post-credit scene... I genuinely have no idea where Marvel is heading next, and I love that. It leaves you excited without giving too much away.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is emotional, thrilling, surprising, and everything I wanted from a Spider-Man film. It honors Peter's journey, delivers unforgettable moments, and proves that even after No Way Home, there's still plenty of magic left in this story.

title: A surprise full of heart and affection for the characters
review: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is undoubtedly the best Spider-Man film with Tom Holland, a mature piece of cinema that can finally stand on par with Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2. Destin Daniel Cretton's direction is significantly superior to the previous trilogy-it is well-thought-out, dark, and perfectly tailored to the characters' darker sides. Cretton masterfully plays with heights, skyscrapers, and the structural angles of New York City, making the city itself feel alive and like a core character once again. The cinematography beautifully supports this vision, favoring melanoma tones, breathtaking sunsets, glass reflections, and neon lights that highlight the real New York. The acting is extraordinary. Tom Holland is simply perfect; seeing his face more often underneath the mask-battered by fights, wounds, and the sheer weight of life-brings an incredible sense of humanity. The script clearly loves its characters, crafting flawless narrative arcs. You can truly feel the deep love Peter holds for those around him: from Frank to MJ, to his connections with Aunt May's memory, Detective DeWolff, Ned, and Bruce. But the most beyond-measure surprise is Sadie Sink as Jean Grey. Jean has been my absolute favorite comic book character since I was 5 years old. I truly loved the previous on-screen portrayals by Famke Janssen and Sophie Turner, but unfortunately, the iconic Dark Phoenix Saga ended up being a bit of a disaster script-wise with both actresses. This time, however, the relationship between Peter and Jean is the most successful element of the entire film. They share loneliness, pain, and the temptation to give in to their dark sides, but they ultimately find a deep connection and reclaim their lives with hope. It is an amazing duo that absolutely needs to be explored further, and this introduction finally makes me confident that they will do justice to Jean and the legendary Phoenix storyline. Yelena's office scene was also a highly intriguing addition. If I have to find a flaw, the handling of Damage Control sets up great future potential but feels too rushed and underdeveloped. However, despite having so much on its plate, the final result is superlative thanks to an excellent and surprising balance. Rating: 9/10.

title: Good, but could have been great.
review:
I really enjoyed this film, but it's far from perfect. There was so much good to enjoy, but the writing was what stopped it from being great...

There was far more good than bad in this film. For example, the chemistry between Frank and Peter was legendary and their banter was perfect. The way they added to Peter's relationship with Ned and MJ without ruining No Way Homes ending was perfectly done, and although I wasn't a huge fan of the idea of Peter becoming more spider like, I thought that it was executed very well. I love how they leant very heavily (in the first half of the movie) on Peter becoming more so the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man who banters with his street level villains and the police rather than facing multiversal or world ending threats. Spider-Mans new suit was also very cool.

However, Brand New Day was unfortunately also very cliche, which was its biggest downfall (I won't go into specifics to avoid spoilers, as most of the cliques are in the second half). Even Peter's character development, which was perfectly fine and not bad, was still very basic, and we've seen very similar before in other films countless times.

A lot of plot points were really quite generic, and can be seen in many other films. They also brush over certain plot points super quickly, such as the Spider-Man vs Hulk fight, which was over almost as soon as it started, it ended in the most predictable way possible, and the power scaling was way off.

The film also leaned heavily into mystery, but since we knew who was playing the villain and who the villain was, the mystery didn't end up being all that mysterious, and it was really quite predictable. (There's also another big issue with the villain... but saying what would spoil the film.)

If I'm being completely honest I was expecting it to be better than it was, but I'm not insanely disappointed or anything, it was still a fun Spider-Man film and put a smile on my face.

Overall verdict: The first half was genuinely great and had fewer problems than the second half, and so gets a 7/10.

The second half however is incredibly clique, but still fun, and so gets a 6/10.

It's a good movie that could have been great, so it gets an overall score of 6/10 from me.

If you're a Marvel fan then I definitely recommend this movie, but don't expect anything incrediblely original.

author: Alex_imdb18

title: Spider-man: Brand Mid Day
review:
While not outright horrible, Brand New Day lacks depth and leaves many of its strongest ideas underdeveloped.

Let's talk about the characters.

Scorpion Scorpion is one of the few iconic, "untouched" Spider-Man villains. He was teased back in 2017, yet three movies and nine years later, he gets about ten minutes of screen time.

The problem is not simply the amount of screen time. A character can make a strong impression in ten minutes. The problem is that such a long-running tease ultimately leads to an almost incidental appearance, with no substantial arc and little influence on Peter or the main story. That alone shows where the movie's priorities lie.

Ned Did everyone, including Ned himself, simply forget that he has magical abilities? What college are we even talking about? The guy needs to go and study magic under Wong. But I guess we are not seeing Hobgoblin anytime soon.

Hulk While I am happy to see Hulk on the big screen again, are we just going to ignore the fact that Bruce and Hulk merged in Endgame?

Professor Hulk is suddenly gone, and the movie barely explains why. This makes Bruce's entire previous character development feel strangely disposable. Why spend years building toward the integration of Bruce and Hulk if it can simply be reversed whenever the next movie needs a more traditional Hulk?

Jean Grey Although she is brilliantly cast and acted, Jean Grey is one of the most random characters Spider-Man could possibly fight. But fine-let's bring in the X-Men.

Her history is barely explored, and her powers work however the screenwriters need them to work in any given scene. Are you seriously telling me that the Big Bad Organization captured her sister but left Jean alone while she was standing right in front of them?

The twist that Jean is not actually a villain and is merely trying to save her sister is not bad. However, once you think about it, it leaves the movie without a proper villain.

No Real Villain Bill Metzger, ironically and greatly played by Tramell Tillman-best known for playing the corporate supervisor Mr. Milchick-is far too underdeveloped to work as the movie's twist villain.

The moment the twist is revealed, he immediately folds and then disappears from the story. He never becomes a serious physical, emotional or ideological threat to Peter.

Punisher Punisher's dynamic with Spider-Man is entertaining, and their contrasting personalities create some of the movie's funniest moments. However, his presence still feels forced, and the film completely avoids the moral conflict that should define their relationship.

Punisher is prepared to murder a child. An extremely dangerous child, granted, but still a child.

The problem is not that Punisher considers it. That is consistent with his worldview. Frank Castle judges people according to the threat they pose, not according to their age, legal status or capacity for redemption. He is willing to kill whenever he believes it will prevent further deaths.

The problem is that Peter barely reacts.

Spider-Man is fundamentally opposed to killing. He repeatedly risks his own life to save enemies who have tried to murder him. He believes that people can be stopped without being executed and that power does not give someone the right to decide who deserves to live.

Punisher attempting to kill a child should therefore create a major rupture between them. Peter should be furious, disgusted or at least deeply distrustful of Frank afterward. He should confront him, refuse to work with him or actively prevent him from trying again.

Instead, the film quickly returns them to their quirky buddy dynamic as though nothing significant happened.

This weakens both characters. Punisher's attempted killing becomes little more than a temporary action beat, while Spider-Man's moral code suddenly appears negotiable whenever the screenplay wants the two characters to continue exchanging jokes.

Their conflict should not merely be tactical. It should be ideological. Punisher believes some people must die. Spider-Man believes nobody should be casually reduced to a target. The film places that conflict directly in front of us and then refuses to engage with it.

The Arachnoid DNA Plot This is by far the best part of the movie.

Peter undergoing changes that will ultimately make him stronger is a great idea. Making him lose control and become ruthless is also an effective substitute for another symbiote storyline.

Unfortunately, the entire plot feels like background noise compared with the main story, and it is resolved far too easily.

This should have been the central conflict of the movie. Peter becoming stronger while gradually losing control could have connected directly to his relationships with Punisher, Jean Grey and MJ. Instead, it remains one more underdeveloped subplot in an already overcrowded story.

The Complete Absence of Black Cat/Felicia Hardy Okay, now this is serious.

Ask yourself: wouldn't it have been more interesting if Spider-Man had to choose between returning to MJ, effectively "reviving" Peter Parker and his old life, or starting over with someone new?

Felicia Hardy could not care less about Peter Parker. She would be interested in Spider-Man himself.

Instead of spending two hours watching Peter awkwardly embarrass himself in front of his "ex," the movie could have given him a genuine romantic alternative-one that would create actual conflict.

The romantic plot could have become a proper love triangle:Black Cat ↔ Spider-Man/Peter Parker ↔ MJ MJ would represent Peter's lost life, his old identity and the possibility of restoring what was taken from him. Felicia would represent a new beginning built around Spider-Man rather than Peter Parker.

That would turn the romance into an actual thematic choice rather than another series of awkward encounters.

I guess Marvel executives have a cat allergy, because I honestly do not understand how we have had nine Spider-Man movies without even a hint of Black Cat. (Apparently, there was plenty of time for Jean Grey, Hulk, Punisher and Black Widow-the first characters who come to mind when you hear "Spider-Man," right? No.) The Sudden and Complete Absence of J. Jonah Jameson Seriously, where is he?

Who is going to tell New Yorkers that Spider-Man is a crook and a fraud?) The universal praise Spider-Man receives in these movies is one-sided and boring. The city needs someone who openly distrusts him, challenges his public image and turns public opinion against him. J. Jonah Jameson is not just a source of jokes. He represents public suspicion, media manipulation and the possibility that Spider-Man's actions may be interpreted in the worst possible way.

Removing him also removes one of the most important forms of pressure on Peter.

In the end, the movie is not bad. It has some great visuals and action sequences, plenty of humour and several genuinely emotional moments.

Its central problem is that it tries to be too many movies at once: a story about Peter rebuilding his life, a mutation storyline, an introduction to the X-Men, a Punisher crossover, a Hulk movie and a conspiracy thriller.

As a result, none of these ideas receives enough attention to become the actual heart of the film.

It could have been much better.

P. S. I could watch an entire movie about Spider-Man fighting the Hand Clan. Those guys are awesome.

title: A Grounded Masterpiece That Shows MCU Spider-Man at His Absolute Best
review:
Wow, although my anticipation was somewhat high, I didn't know it was gonna be this good. My experiences with this Spider-Man series vary a lot, apparently: 3.5 stars for Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), 4.5 for Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019), 3 for Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021), and now this: full jackpot!

There are always a few minor nitpicks, but Spider-Man: Brand New Day is so well executed from start to finish that I don't see why I shouldn't give it 5 stars. It's so much more grounded, and I love that the movie feels heavier and more physical. You don't get that typical MCU vibe with flat visuals-you actually feel fully invested in the story.

I love the direction it takes with Peter Parker's psychological and physical transformation-the way he technically becomes more and more like a real spider. He struggles to stop and reverse it, but when we finally see him in the third act as a powerful, anatomical Spider-Man, he feels twice as formidable. In parallel, the focus on how much Peter has matured fits seamlessly alongside his evolved abilities.

One minor complaint is that Jean Grey gets revealed a little too early. I wish her presence remained a mystery just a bit longer. Either way, her part of the story is great, and the film feels so dynamic because of her abilities and how she manipulates people.

The emotional core is definitely the relationship between Peter and MJ. Tom Holland plays the character to perfection, and the way he conveys Peter's deep desire to make MJ remember him is heartbreaking and powerful. I wasn't a fan of the plot in No Way Home because the whole spell concept felt like a cheap shortcut, but Brand New Day actually uses it to deliver something truly meaningful, and I loved that.

There's so much more I could say. It's been a while since I wrote a review this long, but I guess there's a good reason for it!

Also, the script is also far more cohesive, grounded, and restrained than I anticipated.. I expected things to be dumner, for some reason. And it has emotional moments that carry real weight, and pretty much every actor and element is used well.

Some subplots feel a little outside of Spider-Man's territory, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. They keep the story feeling fresh and lead to genuinely unexpected developments, which helps keep the audience engaged.

I still think Homecoming introduced this version of Spider-Man extremely well! But the sequels, despite having strong ideas and moments at the time (Mysterio and Spidey friends), felt ultimately underwritten. And this film continues lashing Peter's emotional state with endless turmoil, which can feel repetitive and tiresome.. not because it doesn't fit the character (suffering is in Spider-Man's DNA), but because the previous films got in the way of that momentum, as the arc felt finished before it started (no explanation needed), then stagnated in the middle, and then started over from scratch (with the Aunt May incident surprisingly late and unnecessary and such). As a result, this movie almost feels like it's still completing Peter's introduction and rethreading ground in parts, instead of moving him into new stuff. Surprisingly, though, it works in the end! If you can forget the previous two, this works as a great sequel. Anyway, the film stands well on its own, even if you can't help but feel it's laying the groundwork for what's next.. or realize that the whole thing would be solved if characters just talked to each other about their problemas like people.

Overall, a solid outing with some great action and new characters. But knowing what's immediately after gets in the way of that hope of them gently continuing this journey.. as their "desperation" sets in.

title: Spidey and Peter, Holland Can Play Both
review:
Finally got to watch this movie, and I'm in awe. Well, I'm a bit biased towards Spidey, so the review may reflect that. This is the fan in me talking.

Firstly, I want to talk about Tom Holland because this is his movie. He commands it, completely immersing himself in the character. You can totally feel that he now owns the screen rather than just taking orders.

The movie deals with loneliness, emotion, maturity... some pretty heavy stuff, and you feel it. Peter is lonely, and that's why he has made Spider-Man his whole identity. As the story progresses, with the help of the supporting characters, he evolves. Peter's character arc is the core of this movie.

Jean Grey, played by Sadie Sink, surely leaves an impression. At some point, it even feels like the movie is about her, which can be seen as both a positive and a negative aspect of the film.

Zendaya does justice to the emotional portrayal of MJ, and I'm glad the director didn't squander the development from the previous movie. I love that they didn't just redo everything.

A big shout-out to director Destin Daniel Cretton, especially for the action and swinging sequences. Those are some of the best I've witnessed on screen.

Having said all that, I was really disappointed with the treatment of the Punisher. He was mainly used for comic relief when he could've been given a much more serious tone. The colour palette sometimes feels very MCU-ish. The VFX in the first quarter of the movie also felt cheap and underdeveloped. Most importantly, the first half felt sluggish, which is definitely a minus.

However, this is a movie with substance, not just fan service. It has its flaws, but nonetheless, it's a well-made movie that definitely warrants a repeat watch. 8.5/10.

title: The marketing spoiled too much
review:
I had mixed expectations going into Spider-Man: Brand New Day. On one hand, I was excited to see how Peter Parker would deal with the loneliness and anonymity left behind after Spider-Man: No Way Home. On the other, I felt it would be almost impossible to match the emotional impact and spectacle of its predecessor.

Fortunately, it's still a solid MCU entry. The mystery surrounding the villain is engaging, especially as we slowly uncover their identity, motivations, and ability to possess other people. I also appreciated the more personal approach to Peter Parker, who is forced to fully embrace the consequences of "with great power comes great responsibility."

That said, not everything works. Peter's mutations had plenty of potential but never feel fully developed, and I was left wanting much more from that storyline. My biggest disappointment, however, wasn't the film itself but the marketing. The trailers and countless leaks revealed far too much. Characters like The Punisher and Hulk would have been fantastic surprises, but their appearances had already lost most of their impact before I even entered the theater. The same happened with another major character whose identity had been spoiled months in advance, making what should have been a shocking reveal feel predictable.

Even so, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an entertaining blockbuster that never becomes boring. It simply doesn't reach the emotional highs or the sense of wonder that made No Way Home so special.

I'd definitely recommend watching it, especially if you've followed Tom Holland's Spider-Man from the beginning. Just avoid trailers, leaks, and spoilers if you can. Your experience will be much better.

For me, it's the weakest of Tom Holland's four Spider-Man films. But that's not really an insult, because I still think all four are good. This is simply the one that left the smallest impression on me.

title: The definitive Spider-Man adventure.
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is everything a modern Spider-Man film should aspire to be: thrilling, heartfelt, visually spectacular, and deeply human. Rather than relying solely on nostalgia or universe-shattering spectacle, the film returns its focus to Peter Parker himself, reminding us why he remains one of Marvel's most enduring heroes.

Tom Holland delivers his most emotionally nuanced performance yet, portraying a Peter who has matured through hardship while never losing his compassion or sense of responsibility. The supporting cast shines as well, with Zendaya bringing warmth and emotional depth, while Sadie Sink proves to be an excellent addition, injecting fresh energy and charisma into the story.

The action is nothing short of exhilarating. Spider-Man's acrobatic combat and web-swinging have never looked more dynamic, with inventive set pieces that balance excitement with genuine stakes. The visual effects are consistently impressive, enhancing rather than overwhelming the storytelling.

What truly elevates the film is its emotional core. Themes of identity, sacrifice, and hope resonate throughout, creating moments that feel earned instead of manufactured. Even quieter scenes carry weight, allowing the characters room to grow between the blockbuster spectacle.

The film isn't flawless. The ambitious plot occasionally feels overcrowded, with multiple story threads competing for attention, and a few supporting characters could have benefited from additional development. Despite this, the pacing remains engaging enough that these issues rarely diminish the overall experience.

Ultimately, Spider-Man: Brand New Day captures the heart of the character while delivering blockbuster entertainment of the highest order. It's funny, emotional, action-packed, and inspiring; a superhero adventure that balances spectacle with soul. This is Spider-Man at his very best, and one of the strongest entries in the franchise.

title: Masterclass in Heart: Why Spider-Man: Brand New Day is Deserving of Every Record
review:
If there is one glaring issue that has plagued modern blockbuster cinema, and superhero movies in particular, over recent years, it is the absolute absence of a beating pulse. We have been fed endless spectacles of CGI destruction, fatigue and hollow quips, often leaving cinemas feeling completely empty. Enter Spider-Man: Brand New Day, a film that does not just course-correct the genre, but completely redefines it by packing every single frame with raw, genuine heart.

Yes, let us get the obvious out of the way first: the action is phenomenal, inventive and pulse-pounding. The performances are top-tier across the board, anchored by a lead cast delivering deeply mature, emotionally resonant work. The storyline weaves a complex, gripping web that honestly keeps you hooked from the opening frame to the credits.

However, what elevates this movie from just another good blockbuster to a true cinematic masterpiece is its profound emotional weight.

This film brilliantly tackles deep internal turmoil. We see a Peter Parker who is carrying the invisible, crushing weight of a world that has fundamentally changed around him. The movie explores the agonizing worry of watching the people you love move on, thrive and find happiness, all while navigating the delicate boundaries of human connection.

Crucially, the film also does an incredible job of celebrating friendship in all shapes and sizes. It highlights the unexpected bonds, the ride-or-die companionships and the different ways people show up for each other when the chips are down. These relationships feel lived-in, authentic and genuinely vital to the emotional core of the story rather than just forced plot points.

Furthermore, Brand New Day handles grief and loss in a remarkably mature, grounded way. It does not use tragedy as a cheap trick, instead it actually sits with the pain, explores the psychological fractures it leaves behind and shows the messy, beautiful journey of human healing. When the film leans into these quiet, devastatingly human moments, it achieves a level of emotional resonance that modern movies so desperately lack.

It reminds us why we fell in love with these characters in the first place: not because of the masks they wear or the powers they possess, but because of their core vulnerability.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a triumph of storytelling, character work and emotional depth. It has scale, it has spectacle, but above all else, it has a soul. It is a rare cinematic masterpiece that is wholly and indisputably deserving of every single box-office record it continues to shatter. Do not miss this on the big screen.

title: A Frustrating Chapter That Struggles Between Hope and Consequences
review:
After watching Spider-Man: Brand New Day, I was left with a strong sense of disappointment.

To its credit, the film shows clear improvements over previous installments in several technical areas, including dialogue-driven scenes, action choreography, visual presentation, color grading, and sound design. However, despite these strengths, I found the overall experience emotionally frustrating.

One of the most interesting characters for me was Gretchen. Like Peter Parker, she is a character shaped by pain and loss, but I found her motivations and desire for revenge more understandable. Unfortunately, the story ultimately follows a familiar path where Peter convinces her to abandon her anger and choose forgiveness. While this message fits with Spider-Man's traditional values, the execution felt somewhat predictable and disconnected from the darker emotions the film had built up.

Peter's compassion has always been one of his defining qualities, and I respect that the character remains committed to doing the right thing. However, in this story, his unwavering optimism sometimes felt less inspiring and more emotionally difficult to accept, especially when the consequences faced by other characters were so severe.

The handling of Peter and MJ's relationship was another disappointing aspect for me. Seeing MJ move forward with her life while having little connection to their shared past created a sense of sadness rather than emotional closure. For viewers who were invested in their relationship, this choice may feel difficult to connect with.

In a darker and more complicated world, many audiences naturally look for stories that explore consequences, justice, and emotional catharsis. Spider-Man: Brand New Day chooses instead to emphasize forgiveness and hope, which is consistent with Spider-Man's philosophy, but the balance between idealism and reality did not fully work for me.

Spider-Man should remain a symbol of kindness and responsibility, but a story about hope can still acknowledge anger, loss, and the consequences of people's actions. Unfortunately, this film left me wishing it had explored those themes more deeply.

title: Best Spider-Man movie yet

Peter also learns that he'll have to adapt to the fact that the new MJ doesn't love him. There was a scene in the movie that I thought was a little weird. He's so fed up with not being able to remind his friends who he is, and ends up following, and almost stalking Ned. He literally follows Ned to a party that Peter wasn't even invited to. He could have at least tried to be friends with Ned, so he can slowly reveal who he is eventually. Moving away from the whole philosophy behind the movie, let's talk about the main threat. Of all the villains I've seen Spider-Man fight, Jean Grey, is by far one of the most interesting. Like Mysterio, she can easily confuse people; like venom, she can control different victims; like the Wizard (from the comics and TV shows), she can manipulate objects; and forget about the strength of the Lizard, she was able to control the Hulk. I also have to say, I love the character design for Scorpion in this movie. They didn't just attach a random scorpion tail to the Scorpion, you could see the mechanics of the tail. I think it's trying to imply that Spider-Man will be in space in the next movie, but they showed it in the most boring way possible. It just shows the Spider-Man tracking app, and it's reading a signal from space. Way worse than the end-credit scene of Into the Spider-Verse. So I doubt you need to see the end-credit scene before watching Avengers: Doomsday. As someone who hasn't seen Thunderbolts* yet, I was a little confused. I know the Thunderbolts were going to be like the Avengers, but I didn't think they'd be the literal new Avengers. So I was a little confused why he was meeting Black Widow's sister. I think they were trying to show that Black Widow's sister is the new Black Widow. Overall I'd say Spider-Man: Brand New Day is my 2nd favorite Marvel movie (with Guardians of Galaxy vol 3 being my favorite).

title: Spider-Man At His Absolute Best!
review:
5 years after the last Spider Man movie released in cinemas, Spider-Man: Brand New Day manages to not only be a great movie, but it also adds a new evolution for Peter Parker's story.

Starting with the positives, I really enjoyed the direction this film went for. Destin Daniel Cretton did a fantastic job making this film mature, realistic and grounded through the use of different camera angles, storytelling, and practical effects. Thanks to the great direction, the action of the film felt exciting to watch(especially the web slinging), and the story was able to be engaging. The main plot itself I found to be interesting, with the mystery surrounding the villain of the film and Peter trying to grapple being Spider-Man full time. Additionally, the message of the film was such a profound one. The themes of loneliness, depression, and racism were all handled so well here. Those themes being explored through Peter, Jean, and Punisher, who have all lost family but handled those losses differently, was such an amazing touch to see. I especially enjoyed the parallel between Peter and Jean, where one wasn't consumed by grief but one was.

However, the characters for me are the best part of this film, with every single actor/actress doing a great job playing his/her character. Peter Parker's struggles throughout the film were so interesting to watch, and I'm so glad the film didn't erase the consequences of previous films, regarding Ned and MJ. I thought Ned and MJ were handled well enough. As for Jean Grey, this was a nice introduction to her character. I liked how it was simple to understand her motivation and powers, without needing to watch any X-Men media. Finally, I was surprised at how much I enjoyed The Punisher. His rivalry with Peter was fun to watch, and I liked the contrast between his and Peter's worldviews, which made their dynamic more interesting.

Even though I enjoyed most aspects of this film, there are some minor criticisms I have with it. The pacing, while not awful, can sometimes vary in going too slow or too fast. Additionally, the character of Bruce Banner felt like a plot device, only really serving to help Peter and fight him, before disappearing from the film.

Overall, Spider Man: Brand New Day was such a great delight to watch in theaters. Despite some minor issues like the pacing and some characters, they didn't take away from the experience for me. I think this is a step in the right direction for the MCU, but it is a great Spider Man film first! I would highly recommend this film!

9/10.

In Brand New Day, almost every hero/villain is some kind of mix. Oh, they're just misunderstood. Or they're losing control so they nearly hurt people. No. Spider-man should be good. Not perfect, but always good. Always trying to do the right thing, always using common sense, always communicating.

And with villains, as soon as you attack innocent people, threaten them, torture them, kill them, no, you can't be saved. You should be stopped and punished (no pun intended). Prison time. No forgiveness because you had a rough childhood or you didn't really mean it. It's so ridiculous.

I hated the look and style of this movie, or at least most of it. It reminded me of Everything Everywhere All at Once which I barely got about 10 minutes into at the time. It feels so messy, noisy, dirty, etc. Not cinematic, not cool. Like a dirty old basement. That's what the movie looks like. I like style, contrast, some kind of consistent palette or something.

The same with the music. It's terrible. It's forgettable. Worse than that, the director lazily relies on songs about 5 times. I didn't like the songs and they do nothing to push cinema forward. Compare it to The Odyssey which had at least 3 common actors with this movie. Goransson's music is bizarre, crazy, intense and interesting. The ending song was awesome as well. Not this movie.

So, compared to Raimi's Spider-man 1&2, Burton's Batman 1&2, Nolan's trilogy, Superman 1978 and many others, this movie pales in comparison in terms of music, style, originality, themes, etc.

I want my money back. I regret watching this. The director also made Shang Chi which I also found to be a big disappointment. But the IMDb rating was high. I feel lied to. I should have trusted my instincts and waited. This movie reminded me of Shang Chi, Deadpool & Wolverine and partially Homecoming. In bad ways. The weaknesses of those movies combined. If you loved those, you may well love this. If you have good taste like me and didn't enjoy those other ones that much, you will also hate this movie like me.

Some of the action was okay, especially parts with the Hulk or with a tank. But even those parts looked drab and had rushed, messy camera work.

Bad acting, bad music, terrible values, questionable casting, flat humour and a terrible ending. Give me my money and time back! The theatre was packed and it felt like there was ZERO energy in the air. The post credits "scene" was also the worst I've ever seen. A huge waste to wait for about 15 seconds of absolutely nothing. Highly not recommended.

title: Grounded and Emotionally Raw
review:
Spider Man: Brand New Day delivers Tom Holland's most grounded and emotionally raw performance yet. This chapter strips Peter Parker down to his core, forcing him to rebuild his life from nothing while protecting a city that no longer knows his name. The film leans into street level storytelling, giving New York a gritty, lived in presence that pushes Peter forward and knocks him down in equal measure.

The action is sharp and intimate, and the cinematography gives the film a handmade, almost vulnerable feel that matches Peter's new reality. At the center of the story is a mysterious, broken antagonist whose presence shapes the entire film without ever revealing too much. Their pain, motives, and connection to Peter add a tension that keeps the movie grounded and unpredictable.

That said, certain parts of the movie move slowly, especially in the middle act where the film focuses heavily on Peter's isolation and day to day struggles. It's meaningful, but it does drag at times. And while the movie delivers a powerful emotional arc, there were things I hoped to see that simply didn't happen moments, characters, or developments that felt just out of reach. The film chooses restraint over fan service, which works for the story but leaves a few wishes unfulfilled.

Even with those drawbacks, Brand New Day stands as a bold, personal rebirth for Spider Man a story about rebuilding, rediscovering, and choosing responsibility even when the world has forgotten you.

title: Knowing Yourself When No One Else Does
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the best Tom Holland Spider-Man film, which is a meaningful distinction for a franchise that has always struggled to fully balance its personal and blockbuster dimensions. Destin Daniel Cretton finds that balance more successfully than his predecessors, building a superhero film around a genuinely relatable emotional core and trusting Tom Holland to carry it with the specificity and vulnerability the material demands.

The film's central premise is its greatest strength. Peter Parker living anonymously in a world that has forgotten him is not merely a plot device but a genuine emotional condition, and the film explores it with a specificity that makes his isolation feel real rather than convenient. But the external isolation is only half the challenge. Peter's powers are simultaneously changing and beginning to threaten his control over himself, meaning the chaos he must navigate is not just social but deeply internal. The film's central conflict runs in two directions at once, and that dual pressure gives the story a weight that most superhero films never attempt. He cannot control what others remember or feel, and he cannot fully trust his own body. What he can control is who he chooses to be within those circumstances, and watching him arrive at that understanding is the film's most satisfying emotional journey.

The tension between his desperate desire to reconnect with MJ and his understanding that protecting her means staying away is agonizing in the best possible way. Holland makes every moment of that conflict feel inhabited and human, turning what could have been a superhero abstraction into something universally recognizable about love, powerlessness, and the painful distance between what we want and what we can control.

The scenes involving Ned are among the film's finest despite being few in number. Their friendship offers Peter something his existence as Spider-Man cannot, the simple experience of being known as a person rather than a symbol. With Ned he can simply be himself, and those moments of ordinary human connection carry an emotional weight that the film's larger set pieces cannot match. They are a quiet reminder of what the entire film is ultimately about.

Sadie Sink and Jon Bernthal both bring genuine chemistry with Holland and add emotional stakes that are impressive given how new both characters are to this corner of the Marvel universe. Sink's Jean Grey serves an interesting thematic function as a parallel to Peter's own journey, another person learning to navigate and control enormous changes rather than be defined by them. The comparison deepens both characters without the film ever making it explicit. Tramell Tillman is exceptional as the film's true antagonist, elevating what is otherwise a familiar Damage Control storyline through sheer force of presence and precision.

The film's limitations are real but manageable. Peter's isolation, while emotionally effective, also restricts the film's relational world considerably, leaving few opportunities to connect with anyone beyond him. The MCU connective tissue occasionally pulls the story toward a larger scale than the more intimate film at its center warrants. And the Damage Control reveal follows a blueprint the franchise has used before, arriving with less surprise than the film seems to expect.

What remains is a superhero film that genuinely earns its emotional moments, trusts its lead to carry considerable dramatic weight, and finds something true to say about identity, selfhood, and the importance of knowing yourself when everything around you and within you is changing. That is considerably more than most entries in this genre manage.

title: A Masterclass in Emotional Maturity and Psychological Warfare
review:
The premise of Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) grounds the iconic web-slinger in a hauntingly intimate, heartbreaking reality: stripped of his legacy, erased from the memories of everyone he ever loved, a completely forgotten Peter Parker lives a solitary existence in a small apartment, pouring 100% of his life into being a full-time Spider-Man. But as the crushing weight of total isolation, grief, and relentless crime-fighting accumulates, the psychological pressure triggers a dangerous, dark transformation within him just as a lethal new adversary emerges. As expected from a top-tier Spider-Man film, it is overflowing with emotional and character complexity-yet the sheer seriousness and depth of the screenwriting elevates this entry into something truly legendary.

Character Growth Through Real Maturity Let's celebrate the absolute core strength of this film: a script written with undeniable intellectual weight and seriousness (naskahnya benar-benar ditulis dengan serius). Instead of treating Peter's trauma as cheap background noise or resolving his problems with easy magical shortcuts, the screenwriters showcase how raw, painful emotions actively forge a developing character.

However, the film makes a crucial, profoundly mature point: emotional pain alone doesn't save you-true resolution can only be achieved through intellectual and emotional maturity (kedewasaan berpikir). Watching Peter navigate his isolation and make grueling, selfless choices based on real adult logic rather than childish impulse is a deeply rewarding experience.

The War Within The philosophical brilliance of Brand New Day lies in its subversion of traditional superhero tropes. The film boldly emphasizes that the most terrifying, powerful enemy facing a hero isn't a giant mutated monster, an alien threat, or a villain in a high-tech suit-it is the internal darkness, grief, and self-destruction lingering within oneself (musuh yang kuat bukanlah monster... melainkan pada diri sendiri).

By forcing Peter to fight an intense psychological battle against his own inner demons before he can defeat his physical threat, the filmmakers deliver an airtight, emotionally resonant narrative that hits like a sledgehammer.

Final Thoughts Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an absolute triumph. By pairing complex emotional stakes with a deeply serious, mature script and shifting the primary conflict inward, it creates a deeply moving masterpiece that refuses to disappoint (benar-benar tidak mengecewakan).

A profound, beautifully written superhero epic that proves the greatest battle is the one fought within.

title: *Spider\-Man: Brand New Day* completely exceeded my expectations\.
review:
Spider Man: Brand New Day completely exceeded my expectations. This is more than just another superhero movie with great action and visual effects. At its heart, it's a story about responsibility, identity, relationships, and what it truly means to be Spider Man. The movie takes its time developing its characters, and because of that, every emotional moment feels earned instead of forced.

I found myself genuinely emotionally connected to the story. There were several moments that made me tear up because the performances felt so natural and authentic. The emotions never felt like they were trying to manipulate the audience. Instead, they came from watching characters you care about face difficult situations in a believable way. That emotional connection is what makes this movie so special.

Tom Holland delivers what I believe is his best performance as Spider Man. Peter Parker feels more mature, more experienced, and more confident while still keeping the humor, kindness, and heart that make him such an incredible character. The chemistry between the cast is outstanding, and every relationship feels genuine, making the emotional scenes even more powerful.

The action is incredible, but what impressed me the most was the balance between exciting set pieces and meaningful character moments. The movie knows when to slow down and let the story breathe, which makes every major scene feel even more impactful.

Without spoiling anything, make sure you stay through the credits. The final scene doesn't rely only on surprise. Instead, it leaves you thinking about what could come next and gets you excited for Spider Man's future.

I saw this on opening day in a packed theater filled with Spider Man fans, and it was one of the best movie experiences I've had in a long time. The audience reactions, the emotion, and the excitement made the experience unforgettable.

Overall, this is one of my favorite Spider Man movies ever made. It is emotional, exciting, heartfelt, funny, and beautifully paced from beginning to end. I never wanted to leave my seat.

I highly recommend this movie to every Spider Man fan and anyone looking for a genuinely great film.

10 out of 10.

title: MCU Spider-Man at his full potential
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day fulfils the exciting promise of No Way Home's ending by being a pretty self-contained and more mature street level story that can still connect to the wider MCU in mostly unobtrusive ways. Some of the elements here are just quintessential Spider-Man stuff as he suffers even after doing the right thing and the mystery at its centre ties all the different plot beats together and earns the 145 minute run time. It's at its strongest when embracing the feels which haven't been this potent since the Raimi era.

Tom Holland is now the only Spider-Man to lead four films and he only gets better as the character. He's clearly grown so much since last time and that allows him to add more angst to Peter Parker at his most isolated without losing the warmth, quips or kindness. He spends the majority of his screen time in the costume so it helps that this is easily his best looking one because it doesn't feel over designed, mixes in the best aspects from previous Spider-Men outfits and it's actually allowed to show creases when moving.

Jon Bernthal finally gets to bring his bruising version of The Punisher to the big screen whilst being a lot more fun than usual thanks to his very natural comedic rapport with Tom Holland born from their real life friendship but the tragedy of the character isn't forgotten about. Sadie Sink is great in her part too. Zendaya gets a bit less to do for obvious reasons but she brings plenty of emotional heft to her scenes and her chemistry with Tom Holland and Jacob Batalon (really funny) benefits from a new dynamic between them.

Destin Daniel Cretton's direction succeeds in fixing the issues with the previous trilogy even when working inside the usual house style by making New York & its citizens feel more alive than they ever have been in the MCU and delivering web swinging sequences that have an energetic perspective alongside quality action scenes which mix in moves from the PS4 game. Brett Pawlak's cinematography achieves something similar thanks to stronger lighting, contrast and some really striking shot composition ripped straight from the comics.

title: A decent Marvel movie but not the Spider-Man story we needed
review:
I saw the Spider-Man Brand New Day in the cinema today and I was pleasantly surprised in the beginning of the movie. They pick up very nicely from where the previous film left off and attempts to move it into more darker and mature territories, exploring themes such as trauma, loss and adult challenges. In many ways it also succeeds in doing so.

The scenes with MJ, Peter, and Ned were among the strong moments in the film, atleast for me. There is a genuine emotional thread here that I believe could have been explored much further. Unfortunately, the pacing often falls into a rhythm that felt a bit off in the sense that it was: melodrama, action, melodrama, action, and at some points I found myself thinking in one of the scenes: "Why do I feel like that the movie is trying to force an emotional reaction out of me" at a point where it made less sense for the story? I think the older Spider Man movies had a better balance between emotional moments and overall story progression.

One of the biggest issues in Brand New Day is that it often feels divided between telling a story about Spider-Man and setting up the next major MCU storyline. To me, it feels like Spider-Man was hijacked by Marvels future plans. The movie introduces a lot of material, new threads, hints at where the universe is going, but it is all at the cost of Peter Parker himself. Instead of feeling like these elements naturally serve the story of Spider-man, it often feels more like franchise expansion. But in trying to cover so many new directions, it disrupts the balance of the movie, which thrives when it focuses on Peter's inner turmoil and more often than not stumbles when it pauses to introduce new elements.

One could argue that the big swings in the movie is not about Peter, but rather about the MCU universe and the pseudo-family he was placed in.

Another issue is the lack of a truly compelling main villain. The introduction of several villains as well as the main villain creates a lot of excitement and I remember thinking "Woah where is this going!". Kind of reminded me of Age of Ultron when they introduced the Main Villain and the challenge it could be. The first half sets up a lot of interesting possibilities but the film just doesnt fully capitalize on the opporunities and that momentum. They ended up focusing a lot on humanizing the main villain, explaining the main villain, because it likely will seem important to the future stories. I am desperately trying to avoid spoilers, but overall take is the feeling that there is more focus on building the future of MCu rather than fully exploring what this particular spider-man movie could have been.

A Brand New Day has all the ingredients to be an incredible superhero movie. It certainly got the crowd-pleasing moments and Easter Eggs that will make the fandom cheer. A bit too much CGI with the fighting scenes but okay for me. Great moments. Acting performance, action moments, emotional moments and darker themes. However, In all of this I miss a more clear idea of what it means to be Spider-Man.

The movie is darker, but not necessarily more mature. It has grief, anxiety and serious themes, but sometimes it lacks the depth that makes Peter Parker's struggles truly meaningful. Being serious is not the same as saying something is meaningful. The movie occasionally falls back on familiar bromides like "you're special" or "be yourself," and after a while, I started to feel some fatigue with these kinds of messages. The excitement of thinking where this could go in the first half beat the experience of where it did go. The revelations did lay good groundwork for future movies to come but it also had me feeling like "I guess thats it"

The biggest problem is that the MCU-machine feels more important than their most iconic hero. A very entertaining movie with a lot of fantastic elements, but also a movie that tries to build the next phase of Marvel, before it tries to focus on the actual name that is on the poster of the movie.

Brand new day tries to move forward, but is a bit held back by all the different directions in which it tries to move forward.

I may have been harsh with my rating but I feel it is around 6-7. I will revisit the rating after I end up watching it again, which I probably will.

title: I expected more tbh
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day - Review

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an exciting and refreshing addition to Spider-Man's story. The movie successfully brings Peter Parker back to his roots after the emotional events of previous films. Instead of focusing on world-ending threats, it tells a more personal story about responsibility, sacrifice, and finding hope even after losing everything.

One of the movie's biggest strengths is its portrayal of Peter Parker. He feels more relatable than ever, struggling to balance his everyday life with the challenges of being Spider-Man. His determination to protect others, despite the hardships he faces, reminds audiences why he is one of Marvel's most beloved heroes. The action scenes are thrilling and creative, making great use of Spider-Man's agility, web-swinging, and quick thinking.

The film also introduces interesting new characters while giving familiar faces meaningful roles. The relationships feel natural, and the emotional moments have a strong impact without slowing down the pace of the story. The humor is well balanced with the more serious themes, creating an enjoyable experience for viewers of all ages.

Visually, Brand New Day is impressive. The special effects, cinematography, and soundtrack work together to create memorable scenes that capture the excitement of Spider-Man's adventures across New York City. The movie maintains a steady pace, keeping the audience engaged from beginning to end.

Although some plot points may feel predictable to longtime Spider-Man fans, the film's strong performances, emotional storytelling, and entertaining action make up for these minor flaws. It respects Spider-Man's legacy while offering a fresh direction for the character's future.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a fun, heartfelt, and inspiring superhero film. It reminds audiences that true heroism comes from perseverance, kindness, and the willingness to do the right thing, even when no one knows who you are. It is a worthy chapter in Spider-Man's journey.
