title: Why did it take so long to get the Spiderman/Punisher duo? A much-needed movie...
review:
And one day we got the Peter Parker of Tom Holland we wanted!

I just saw the movie and I was pleasantly surprised.

It's not that the trailers didn't spoil some of the film or that certain actors already had leading roles assigned. However, I'm grateful to have pleasantly surprised you with the dynamics and heart of this film.

First of all, I think the main reason for this is Destin Daniel Cretton, who had already demonstrated in "Shang-Chi" and "Wonderman" that he understands comics and character development quite well. Thanks to him and his personal touch, I think we got the movie that most of us, I assume, can empathize with regarding Spider-Man and his situation.

Going back to what I said, as a product, it's the best Spider-Man film the MCU has given us. It's the one many of us believed it should have been from the beginning, but better late than never, as the saying goes. Peter's character development, his depression, his chemistry with Frank, the roles assigned to the supporting characters, and the fight choreography are all top-notch.

Furthermore, the inclusion of Sadie Sink, whom we already know well and whose talent we know, greatly enhances the dynamic on screen.

It's a very comic book-like film, which I really like. Those cameos from Hulk, Yelena, villains like Scorpion, and others make fans celebrate.

I want to highlight the chemistry between Peter and Frank; it's by far the best thing about the film. We all knew the Punisher would appear, but I never imagined he'd have such a significant role and complement the protagonist so perfectly. Clearly, their off-screen friendship creates a special chemistry between them. A chemistry that, by the way, is undoubtedly also present with Zendaya. He has limited screen time, but his moments are crucial to Peter's development, especially that conversation after the letter and the "I don't love you, I don't even know you" was pivotal.

As for the villains, we can say that Jean Grey, and Damage Control, are partly responsible for this dynamic. I understand the research and development behind Sadie Sink's character, but I was a little disappointed that it was Peter who brought her back from the Dark Side and not another character, as we all wanted: Professor Xavier. Beyond that, her use of telepathy and other abilities are excellently portrayed.

I feel there are some flaws in the film: Peter's introduction, which is quite depressing, doesn't bother to show anything else that fans wanted to see: how does he support himself? Because clearly, without an education, he must be working as a photographer; a great opportunity was missed there. The CGI in the swinging between buildings and some of the fight scenes doesn't look that great, and the soundtrack, except for Michael Giachino's final theme, is a bit lacking.

However, what bothered me most was the post-credits scene... I simply expected more.

In the end, Peter returns to square one, back to being with his friends, and this might not appeal to everyone, but considering his development and the allegory of maturing and growing with the change in his powers and accepting them as they are, I think it's fine. It's definitely the best of Tom Holland's four Spider-Man films and a clear demonstration that this new MCU should be based on Spider-Man, the X-Men, and little else...

title: A Fun Return That Doesn't Quite Reach Its Full Potential
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an entertaining superhero movie with some exciting action sequences and strong performances, but it struggles to live up to the emotional impact of its predecessor.

The story follows Peter Parker as he tries to rebuild his life after the events of No Way Home. While staying true to Spider-Man's themes of responsibility and hope, the plot feels uneven at times. The first half builds interesting ideas, but the second half becomes predictable and rushes through several important character moments. Some new characters are enjoyable, though a few of them don't receive enough development to leave a lasting impression.

Tom Holland once again delivers a likable and heartfelt performance as Peter Parker, balancing humor with emotional vulnerability. The action scenes are visually impressive and feature creative web-slinging sequences, but the film relies a bit too much on familiar Marvel formulas.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a fun blockbuster with enough heart to satisfy Spider-Man fans, even if it never reaches the heights of the best films in the series. It's an enjoyable watch, but not one of the strongest entries in the Spider-Man franchise.

title: Going as the +1 of a fan
review:
The first half doesn't have as many sentimental moments that go: 'remember when X happend' like we've become used to from Marvel movies (and if you're a fan, you probably like those moments). For me, as someone who doesnt get the callbacks, I was pleasantly surprised at the pacing of the first half. It was generally just a continuation of the last movies' plot and set-up for this one.

The second half however, felt like a drag (and with its ~2:30 runtime the pacing of the movie slowing really hits hard). Maybe it's because the set-up in the first half exeeded my expectations and I became slightly invested, but the second half really is like any other marvel/bond movie: a lot of "tell don't show" to make sure everyone is keeping up and some plotholes that signal that the story isnt the filmmakers #1 priority. If that's what you come in to the theater expecting, you will find yourself waiting for fight scenes to be over and almost purposefully ridiculed by the writers lack of filling plotholes.

But, at the end of the day, one must appreciate the machine that is Marvel. With a clear goal to reach as wide an audience and to make them invested in both the characters and the actors playing them, these movies are economically genius. If you go in expecting a niche cinematografical masterpiece and laughing at your own disappointment, you must ask yourself: who is the fool? The spiderman fan having a good time watching his favorite character beat up the bad guy? Or you: the only person who feels he wasted his evening.

Actual movie rating (6/10).

If, like my girlfriend, you just just like spiderman and popcorn (9/10).

title: Based
review:
Brand New Day was some serious gourmet food. Nah, but I loved it, and boy is there a lot to talk about.

I think the commentary on loneliness, and what it can do to you is such a breath of fresh air.

While I like Superhero films as a whole, it's so disappointing to see so many of those films have the potential to explore real world problems in meaningful ways, and just choose not to in favor of action & explosions. While I think they've generally gotten better with it (tho can't really say that for the previous two Superhero films that still keep themes to a surface level) there's still room for improvement, I'm really glad that Brand New Day does this well, and I think it should serve as a blueprint for future Superhero films..

I think it works quite well as an introduction for the X-Men to the MCU. I think it'd be impossible to do it flawlessly considering how many years of this franchise we've had, but I think it worked well here. I also love how they handled Jean Grey (yup, to no one's surprise, that's who Sadie Sink is playing, really wish there wasn't so much discourse surrounding modern films, makes things like this impossible to keep secret, and film opinions are being shoved in your face constantly, like god darn). Making her the secret villain I was referring to earlier, before turning her into more of a hero with a very heartfelt conversation with Aunt May of all people (she got into his mind which is how it happened lol).

I also like how Spider-Man is more honed in on his craft, and it shows in his fight scenes and web swinging, speaking of, this film looks much better than the previous ones, even Hulk looks pretty good here. Tho, I do think it was a bit messy (which wasn't a surprise), I'm disappointed that Scorpion didn't have much of a role, I thought they'd fill in from the Homecoming post-credits scene, but he only gets a small role here (probably my biggest problem with it).

There's a fair amount of exposition dump to catch up people who hadn't seen the previous trilogy, it does make some parts feel a little messy, tho it did help people like my Uncle who hasn't seen any MCU movie besides Deadpool & Wolverine. There's also a LOT of characters, most of who play an integral role in the story, that also made things feel a little messy here. I'm a little conflicted on how they handled Punisher, don't really like him trying to kill a child (even if it's for fair reasons), tho at least it led to a great ending. I don't really know his character, and after thinking more about it, I quite like how he was handled here, especially when he put on Peter's mask (after he waited at the hospital) to cover up for him, that was a sweet moment.

Hulk is pretty good, I think this film's a step in the right direction for his character, he is quite scary here, and I like how Hulk actually sacrificed himself after a talk with Peter (he didn't die, just not sure how to word it properly), tho again, I'm disappointed that we didn't really see him create his inhibitor, especially with how major the invention is, tho that's more of a general MCU problem, not necessarily just with Brand New Day. I think the side characters are handled better here than in the previous films. Even Aunt May, who isn't supposed to be alive, gets her best scene in this film. MJ telling Peter she doesn't love him (since she doesn't remember him) was so brutal, I was a little teary eyed leaving the theater after that to go to the bathroom, this is MJ at her best (not a high bar tho).

Ned is alright, his Spider-Man obsession is logical, and I like him at the start, but he does fall victim to this films messy nature. Lastly, the ending is so good at the hospital where Peter realizes that the city loves him, and I liked his final reunion with Ned too. Overall such a great film, I wouldn't put it over the Spider-Verse films, but it's easily the best live-action Spider-Man film, and Tom Holland in particular is at his best.

title: The worst of the quartet
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an entertaining superhero movie that delivers plenty of action, humor, and emotional moments, even if it doesn't always reach the heights expected from a new Spider-Man adventure. With its familiar hero at the center, the film feels energetic and accessible, but some of its story choices and pacing prevent it from being truly outstanding.

The biggest strength is Spider-Man himself. His character remains likable, funny, and relatable, while the film gives him enough personal challenges to make the story feel more meaningful than a simple action spectacle. The action sequences are generally exciting, with impressive visuals and creative web-slinging moments. The movie also understands the lighter side of Spider-Man, balancing jokes with more serious scenes without completely losing its emotional focus.

However, the screenplay is less consistent. Some story developments feel predictable, and certain characters could have been given more depth. The movie occasionally relies too heavily on familiar superhero formulas, making parts of the plot feel like something audiences have seen before. The pacing also becomes uneven, particularly when the film tries to balance its character drama with large-scale action.

Despite these flaws, Brand New Day remains an enjoyable addition to the Spider-Man franchise. It has enough personality, spectacle, and heart to keep audiences engaged, even when the story itself is not especially surprising. The performances help carry weaker moments, and the overall presentation makes it an entertaining theater experience.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a solid but imperfect superhero movie. It succeeds as fun popcorn entertainment while leaving room for a stronger story and deeper character development. 3/5 stars.

title: The Best Tom Holland Spider-Man Film
review:
When it comes to superhero movies, I'm definitely not a huge fanboy. Sure, I have loved some films, like Superman, Guardians Vol. 3, and The Batman, which are great films. However, most of the time the genre either leaves me thinking between "Yeah, this is pretty good" or "Oh my God, why am I even watching this garbage?" (Thor: Love and Thunder) Regardless of what happens in the coming years for comic book movies, only two superheroes will reliably get me seated inside a cinema: Batman and SPIDERMAN.

After having had three manufactured factory-made Jon Watts Spider-Man movies, it has finally been a breath of fresh air to get a different perspective on the web-slinger. It is finally time to move away from the "Ironman Junior" phase. Watts' approach to the character- his perspective was always dull and aesthetically unpleasing when it comes to such a dynamic character like Spider-Man. (Of course, you can say whatever you want about "The Amazing Spider-Man"; the script might have been completely trash, but at least they knew how to swing)

First things first - looks. Cinematography is definitely the best we have gotten for the MCU iteration of Spider-Man. No, it doesn't compete with the Sam Raimi films, but compared to the Home trilogy visuals? I'll be happier with this. Both previous MCU Spider-Man movies looked like car commercials. No Way Home gets bronze for actually trying to look cinematic, but those green-screen effects, yikes! Cretton brings real kinetic energy when filming action sequences. The way he films and directs the visuals in the fight scenes? Just amazing 👍. This man gives a sense of physicality to the action, which is just awesome, especially in the climactic action sequence. But in the dialogue scenes? 👎 Complete snooze fest. Just boring and standard shot reverse shot stuff in conversations. Nothing is exciting in it, just standard stuff. Compared to the Rami films I remember, the dialogue was more dynamic, fluid, well-composed, well-shot, well-framed, and well-lit-just as good, if not better than the action. I wish Marvel gave their directors as much freedom to be stylistically interesting while filming dialogue scenes as they do in CGI action scenes, but I guess it's wishful thinking for wanting a Marvel film to have a Sam Raimi style to it or any unique auteur style.

The cast is solid. Tom Holland, Zendaya, Sadie Sink, Jacob Batalon, and Jon Bernthal all do a good job in this movie. But if I had to pick the MVP, then it goes without saying that it is Zendaya. She delivers a really good performance as always. However, it does not mean that the other members of the cast have failed; she is simply the best among them all. On the other hand, the member of the cast who has performed poorly in this movie is Jon Bernthal. He does not perform badly; he simply performs the same type of brooding tough guy act that I have seen him do in every movie I've seen him in, including The Odyssey.

Now, on to the more blatant criticisms. Apart from the CGI being quite bad in some parts (although the overall production is quite good) and the cinematography for the dialogue being subpar, my biggest disappointment is the score. After finding out that Michael Giacchino was the person responsible for the score of this movie, my jaw hit the floor. This is the same person who scored The Incredibles and The Batman. How did he manage to produce such a mediocre score? Other than a couple of needle drops, there isn't a single piece of original music that stayed with me. Danny Elfman made a generational score for the Raimi trilogy-I could hum the leitmotifs from Spider-Man 1, 2, and 3 right now, but this film, just like in the rest of the Holland era, the orchestral score went in one ear and out the other.

So, does this movie fall into that "pretty good to really good category? Yes, absolutely. "Will I increase my rating on a second viewing down the line?" Probably not, but is this one of the better Spider-Man movies in recent years that isn't part of the Spider-Verse franchise? Sure, why not.

title: It's a Brand New Day
review:

This movie takes itself a lot more seriously in its tone, the comedic aspects of the movie are scattered around where you don't actually feel like everything you're watching is just played for laughs, but rather take part of what's happening in the story in subtle ways.

Sadie Sink's character is a standout in the story, while obviously not having the same screentime as Tom Holland she still managed to own every scene she was in. While this is definitely for me the best Spider-Man live action movie since Spider-Man 2, in the aspect of emotion, entertainment and story, I did feel like it dragged out just a bit, some scenes feel a bit repetitive but it wasn't enough to ruin this for me in any way.

title: A good Spider-Man movie that had the potential to be something much greater.
review:
I really enjoyed this movie, especially the visual effects, the action sequences, and the way Spider-Man feels more mature and human this time. Peter Parker finally feels like someone who has grown from his past experiences, and I appreciated seeing a more experienced version of the character.

One of the highlights for me was The Punisher. His presence brought a more serious tone to the movie, and his comments and attitude gave some of the most memorable moments. He was a great contrast to Spider-Man's personality and added a darker edge that the story needed.

However, I think the movie played things a little too safe. The main villain and the central storyline involving the telepathic girl were not as engaging as I hoped they would be. The concept had a lot of potential, but the development felt underwhelming.

My biggest disappointment was how they handled Peter's mutation and the changes happening to his powers. I was expecting something much more dramatic and psychological - a Peter who slowly loses control, changes as a person, and starts becoming someone even he is afraid of. Something closer to the darker side of Spider-Man, like what we saw with Tobey Maguire's version when he was affected by the symbiote.

The movie had all the ingredients to become a darker and more memorable Spider-Man story, but it never fully committed to that direction. It was still an entertaining experience with great action and a more mature Peter Parker, but I left the theater feeling that it could have been much more ambitious.

Final rating: 6/10.

title: The Best Tom Holland Spider-Man Movie
review:
Marvel has not made such a tightly organized movie for a while. This movie is well scripted, smart, and very well executed. Everything makes sense, and the action is really good. No wonder the director is the same director as Shang-Chi. He knows how to handle action while still keeping the emotional depth accurate.

Spider-Man working with the police officer is very smart. He does not come in and steal her role or make the police look useless. He works with her, slowly earns her trust, and gradually becomes part of the community. This is how Spider-Man should be written. He is powerful, but he still needs to build trust with normal people.

Jean Grey is also a very strong antagonist because she has her own story and pain behind her. She is not just another villain who wants to destroy the world. Her conflict with Peter has meaning because both of them have lost someone, but they deal with that pain differently.

The first scene where MJ seems to remember Peter was very rough. At first, I thought the movie was trying to bring back her memory too easily. But when it turns out that Jean possessed MJ, the scene makes sense again. Jean was using Peter's hope against him, which was a very good idea.

The real MJ finding out about Peter was also very well scripted and handled. It makes sense that she would be angry because Peter hid the truth from her for so long. It also makes sense that she does not automatically love him again because she has no memory of their relationship.

However, that scene needed a better transition. MJ goes from being angry that Peter hid everything from her to honestly saying she does not feel anything for him. Both reactions make sense, but the movie moves between them too quickly. It needed one more moment for MJ to explain that she understands they had a relationship, but that relationship only exists in Peter's memory now.

The fight between Jean and Peter was also very well developed. But when Peter says he is both Peter Parker and Spider-Man, the movie does not give enough depth to the power upgrade. It is a good idea, but the transition is too fast. The movie needed to show more clearly how accepting both sides of himself changed the way he used his power.

The same problem happens when Jean hears Aunt May's speech and realizes that Peter also lost someone. The idea is meaningful, but Jean puts her guard down too quickly. The movie needed to develop that emotional change a little more before reaching that moment.

These are not major plot problems. The ideas all make sense. The movie is just missing a little development between some of the emotional moments.

Overall, this is the best Tom Holland Spider-Man movie. No Way Home was a bigger event because of the old Spider-Men, but Brand New Day is a better Tom Holland Spider-Man story. Peter finally carries his own movie, the villain has real emotional depth, the action is excellent, and the characters behave logically.

For the first time in a long while, Marvel feels like Marvel again.

I genuinely feel bad for Tom Holland because he finally delivers the Spider-Man performance many fans have been waiting for, but it's trapped inside a weak film with an underwhelming script. title: The Best Spider-Man Movie Ever Made ?
review:
For the longest time, Andrew Garfield held the undisputed crown as the absolute best Spider-Man to ever swing across the silver screen. To me, he was perfection personified-the unmatched acrobatics, the hyper-realistic web-slinging style, the pitch-perfect wit, and the deeply relatable, messy teen struggles made him feel startlingly alive. No other live-action web-slinger came close.

That was the absolute truth... right up until the credits rolled on Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

I mean... wow. What did I just watch?! It is, quite literally, mind-blowing. I was so completely immersed that I genuinely didn't want the movie to ever end.

Growing Up, Getting Gritty The single greatest triumph of Brand New Day is how fearlessly it dives into the raw psychology and mental weight of Peter Parker's dual existence. The "kid" phase is officially over. Peter is a full-grown adult now, crushed under the heavy, unrelenting realities of genuine responsibility.

And oh, how glorious it is to have classic Spider-Man back where he belongs: tackling grimy, grounded New York City problems, diving into brutal street-level brawls, and fighting in tight, claustrophobic spaces. This is the real Spider-Man we've been craving. The movie shines brightest when it dissects the exhausting drama and emotional toll of balancing Peter Parker's broken personal life with Spider-Man's endless crusade.

The Ultimate Dynamic Duo If you told me before walking into the theater that Spider-Man and The Punisher would share the screen, I wouldn't have expected lightning in a bottle. Yet, the chemistry between them is nothing short of legendary. Their duo is the best pairing in the entire cinematic universe so far-they played off each other with such effortless friction and mutual grit that it felt like they'd been sharing the screen for five straight years.

Another massive win? Dialing back the heavy romance. By refusing to let the MJ drama overshadow the narrative, the film keeps the laser focus firmly where it belongs: on Peter Parker himself.

The Only Flaw... Every masterpiece has its scratch. The only thing that truly bothered me was how they spent about half of the movie introducing the world of the new X-Men, starting with Jean Grey. I just wanted to live and breathe with Spider-Man for the entire runtime! That being said, the Jean Grey sequence was actually really well done, and she completely killed the role-I loved it anyway.

Without a shadow of a doubt, this is the best Spider-Man movie I have ever watched.

Thank you guys for reading my review, and I hope we see you all in Avengers: Doomsday!

title: Spider-Man Brand New Day: A Grounded Story of Peter's Personal and Heroic Struggles
review:
Tom Holland has a very solid run when it comes to the Spider-Man movies in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Although I did not love Homecoming all that much, I came around loving his character as I enjoyed Far From Home and No Way Home. And so, I was surprised to know that he was getting a fourth movie called Brand New Day and I wonder how this would expand on Peter Parker's journey post-third movie. I have to say, Brand New Day was another solid entertaining movie because of Tom Holland's relatable Spider-Man, street-level stylistic choices, and an entertaining story despite some narrative choices that puzzled me.

Peter Parker as Peter Parker, aka Spider-Man, shows the journey that he went through and how he has grown in becoming a hero. Just like in the previous movies, he still shows that funny and gullible side as shown in the funny moments whenever he interacts with other MCU characters or causes accidents in public. And yet, you can also see the emotional development and struggles that Peter carries after the events of Far From Home with E. V. as his technical assistant as well as No Way Home after losing literally everyone and trying to cope with his loneliness through heroism. Hence, this idea of him working as their friendly neighborhood Spider-Man alongside the police force finally adds this level of groundedness, especially with a new problem surrounding his use of web powers without needing technology. Surprisingly enough, even though I have never seen the television show or the special for this eponymous character, Jon Bernthal as Frank Castle / The Punisher. The back and forth bickering and even those somewhat father and son moments are so hard to resist because it shows the friendship and rivalry that was formed between Peter and Frank, to the point that they trust each other. Meanwhile, Zendaya as MJ and Jacob Batalon as Ned were good in their small moments, especially the former in providing a conclusion to Peter's mental conflict while Floren Pugh as Yelena Belova never fails to deliver funny dialogue and it is nice to see Mark Ruffalo playing as the Hulk again in his fighting sequences with Spider-Man. So yes, Holland literally carried all the way through and I was never bored seeing him in his interactions with the other characters as well as his struggles in becoming Peter Parker and Spider-Man.

In terms of the filmmaking, the ones that stood out for me were the costume design, cinematography, visual effects and editing. As I was comparing the Spider-Man suits across all four films of Tom Holland, each of them reflect the evolution of Peter Parker as shown in the fourth one. With the first being reflected on becoming a hero, as the second and third movies showing his adaptation with technology and such, the fourth movie showcases a suit that definitely reminds me of the comic book outfit which does symbolize the street-level Spider-Man that most fans wanted. For his first work into the MCU, Brett Palwak's cinematography did a solid job in capturing the action sequences that were directed by Destin Daniel Cretton and even the scope of the threat Spider-Man is facing. The scene with Spider-Man vs. The Hulk as well as the one with the Hand showcases probably one of the best action sequences I have seen from the franchise. Even the visual effects are awesome to look at because it delivers the smaller and bigger intense action moments. Whether that is through the iconic look of the Hulk once more rampaging just like in the previous X-Men movies, as well as the scene where a large scope of New York is in danger, it just adds more entertainment to the movie. The people behind the scenes were able to deliver a visual feast to the eyes of the fans that they would find it difficult to be bored by.

I definitely enjoyed the movie all the way through but there is this character choice that made me puzzled as to why the filmmakers went with it. In terms of the tone, it never deterred me nor undercut the important moments in the movie. Like whether it's the hilarious moments of Spider-Man with Yelena and Frank, or even the emotional scenes of him with MJ and Ned, they never felt out of place and instead provided entertainment. Even the pacing of the movie was straightforward all the way through without any signs of becoming boring. It was able to balance out the cool action moments of Spider-Man and personal moments of Peter Parker, with one underlying connective tissue of the theme of what it means to cope with loneliness and adapting to a new style of power that he needs to accept later on. The biggest issue for me has something to do with the way they used Sadie Sink's character and its implications for the introduction to a new roster into the universe. Without giving too much spoilers, as a fan of this team, having one of its members be depicted in this story might make fans wonder why, especially since she is a main part of the movie alongside how they interpreted her differently from the comics in terms of relatives and power set even if it makes sense to fit the movie's story. If anything, I like almost everything that happened in the movie except for Sink's character which has nothing to do with her performance because she was great, it is mostly on the direction and writing.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is another solid installment to Tom Holland's Spider-Man franchise. If I were to rank all four of them, it would rank third - above Homecoming which is in last and behind No Way Home and Far From Home which are my first and second favorites respectively. It was nice to see Holland again playing as the titular character as well as what Cretton directed despite some of the narrative choices that did not sit with me at all. But seeing how much it brought a lot of people to theaters, it would not be surprising for me to say that this is a movie that will entertain you and get excited for what is to come in the lead-up to not just Doomsday and Secret Wars but to the future of the MCU in general.

title: Amazingly relatable and genuinely emotionally-resonant

It seems like a no-brainer but too many recent superhero (and big-budget action films in general) seem to be woefully deficient in the arena of genuine "Heart & Soul" that "Spiderman BND" generates in abundance.

Of course, a huge reason this all works so well is due to the amazing multi-Layered performance of Tom Holland who embodies the essential qualities that made the original Marvel Comics (Stan Lee & Steve Ditko) version of Peter Parker so revolutionary in the early 1960s, portraying Parker as exceedingly smart, diligent + compassionate, but at times socially awkward, just trying his best to deal with Life's emotional highs & Lows while still navigating the 'great responsibility emanating from great power' dynamic.

Audiences can totally relate and see parts of themselves within daily interactions of Peter, MJ, Ned, and it is most definitely the undeniable talents/ thespian artistry of Tom Holland, Zendaya, Jacob Batalon whose personal chemistry and believability transcends the confines of a movie theater. Another key is that perhaps more than any other Marvel-based movie, the Spiderman series of films has captured the essence of that most classic era of Spiderman comics not just in authentic characters but also the visual Look that oftentimes seems to 'burst' thru as if the most classic comic scenarios have come to Life.

Other high-points are definitely Jon Bernthal's portrayal of the 'Punisher' whose merciless efficiency and lone-wolf stoicism are undermined (in a good way) by Spiderman's inherent compassion that breaks down at least a bit of 'Frank Castle's' impenetrably hardened emotional barriers. Sadie Sink is surprisingly effective (and genuinely frightening) as the burgeoning super-mutant (who shall remain nameless, although most people probably know by now).

Spiderman Brand New Day has most certainly broken the fever of 'superhero fatigue' and thankfully shed much of the 'madness' of the over-complicated multiverse, instead focusing on what made the original Marvel comics so great in the first-place (prior to the creation of cinematic MCU) with laser-focus on emotionally-resonant character development and relatability, while fully allowing the Spiderman action-sequences to seamlessly leap out of the classic-comic pages, kudos to Director Destin Daniel Cretton!

author: akking-74139

title: Peter Parker behind the wheel.
review:
After so many years where everything seemed bigger than him, Brand New Day finally reminds us that Peter Parker works best when the world fits around his own body, when he stumbles, chats, forms bonds, and confronts the sheer weight of the burden he carries and the symbol he represents. Before being a Marvel hero, he needed to go back to being the kid who knows every street corner in the city, and to question whether he misses simply being that person.

The film still carries some habits that seem impossible to shake. Much of the dramatic weight retreads ground Thunderbolts had already explored, while the narrative constantly recycles images, conflicts, and moments that defined earlier versions of the character. It is a clear nod to those who have followed the franchise for decades, but also a rather safe way to elicit emotion. The big moments rely more on the viewer's memories than on the film's own construction.

Even so, there is a visual care that makes a difference.

Destin Daniel Cretton, alongside Brett Pawlak, brings back elements that seem basic but have been largely abandoned by recent blockbusters: contrast, color, saturation, and real locations. Even when shallow depth of field is overused, there is a living world that seems to exist behind the characters. The city regains its texture; the streets feel inhabited again. For the first time in a long while, Spider-Man truly belongs in the space he occupies.

That changes everything; Daniel explores the hero's specific connection to New York, albeit superficially, through beautiful framing.

A sense of humanity emerges precisely from this tangibility. The framing makes Peter appear smaller against the backdrop of the city, without turning him into a figure crushed by digital effects. The image breathes again. There is composition, there is light, and there is a genuine effort to make New York a participant in the narrative rather than just a backdrop for CGI. The fight scenes are engaging, featuring beautiful nods to everything from John Woo to House of Flying Daggers.

The relationships also take a more interesting turn. The dynamic between Yelena and Peter possesses a lovely, unexpected lightness, almost maternal in nature. The two work well together because the film allows them to talk and care for one another beyond their superhero personas; there is friction, humor, and genuine curiosity between them. Meanwhile, the presence of the Punisher seems to finally confront one of the biggest weaknesses of recent films: the struggle to build relationships that truly transform Peter over time. For the first time in a long while, the people around him seem to leave a lasting mark.

Brand New Day still looks backward too much, sometimes excessively so, and seems afraid to fully commit. It misses opportunities for moments of emotional confrontation, like those found in its counterpart, Thunderbolt, by feeling the need to crack a joke at the very end, thereby deflating the tension. Yet, perhaps that step was precisely what was needed; sometimes, one step back leads to two steps forward. As they attempt to breathe soul back into Spider-Man, Daniel and Tom remind us that he needed to be the protagonist of his own movie, not just the face on the poster.

title: The Brand New Avatar of Spidey Saves MCU Again
review:
Spider-Man Brand New Day (2026) : Movie Review -

Spider-Man is back to save the MCU once again. The last time Marvel delivered a massive blockbuster was with Spider-Man No Way Home (2021), and now they might just have the next one with Spider-Man Brand New Day. No Way Home was all about action and nostalgia, and it is nearly impossible for Marvel to recreate that magic again-unless they bring together three Spideys once more in the future. Brand New Day suffers from the pressure of its predecessor, but this time, it's understandable. This one focuses more on Peter Parker's inner battle rather than the outer world, as he struggles with the trauma of losing his loved ones. The film introduces a new villain who operates through mind games, which aligns well with Spider-Man's ongoing emotional conflict. That's the core trick the writers rely on, and it works in parts. Add to that the action-packed spectacle, and it becomes a big-screen experience that fans simply can't afford to miss.

Spider-Man Brand New Day begins after the events of No Way Home, with Spider-Man (Tom Holland) becoming the popular hero once again after the world forgets Peter Parker. A mysterious new entity arrives in the city and attacks the Damage Control bureau. It is searching for something called "V-Max," and no one knows what it really is. This invisible force can enter people's minds and control them at will-except for one man: Spider-Man. As Spider-Man teams up with Damage Control to stop the threat, things take a devastating turn when the entity targets MJ. It even takes control of Hulk's mind, making the situation far more dangerous for Spidey. The big question remains-will Spider-Man be able to defeat it and save the people he loves?

As mentioned earlier, this film is largely about Spider-Man's internal conflict and emotional scars. Towards the end, he is forced to choose between being Spider-Man and Peter Parker, and the choice he makes will leave you always screaming. The idea feels somewhat similar to Bruce Wayne's dilemma in The Dark Knight, though the level of intellectual depth here is comparatively lower. The new villain also carries shades of characters from X-Men, and you can't miss out on hints of Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 3 (2007). The action sequences are designed for the big screen, especially in 3D, with the Hulk vs Spider-Man sequence standing out as a major highlight. However, I do wish it had been longer-something on the scale of Hulk vs Iron Man from Civil War would have elevated it further.

That said, the film does suffer from a few logical inconsistencies that are hard to ignore. If a bullet could kill Spider-Man, he would have been dead long ago-I'm not buying that at all. The writers should have handled that better. In another scene, Peter is seen swinging across the city without his mask, which feels highly illogical. These flaws, along with some slow emotional melodrama, may slightly affect your overall experience, but not enough to derail it completely. In the end, it still works as a fine Spider-Man outing.

The performances are once again satisfactory. Tom Holland gets more room to explore his acting range, as the character is more grounded this time. He doesn't come across as a larger-than-life superhero but rather as a vulnerable human being, and Holland delivers that convincingly. Zendaya has limited screen time but does a decent job. Jon Bernthal brings intensity with his kick-ass role, while Jacob Batalon feels sidelined. The real surprise package is Sadie Sink-she is fantastic here. Without revealing much, she's definitely worth the wait, even if she appears later in the film. Tramell Tillman and Michael Mando are solid, and Mark Ruffalo finally gets a chance to shine in his own space. The rest of the supporting cast does a fair job.

Technically, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an action spectacle. Cinematographer Brett Pawlak delivers some visually striking frames-some are upside down, some rotate dynamically, and a few slow-motion sequences look stunning in 3D. The visual effects are impressive once again, although the 3D quality felt average during our screening due to a poor theatre setup, which slightly dampened the experience. The sound design is decent, and the production design stands out as one of the film's strengths. Writers Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers could have done a better job tightening the script, but considering the massive expectations following No Way Home, the pressure was immense. I understand that. However, Destin Cretton could have masked some of those flaws with sharper direction, which unfortunately doesn't happen here. Because of that, the film doesn't quite reach extraordinary heights. Despite its shortcomings, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a pretty good watch. It works as a much-needed boost for the MCU, which hasn't been in the best shape lately. Go and enjoy it on the big screen-and don't forget, "Spider-Man will return..."

RATING - 6/10*
author: SAMTHEBESTEST

title: The Spider-Man I'd Been Waiting For
review:
If the previous movies hadn't made so many mistakes with this version of Peter Parker, I genuinely believe Spider-Man: Brand New Day would have been the greatest live-action Spider-Man movie ever made.

In my opinion, this is the best-written Spider-Man film starring Tom Holland. The pacing is excellent, the direction is confident, the emotional moments finally land, and for the first time, it truly understands why Peter Parker has remained one of the most beloved superheroes in comic book history.

The biggest relief comes from the movie's new direction.

Gone are the Iron Spider suits, the obsession with making Peter feel like Iron Man's successor, and the constant need for world-ending threats. Instead, we're finally back to the Spider-Man I grew up with: swinging through New York, stopping ordinary criminals, talking to civilians, making mistakes, and struggling to balance his own life with the responsibility of wearing the mask.

That's Spider-Man.

One of the film's greatest strengths is that Peter Parker finally feels like a person again.

Both Peter and Spider-Man interact with others in a much more natural way. He asks for help, forms genuine friendships, struggles emotionally, and actually feels vulnerable. Instead of simply moving from one action scene to another, the movie allows him to exist as a normal young man.

One line perfectly captures that feeling:

"I'm so happy to see that this sad man has friends."

It's such a simple sentence, yet it says everything.

For the first time in Tom Holland's Spider-Man films, someone isn't just worried about Spider-Man saving the city. Someone is worried about Spider-Man himself.

That single line humanizes him more than entire sections of the previous movies.

The movie also understands something that I felt the earlier films completely missed.

Spider-Man has never been interesting because he's powerful.

He's interesting because Peter Parker suffers.

One of my favorite aspects of the film is that Peter is finally allowed to be human again. He experiences loneliness, heartbreak, regret, and moments where all he wants is a normal life. He watches life move forward without him, feels the weight of the choices he's made, and still has to put the mask back on because people need Spider-Man.

That, to me, has always been the essence of the character.

Spider-Man isn't a hero because he's the strongest person in the room.

He's a hero because he keeps choosing to help people while his own life is falling apart.

Anyone can save the world when everything is going well.

Peter saves it while he's miserable.

That's what makes him inspiring.

MJ was another huge surprise.

I honestly never cared much about her in the previous films. She often felt awkward without much depth, and I struggled to understand why Peter loved her so much.

Here, she finally feels like a real person.

She doesn't always say what we want to hear, and some of her dialogue genuinely hurts to listen to. Not because she's trying to be cruel, but because she's honest. She finally displays emotional complexity, and by the end of the film I found myself appreciating her far more than I ever expected.

The film's antagonist is, without question, my favorite from Tom Holland's Spider-Man movies.

From the very beginning, the mystery surrounding this character is handled brilliantly. Peter discovers the truth at the same pace as the audience, making every revelation feel earned instead of forced.

But what impressed me most is that this isn't really a typical hero-versus-villain story.

There are several moments where it becomes obvious that this person could have made things much easier by simply killing Spider-Man or attacking the people closest to him.

Instead, the conflict becomes psychological.

Personal.

Emotional.

It feels less like two enemies trying to destroy one another and more like two people who believe they're trying to save each other.

I won't say more because it's one of the film's biggest strengths, and it's something everyone should experience for themselves.

The action is fantastic.

Spider-Man finally moves the way Spider-Man should. The humor is placed exactly where it belongs, never interrupting emotional moments, and the movie balances comedy, drama, suspense, and heroism better than any previous Tom Holland Spider-Man film.

If I have one criticism, it's one the movie simply can't fix.

This Peter Parker still carries the baggage of the previous films.

Even though Brand New Day finally understands who Peter Parker should be, it arrives after years of characterization that I never fully connected with. Because of that, some emotional moments don't hit as hard as they could have if this had been the foundation of his story from the very beginning.

Imagine if this had been his first movie.

If this grounded, lonely, street-level Spider-Man had been the Peter Parker we met before all the Avengers, before the multiverse, before Iron Man.

I honestly think we'd be talking about one of the greatest superhero films ever made.

Even with that limitation, Brand New Day feels like a love letter to everything that has kept Spider-Man relevant for generations.

Heroism.

Humanity.

Humor.

Heart.

Not because Peter has incredible powers.

Not because he saves the city.

But because no matter how lonely, exhausted, or broken he feels, he still chooses to put on the mask.

And for the first time in Tom Holland's Spider-Man films, I didn't leave the theater thinking about the action.

I left thinking about Peter Parker.

To me, that's the greatest compliment any Spider-Man movie can receive.

title: Surprisingly emotional
review:
After the bombastic spectacle that was No Way Home, as well as its heart breaking ending, this fourth film in the series thankfully goes for a more grounded, character driven story. And to its credit, it does it really good. Sure, I predicted who the villain was pretty much the second they were introduced, but the film isn't really about them. It's about Spidey and one other character, how they're similar in pasts and their places in the world, the different ways they handle their circumstances, and ultimately, their shared redemption. All of this is well handled, paced, and written, as well as held up by the cast. Tom Holland gives a personal best performance here as a Peter Parker forced to live alone for years and constantly on the edge. Sadie Sink makes an excellent transition to film that shows solid range as an actor. Jon Bernthal is fun as always. And the rest of the cast, even the small cameos, do a good job, too. There's even one scene that got me close to tears. Unfortunately, as good as the inner stuff is, the outer stuff feels like a lot of buildup with not that much payoff, with lots of neat ideas that have only just started by the end.

The director really nailed the look and feel of Spidey's everyday life in just the opening scenes alone. The editing, visual effects, and music all come together to showcase how completely overhauled his life has become. Then, once the main plot gets going, it really picks up and becomes a ton of fun. Thr action is some of the best in any Spiderman movie, especially his awesome fight with the Hulk (that's not a spoiler; it was in the trailer). But, some of the best stuff in the film isn't even the action. It's the scenes where Peter discovers his powers acting up, the different ways they affect him, and the methods he uses to cope. Just the different things he does with his webbing get some great thrills.

Overall, Spiderman Brand New Day is up there with the best Spidey films and a return to form for the MCU. I still prefer 2 and No Way Home (at least in live action), but this one's still a good time.

title: **A Good Spider\-Man Movie Buried Under Too Much Marvel**
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an enjoyable superhero movie that leaves a better impression while you are watching it than when you start examining how everything fits together.

Its greatest strength is that Peter Parker still has a genuine character arc. Tom Holland remains engaging, and the film allows Peter to begin in one emotional place and end somewhere meaningfully different. The world-building is also surprisingly effective. New York feels both modern and timeless, blending advanced technology with the theatrical robberies and visual language of older Spider-Man comics. The swinging sequences are especially inventive, using shifting, almost spherical perspectives to reflect how Spider-Man experiences the city from every possible angle.

Unfortunately, the film never trusts those strengths enough. Yelena, Hulk, Punisher, The Hand, numerous cameos and an exhausting number of action scenes make the movie feel considerably longer than its runtime. Several characters exist primarily to create marketable encounters rather than improve the story.

There is a genuinely good Spider-Man film here, but it is buried beneath an overstuffed MCU package. Pleasant, visually imaginative and emotionally sincere-but also disposable enough that one viewing will probably be sufficient.

title: "The mask stay's on"
review:
I don't think Spider-Man: Brand New Day reaches the heights of the best Spider-Man films, but it's still a genuinely fun watch that reminded me why I love this character. After the ending of No Way Home, I was really interested to see Peter completely on his own, and the film leans into that grounded, street-level approach really well. It feels smaller in scale, but in a good way.

Tom Holland gives another great performance. This version of Peter Parker finally feels like he's forced to grow up, and you can really feel the loneliness that comes with everyone forgetting who he is. Seeing him struggle without May, MJ or Ned by his side gives the character a much more emotional edge. The action is also a huge step up. The swinging scenes are some of the best we've seen from Holland's Spider-Man, and the practical-feeling choreography makes every fight feel personal rather than just another CGI spectacle.

The cinematography surprised me too. There are some genuinely beautiful shots throughout the film, especially during the night sequences, and the score fits the more grounded tone perfectly. I also loved that the movie focused more on Peter being the "friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man" again instead of constantly trying to save the entire universe.

That being said, the film definitely has its problems. The story can feel a little predictable at times, and some of the emotional moments don't hit as hard as they probably should. A few supporting characters don't get enough development, and the pacing in the middle drags before the final act finally kicks into gear. Some of the dialogue is a bit cheesy as well, and I think the villain could have used more depth.

Spoilers: Peter choosing to keep his distance from MJ and Ned after everything they've been through is still heartbreaking, and I liked that the film didn't immediately undo the consequences of No Way Home. It would've been easy to give us the happy reunion everyone wanted, but instead it sticks with the idea that being Spider-Man means making sacrifices. That ending left me excited to see where his story goes next.

Overall, I had a great time with Brand New Day. It isn't one of the best Spider-Man films, but it's a solid return to a more grounded Peter Parker, with great action, strong performances and plenty of heart. It has a few story issues that stop it from being truly great, but it's a film I'm definitely looking forward to rewatching.

title: Back to Basics
review:
Since the ending of Spider-Man: No Way Home, it looked like we were finally going back to Spider-Man's roots as a local broke street level superhero...almost 5 years later we got it! Spider Man: Brand New Day, is one of the best Spider-Man movies to date. Tom Holland is the definitive live action Spider-Man in my opinion after this. The movie is mature, grounded, emotionally profound and full of heart filled with great Spider-Man action that will leave your eyes webbed to the screen from beginning to end.

The movie does not shy away from the ending of the last one. Peter suffers the reprecussions of his choice. Isolation and loneliness plague him throughout the film. Parallels between this and Spider-Man 2(2004) are apparent but never completely imitated.

Characters like Frank Castle and Bruce Banner mirror his character, subsequently making great dynamics with Peter and his journey. Especially Jon Bernthal's Punisher. It was great and surreal seeing him on the big screen after all these years of being a streaming exclusive.

His dynamic with Spider-Man is hilarious and compelling at the same time. He is still The Punisher we know from the Netflix Era, just fitting in the tone of Spider-Man's world. Mark Ruffalos Hulk is also a compelling part of the plot, and not used for a cheap cameo appearance. It was great to see him BACK as THE HULK after 8 years. Professor Hulk good riddance. Now I want to touch on the "surprise" villain without spoiling it.

Sadie Sinks character is the driving force of the 3rd act. She is a sympathetic villain for the most part. She also reflects Peter's journey throughout the film but in a more malignant way. I enjoyed her character, but my god she is a VILLAIN. Feeling sympathy/empathy towards her is put aside sometimes. That is my only big complaint for the movie.

Overall Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a love letter to past Spider-Man stories from the comics to the past films, taking him back to the big apple reminding us why he one of the greatest and most relatable Superhero's of all time.

author: mariakalya

title: Same Old Good Day
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the 4th entry in Tom Holland's iteration of the webslinger. This movie opens with a montage and some narration by Peter. I thought that this was a really fun montage to watch, and I honestly wished there was more. The movie continues to have a mystery villain revealed to be Jean Grey. Honestly, I didn't really like the Jean Grey plot. She was yet another misunderstood villain trope that is quite annoying since the movie had no primary villain. It also made the film feel like a set-up for X-Men movies. It also sidelined other villains that should have been the main villain in this, such as Scorpion and Tombstone. Scorpion was barely in the movie, and Tombstone would have been such a great main villain here, but he appeared for like 5 seconds. The pacing was a little weird too. We spent more minutes than needed with the plot exposition and the Jean Grey chasing. The stuff I liked about the plot was Peter's internal struggles, his relationship dilemma, and his character themes.

Peter goes through his life in this movie, fixing relationships while juggling with his personal life. I did want more scenes of this. We didn't see him go to work or go to school. I wanted more scenes of ordinary life, like what Spider-Man 2 did. His dynamic with Frank, who serves as his foil, is really enjoyable. It was fun having that moral difference banter. Dr Banner was also a surprisingly good addition. His talk with Peter about science stuff was pretty fun. The prime Hulk finally came back, and it did make me happy to see them adapt that one comic panel where the Hulk remembered Peter. Jean, played by Sadie Sink, looks good, but I really didn't like her story here since it just looks really out of place and seems to just push for the MCU's future. I loved the callbacks and the dynamic of his relationships with Ned(CEO) and MJ. I thought that they were the heart of the movie. I do hope that Peter moves on with someone else, like Black Cat or Gwen, instead of going back to MJ since that would kind of be redundant and would feel safe instead of something fresh going forward.

The visuals were great, featuring a darker palette that matches the more mature tone of the movie. I didn't like the slow-motion scenes too much, though. I did also really love the suit in this one. I do think it's the best one Holland's version has ever worn. This is also some of the best webslinging the MCU's version has ever seen. This looks a lot like Insomniac's Spider-Man. The Easter eggs were also fun. We got references to Tobey and Andrew's iterations, a Delmar Deli's shirt, and pictures of Flash and their high school teacher.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day feels like the same old day, as it follows a very common trope while retaining its MCU formula. It has pacing issues and a nonexistent villain. Still, it's a fun movie that features good performances, visuals, web-swinging, and core Spider-Man themes.

title: My new favorite live-action Spider-Man movie and a top 5 MCU film!!
review:
I'm gonna cut right to the chase. This is the greatest live action Spider-Man movie of all time, the best MCU movie to release after Endgame, and a top 5 MCU movie. Better than Spider-Man 2, better than No Way Home, EASILY. I cried twice; once due to emotional stuff in the film and the second time because of joy during the end credits.

I feel so vindicated. Spider-Man is probably my all-time favorite character across all types of media. I don't think there's a single truly bad Spider-Man movie, and I think all 3 actors are great. And while the original Tom Holland trilogy is amazing, we were being absolutely ROBBED. This movie is the most Spider-Man movie out of all of them. The swinging is incredible, the directing is incredible, the action is some of the best in the entire MCU, and Tom Holland CRUSHES it with his performance.

There's so, so much I want to get into I actually feel floored rn. I'll start with the writing. The plot is a TAD unfocused at times, but dang it is really good. I'm sure everyone knows by now, but Jean Grey is in fact the villain. And omg they gave her a VERY good introduction, I think she's already surpassed her two predecessors (because she was butchered in all of the X-Men films unfortunately). Thematically this movie is very similar to Thunderbolts and Jean is a huge reason why. Her and Peter both share traumatizing backstories and crippling loneliness. Loneliness and isolation are the main themes of the film, and I'm a huge sucker for when movies tackle that so I LOVEDDD it (but I did feel a bit targeted). I don't feel like comparing this to Thunderbolts because both are incredible and handle the subject matter very well. Jean and Spider-Man are simply handled perfectly. Tom Holland glows in his performance as an isolated, depressed Spider-Man losing control of his mental health.

I was also very impressed with the way MJ and Ned were handled. They somehow found a way to reveal Spider-Man's identity without ruining the ending of No Way Home. That "I don't love you" from MJ absolutely broke me 😭 Lastly I wanna talk about how comic-booky this movie really is. This is the first MCU movie in a long time that actually feels like an MCU film. There are so many characters and villains we've seen in other projects, but they're cameos that only work because of the connective tissue that is the MCU timeline. I was so happy to see Yelena in particular, that scene was really fun. Punisher's dynamic with Peter is surprisingly amazing, their banter is hilarious. Hulk doesn't get a whole lot of screen time, but he shines too.

Lastly, I NEED to talk about how incredible the action and camera work in this movie is. Jon Watts, WHAT WERE YOU DOING?? Looking back makes those movies look PUNY now omgggg!! Destin Daniel Crettin delivered some of the best action and cinematography in the entire MCU. All of Spider-Man's swinging scenes made me grin so hard. The action scenes are stylized and far more interesting than any from the Home trilogy.

But yeah this was EVERYTHING I could've asked for in a Spider-Man movie, and I think it is quite easily the greatest (live-action) of them all, and dare I say one of the best in the entire MCU. I am beyond happy right now.. Give Destin the keys to the whole franchise immediately.

title: Pretty Good Movie
review:
Rating - 7.8: Overall, 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' is a very solid, entertaining film showcasing the more grounded direction the MCU is heading as Tom Holland connects a web of past and present relationships to capture Peter Parker's depression and loneliness, supported by Jon Bernthal and Sadie Sink; while the action is fun and the humor definitely lands, the film is held back by tacky cinematography/editing choices and its lack of originality as the story feels almost identical to 'Thunderbolts*'.

Direction - Pretty Good: The macroscale is what you would expect from a Marvel Spider-Man action movie, though they try a few more stylistic choices to make it feel like a comic book movie that feel a bit tacky; while I wasn't too big of a fan of the new fight choreography, I cannot deny that the action sequences were entertaining and fun to watch; the microscale is surprisingly pretty good for a Marvel movie as Peter Parker acts like a spider in the middle of a web, serving as the center of interactions connecting old and new relationships; this movie is very much a more grounded MCU movie as it is about Peter Parker coming to terms with his depression and loneliness after the events of the last movie; storytelling is pretty standard for Marvel, taking a lot from Thunderbolts with how it uses emotion, empathy towards the protagonist's struggles, and character relationships to move the story forward; tension uses your emotional connection to the characters, and while the ending builds pretty good tension, knowing this is the first movie of a new trilogy gives the characters plot armor so you don't feel super uneasy or tense

Story - Pretty Good: The concept is interesting and deals with Peter Parker's loneliness as he watches the world move on without being able to be part of his old past or connect with his old friends after No Way Home; the plot structure is a linear story that feels very much like a copy-cat of Thunderbolts in how the main character suffers from depression, the antagonist is framed as a misunderstood superhero with the government as the true threat, and they end up befriending them; character writing is surprisingly pretty good, painting Peter as more depressed and showing how distant Ned and MJ now feel, while giving the Punisher and the antagonist more empathy and humanity; the strength of the relationships also strengthens the character writing as it creates the web that centers around Peter Parker

Screenplay - Pretty Good to Good: The dialogue is pretty standard Marvel dialogue, being the playful and friendly tone you would expect from a Spider-Man movie; the humor is standard Marvel and Spider-Man humor, with a decent hit rate; the symbolism is decently strong, exploring concepts of loneliness, duty, and depression as Peter Parker feels isolated in a world without his former friends; while I did enjoy the symbolism for this movie, it is very similar to Thunderbolts; the foreshadowing is standard for Marvel, though it makes the ending feel a bit predictable

Acting - Pretty Good to Good: Tom Holland - Good (Does a great job capturing Peter Parker's grounded, lonely, and depressed nature while building a web of relationships between his former friends and new companions, acting as the center of all the relationships in this movie), Zendaya - Pretty Good (Given less material to work with this time around, but delivers a good performance and shares great real-life chemistry with Holland), Sadie Sink - Good (A major standout in the movie who brings her character to life with great presence, sharing a strong dynamic with Holland and proving she can shine beyond Stranger Things), Jacob Batalon - Pretty Good to Good (The CEO has done it again, serving as comic relief and doing a good job with his limited screen time, maintaining good chemistry with Holland that highlights their former friendship), Jon Bernthal - Good (One of the best performances in the movie, portraying a hardened, tough-guy anti-hero as The Punisher and sharing electric chemistry with Holland), Tramell Tillman - Decent (Plays a pretty generic character as he is not really given that much material to work with; kinda just bland and monotonous as he gets the job done), Mark Ruffalo - Pretty Good (Is kind of just thrown into this movie as he uses his past experience playing the character as the real driving force for this performance, making this ultimately feel like a "fulfilling his MCU contract" type of performance), Rest of the cast - Pretty Good (Solid ensemble performance that thrives on strong chemistry, successfully building a web of relationships connecting Peter's past and present)

Score - Pretty Good: Continues what was left off in the previous films, serving primarily for character building, tension, and tone without overshadowing the movie or providing memorable new themes

Soundtrack - Pretty Bad: Typical high-budget Marvel blockbuster needle drops; while the Tame Impala needle drop was okay, the Bad Bunny needle drop was terribly mixed into the scene, cutting off awkwardly and feeling very forced

Cinematography - Bad to Pretty Bad: Felt tacky and poorly executed, trying to be innovative with a comic book feel and motion shots that didn't land; additionally, the blue color palette felt very dull and it was overly obvious the movie was framed for ScreenX, making the aspect ratio and composition feel off; after you get used to the cinematography in the first hour, it is not so bad in the second half

Editing - Bad to Pretty Bad: Tries too hard to turn this into a comic book movie, feeling very on-the-nose and a bit tacky alongside the cinematography choices

Sound - Good: Pretty strong sound design, delivering what you expect from a high-budget Marvel action movie

Visual Effects - Good: Standard high-budget Marvel visual effects where nothing really blows you away; it feels a little too much at times, but looks good overall with some places better than others

Production Design - Pretty Good: Captures New York fine, though it feels like a lot of it was shot on sound stages and interior sets rather than on-location in real New York

Makeup - Pretty Good: Does a pretty good job, particularly showing the bruising Peter Parker and The Punisher get throughout his fights

Costumes - Good: Good costume design; Spider-Man's suit is kept clean and un-overcomplicated, feeling reminiscent of Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield's suits rather than overly techy, and the Punisher gets a good suit as well

Pacing - Pacing was pretty good for the most part; even at 2 hours and 25 minutes, it feels like a fun time that moves along just right

Climax - Well-executed and gives great closure to many of the characters, even if it is pretty predictable

Tone - Tonally it is a grounded Spider-Man Marvel movie, taking on darker and deeper themes of depression and loneliness similar to Thunderbolts; despite its more grounded feeling, this movie does feel like a playful Spider-Man movie you would expect from the MCU

Final Notes - The product placement in the first hour is egregious (Little Caesars, BMW, Bero, Takis, etc.)

title: Spider-Man has finally arrived in the MCU!!
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day isn't just the best live-action Spider-Man film it's the definitive Spider-Man movie. This is everything I've ever wanted from a Spider-Man story, and it absolutely delivers.

The story is incredible, with a perfect balance of low, personal stakes that gradually build into something much bigger without ever losing sight of Peter Parker. It understands that Spider-Man isn't just about saving the world it's about saving people while trying to hold your own life together.

Tom Holland gives the performance of his career. Peter Parker feels mature, relatable, and completely authentic, while Spider-Man is confident, funny, and endlessly heroic. The humour lands perfectly, the emotional moments hit hard, and the action is spectacular. Every swing, every fight, every sound effect makes you feel like you're watching Spider-Man leap straight from the comics.

The suit is absolutely phenomenal. It's easily the most comic-accurate live-action Spider-Man suit we've ever had, capturing everything that makes the classic design so iconic while looking incredible on screen. Every detail, from the colours to the webbing and the expressive eyes, feels like it was pulled straight off the page.

What impressed me most was how this film feels like the perfect combination of what Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield brought to the character, while still allowing Tom Holland to make the role completely his own. You can feel the influence of the previous Spider-Man films, and with the guidance of the previous directors and creative teams, they've crafted the Spider-Man fans have been asking for. It honours the past while confidently creating its own identity.

New York City deserves just as much praise. This is the best the city has ever looked in a Spider-Man movie. It feels massive, alive, beautiful, and full of personality. Spider-Man doesn't just swing through New York he interacts with it, uses it, and moves through it in ways that make the city feel like another character in the story.

The supporting cast is fantastic, and every cameo feels meaningful rather than just being there for fan service. Each appearance adds something to the story, develops the characters, or pushes the plot forward, making the entire world feel connected and lived in.

The villains are absolutely nailed. Instead of relying on just one standout antagonist, the film gives us multiple memorable threats that each bring something different to the story. They feel dangerous, layered, and genuinely challenge Peter both physically and emotionally.

From a technical standpoint, this film is stunning. The CGI is some of the best we've seen in a superhero movie, making every swing, fight, and visual effect feel seamless and believable. The cinematography is equally outstanding, perfectly capturing both the scale of New York and the intimacy of Peter's journey. Every frame feels carefully crafted to immerse you in Spider-Man's world.

As someone who has always been a massive Andrew Garfield fan and considered him my Spider-Man, I never thought another actor would take that place. But after watching Brand New Day, I can honestly say Tom Holland is finally my Spider-Man.

Spider-Man is home, baby.

10/10. The greatest live-action Spider-Man film ever made to date.

title: The Best and Worst of the MCU
review:
It's Spider-Man 4, Brand New Day. Man, it's hard to believe this movie even exists. I mean, how many movie franchises have managed to make a successful trilogy, let alone a tetralogy? I don't think I'm the first to say this, but Spider-Man was one of the best things to come out of the MCU. They definitely took there time releasing these movies, but in the long run, it definitely payed off. With that being said, I wouldn't go as far as to call it the best Spider-Man Movie.

It's still really good, don't get me wrong. But a part of me couldn't ignore the modern MCU writing starting to clash with the good MCU writing. Their's a scene for instance in the first act, where Spider-Man is getting information from Black Widow, and she forces him to strip down to his underwear. The whole scene is super uncomfortable. The jokes don't land, it's really slow, Widow constantly brags about the Thunderbolts, it's really bad. A part of me was worried the entire movie was going to be like this.

But as I kept watching, the bad writing started to disappear. Seeing Peter entering adulthood and trying to navigate his new world was really engaging. I really like how closed off he is at the beginning of the movie, with the gray rain imagery visually showing how he feels mentally. But as the movie goes on, everything starts to become more colorful.

I love the adult conversations he has with his former friends, I love how the main villain messes with his head by possessing the people he loves, I love the buddy cop relationship he shares with the Punisher, this is really great stuff. It's just that, you have to sit through one awful scene to get to it.

I'm not sure if Avengers Doomsday is going to suffer through the same issues. But if the MCU wants really wants to get back on track, I have a few requests. First off, the comedy needs to be upped. I only laughed twice in this entire movie, I really don't want to see more half naked hero jokes in any future movies. And second, I do want Spider-Man to fight more Spider-Man villains in the future. I know the Scorpion is in this movie, but he's just a side villain at best.

Once I learned who the true villain really was, it did start to feel more like a Marvel movie than a Spider-Man movie. The climax is still good. But I did want to see Spider-Man fight an actually Spider-Man villain at the end. Maybe if Sony wasn't busy making that terrible Kraven movie, we could actually have Spider-Man fight him for once. Overall, I think this movie good. Though a part of me is still cautiously excited about Doomsday.

title: Forced, predictable, and full of inconsistencies
review:
The double standard bothered me from the start. A naked adult Russian woman sexually harassing an underage boy is played for laughs. Imagine reversing the genders: an adult naked man harassing an underage girl. Would that still be considered funny? The movie also relies on unnecessarily sexual jokes and random references, like the joke about Spider-Man having a boyfriend, that feel inserted rather than naturally part of the story.

But the biggest problem is the writing. The script constantly sacrifices logic and character development to reach a predetermined outcome. Jean can read and control minds, yet conveniently doesn't read the obvious villain's mind when it would immediately solve the mystery. Peter can build an incredibly sophisticated device overnight but somehow doesn't anticipate something as basic as magnetic interference from his glasses.

MJ confronts Peter for not fighting for their relationship, only to tell him shortly afterward that she doesn't love him. His friend practically recognizes Peter from a simple greeting, while MJ needs a kiss. The rules seem to change whenever the plot needs them to.

Black Widow and Scorpion also feel forced into the story, and the Spider-Man tracking app makes no sense. Why would a superhero publicly broadcast his real-time location for criminals to follow? And somehow the app can track him into space? It feels like a forced joke that exists only to set up the next movie.

There are entertaining moments and good action, but too much happens because the writers need it to happen, not because the story naturally leads there. Predictable, inconsistent, and extremely forced.

title: Good but half cooked
review:
First and foremost, I thought the marketing for this movie was incredibly misleading.

We were presented with the idea of a grounded, street-level Spider-Man story featuring lesser-known villains like Tombstone and Scorpion alongside a darker focus on Peter's personal life and struggles.

Instead, the filmmakers completely abandoned that premise to deliver a half-cooked Jean Grey movie.

Even with that shift, Jean Grey wasn't presented well at all. The character was highly mischaracterized, even though Sadie Sink gave a decent performance.

Another thing I felt was pointless was MJ and Ned coming back only for them to barely evolve in the movie. Their relationships end up confusing and almost the same as when the movie started instead of the film introducing new characters like Harry and Gwen.

That being said, the film does have some incredible highlights.

Spider-Man and Punisher were the absolute highlight of the entire movie. Their chemistry was fantastic, radiating a chaotic Spider-Man/Deadpool energy that was easily the most entertaining part of the film

Seeing Yelena Belova was a brilliant welcome surprise. Her dynamic with Spidey and the connection to the New Avengers worked incredibly well.

Destin Daniel Cretton did a great job directing. The fight scenes and cinematography were pretty decent, and if you catch it in ScreenX, the visual experience is genuinely great. The intro was solid but felt a bit like an extended version of the trailer.

Overall, I thought it functioned well as a good MCU movie, but it stands as a disappointing Spider-Man one.
