title: A solid comeback of the movie series: engaging story, good costumes and wonderful photography.
review:
The movie resumes exactly from where "No Way Home" left off. We see Peter Parker focused entirely on fighting to lower the NYC crime rate, pushing himself and isolating from everyone.

The title "Brand New Day" absolutely matches with the overall direction of the franchise, it feels like a soft reboot of the Tom Holland series, one that actually resolved some of the issues that I complained about in the previous trilogy. The CGI was nicely done, it does not look cheap. I believe that the secret here was the mix between practical effects and physical acting, with the addition of simpler VFX, that made the film more pleasing to the eye. On top of this, it was shot on real locations, rather than being done entirely on a green screen.

The photography is amazing; there are some dynamic POV shots, providing a more immersive experience during the most tense fights. There are a lot of actual stunts that made everything more credible, rather than just using animations. This alone made the experience better, as I did not feel that I was watching videogames cutscenes.

Narratively speaking, I think that the screenwriters reached a very nice balance between action-packed sequences, character development and comedic beats. The jokes were never over-the-top and were delivered at the right moments, to ease the tension. The screenplay explored interesting topics: we see Peter abandoned and completely lost, heading down a dangerous emotional self-destruction path that is making him increasingly lonely. We see that he is struggling and he wants to reunite with his friends, finding that genuine connection again that was enriching his life. The Punisher steps outside his usual dynamics and he is more like a fatherly figure that plays a fundamental part during Peter's journey.

The age of the actors starts to be debilitating for the franchise. When the series started with Holland and Zendaya, the actors were in their early 20s and they looked right for their respective roles. Now that both are in their 30s, in my perspective their physical appearance tells me that they are ready for more mature parts. It looked like watching grown-ups trying to forcibly play grad-students. It just does not work.

The film is solid and the two hours and a half runtime flew by in an instant, never really feeling bored or frustrated. I liked the ending and it definitely gives much room for further developments. My final rating is 7 out of 10.

title: The World's a Rollercoaster and My Hands are Busy in the Air saying I Wish You Were Here
review:
Since 1962, a core part of Spiderman's ethos has been about loss and the overcoming of it to be a hero and to do heroic things.

Destin Daniel Cretton and writers Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, and the OG Stan Lee make that a reality here for Spiderman and Tom Holland's Peter in a deeper and lasting way, more than any other previous movie rendition.

Throughout the four years in which this movie takes place, Peter both pines through social media for his love MJ, his best friend Ned, and consistently visits the grave site of his Aunt May with flowers, illustrating his loss and isolation and suffering.

Finally working up the courage to join Ned and his now roommate MJ at a party fairly early in the film, and seeing them in person living life with each other and without Peter, you feel the ghostly pain of separation which Peter feels.

Later in the story, when MJ finds Peter's hand-written note to her, the dialogue between them acknowledging each other, but also being honest in regards to how each of them feels (and doesn't feel) about love and each other, is heartbreaking, but incredibly powerful.

In the finale, when Jean Gray enters Peter's mind, and gets the first opportunity in a long time (maybe ever) to be encouraged by a memory of Aunt May, and then further supported (and defended in reality) by Peter himself, the story really encapsulates a number of emotions in relation to love, isolation, sacrifice, loneliness, resilience, and most importantly, the need for community in this life, whether you're a different and special person, or just a normal person with a normal life.

Marvel and the MCU specifically keep returning to this emotional core of leaving a legacy, and how that legacy often comes with the burden of what our heroes leave behind and sacrifice in their choosing the greater heroic responsibility.

The silver lining, exemplified in the end of this story specifically, is that Peter and Jean, and even Frank Castle, show us that there is still room for healing and new versions of love and community in the midst of loss and tragedy.

Making this one of the better stories, that we have not seen in awhile.

title: Great Vibes, Questionable Plot
review:
The vibes. The vibes in this movie were genuinely incredible. I can already see myself becoming nostalgic for this movie years from now, and I'll definitely remember it as one of the peaks of summer 2026. This is the first Tom Holland Spider-Man movie that, in my opinion, truly captures the feeling of a Spider-Man story, and I loved the inspiration they took from Insomniac's adaptation. It fit incredibly well into the movie and helped give it a distinct identity.

The movie was gorgeous, creative, and full of memorable scenes and great music choices. The choreography was spectacular, and there was a real sense that they were trying to make this movie feel special. Tom Holland's acting was excellent as well, probably his best performance as Spider-Man so far. I also really liked the subtle appearances and references to different MCU characters. They made it clear that Peter still exists within this larger universe and gave the MCU around him more life, while still keeping the movie firmly grounded as a Spider-Man story. I think they handled that much better here than in the previous movies.

As I said, the biggest strength of this movie for me was its atmosphere and creativity. Unfortunately, this is also where the plot starts holding the movie back from getting a higher score.

I have no problem with Jean Grey being the main antagonist, or rather initially appearing to be the antagonist. I thought she was handled well, and the writers did a good job giving her character depth while also setting up a future for her in the MCU. My problem is that once she redeems herself and the Damage Control department becomes the actual villain, the movie loses some of the feeling of having a true central antagonist. Having the Hulk, the Hand, and Scorpion involved as well only makes that problem more noticeable. There are simply too many different antagonistic forces competing for attention without one of them feeling like the definitive threat.

I also feel like MJ and Ned were left without a definitive conclusion regarding their relationship with Peter. It almost feels like the writers were unsure of what direction the audience would prefer and decided to leave the answer open for us to figure out ourselves. I understand that this is supposedly only the first movie of a new trilogy, so there is obviously still time to develop this, but I still found it somewhat unsatisfying.

Personally, I initially hoped MJ and Ned wouldn't appear at all. I wanted to see Peter slowly embrace his new life, let go of his old one, and fully accept that he has to move forward, while still acknowledging the lesson he learns throughout the movie: that complete isolation isn't sustainable. Unfortunately, once I saw them in the trailer, I already knew Marvel probably wasn't going to completely let them go.

At that point, I hoped they would remain decent friends with Peter. Instead, the ending gives us that confusing scene where we're left wondering whether MJ and Ned actually remembered him. Now we're potentially left waiting years to find out whether they will become close friends with Peter again, or whether Ned simply realized that Peter is Spider-Man and they will remain the kind of friends Peter occasionally hangs out with. Personally, I hope it's the second one. My ideal scenario would actually be for Peter to eventually develop a completely new love interest, perhaps the blonde girl who lives on his floor.

I have one final nitpick as well. Throughout the entire movie, I felt like something was missing, and eventually I realized what it was: Peter has no job, and there is no J. Jonah Jameson. It made me wonder how Peter is even making money. Peter being broke and having to balance his responsibilities as Spider-Man with an ordinary job has always been an important part of his character, so I found its absence noticeable.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a decent movie with an excellent atmosphere and a huge amount of creativity behind it. The cinematography, music, choreography, and overall Spider-Man aesthetic make the movie incredibly enjoyable and give it an identity that I feel the previous Tom Holland movies sometimes lacked. However, the plot holds it back from being something truly great. Some of the decisions regarding the antagonists and Peter's relationships with MJ and Ned feel questionable or deliberately indefinite, leaving me without the sense of complete satisfaction I wanted after the credits rolled.

Still, the experience itself was extremely enjoyable, and I can already tell that the atmosphere of this movie will be what I remember most about it.

7/10.

title: Best Spiderman movie ever.
review:
This movie made me feel things that no other Marvel movie ever has. It's so relatable and just so awesome. The action scenes are incredible, especially the swinging sequences, which I felt were missing from the previous movies. In this one, they felt like the perfect blend of Tobey Maguire's and Andrew Garfield's Spider-Man films.

But the best part of the movie isn't even the action it's the quiet, emotional moments. For example, when Peter sees MJ with her boyfriend, when she finds the letter Peter never gave her, and the "I don't love you" scene... those moments absolutely broke me. And the conversation between Peter and Jean Grey when she enters his mind was amazing.

What I loved most is that throughout the entire movie, Peter doesn't want to be Peter anymore he just wants to be Spider-Man. But in the end, when Jean asks him, "Who are you? Peter or Spider-Man?" and he answers, "Both," it shows that he's finally accepted who he is and embraced his new powers. I thought that was such a powerful moment.

I also really liked that the movie ended on such an emotional note. Sure, there was the big fight with the hand, but the scenes between Peter and Jean, without any action, were the real highlight for me. And finally, when Peter is in the hospital and all of New York is gathered outside, hoping he's okay... that scene felt absolutely magical.

title: A Great Movie, But Not A Great Spiderman Movie
review:
I wanna start off with the positives of this film because yes, there were.

---------------------- The Suit was absolutely peak, the visuals were stunning, the acting was amazing, seeing Hulk, Punisher and Spiderman was peak. After 9 years we finally saw an "Incredible Hulk". Hulk was for sure one of the highlights for me, all of his scenes worked, and I just enjoyed the hell out of them. Seeing some of Spiderman's rouges gallery was neat (even if they were barely in the film, it still worked for me) Yelena was alright I guess. And I loved the callbacks to Tobey's spiderman, that was awesome. And they nailed the lonely mature Peter Parker in the first half of the film. The street level spiderman is exactly what I've wanted for a long time and it showed as well.

Now let's get on with my criticisms.

---------------------- Punisher felt kinda goofy to me... as someone who's seen him since the OG Daredevil days he felt a bit different, while it's not a major critique, I still felt it was a bit off.

---------------------- Spiderman's mutation cycle was hyped up to be super intense and insanely hard for Peter to control, which it was at the start, it felt dangerously cool, and yet in around the latter half of the film he got full control of it while fighting the hand. Just by remembering his friends. Felt underwhelming and I felt like they could've done so much more with it.

---------------------- Ned and MJ weren't handled well in this film for me. I thought we were seriously getting a "Brand New Day", Peter's new start. But by the end of this film he's back to being friends with them (even if they don't have their old memories) This feels like a robbery to the ending for No Way Home for me. This film could've been Ned and MJ's last appearance, marking a final goodbye, and for Peter to start fresh. Instead MJ found Peter's note, rejected him yet remained friends with him? And the last scene of the film being Peter doing his signature handshake with Ned and Ned instantly remembering him as his best buddy felt cheesy and unearned to me. Even the theater was fully silent and disappointed during it. This clearly was not a Brand New Day, which isn't inherently wrong, but the marketing of the film suggested otherwise.

---------------------- The antgonist did not make sense at all. Sadie Sink was amazing in this role and nailed it, but why did we need Jean Gray in a spiderman movie? Especially as the MAIN antagonist. At times the film felt like it was HER film due to how much focus was on her. We learned her origin story, we were hit with a predictable plot twist that she wasn't the true bad guy, she got a power boost, and in classic tradition, lost through the power of friendship. Now I know Jean isn't a villain, and that is exactly why having her as the main antagonist just didn't work for me, ESPECIALLY in a spiderman movie. Felt like a backdoor pilot for some future X men project.

---------------------- Some jokes landed, some were cheesy and didn't. All I gotta say lmao ----------------------

Overall, I enjoyed the film. It was a fun time, especially in the theaters. I can not stress enough how great the visuals were. But I was let down due to lazy writing and the semi undoing of No Way Home's ending. Which is why I rate it a 7/10.

title: **A Triumph of the Friendly Neighborhood: Cretton's Masterpiece Redefines the Web-Slinger**
review:
Four years after the heartbreaking climax of *No Way Home*, director Destin Daniel Cretton picks up the cinematic threads with *Spider-Man: Brand New Day*, delivering what is undoubtedly the most mature, emotionally resonant, and cerebral installment in the franchise to date. Anchored by themes of profound isolation and the burdens of adulthood, the film follows a lonely Peter Parker (Tom Holland) dedicating every waking second to street-level vigilantism in a New York City that has entirely forgotten him. As Peter grapples with his fractured reality and the pressure of watching former friends MJ (Zendaya) and Ned (Jacob Batalon) move on without him, his powers begin a startling, aggressive evolution. This biological metamorphosis coincides with a formidable new psychic threat and an unlikely alliance with Jon Bernthal's uncompromising Punisher, thrusting our hero into a narrative that is equal parts psychological thriller and kinetic action epic.

The performances elevate the material far beyond standard comic book fare. Tom Holland cements his legacy as the definitive Peter Parker, offering a career-best turn that masterfully balances a bruised, brooding exterior with the inherent, irrepressible heart of the character. He is matched beautifully by Sadie Sink's revelatory integration into the MCU as Jean Grey, whose complex, nuanced introduction serves as a dark mirror to Peter's own internal struggles. Cretton's direction is immaculate; he expertly weaves spectacular, video game-inspired web-swinging sequences with intimate, character-driven moments of pure vulnerability. The camera work by Brett Pawlak captures a grittier, more grounded New York, heavily recalling the emotional weight of Sam Raimi's *Spider-Man 2* while entirely forging its own visionary path.

*Spider-Man: Brand New Day* achieves the impossible: it deconstructs its iconic hero only to rebuild him into something richer, darker, and deeply human. By stripping away the high-tech safety nets and Avengers-level spectacle, the film forces Peter-and the audience-to confront the terrifying reality of great responsibility. Flawlessly paced, brilliantly acted, and overwhelmingly poignant, this is not just the MCU's crowning achievement of Phase Six, but a bona fide cinematic triumph. An absolute masterpiece and essential viewing for anyone who has ever worn the mask. **10/10**

title: The best tom Holland spider man movie
review:
Spider-Man isn't really about the superhero-it's about Peter Parker.

What stayed with me after watching this movie wasn't the action or the web-swinging. It was Peter Parker's loneliness.

The film beautifully shows the life of a young man who has lost almost everyone. He carries the weight of being Spider-Man, but when he takes off the mask, he's just Peter-a lonely person trying to move forward. He has no family beside him, no friends who remember him, and no one to share his pain with.

The most heartbreaking moment is when he goes to meet MJ. She reads the letter he wrote, but Peter realizes that telling her the truth would bring danger and disrupt the new life she's building. Instead of asking her to remember him, he quietly lets go. He walks away carrying the pain alone, sacrificing his own happiness for the people he loves.

That moment reminds us that Peter Parker's greatest battles aren't against villains-they're against loneliness, heartbreak, and the sacrifices he makes every single day. That's why Spider-Man is more than a superhero story. It's the story of an ordinary man who keeps choosing responsibility, even when it means living with a broken heart.

In the end, the hero isn't Spider-Man. The hero is Peter Parker.

review:

The emotional aspects of the movie are so good, but it doesn't really reach its potential to be truly heartbreaking as it could have. The action felt like it was made by people who have the ability to make something great but are being held back.

Despite my frustration with how it felt like this could've been so much better, it's still a very good film that is also visually the best-looking Spider-Man movie in the MCU, which is honestly not a huge bar. Tom Holland gives his best Spider-Man performance, and this time he really made it feel like he doesn't need someone else to carry his movie, unlike the three previous ones. This time, I also noticed how Zendaya plays MJ with consistency from the previous movies that is clearly very different from how she plays her other characters, giving the character a weird energy. Sadie Sink was incredible in this movie, but her character arc and the way the movie ends felt like something the MCU liked from some of the previous movies and put together here. Most of the twists and turns were predictable, but that's not necessarily an issue because of the performances.

author: Measson-1er

title: Sometimes Less Is More
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day, largely stripped of the multiverse, multiple timelines, and cameo appearances designed to sell the next film, returns to the emotional core that made the Stan Lee-Steve Ditko comics of the early '60s a staple for so many generations. The comic book was essentially a story about teens and young adults trying to find themselves in the world during a tender, transitional period in their lives.

I grew up with comic books, walking down from my dad's office in downtown Worcester by myself to the local magazine store (yes, I am dating myself), where I would spend hours leafing through the many comics on the rack. My favorites were the comics that used the superhero setup to explore issues of loneliness and family. The Fantastic Four was my favorite because it was not only a story about saving the world, but about how a family struggling to save each other can somehow do their duty and save the world.

Spider-Man had a similar appeal. Focusing on teen and early-young-adult Peter Parker, gaining superpowers and taking on new responsibilities while trying to forge adult relationships sounds a lot like what we all go through-if you substitute a new awareness, intellect, and independence for Parker's actual superpowers.

At the heart of most of these stories, Fantastic Four and Spider-Man included, was always an important question: Given our responsibilities to ourselves, our families, our friends, and the world, what is the right thing to do? There were never simple answers, even if the stories could sometimes be a bit hackneyed.

So it is with some nostalgic baggage that I always walk into a superhero film. The Marvel universe has a spotty record of translating these emotional and moral cores in an entertaining way. The first two Tobey Maguire Spider-Man movies were largely successful, as were the two near-masterpiece Spider-Verse animated features. (The animated films showed how every metaphysical trick in the book could actually aid the story's core, not mask it.)

Yet too often, particularly recently, the characters and stories have gotten lost in a blizzard of bad special effects, multiple timelines, multiverse high jinks that stopped being interesting years ago, and the need to use standard, well-known properties like Spider-Man to launch other movies. The last Spider-Man movie, which had fun with multiple different versions of Spider-Man at once, did have an emotional core, but buried that core under a plot so convoluted I could not explain what happened and why. And honestly, the film didn't make me care enough to try.

Which brings us to Brand New Day.

The film is able to press reset on the storyline while still retaining the same characters from the previous film, unlike a full reboot. The contrivance in No Way Home of Doctor Strange wiping everyone's memory of Peter Parker felt like a contrivance in that film. Yet it works here, allowing the audience to retain its emotional connection to the lead characters while providing a storyline freed from the many plot complications that arose once so many people knew Peter Parker's secret.

Brand New Day is not a masterpiece, maybe not even a great film. But it is a poignant one.

We are able to feel Peter's loneliness as his friends move on together without him, something many of us experience in our early 20s as our dearest friends head off to different colleges and jobs. We're also able to relate to Peter's insistence that he do it alone. Peter throwing himself into his work while giving up his friends for their sake is both a justified rationale and an excuse for not dealing with complex emotional issues. And the inclusion of the villain who, as insiders know, brought the potential for great hope and destruction gives Brand New Day some heft on a cosmic scale.

There is enough adventure and cheeky good fun, much of it provided by Florence Pugh's pitch-perfect comic relief as Yelena Belova, the new Black Widow, to add balance to the film. The film's core message-that we need each other-is simplistic, and the film doesn't really have a lot to say about it, or about any of the other issues it raises.

But the film does not overreach either.

So if Brand New Day feels like little more than spending a few hours with friends we care about, I think that's the point.

title: With a great script and direction, comes a great superhero movie, Tom Holland gives one of his best performances
review:
The reviews I read said how this was a great superhero film, and after watching it I can agree. Spider-Man: Brand New Day brought us a well written story full of emotion, and characters that are important to the story, accompanied by action sequences that remind you of the Insomniac Spider-Man games. The visual effects and CGI, which have been terrible in most Marvel films these couple of years aren't found in this film, instead Brand New Day offers you great CGI and none of those visible and unfinished green screen shots. By the heart of the film is Tom Holland, the star in front of the camera and behind it, as Holland was more involved in the production and development of the film. Tom Holland shows once again the passion he has for the character, for the story (the film adapts the 2008 comic book storyline "Brand New Day"), and he gives one of his best performances in this film. Whilst the film offers humor and entertaining dialogue, we also have dialogue that gives Holland scenes where he can shine. It's fun in a way, how he starred in The Odyssey, but his best performance this year comes in this Spider-Man film. There might be a reason for that, the direction Destin Daniel Cretton gave him. Cretton did such an incredible job with this film, making sure the themes is executed perfectly but also giving direction to actors who all did great. The cinematography was also really great, reminding me of the cinematography in Sam Raimi's Spider-Man trilogy and the first Andrew Garfield Spiderman film.

The film's premise: A forgotten Peter Parker lives alone as a full-time Spider-Man until mounting pressure triggers a dangerous change and a powerful new enemy emerges.

The cast includes: Tom Holland stars as Peter Parker / Spider-Man, alongside Zendaya as Michelle "MJ" Jones-Watson, Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Jacob Batalon as Ned Leeds, Jon Bernthal as Frank Castle / Punisher, Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova / Black Widow, Tramell Tillman as William "Bill" Metzger, Marisa Tomei as May Parker, and Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner / Hulk. Additional actors reprising their MCU roles include Michael Mando as Mac Gargan / Scorpion, a criminal who was previously captured by Spider-Man and arrested in the film Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), now wearing a suit of armor equipped with a mechanized scorpion-like tail. Also Zabryna Guevara as Sheila Rivera, the new mayor of New York City. In minor roles: Liza Colón-Zayas portrays Jean DeWolff, a New York City Police Department (NYPD) detective. Marvin Jones III portrays Lonnie Lincoln / Tombstone, a crime boss with albinism, near-indestructible skin, and superhuman strength. This is a cast full of great characters, and you can't forget The Hand which appears in the film, a reduced role than in Daredevil and is solely there for a cool action sequence in its third act. Cool and great in so many ways, choreography and cinematography to how it's directed.

At first glance you might notice the run time (2h 25m) and think it's too long, but a shorter film wouldn't have worked because of how important Peter Parker / Spiderman is to the film. There's character development and he's not in high school any more, and also what he has experienced. Peter Parker has a great character arc in this film and I absolutely loved the screenplay Marvel Studios vets Erik Sommers and Chris McKenna wrote, more mature and far from Jon Watts trilogy which leaned more into young adult themes. Here we have trauma and loss that are front and center, and I would also say of identity. They also hit differently now that Spiderman is stripped to the bare essentials, creating a more grounded character and thus a story and antagonist. These writers' work combined with Cretton's direction is why the film has such great emotional depth, as there's not many films that make you feel something. In recent MCU films I would say Guardians of the Galaxy 3 where the emotional weight and depth was so high, kudos to these people. Like that film, Brand New Day has a great cast that is full of three dimensional characters. You see, every character works so well because of how they connect to Peter in some way, having gone through some of the things that he's been through. I think that Destin Daniel Cretton was the right director for this film, if you look at his filmography we have "Just Mercy" which is a great drama with a great performance from its lead, then we have his previous MCU film "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings" and well it's a blockbuster film. With this Spider-Man film he does both and succeeds in making a character focused film. It's so easy to connect with the grief and trauma that has shaped Peter Parker's life, the loss and trauma Frank Castle has, and Jean Grey. This is a character that everyone knew would be in the film, but what capacity and what role? That was something no one knew, and her role in the film worked so well. We also get to see her backstory unfold and that has a deep meaning to the upcoming Doomsday film and the Mutants storyline. I really liked Sadie Sink's performance. She too has a trauma and loss, what happened to her sister and what William "Bill" Metzger put them through. I'm sorry but I can only see Seth Milchick in the role of Metzger, Tramell Tillman is great in the role but I wish he played a different role next time. He does a fine job here, don't get me wrong and I'm glad he's getting the recognition he deserves. Jean Grey is the antagonist of the film, which works really well in terms of her powers and backstory, in terms of Peter Parker's own arc. But she's not a villain, instead she is one of the most human character in the MCU. Most of the characters in this film feel real, although Scorpion doesn't have a big role to play, it's so nice to see him in the film, as he's the villain for the first act. There's also a subplot where Bruce Banner helps Peter Parker without knowing he's Spiderman in creating a way for him to stay normal and not be unstable because of his Spider DNA enhancing. I really liked this subplot and I love how it concludes. The subplot ends with him becoming The Hulk for the first time since Infinity War. It offers you one of the best action sequences in recent times, and a highlight in the film. Peter Parker also comes to terms with his change through character development throughout the film, in the final action sequence. Every single scene was so well thought out, brilliantly directed and written, and edited.

Erik Kain summarizes it perfectly, "The movie works because it's a good story that moves along at a great clip and throws in plenty of action and humor to balance out its more somber themes. Plenty of web-slinging, plenty of antics, plenty of things going boom. Holland is perfect as Peter Parker, and the various familiar faces he comes into contact with are all fun - especially Yelena Belova (Florence Pugh) and her amazing office." He then finishes with, "Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an exciting, emotionally powerful, often hilarious action-adventure movie that breathes new life into the superhero genre." I agree fully with him. The pacing is fast but also not too fast as there are numerous scenes that go deep in Peter Parker as a character, but most importantly, those scenes never become too long and too boring. They were actually really well written and I wish they would have been longer, wouldn't have been interrupted by something else. But for the sake of the whole audience, they were right to interrupt those scenes, for pacing reasons. The editing in the film was great, truly fantastic. The mix of character drama and superhero action makes for a compelling drama whilst also giving us some of the finest that this superhero genre has to offer. I found the length to be fine and I think the antagonists and more grounded take contributed in making the length meanwhile, thus crafting a narrative that is more relatable and with more emotional depth. That's why I disliked Far From Home, the villain seemed too outlandish and not grounded enough, there was also other things I disliked about that film. But two themes that have been consistent with these films are the themes of loss and identity, and I think this gotta be the film that executed the theme of loss the best. Spider-Man: Brand New Day surprised me in lots of ways and I never thought I would hold another Spider-Man film as high as Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 1 and 2, but Brand New Day is there with them, thanks to its superb script and direction and also an unforgettable performance from Tom Holland.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is, by far, the best Tom Holland Spider-Man movie to date.
review:
I watched the previous three Tom Holland Spider-Man films quite a while ago, and although I found them somewhat generic, with fairly cliché characters, they were still entertaining and fun. However, this movie completely exceeded my expectations.

The story picks up right where *No Way Home* left off, with everyone forgetting who Peter Parker is. One of the film's biggest strengths is Peter's character development. It does an excellent job of showing how he struggles with loneliness and melancholy while forcing himself to keep his distance from MJ and Ned. The movie also balances this emotional storyline with the main plot very well, giving both enough time to develop naturally.

The cinematography is stunning. At its weakest, it's still impressive, and at its best, it's absolutely breathtaking, especially the shots of Spider-Man swinging between New York's skyscrapers. From a production standpoint, I have no complaints either. The editing is excellent, the soundtrack is great, and the action choreography is possibly the best in the entire Tom Holland Spider-Man series.

Another highlight is Jean. She's a threatening and elusive character, and she has a great plot twist near the end when it's revealed that her only goal was to save her sister. Her powers are also incredibly cool, allowing her to infiltrate a maximum-security facility entirely on her own.

One of my favorite scenes is when she loses control of her powers and ends up paralyzing half of New York. I also loved her final conversation with Spider-Man, when he makes her realize that he, too, has lost everything because of who he is. This scene perfectly showcases Peter's growth throughout the movie. That said, I do wish Jean had received a bit more development, as I felt there was still more to explore with her character.

The only thing I didn't like was the twist villain. The movie seemed to be aiming for something similar to what *Captain America: The Winter Soldier* did, but it barely hinted that this character was the real antagonist. Once the reveal happens, the character isn't explored any further, and their motivations are never properly explained. As a result, the twist feels underwhelming, and the villain never comes across as particularly intimidating.

Overall, **Spider-Man: Brand New Day** is one of the best movies of the post-*Endgame* era and an excellent lead-in to *Avengers: Doomsday*.

title: Not perfect, but at this point... I'll take it
review:
A nice surprise, given the current climate of the MCU. A lower stakes and more "grounded" Spider-Man film, that felt more akin to the Sam Raimi trilogy, and helps it stand out in a better way when compared to the previous films.

A big reason for that is most definitely from the assured direction of Destin Daniel Cretton. While not overly flashy (how can it be in a Marvel film?), it is however imbued with enough flourishes and detail to elevate it above some of the standard stuff we've been getting lately. Most of the action is quite creative and well paced, with a distinct New York vibe that is very well realised throughout the film.

The whole cast do great, with Zendaya delivering probably her best performance of MJ's character yet and Tom Holland is so effortless with his levity and humour as Spider-Man. Supporting roles from familiar MCU characters are all fine, and it was great to see Michael Mando finally get more to do as Scorpion this time round. The big stand out was easily Jon Bernthal as the Punisher, reminding us once again how perfectly casted he is for the character, and it was great to see how well he vibed with Spiderman.

Not all the cast though fair as good, with the newer additions to the character line up delivering decent performances, despite suffering from the plots weaker elements. Tramell Tillman is wasted in a role that truly doesn't allow his talents to truly shine, and I definitely would have liked more of Liza Colón-Zayas interesting character in the story. But it's Sadie Sink's villain that feels like the most under severed. Despite a well intentioned focus on her toward the end of the film, the attempts at redemption & empathy come a little too easy, with no real repercussions or consequences for the genuine harm her character commits (a particular moment from her is quite vindictive and cruel that never really gets enough follow up).

However, despite the stories weaker parts, it's the creative vision from Destin Daniel Cretton and contributions from a great cast that elevate this film as great change of pace for the MCU, especially when they could have so easily made it just made it as a set up for "Avengers: Doomsday". Instead they allowed the story to stand on its own and it's all the better for it.

title: SPOILER REVIEW - Spider-Man: Brand New Day
review:
The beginning relies on one-second action montages, similar to The Fantastic Four. Fight scenes make up roughly 10% of the movie, which is embarrassing. There isn't a single major fight that wasn't already heavily shown in the trailers or TV spots.

Characters like Tombstone and Scorpion receive almost no screen time and are given practically no story arc. The movie introduces several actual Spider-Man villains, only to reduce most of them to brief appearances before shifting almost all of its attention toward characters and storylines that feel disconnected from Spider-Man's world.

Jean Grey did not need to be in this movie. The movie dedicates a massive amount of attention to an Omega-level mutant while several actual Spider-Man villains were already available and deserved to be developed. A character that powerful had no business being placed at the center of a Spider-Man movie. Instead of feeling like a natural part of Peter's story, much of the movie feels like it is being used to introduce Jean Grey and set up the MCU's future X-Men storyline.

The Hulk sequence feels like the disappointing Red Hulk showcase from Captain America: Brave New World. Most of it was already revealed in the marketing, and the full scene is short and underwhelming. Hulk is mainly inserted into the story after Jean takes control of him at the DODC headquarters, but the entire sequence feels more like something designed for the trailers than something the movie actually needed.

On top of that, because the DODC ultimately ends up being the main villain, the movie had the perfect opportunity to tell a much better story using characters like the Hand, Scorpion, Tombstone, Tarantula and others. They could have been brought together to form the Sinister Six, giving Spider-Man a group of grounded but dangerous enemies who actually belong in his world.

Punisher gets done extremely dirty. He feels about as capable as Happy Hogan, despite being someone who can go toe-to-toe with characters like the Winter Soldier in the comics. None of his usual presence or aura comes through.

That alternative direction also would have allowed Punisher to properly display his aura and create genuine fear. Watching him hunt, intimidate and fight members of the Sinister Six could have demonstrated why criminals are terrified of him while still keeping Spider-Man at the center of the movie. Instead, we got none of that, and Punisher was reduced to a character who never feels especially dangerous or important.

Overall, the movie feels like 50% Peter Parker, 40% Sadie Sink and only 10% meaningful action. I'd give it a 5/10 and rank it as the third-best Tom Holland Spider-Man movie.

title: GOATED MOVIE!
review:
I went into *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* hoping for a decent reset after the heavy multiverse chaos, but I honestly was not expecting it to hit this hard. Director Destin Daniel Cretton took the franchise back to its street-level roots, delivering the most grounded, heart-wrenching, and authentic Spidey story in years.

First off, the visual effects and cinematography are next-level. New York finally feels like a real, living character again rather than a flat digital backdrop. The web-swinging sequences are breathtaking-the camera swoops alongside Peter with a genuine sense of height, speed, and vertigo that makes your stomach drop. When Peter's physical evolution starts glitching his powers, the visual execution is visceral and intense without ever sacrificing clarity.

Story-wise, this is Tom Holland's absolute best work as Peter Parker. Living in total isolation after the world forgot who he was, his quiet grief and loneliness bleed through every scene. The narrative gives him actual room to breathe. The dynamic between his optimistic, rule-following Spidey and Jon Bernthal's ruthless, gritty Punisher creates unbelievable tension, while Sadie Sink delivers a subtle, magnetic performance that steals every moment she's in.

What truly makes this movie shine is its willingness to prioritize personal stakes over world-ending explosions. It doesn't rely on cheap nostalgia or forced cameos to pull at your heartstrings-it trusts the tragedy and quiet heroism built into Peter's DNA. By the time the climax hits, every emotional blow lands just as heavily as the physical punches.

It's thrilling, visually stunning, and deeply moving. Easily an top-tier Marvel entry.
author: Dhiraj-374

title: Best spiderman movie since first two Sam Raimi's Spiderman movies!!
review:
Spiderman Brand New Day feels like the moment the franchise finally decided to grow up. In my view, it's the best SpiderMan movie to date, only followed closely by the first two Sam Raimi films, which still hold a special place for me. This new chapter delivers an adventure that's explosive, unpredictable, and emotionally charged in a way the Tom Holland trilogy never quite reached. Holland gives the most nuanced performance of his run as Peter Parker, and Sadie Sink matches him beat for beat with a presence that feels raw, grounded, and refreshingly human. The rest of the cast elevates the story instead of crowding it, something that earlier Holland films struggled with.

What makes Brand New Day stand out is how confidently it embraces a darker, more mature tone. The stakes feel heavier, the consequences sharper, and the emotional beats hit with a sincerity that surprised me. Unlike Holland's first two movies fun, sure, but often too childish and overly tied to Tony Stark to let Peter breathe this film finally lets SpiderMan be SpiderMan. He's no one's sidekick, no one's "mascot," and the story doesn't rely on flashy tech or mentor figures to carry the weight. It's Peter alone, facing a world that isn't holding his hand anymore.

Even No Way Home, which I enjoyed, leaned heavily on nostalgia and fan service. Brand New Day doesn't need that. It's bold enough to stand on its own, and that confidence pays off. The action sequences are brutal and beautifully choreographed, the emotional tension never lets up, and the narrative keeps twisting in ways that feel earned rather than gimmicky. It's the kind of SpiderMan story that lingers with you after the credits roll.

For me, this is the most mature, most emotionally resonant, and darkest SpiderMan film ever made. It's the one where Holland truly shines, where the character finally steps out of the shadow of past interpretations, and where the franchise proves it still has new stories worth telling. If you're a fan of the wall.crawler, this movie isn't just recommended, it's essential.

I will also have to admit I am still suffering from superhero fatigue. Taking a pause from the last Spiderman film was a good call. For one thing, the emotional hook at the end of the last film seemed to really motivate audiences to see this one. But really, honestly, I liked this movie. I have the last three Holland versions in my movie collection and find them all fun and engaging (less the Europe school trip one).

This reset brings back our favourite characters, and Peter's inner struggle of whether to reconnect with them or not. Familiar themes are threaded throughout. Tried and true, like the same setup in Guardians of the Galaxy, where the hero must deal with a former love interest no longer having feelings for him (or even knowing who he is). Another is finding sympathy for the villain. Another is the government having sinister intentions.

I have always liked the Peter Parker character. Well grounded, good humour, makes mistakes. The re-introduction to his friends was handled well, with a nice twist for the MJ character. The screenplay combines different characters as a way to explore how their personalities would interact. What if you combine MJ and Punisher? What if Peter hides his identity to MJ? What if he reveals his identity? What if MJ remembered who Peter was? What if you combine Peter and The Hulk? What if you toss in Black Widow meeting Spiderman? (answer: a waste of time) What if Spiderman and the Villain had a therapy session?

What I noticed during the high energy action scenes is a lot of green screen and CGI backgrounds. I guess these scenes still succeed because they are put together well. One particular of note is a group of Ninjas performing acrobatics. If you like that kind of dynamic action, check out "Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon" from 2000. Another literal cliffhanger version of this kind of battle can be seen in "G. I. Joe: Retaliation". If you like how the villain can jump from body to body, check out "The Hidden" from 1987. I'm not knocking Spiderman 9 for finding inspiration in these other movies. Many modern action films take ideas from older films and do well with them.

So little to complain about except some scenes were repeated (like two scenes with the dead aunt where one would do). Other times something is setup only to be negated. Speculation about producers dictating certain story elements seems pretty evident. Also the blatant product placement made me groan. But again, the movie is well put together, with Tom Holland nailing the lead. I give a 7 out of 10, a fun outing with just a few to many story beats.

title: 10 out of 10
review:
The 37th MCU film, and the second film in Phase 6.

The greatest Spider-Man movie ever made.

No, it was the greatest movie in the entire MCU.

I was crying nonstop from the middle of the movie onward.

10 out of 10 This is the first time I've given a perfect score to an MCU film.

To be honest, I wasn't really into the previous film, *No Way Home*. I understand that it achieved a feat that will go down in film history, but the clumsy screenplay made it impossible for me to connect emotionally. However, with this film, I cried nonstop from the middle onward. There may never have been a film in the past that made me cry this relentlessly.

It's a brilliant screenplay that unravels the hero's torment-embodied by the phrase "With great power comes great responsibility"-while simultaneously depicting the awakening of new powers. Furthermore, the hero's suffering is intertwined with that of this film's villain, illustrating the precariousness of heroes with superpowers-a hallmark of the Marvel universe. And amidst it all, salvation is portrayed as a ray of light. I want to commend the screenplay for making such effective use of the death of a loved one-an event that felt abrupt and meaningless in the previous film.

Previous films devoted a lot of time to the romantic subplot with MJ, which I felt somewhat lacked tension, but in this film, the balance was excellent. As a superhero story, the main focus is, after all, the hero and the villain-and their battle. It is precisely because the villain's motives, true identity, and suffering are so thoroughly portrayed that the hero's own suffering shines through.

This is the first MCU film that has made me cry my eyes out to this extent, and I'm giving it a perfect score-something I didn't even give to *Endgame*. The action is great, the script is great-what more could you ask for? This might just be the masterpiece of the year.

I think it will be hard to top this level of emotional impact, but just as this film moved me, I can't help but hope that future installments will continue to pleasantly surprise me. I strongly urge even those who drifted away from the MCU during Phases 4, 5, and 6 to watch this. It will surprise you all over again.

title: Great Action and Visuals, But the Script Goes Entirely Haywire in the Third Act
review:
I was insanely hyped for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, and for the first two acts, it really delivers on the fun, high-octane superhero spectacle. However, once you reach the climax and ending, the story unravels into a confusing mess of weird character choices and a lack of real direction.

The Highlights: Great Visuals, Action & Humor: Stunning visual effects and cinematography throughout. The comedy lands well, and the high-energy action set pieces hit hard.

Hulk Unleashed: Watching Hulk absolutely demolish stuff and then immediately try to play innocent/bystander was easily one of the best running gags in the film.

The Punisher Dynamic: Frank Castle stole every scene he was in. His banter with Peter added grounded grit and great comedic timing.

Grounded Peter Parker: Spidey takes a real physical beating in this movie. Seeing him hospitalized, bleeding, and dealing with human limits kept him deeply grounded.

Where It Falls Apart: No Real Villain: Incorporating X-Men's Jean Grey felt forced. She isn't a villain; she's just possessing people and causing chaos while searching for her lost sister. Once she finds out her sister is dead, she goes on a rampage, only for Peter to stop her by showing her his memories of Aunt May. Without a core antagonist, the plot feels directionless.

The MJ Dilemma: Peter is torn between wanting MJ back and keeping her safe. But unmasking to her again when she has zero memory of their romance makes no operational sense and lacks emotional payoff.

Baffling Identity Reveals: Revealing his face to Frank Castle made total sense-Frank earned his trust after Peter took a sniper bullet meant for Jean. But Ned instantly remembering Peter's identity from a single handshake at the end? Completely illogical and cheapens the memory spell logic.

Verdict: If you're a die-hard Spider-Man fan, you'll find enough cool moments, top-tier visuals, and fun character interactions to enjoy it. But if you're a casual viewer looking for a tight, coherent story, the bloated narrative and bizarre third-act choices will leave you disappointed.

Strictly a one-time watch or skippable.

Every Tom Holland Spider-Man movie has had so many supporting characters and major MCU connections that Peter Parker himself sometimes feels like a secondary character in his own movies. And now, they've completely scrapped the opportunity to properly explore Peter's college life, his struggles as a young adult, his relationships, his identity, and the classic Spider-Man experience.

We finally had the perfect opportunity to give Tom Holland's Spider-Man a more grounded, personal story-Peter balancing college, money, relationships, responsibility, and being Spider-Man. Instead, Jean Grey seems to be stealing the spotlight.

Introduce the X-Men, sure. Expand the MCU, absolutely. But don't take the Spider-Man out of a Spider-Man movie.

title: Small Patato
review:
By far the best Tom Holland Spider-Man entry ever (not counting No Way Home, of course). This movie does something unique that the other two Tom Holland Spider-Man entries couldn't: it really makes him feel like the Spider-Man. This is a great sequel to No Way Home.

I liked how they went with Spider-Man catching every villain, just like in Sam Raimi's idea for the beginning of Spider-Man 4. That was a great touch, and it shows the consequences of No Way Home-Peter alone, trying to live as Spider-Man, not Peter Parker. He's sad, tired, and alone. The movie actually reminds us of this a lot. No Way Home wasn't just a fan-service movie made to print money; it gave Tom Holland's Spider-Man the best character development he could ever imagine.

Sadie Sink's Jean Grey carries the movie from start to finish. I liked how they showed a not-fully-reached-potential Jean who's insanely powerful in the MCU universe. This is a really great way to introduce mutants to the MCU. At first I thought Jean Grey in a Spider-Man movie didn't make sense at all, but I've got to be honest-they nailed it really well.

Not just Jean-every other character in this movie has a purpose, not some cameo slop. I love Spider-Man and Punisher's chemistry; their scenes stole the movie for me. And Frank's character is better written than he ever has been. It's insane, but the MCU did Punisher better for me.

Then we have Hulk / Professor Banner. I didn't actually get how they were going to tie his story into this Spider-Man movie, but it made great sense. Peter seeks help for his mutation, and who knows mutation better than the strongest Avenger himself? And YES-they did Hulk justice. Marvel is finally realizing Hulk is much more than a joke; he really is the strongest. You can see that from people's reactions-they don't want to go against him. And Spider-Man, who beat Doctor Strange in No Way Home, couldn't beat Hulk. He had to reach Banner in order to live. This was important to me, because from the trailers I thought they were going to make Spidey beat Hulk just because it's his movie. Glad they proved me wrong.

And please, Marvel-I beg you-for the next Spider-Man movie, use other Spider-Man love interests. Little spoiler incoming here: the spell actually worked really well. MJ says she doesn't remember and doesn't love Peter. That's not his MJ anymore. I think this is a great chance to put Felicia or Gwen in the next Spider-Man movie, because Spider-Man gives up on MJ so she can live a peaceful, healthy life. That's it-he made the sacrifice. Don't undo that. It would really hit better if they go with someone else for Spidey, and they have the people for it.

Anyway, this is a great Marvel movie with insanely good fight sequences and a great story. Can't wait for more, and hopefully this movie builds up for a solo Hulk movie in the future. Can't wait!!!

title: Great action and a heavy emotional core, even if it doesn't quite hit the absolute peak of the franchise.

While it may not eclipse the absolute pinnacle of Spider-Man cinema, it succeeds as a compelling, character-driven drama that honors the hero's rich comic book legacy.

The film shines brightest in its exploration of Peter Parker's central conflict: the grueling, everyday struggle to balance a personal identity with the unyielding responsibilities of being Spider-Man. Stripped of familiar safety nets, Peter's isolation forces a deep dive into the human cost of self-sacrifice, grounding the superhero spectacle in genuine emotional stakes.

Visually, the film excels with crisp, visceral action choreography that makes every street-level battle and dynamic web-slinging sequence feel weighty and impactful. Supported by strong dramatic performances during its quietest moments, the narrative successfully captures the enduring friction between duty and personal life, making Brand New Day a thoroughly engaging and emotionally resonant installment.

an actual Spider-Man comic book and merge them with a mature, emotionally resonant film about loneliness and personal transformation. This is Peter Parker's movie one hundred percent and although there are other comic book heroes in the mix, this isn't like the earlier films.. This is entirely a street level Spider-Man story ( all in NYC) , one grounded in dramatic stakes as Peter copes with the consequences of the choice he made in No Way Home.


* It's the best looking comic book movie I've ever seen. I've been watching big budget live action Spider-Man movies since 2002 and his web-slinging, agility and costume have never been as comics accurate as they are here. It's like watching comic book panels come to life on screen. I thought this was even more impressive visually than Endgame.



* This is my new favorite Marvel movie. Not only do I think it's going to break all the box office records in the MCU, I think there's a real chance Doomsday may actually suffer by comparison to Brand New Day. This movie has so much heart and soul mixed in with the eye popping spectacle that it's hard to imagine what's essentially a giant stunt movie designed to rescue the MCU from waning interest will top this, even with the debut of Doctor Doom.. I'm sure Doomsday will make millions, but in terms of quality? I honestly don't know if it's going to touch Brand New Day.


Finally, Spider-Man and the Punisher are the onscreen team I needed without realizing it. While Peter's coming to terms with Ned and MJ getting on with their lives without him is at the heart of the story, the chemistry between real life friends John Bernthal and Tom Holland as Frank Castle and Peter Parker respectively is the number one reason I would recommend the movie. Every time they're on screen trading quips it's pure gold. And no, they really didn't sanitize the Punisher all that much. He's not exactly R rated, but he's definitely pushing the edge of that PG-13 . Subsequently, Brand New Day also has the unusual distinction of having the most profanity of any Spider-Man movie. And somehow it works in the film's favor.

Do not let anyone spoil this for you if you can avoid it. There are some nice surprises here.

Right now, Brand New Day is my number one movie of 2026. In fact, I was so impressed with the movie overall, I may head back to the theater to catch the 3-D version, because I want to see what those web-slinging sequences look like in the format. I'm not kidding - you've never seen Spidey move the way he does in this movie.

Some reviews say it gets bogged down and overstuffed in the third act, but I didn't feel that at ALL. In fact, I was impressed with how deftly director Destin Daniel Crettin balanced all of the plot threads and eventually tied them together. And the final scene in the movie ( not the post credits scene, but the actual final scene in the movie proper) is such a rewarding, pitch perfect note to end on. I have high hopes for whatever comes next.

It took over two decades, but I finally saw the Spider-Man movie I would say is better than Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2... and if you know how I feel about that movie, you'll know that's a saying a LOT.

Do NOT wait to watch this at home..The first viewing of Spider-Man Brand New Day should be on the biggest screen you can find.

I don't know if this will revive the MCU , but for 2026 at least, Marvel has swung their way right back to the top. Outstanding.

***** out of ***** stars. This is the Spider-Man movie I've been waiting for most of my life.

title: Rebirth & Renewal the Spider-Man Returns
review:
I'm not allowed to give it any lesser score for the huge scope of this story, the near-tragedy of Peter Parker, Spidey, loosing all his friends and contacts at home, work and Avenging, fighting alone in his friendly neighbourhood, having to keep everything anonymous as he keeps the streets clear, and now confronting a new, greater challenge that could transform his life.

And the visual vertigo of New York is the scene stealer in this rollercoaster of adventure, humour and soul-searching drama as he, kind of, teams up with the least likely partner you could ever imagine in the surly Frank Castle, that somehow, for the light and dark contrasts of their characters, works to perfection.

As with much that is Marvelous there is conspiracy and injustice to be uncovered and new dangers and powerful new friends to discover along the journey as Our Hero undergoes a rebirth that will challenge his past and open the way to a new life, leaving us all wondering how, when and where he will swing down to save us again.

This should be savoured for the beautiful photography of the city, and special effects which really deliver the kind of kinetic impact (outch!) that's often missing in other rubbery CGI-filled films as Spidey bounces, crashes and falls a lot, around the city. Tremendous character, humour and construction, with deep reflections into the nature of power and responsibility, whether it is Spidey's own powers or the implications of his work, all vie for attention and add to the length of the film, but all the richer for these moments of normal humanity.

As for laying down the foundations for further Marvel movies. Without an Iron Man around Peter Parker looks to be the anchor character everyone will love and hope to revisit in this universe.
author: TheWorldmaker

title: BELIEVE THE HYPE!
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is, for me, the best live-action Spider-Man movie ever made. It perfectly balances heart, action, emotion, and spectacle, delivering a Spider-Man story that exceeded all my expectations from start to finish.

The action sequences are absolutely breathtaking and visually stunning. Every set piece feels massive, creative, and exciting, with incredible cinematography and effects that make every swing, fight, and emotional moment hit even harder.

Tom Holland gives what I believe is the strongest Spider-Man performance ever. He completely owns the role, delivering the perfect mix of humour, vulnerability, and determination. This is easily his best outing as Peter Parker.

Sadie Sink is fantastic as Jean Grey, bringing real emotion and depth to the character. She plays such an important emotional role in the story, and her chemistry with the rest of the cast is excellent. Zendaya and Jon Bernthal are also brilliant in their respective roles, both making a huge impact whenever they're on screen.

For a movie that's around two and a half hours long, the pacing is outstanding. It never drags, always has something happening, and constantly keeps you invested without feeling rushed.

A fun highlight was Florence Pugh's cameo appearances. She absolutely steals every scene she's in, and for me she's up there as the most attractive character in the MCU.

The ending is everything I wanted: emotional, epic, and incredibly rewarding. It wraps up the story in a way that feels satisfying while leaving you excited for what's next.

My only criticism is Jean Grey's reveal. Considering how much the film builds towards it, I thought the payoff could have been just a little stronger.

Overall, I absolutely loved Spider-Man: Brand New Day. It's an unforgettable superhero movie that, in my opinion, has put the MCU back on the map.

author: Litenbob

title: A SPOILER Review
review:
After months of waiting, a new Spider-Man movie has been released and to most audience members, it's a top 3 Spider-Man movie of all time. However, I can't agree with this sentiment. I'd full bet that this is the honeymoon phase and most will come down on the movie as I fully believe it's a fine movie, an enjoyable Spider-Man movie as well, but to say this is a one of, if not the best Spider-Man movie is so insane I don't understand. To explain why I feel this way, I sadly will be talking about spoilers in this movie so I can explain why this movie is fine, but not great. If you haven't seen this film yet, go watch it as I don't want to spoil it for you if you haven't seen the film yet. With that said, let's dive into probably my longest review I ever wrote with, Spider-Man Brand New Day.

Firstly I'd be remiss if I didn't discuss what I liked about the film. Firstly, I loved the iconic scenes that were ripped from the comics. It was so cool and felt like I was watching a live action comic at times. Next I want to discuss the cast. As I have never reviewed any Spider-Man movie yet, something I plan to do at some point in the future, I want to discuss the cast here. Tom Holland, in my opinion, is the best live action Spider-Man we have ever had. His Spider-Man is so relatable, memorable, and has a great dichotomy between Peter Parker and Spider-Man. Also his accent is really great too. Zendaya isn't a bad MJ either and I think in this movie she's really great since she doesn't remember who Peter Parker is. As for Ned, I always liked him, he's so funny and I also feel so bad that he can't remember his friendship with Peter. Going off of how nobody remembers who Peter is, I loved how we don't try and undo everyone forgetting who Peter was in the movie or even within the first hour of the movie making him tackle the events in the film all by himself. I enjoyed that we don't explore the people in his life remembering him until the very end of the film leaving it possible they can get their memories of him back in the future, but it'll take awhile. Lastly for characters, I want to mention Jon Bernthal as Punisher. He was my favorite character in this film and I never saw him as the Punisher before so seeing him here was great and I loved his and Peter's interactions (I never saw the Netflix series he is in, nor did I watch Daredevil). Besides that, the setting camera work was all really good too and the plot was fine, but I'm left a bit indifferent with it so I'll be going over it in the parts I didn't like. Also I did love his suit in this film. I was starting to get a bit worn out of all the different STARK suits that he had and was really hoping for a basic homemade suit so I was ecstatic we finally got a basic suit with little to no gadgets to them. Lastly, I loved the messages about loneliness and feeling forgotten about in this film. It was probably my favorite part about the film of people being alone and forgotten about, but still pushing forward no matter how hard it gets.

With the things I like out of the way, I now want to go over the things I really didn't like. While to some these might be nitpicks, I personally feel like they hurt the film and could have been expanded on way better than how it turned out. Firstly Bruce Banner/The Hulk was pointless in this film and could have been removed altogether. I like Mark Ruffalo and I like him as Bruce Banner, but I wish they would have done more besides reminding us that this is a MCU film. We already had a Marvel character with Florence Pugh's Yelena which I think works really great here since this is, at the end of the day, small potato stuff. While I'll admit this is more of a nitpick than most of the other stuff I'll mention, I had to mention this. Now for my first actual issue with this film is the villain. While I liked Sadie Sink as Jean Grey (The worst kept secret of the film) I think this was a bad choice for the film. Spider-Man has the best rogues gallery of any Marvel character (His and Batman's rogues gallery is the best in any comic book character) so to have an X-Men character as a villain I think is truly a bad decision. In this film, we not only had Scorpion, (Who if you ask me was only in the film because his story was left open ended from Homecoming) but also had a cameo from Tombstone. I really wish we could have run a different villain from Spider-Man's rogues gallery like The Jackal, Silver Sable, or any other villain as the main villain of the film. Next, how does Peter afford to buy all these flowers and rent a decent size New York apartment without a job? I can only think it's an inheritance from Aunt May, but I wish they could have mentioned that instead of leaving the viewer to speculate. We've had comics, games, and other movies that had Peter try to balance a work, social, relationship, and Spidey life and I wish this film tried to do that. My next issue is how come this tiny, and might I add extremely thin chip to balance his Spider DNA doesn't break at all. He gets punched through walls, roofs, and floors when he fights The Hulk and other villains but nothing happens to this chip. Not only that, he gets tased as well and this chip doesn't short circuit either. I want to know what this device is made out of since it's impervious to any sort of destruction and electricity. Lastly, and is why this movie forgets 90% of the time that he has Spidersense. He sensed Green Goblin instead of Norman Osborn in the previous film, but when Jean Grey gets knocked out by Metzger and he starts acting all shady, Spider-Man doesn't sense anything wrong with him. I sat there upset because I knew immediately he was the actual threat from the beginning and Spider-Man couldn't figure this out. Now for those that will rebuttal with "But he sees the good in everyone and believes he was doing the right thing," my counterpoint once again is the previous movie where he did the same for Green Goblin, but still recognized the threat he imposed. Then for those that'll say "But he was also having genetic mutations so it could have effected that," my next counter point with that is will first of all, he had the very indestructible chip on so his power levels should have leveled out to sense that Metzger was not only lying, but had other intentions. Now let's also say that he didn't have the chip on just for the fun of it, well then his Spideysense would have been heightened like the rest of his powers as well, and not only would he have been able to see through Metzger within seconds, but I also believe he could have been able to track Jean Grey jumping from person to person easily. I got so mad when he somehow is like "Oh yeah I have Spideysense, let me take the bullet meant for Jean instead." I legit shouted in the theater "Oh now we remember he has Spidersense." due to how annoyed I was at this movie's lack of awareness towards this ability. I will say this though, (to not have this be all negativity) I did legit think we were killing him off in that sense since it was unclear how much longer Tom Holland wants to play the character and this could have been the actual end of his character. The entire scene of him dying and being rushed into the hospital was very emotional because I didn't think he was going to live at first. This, however, did give us the greatest Spider-Man ever in any film, that being Punisher.

Overall I really wish I could like this film like others do, but sadly, I noticed way too many plot issues with this movie to not enjoy it and leave feeling very disappointed and question what others see that's amazing in this film. While I loved the camerawork, effects, and cast in this film, the plot is ok at points. The message of loneliness and trying to push forward when all hope is lost I do think is done well and to some can be very powerful. I would also be remiss if I didn't mention again how his suit was great and one of my favorites ever put to screen since it's a step back from the STARK based suits. Sadly though, the amount of issues with this plot from the villain, to a lack of awareness which left me annoyed at most parts sadly lowers this movie. I truly can't fathom why people think this film is so great when it has so many issues and are calling it "One of, if not the best Spider-Man movie we have ever got." I can not agree with this statement and I don't think I ever will since I see this as a very middle of the road Spider-Man movie. If you think this is a hot take, just wait until I start reviewing all the other Spider-Man movies, I have some serious hot takes that I know some people will be vocal about. It gets the grade below and without a doubt, my biggest let down of a film this year since I was really looking forward to the film. I was hoping it could have been Amazing, Spectacular, or even Ultimate, but sadly it's just an Average Spider-Man.

Final Grade: 5.5/10 (A Average Film) Sorry this review ended up being very long (I think it was my longest one I ever typed up). I really just had alpt to say about it, espically because I'm a huge Spider-Man fan. At the end of the day, I'm glad that people loved it as it gives me hope for more Spider-Man movies with Tom Holland. I hope you enjoyed this extra long review and I didn't come off as to hateful. I look forward to reviewing other Spider-Man films, more movies that come out soon, or even wants that I want to rewatch. I'll see you in the next review.

title: A welcome swing back to form
review:
There are miracles one no longer expects to witness in this life: political honesty, airport food at a reasonable price, or a Marvel film that does not feel like a shareholders' meeting interrupted by explosions. And yet, against all medical expectations, Spider-Man: Brand New Day has a pulse.

What a pleasure it is to find, beneath the industrial dust of the Marvel machine, something resembling a human story. The film brings back the atmosphere of the older Spider-Man movies: sincere, funny, emotional, and almost innocent (which, in the MCU, now feels less like a creative choice and more like an archaeological discovery).

The story is not exactly original. In fact, it is so predictable that halfway through the film one could probably leave the theatre, have dinner, raise a child, return twenty years later, and still correctly guess the ending. But what makes the film work is its emotional core. Peter Parker feels like Peter Parker again: fragile, funny, courageous, crushed by responsibility, and dressed in colours no adult should wear unless employed by a circus.

His character development is touching, the humour lands, and the fight scenes are genuinely enjoyable.

It is also a pleasure to see familiar faces from previous Marvel films return, while new characters from the wider Marvel universe are introduced without making the whole thing feel like a corporate roll call in spandex. The film manages to expand its world while still remembering that Spider-Man works best when the stakes are personal, not when the sky has opened for the seventeenth time that year.

That being said, the film also confirms the great illness of modern Marvel: homework. At this stage, going to see a Marvel movie without having watched the previous films, series, spin-offs, post-credit scenes, animated footnotes, deleted sequences, interviews, and possibly Kevin Feige's childhood diary is an act of reckless cultural negligence. Some people in the audience did not know who Yelena Belova was, why there were new Avengers, or what the post-credit scene meant. Poor souls.

And the post-credit scene itself? Disappointing. Short, underwhelming, and certainly not worth spending fifteen minutes watching names scroll.

Still, despite all this, Brand New Day is a very enjoyable Marvel film. It is funny, touching, well acted, visually pleasant, and it gives Spider-Man the kind of personal journey that made him lovable.

title: Web of Missed Opportunities
review:
With Great Power Comes... an Okay Sequel. I enjoyed parts of it, but it never really reached the emotional highs I was expecting.

Tom Holland is on his own in this film, but it's clear Peter still loves MJ and keeps up with both her and his best friend through social media. One thing that made me laugh was wondering how he even keeps his smartphone in that Spider-Man suit!

The villains didn't leave much of an impression. Scorpion was there, but I never felt emotionally invested in the conflict. I was hoping the film would lean further into Peter becoming more like the classic Spider-Man by exploring his heightened spider-sense, enhanced abilities, and natural web-shooting in more depth. Those elements are included, but I wanted them to play a bigger role.

Grey was great in the role, although I'm not sure I'd even call her a true villain. Seeing the X-Men and Spider-Man together was definitely a cool crossover and something I didn't expect.

The biggest surprise for me was Peter reconnecting with MJ and his best friend near the end. That was a genuinely touching moment and probably my favourite scene in the film.

The confrontation with Hulk felt unnecessary. I'm not even sure it counts as a fight, and most of the action throughout the movie felt a bit pointless because there wasn't much emotional weight behind it.

I also expected more comedy. Spider-Man is usually at his best when he balances humour with drama, but this film leaned much more into Peter's loneliness and exhaustion. He's constantly helping people, sacrificing his own happiness, and never really getting rewarded for it.

As for the title, Brand-New Day seems to refer to Peter trying to build a new life after everything that's happened. It's less about him gaining new powers and more about starting over socially and emotionally while carrying the burden of being Spider-Man. Why was there so much swearing?

Overall, It's a decent film with some strong character moments, but it has has some sticky situations such as lacking memorable villains, doesn't make the most of its action, and could have benefited from more humour.

title: 2 hours of a man being sad in Spandex
review:
Marvel discovers sadness and won't shut up about it

Four years after Peter Parker deleted himself from everyone's memory, Marvel has produced a film built on the same principle: it would very much like you to forget everything that came before, including the parts you paid for.

The premise is a magic trick performed with the house lights on. Peter is a lonely, anonymous crime-fighter in a city that doesn't know him - a setup the movie mistakes for tragedy when it's really just bookkeeping. The last film erased his relationships; this one spends two hours mournfully staring at the hole and calling it depth. Grief requires something to have been lost. What's been lost here is continuity, and no amount of Tom Holland doing his wounded-spaniel face turns a franchise reset into a wound.

The flaws, itemized:


* A villain who apologizes for existing. Sadie Sink is handed an antagonist with such an honorable, sympathetic motivation that the climactic confrontation curdles into a group hug. Conflict requires someone to be wrong. Marvel has apparently decided that's impolite.



* The Punisher as a buddy-comedy sidekick. Frank Castle, a man defined by his refusal to be redeemed, is repurposed into a lonely-hearts-club pal so two IPs can share a poster.



* The Hulk turns up. Not because the story needs him. Because a spreadsheet does.



* Teases for the New Avengers. Teases for the X-Men. A movie ostensibly about a man with nobody left cannot stop introducing you to people you'll meet in 2028. It's a film about isolation that is contractually forbidden from being alone.



* Solemnity mistaken for maturity. Everyone keeps calling this the Empire Strikes Back of Spider-Man films. Empire earned its darkness by losing. This one earns its darkness by removing the color grading and having Peter sit in a chair.



* The tonal whiplash. Torture, blood, automatic gunfire


The action is genuinely well-staged, which is the cruelest part: Destin Daniel Cretton clearly knows how to shoot a body moving through space, and he's been handed a script that keeps stopping the movement to explain its feelings. Somewhere in here is a small, sad, good film about a man who can't let anyone close. Marvel found it, admired it, and then bolted a franchise onto its back until it stopped breathing.
