title: It was good... but it also has problems.
review:
I'm so conflicted about this film, because I did really enjoy it and believe it's Tom Holland's best Spiderman film yet, BUT... it has it's problems.

First, I'll start with the pros: 
* Fantastic camerawork and amongst the best cinematography of the MCU. The director really tried new stuff with this one and even when some shots didn't land, i respect the desire to do something different.



* The best fight choreography of the Spidey films. The jackie chan stunt team were involved and did a fantastic job on this one.



* It finally felt like a SPIDERMAN film for Tom Holland. The web-swinging, the smaller NYC interactions. Up until now it's always felt like he's part of other characters stories, but this was well and truely your friendly neighbourhood spiderman.



* The acting was great. Tom, Zendaya, Sadie all killed it.



* They integrated other characters organically and finally made Hulk the HULK again!


Cons: 
* It leaves a lot of questions about the wider MCU and where this film fits (which can hopefully get answered at some point). It had almost zero acknowledgment of the events in Daredevil Born Again (aside from a torn Fisk poster in an alleyway). How can those city-wide events not even get referenced in the film? Surely they would have impacted Peter or other characters? Not even a mention from Frank who was there?



* The final act of the film, whilst very good, felt slightly disconnected from the other two acts. It drifted into less about Spiderman and more about setting up Jean Grey/Mutants for the MCU.



* How are the Hand there? They were a major part of Daredevil and seemingly destroyed... yet they're suddenly back as henchmen?



* The runtime was LONG! It was a good film, but this was one of the only times when watching an MCU movie that it actually felt long. There was a lot of unnecessary repetition and rehashed tropes that felt... boring at times.



* It had no real villain! Scorpion has been teased for years but ended up as a minor pawn in a larger game by Jean... who was then also a pawn in a larger game by Damage Control - led by a villain who's name I can't remember with motives that I have zero clue about. Damage Control seem to want power just... because? For such a long film, they spent absolutely no time telling us as to why they're doing any of it.


So overall, whilst I think the film suffers from several issues - it does have some of the most fun Spiderman/MCU moments to date. I'd love this new trilogy to continue in the hands of the new director and look forward to seeing whatever he does with it.

title: Spent potential
review:
Overall, I thought the movie was good, and I'd give it a 7.5/10. The biggest highlight for me was definitely Tom Holland's performance. I genuinely think this was one of his best performances as Spider-Man. What I liked the most was that Peter never felt overshadowed by the other characters. Even with Hulk, Punisher, and others in the movie, Peter remained the heart of the story. I also really enjoyed the balance between Peter Parker and Spider-Man. The cinematography was beautiful, and several scenes were visually stunning. My favorite scene was the rooftop conversation between Peter and MJ. At first, I genuinely believed MJ had regained her memories, but when it was revealed that it was actually Jean Grey manipulating her, it completely caught me off guard in the best way. I also loved how Peter managed to overcome Jean Grey in his own mind with the help of Aunt May's words.

That said, I do have some criticisms. I didn't find Jean Grey's motivation very convincing, so I rarely felt that she was a truly threatening villain. The introduction of mutants into the MCU also felt rushed, and I kept wondering how we suddenly reached this point. Punisher, who is usually portrayed as a serious and intimidating character, felt much more comedic here, which didn't work for me. Hulk also seemed underused, almost as if he was included simply to be there rather than to make a meaningful impact on the story.

Another issue I had was Peter's personal life. Throughout most of the movie, he feels like he's Spider-Man 24/7. He barely has a social life, and we don't really get to see enough of Peter Parker's everyday struggles. He doesn't even seem to have a job, yet the movie never explains how he's supporting himself. One of the things I've always loved most about Spider-Man is Peter Parker's ordinary life-struggling to pay bills, working a job, and trying to balance his responsibilities with being Spider-Man. That's what makes the character so relatable, and I wish the movie had spent more time exploring that side of him.

My final criticism is the marketing. I think the trailers revealed far too much, and many of the movie's biggest moments had already been shown before release.

Overall, I had a good time with the movie. Tom Holland finally got to shine in his own Spider-Man story, and the character never felt overshadowed by the rest of the cast. However, because of the weak villain motivation, the underused supporting characters, and the lack of focus on Peter Parker's everyday life, it doesn't reach the level of films like Spider-Man 2 or The Dark Knight for me. Still, I think this is a solid foundation, and if the next movie builds on it, Tom Holland's Spider-Man series could become something truly special.

Tom Holland gives perhaps his most memorable and emotional performance as a very weak and vulnerable Peter Parker/ Spider-Man, this almost feels like the first true comic Spidey film since Homecoming and since this film has many callbacks to the first film (Delmar's for example) you can definitely see how far Spider-Man has come in the MCU since his first appearance a decade ago as just a little more than a cameo in Captain America Civil War as a teen to now when he is a full grown adult Spidey and fully fledged superhero. title: Alone he swings silk threads, tenderness calms the chaos
review:
It's been a long while since I last watched Tom Holland's Spider-Man installments. I feared a sense of detachment after such a long gap, yet the moment the film rolled, Peter's distinct superhero aura washed over me instantly, retaining the timeless charm of this iconic franchise.

The story adopts a dual-track narrative, weaving the overarching hero's rescue mission with Peter's romantic coming-of-age arc. The two threads reinforce one another without the disjointed romance plaguing many superhero flicks, yielding layered storytelling, well-grounded character growth and a well-proportioned narrative scope.

Visually, the film stands out with a grounded aesthetic. Natural lighting, urban on-location shots and intimate handheld camerawork strike a fine balance between New York's everyday vibrancy and the vertigo of web-slinging aerial sequences, crafting restrained, lifelike cinematography.

The antagonist lacks the menacing aura of a scheming mastermind lurking in the shadows. Still, her bond with her younger sister forms the film's emotional core. Departing from rigid good-versus-evil tropes, this bittersweet, mutually redemptive sibling bond lends credible motivation to the villain's choices. This tender, weighty dynamic resonates deeply, serving as a poignant foil to Peter's lonely existence.

Action sequences strike a safe, moderate tone, steering clear of graphic brutality. Combat leans into Spider-Man's clever environmental and web-based maneuvers, with fluid choreography and coherent editing that avoids gratuitous agony. While no groundbreaking set pieces emerge, the clean, approachable action suits all age groups.

Though the picture brings no revolutionary reinvention to the franchise, it preserves Spider-Man's defining essence: beneath crushing fate and bitter conflict lies the innate warmth and empathy of an ordinary person.

title: Best spider man movie yet

It delivers the ultimate balance of classic ground-level drama and innovative superhero action.

## Why It Is a Perfect 10/10

* Back to Basics: Peter is single, broke, and struggling to pay rent in New York City.

* Brain Trust Success: A rotating team of top-tier writers and artists keeps the stories consistently dynamic.

* Fresh Rogues Gallery: Striking new villains like Mister Negative and Menace revitalize Spider-Man's world.

* Stunning Visuals: The art feels energetic, modern, and perfectly suited for fast-paced web-slinging action.

* Pure Fun: It strips away decades of confusing continuity to focus on humor, heart, and high stakes.

## The Verdict This run proves that you can refresh a legendary character without losing their core identity. It is essential reading for both lifelong fans and total newcomers.

Could have gotten a 10/10 if it wasn't for underwhelming third act.

Pls rewatch it.

The biggest problem with this movie is that the villain ends up being 2-dimensional, which could work for a large-scale story like the first Avengers movie.

However, for a small-scale story, the villain should be multi-faceted, like I dont think the villain in this movie had something unique.

Look at Homecoming, it is a small-scale story, However Michael Keaton's Vulture is so good, he is a leader who cares about his employees and sub-ordinates,

but he is also opportunistic ,like he looks at alien tech and immediately thinks about crime,he often pounces at any chance he could use.

He is idealistic, like he has a lot of opinions of the world he lives in, he hates Tony Stark and Avengers and thinks of himself as an ordinary man's frustration towards the world and society.

He is also funny , like he keeps referring to Peter as "Pedro".

He is scary, like Peter gets his ass kicked by him.

He is also a good father.

He is calculative and manipulative.

But most importantly, he is petty in a very subtle way.

Like that's what makes Homecoming feel like a movie and not like an episode.

The villain in this movie has a lot of aura, but definitely isnt multi-faceted.

This is a very character-focused movie so it sticks out when one of the main driving forces of the story has 2-dimensional motivations and doesn't have many traits. Makes it feel like a Video-game side quest after the main plot has ended.

However, the actor playing the villain character is reallyyy good.

The movie is focused on certain themes, that clearly deserved more screentime.

I would prefer a 3hr version of this movie adding some extra layers.

Like, I'm not joking , we are sub-conciously programmed to recognise when the first two-acts of the movie are great, like genuinely.

The first 1hr and 45 min is probably the best spidey story out there. The last act kind of rushed it.

There sshould have been more emphasis on the DODC, they feel like NPCs in this movie.

Remember in The first Avengers movie whenn Nick Fury was secretly working on weaponising the Tesseract behind the Avengers' back, and how the revelation felt like a huge betrayal almost.

There is something very similar in this movie, but its given no weight, it feels like an inconvinience.

Its the main theme of this movie.

The villain is rebellious to the authoritarian agency that is opressive.

Spidey is caught in the cross-fire, that he feels different due to his spider-puberty whilst agreeing with the villain.

All the side characters are set-up perfectly that feel in line of being yourself, like Hulk who is adamant against expressing himself and The Punisher who is adamant about doing things their way.

It was perfect.

Yet, Spider-man feels like his conflict just wafts up into the air, whereas I expected he was going to make another difficult decision, which would have been wayy better.

Like this needs a sequel or a longer edition for sure.

But the best part of this movie and any spider-man movie is how spiderman defeats the villain in this movie.

It is definitely the highlight of spiderman as a character.

This was a great movie go watch it.

title: A brand new day starts now.
review:
After the multiverse madness, Spider-Man: Brand New Day wisely swings back to what makes Spider-Man so enduring: Peter Parker.

This feels like a genuine reset. The smaller scale gives the story room to breathe, letting the emotional consequences of No Way Home finally settle in. Watching Peter navigate a lonely life where no one remembers him is heartbreaking, but it's also the perfect foundation for a classic Spider-Man story. Tom Holland delivers one of his strongest performances yet, balancing optimism, guilt, and relentless determination with ease.

The action is fantastic-fast, inventive, and full of web-slinging sequences that actually make New York feel like Spider-Man's playground again. More importantly, every fight has emotional weight behind it instead of existing just for spectacle.

What impressed me most was its confidence. It doesn't try to outdo the previous film with bigger cameos or crazier multiverse twists. It earns its biggest moments through character, heart, and the reminder that Spider-Man is at his best when life keeps knocking him down and he still chooses to get back up.

A fresh start that honors the past without being trapped by it. Exactly what this franchise needed.

This film perfectly captures that growth without losing the warmth, humor, and heart that make Spider-Man so relatable.

It's not just another superhero movie; it's a story about growing up, accepting responsibility, and finding hope even after loss. For longtime Spider-Man fans, Brand New Day feels like a heartfelt return to what the character has always represented.

title: The first genuine Spider-Man story in the MCU
review:
This is the first MCU Spider-Man film that actually feels like a genuine Spider-Man story straight from the comics.

Outside of the 3rd Act of "No Way Home", I would argue that before "Brand New Day", that we've never gotten a true Spider-Man story in the MCU. Mainly because of certain "un-SpiderMan-like" elements that that were in "Captain America:Civil War" and first 2 1/2 MCU Spider-Man movies.

Uncle Ben being inconsequential in his origin story, thus Peter never learned anything about "With Great Power comes Great Responsibility". Which definitely shows since he exhibited very little responsibility in the movies, especially in Far From Home.

Tom Holland's Peter Parker had no struggles, everything was practically given to him, and his Aunt May wasn't exactly struggling. Especially when they had Tony Stark acting as Peter's mentor & Happy Hogan more or less dating Aunt May. That family was definitely not struggling.

And post-Endgame, Peter was financially well taken care of by Tony and had a ton of access to Stark tech.

Now Post-No Way Home, Peter lost mostly everything. He obviously still has some of that Stark money and tech, cuz apparently that spell only erased people's memories of him, not his bank account. But most importantly, he FINALLY got the "Uncle Ben" speech. It was from Aunt May, though, but at least he got it....3 movies after the fact, but better late than never.

And because of it, Brand New Day is a Spider-Man story in its purest form. It's classic Spidey drama, complete with that Parker luck. And the best thing about it, there's no easy fix, no redo, his situation with his friends aren't magically undone. It actually sticks. And he has to actually work around it. I was genuinely surprised.

As for the rest of movie, in my opinion, for a Spider-Man story it was as close to perfect as you can get. And yeah, it does have a good bit of MCU cameos, but they make sense BECAUSE it's the Marvel Universe. A lot of these characters would be hanging around New York and it Peter would be running into these people from time to time in the comics.

The best part, the cringy "Marvel humor" and the "Whedon-speak" is gone. It's like some kind of miracle. No awkward gags interrupting serious and heartfelt moments, and the jokes that are there have a natural flow in conversations, and not some off the wall nonsense.

If you're a Spider-Man fan, it's practically a requirement to see this movie.

title: Another brand new win for the Spider-Man cinematic universe
review:
Soon to become one of the biggest box-office behemoths of all-time, the 4th solo entry into the Tom Holland Spider-verse that started all the way back in 2017 with the highly enjoyable Homecoming, shows no signs of slowing down as new director Destin Daniel Cretton grounds his first foray into the world of everyone's favourite web-slinger into a more character driven and introspective outing that is sure to keep audiences well and truly pleased.

Following directly on from the series altering events of the wildly fun No Way Home from 2021, Brand New Day finds Holland's Peter Parker/Spider-Man living in a world where those nearest and dearest to him no longer remember their relationships and friendships with the masked crusader of hope, giving a chance for Cretton and audiences to explore a Spidey story that gives added time for the central figure to take centre stage as well as the city of New York itself.

It's quite the feat for the feature film landscape of Spider-Man to still be delivering what feels like fresh and interesting iterations of a character and his story arcs that have now been playing out before us in various mediums since 1962 but that's exactly what Day does here, with Holland and the conflict of Parker the human arguably never better on screen as Cretton and his leading man offer a considered and emotionally resonate approach to their central figure and Holland once and for all stamping his authority over this role that will forever define his careers legacy.

Taking a softer approach to the sometimes-overbearing Marvel attitude towards to their cinematic properties that puts humour front and centre even when it goes too far, the secret weapon to Day's win as an engaging outing is moving past that take on things and while the past Holland escapades have provided us with some great levity and humorous moments, Day does a great job of evening out the ledger, which isn't to say things are all po-faced here, with Jon Bernthal's important role here as Frank Castle/The Punisher ensuring there's still a lot to smile about, but there's an acceptance that for the Spider-Man brand to continue in this form, there needs to be a natural maturing that takes place.

Less reliant on spectacle, which is still here in some well-filmed segments and is undeniable when Spidey is flying through the bustling New York cityscape, Day can't be accused of being a Hollywood blockbuster that is all about bang for buck with many of its best ingredients coming from the quieter moments of Spider-Man's unenviable position and the supporting cast, including the valuable new addition of Sadie Sink in an integral role.

Fresh off her stint in pop-culture beast Stranger Things, Sink is clearly set for big things over the coming years and alongside proven performers here, that includes important turns from proven Spider entities Mark Ruffalo, Zendaya and Jacob Batalon, Sink makes a big mark and her character's integration into the Day plotline is clearly going to be one Marvel can integrate into broader storylines moving forward, in hopefully gripping ways.

Ticking all the right boxes of what we've come to expect from this series that refuses to take the foot off the pedal, Day is going to be a massive winner for cinemagoers and Marvel/Spider-Man fans, proving that while Marvel and the broader comic book movie landscape is facing its challenges, Spider-Man is still flying high and continuing to give us top-quality content to consume thanks to its cared for and considered approach to material so many know and love.

Final Say -

A more introspective take on the Tom Holland era of web-slinging, Spider-Man: Brand New Day delights, surprises and entertains, swinging on its merry way to record breaking box-office hauls and more eager fans keen to see what comes next for our friendly neighbourhood hero.

3 1/2 grand pianos out of 5.

title: A Sour Yarn To End
review:
Drama and action require a balancing act and while No Way Home was all action with no brakes that appealed to my sensibilities this movie takes a dramatic swing. Like a swing it comes down fast and exciting then half way through has to rely on the momentum and an extra nudge to make it all the way up. Visually this is well executed with each pull on the swing present subtly in the foreground. Storytelling wise it fails that final push.

My main criticism in the movie is that it is obviously restrained by the cinematic universe and incorporates aspects of that universe and the broader multiverse that isn't familiar and could not be taken for granted like in phases 1-3. Yelena appears out of nowhere and her scenes could have easily been cut. They should be because it is distracting seeing a character in a 3 billion dollar movie that was introduced and developed in lesser known works. And lesser is an understatement with comparison to this movie.

The movie isn't epic enough to be this bloated. I would cut 10 minutes of fat which include Yelena and all the flashbacks except the final one where Jean looks into Peters mind. I didn't need to see how Jean's sister was captured. I didn't need to see Aunt May 3 times in the same setting. It would have fit in with the theme of this movie where memories are wiped and it's time to move forward. Also the speech at the end by May was complete rubbish and that section could be muted for the most part. Too much talking, just enough showing. The message that you are loved and not it's not good to be alone didn't need to be spelled out. Also I don't want Peter being a cyber security expert. Cut out the facial recognition and security camera nonsense. It doesn't help him in any sense. Scorpion attacked Damage Control. Jeans power could be analysed through his goggles. Cutting 15 minutes would make it fit right in with the first 2 Raimi movies and first 2 Watts movies.

The Punisher steals the show but he should have been developed just a little bit. The show, don't tell rule of storytelling is ignored when it comes to the relationship between Punisher and Spiderman. A cool action sequence establishing their first meeting would add great depth. Something closer to a backstory because he is also a tv only character.

Jean Greys broader role in the universe is kept unexplained. There is no hint to the fact that she is a mutant or associated with the X-Men brand. My friend had no idea who she is and felt that her inclusion was forced because she probably has something to do with comics. Besides being so obscure, her character and development and power scale were handled well and it's impressive how she fits in with Spiderman. Two super powered recluse with total opposite relationships with authorities and systems of government.

The best comic book movies are judged by their villains undoubtedly. It's unfortunate that this movies main antagonist isn't a villain. It's what defines a superhero movie, the bright and colourful supervillain. However, I would say it is more akin to a buddy cop movie like Lethal Weapon.

All the plot points though don't tie up in a neat little bow. The arachnid takeover is mechanically solved. There is no fallout of Damage Control. Jean Grey escapes and is directionless. Spiderman is recovering in the hospital with a cheering crowd outside but how his secret identity is maintained while he recovers isn't explained. Just have Jean Grey heal him or make her the reason as to how Spiderman recovers in a hospital by setting up a force field and wiping the mind of the doctors who operated on him. This could be implied and it's my canon.

At the end of the day I would love to see the percentage of this audience who saw a prior thing Yelena had been in, same for Punisher, and how many connected Jean Grey to the X-Men and not just some unfamiliar red headed teen with mental powers. If you are only familiar with Spiderman and his ancillary media you would never connect him with the lesser known member of the X-Men. They expect a lot from the audience, especially for one of the biggest audiences ever with a very tiny percentage recognising characters established elsewhere or not as popular in pop culture.

As you can see, my major problems come at the very end but there were simple remedies. I'm sad that a sour taste was left after an enjoyable movie. I was yawning and falling asleep at the end. The action on the other hand is top notch. It is worth checking the movie out just on that alone. It is Tom Hollands best portrayal of the character and the dual identities. It incorporates the struggle of lonliness and responsibility, especially to an up and coming adolescent where entering into this new stage of life is intensive and difficult. And it is the best costume of Spiderman ever and we are blest to see in a very large portion of the movie.

In conclusion, if you don't let go of the web at the end of the swing then you will hit something on your way back down. This movie felt that way.

title: One of the best Spidey Movies!
review:
The best thing about Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the introduction of Punisher. Every scene shared between Punisher and Spider-Man is a delight to watch, adding intensity and depth to the story.

Another pleasant surprise is Jean Grey, whose psychic powers create a compelling new threat. Scorpio, on the other hand, has only a brief appearance.

The film also beautifully explores the emotional arc between Peter Parker, MJ, and Ned. As the story progresses, it becomes increasingly heartfelt, culminating in an emotional finale. I especially enjoyed both Punisher and Jean Grey, who leave a lasting impression.

What makes this film stand out is its portrayal of Spider-Man's vulnerable side. It evokes memories of Tobey Maguire's Spider-Man, reminding us that Peter Parker is, above all, a human being. Watching him battle his inner demons while facing powerful external enemies makes the character far more relatable and emotionally engaging.

The action sequences are spectacular, particularly Spider-Man's confrontations with Hulk, which are choreographed brilliantly. Sadie Sink shines as Jean Grey, and her transformation from darkness to hope is the icing on the cake. Another memorable moment is the heartfelt handshake between Peter Parker and Ned in the climax, as Ned finally learns Spider-Man's true identity.

I haven't watched a Punisher film before, but after this movie, I'm eager to do so. Tom Holland once again proves why he is one of the finest actors to portray Spider-Man, second only to Tobey Maguire in my opinion.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a heartfelt superhero film that makes Spider-Man feel more human, vulnerable, and emotionally resonant than ever before. The new director deserves special praise for delivering stunning visuals and exceptional action. This is definitely a film worth experiencing in 3D.

It's also wonderful that the movie was released in India a day ahead of the rest of the world.

My Rating: 10/10

Highly Recommended!

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Review - Peak Spidey Spirit, Flawed Execution
review:
The movie opens with a grounded, street-level atmosphere that captures the authentic "friendly neighborhood" Spider-Man spirit. The production quality, fight choreography, and explosion sequences are top-tier. Tom Holland's acting was genuinely fantastic, bringing fresh life and relatable humor to the role like never before. Zendaya also delivers her finest performance as MJ compared to all her previous movies. His interactions with a detective and their dynamic are portrayed brilliantly, making those scenes an absolute joy to watch.

The classic Spidey humor shines throughout. Moments like his disgust when webs emerge directly out of his own body, stepping into the shower in just his mask and boxers, or stretching his lower back while complaining about getting older give the film a fantastic vibe - almost like playing the PlayStation Spider-Man game - and bring genuine laughs. Punisher's inclusion is handled brilliantly, and the Bruce Banner / Hulk dynamics are seamlessly integrated.

However, as the film progresses, it runs into narrative imbalances and miscasting issues. The actress playing Jean Grey actually delivers a fantastic performance and gives it her all; however, she is simply miscast for Jean Grey specifically. While her acting and positive energy are great, she lacks the dominant, commanding presence that the character demands (with her radiant energy, she could have been a wonderful fit for MJ instead). Furthermore, weak villain motivations in the second half dampen the brilliant setup.

The highs of this film - the acting, production, and humor - are easily a 9/10, but structural flaws drag it down. Spreading this story across a 20-episode TV series would have given the plot the breathing room it desperately needed. Nevertheless, thanks to its great action and true Spider-Man essence, it comfortably locks in a solid 7.5/10.

title: This film made me feel something
review:
I watched Spider-Man Brand New Day yesterday and in my personal opinion this is the best Spider-Man movie ever. First of all it looked very beautiful visually with the color grading, camera shots, and seeing the swinging Spider-Man does.

This is the first Spider-Man movie in a while, where it actually felt like a true Spider-Man movie. The movies we've gotten from the Home trilogy just didn't feel like a proper Spider-Man movie at all, so it's so refreshing seeing a Spider-Man movie that felt like a true Spider-Man film.

Now the emotions in this movie was the strongest element in the film. I liked how they showed Peter Parker's life after having everyone forget about him and how it impacted him physically and mentally. Another thing was that after all these years, MJ found the letter that was written to her and she doesn't love Peter, because she doesn't know who he is. Another thing was when Peter was hanging out with MJ and Ned in the apartment, it was the most fun he had in years, which made me realize how lonely the guy was. I loved the introduction to Jean Grey and I felt she was done really well. It was tragic that the VMax she was looking for turned out to be some air vent that her sister Sara saw before she was killed. And the scene with May, Peter, and Jean was well done, because Peter told her she was not alone despite losing love ones. This whole movie was just emotional and deep, and I felt something from it.

I also loved the comedy, because it was actually funny unlike the humor we've seen from Homecoming, Far from Home and No Way Home.

The only weakness from this movie was the hulk fight scene was too short, and I blame the trailers that showed too much. The post credit scene was disappointing. Yes it shows that he is in space which leads to Doomsday or Secret wars, but through a spidey tracker?

Overall the movie is 9.1/10. Amazing and highly recommend watching.

title: Missing the Magic
review:
My BMW told me I should see this movie so I went. First off, I really enjoyed the movie because I love Spider-Man and the sparse action scenes and swinging through the city were enough to clear my head from the heavy drama that encompassed most of the movie. No Way Home ends on such a melancholy note, I was hoping the trio could reestablish their friendship early so we have more time with them. Instead, it takes Peter Parker 90% of the movie to realize that hey the guy who runs Damage Control is shady af (did Peter learn nothing in Far From Home?) and 100% of the movie to realize that he'd rather have friends than not have friends and that going through spider puberty is actually a good thing.

This doesn't feel like a self contained Spider-Man arc, instead a setup movie for Jean Grey and her Dark Phoenix arc. I'm not crazy about Marvel polluting Spider-Man movies with other characters from the MCU. The hulk added nothing and the punisher was entertaining but the story would have been better and tighter without him. The change in director brought a change in tone, with a lot of heavy drama replacing what were generally pretty fun romps in the Jon Watts trilogy. The action was very clear with some cool slow motion shots and swinging through the city on the big screen was exhilarating. The plot with Spidey's evolving felt unclear. At first it's a problem, even his computer agrees, but in the end it's fine. His depressing era was giving Emo Peter Parker from the Tobey Maguire days.

Having said all that I'm sad for the end of this generation of Spidey. I can't imagine the trio will want to launch another movie and it would get a little strange as Holland gets older and older and older. Definitely an enjoyable movie but missing the ensemble magic of the first three.

Random thoughts: Sadie Sink is great but I found her distracting because she's so recognizable from Stranger Things. I also found the chef from The Bear fairly distracting. Apparently there are 3-d screenings? Peter is so dumb in this. How did Jean get away from the helicopter? The end credits scene is a letdown especially after starving us of the MJ, Peter and Ned shared screentime.

title: A Brand New Day
review:
Finally, an MCU Spider-Man film that feels like a true Spider-Man movie.

A vibrant movie with comic-book colors that's full of heart and true to Peter Parker/Spider-Man. Serious, emotional scenes between characters aren't ruined by forced, unfunny humor and are allowed to play out. The action scenes and set pieces are visually striking and more memorable. And I do mean this whole movie looks colorful and is probably the best-looking Spidey film. The swinging scenes almost gave me motion sickness, which isn't a negative but actually a compliment, as it effectively puts you in his POV during those scenes. Frank Castle, aka The Punisher, and Spidey have great chemistry, and their interactions are pure gold. The performances here are strong, especially from Tom Holland, who has never been better, and from Sadie Sink in that emotional third-act scene. Director Destin Daniel Cretton does wonders with dynamic action, but he also brings a grounded, human touch to the characters and draws out the best in the actors.

Although the visual effects at times look rough, and although I like how the film tries to give New York City a personality this time around, similar to the Sam Raimi movies, which works in parts, in other parts I can't shake the feeling that I'm looking at a street filmed anywhere but in New York, masquerading as the city. The actual villain of the movie isn't anything noteworthy beyond basic evil deeds. The film is a little overstuffed, and I bet there was a lot of cutting around in the editing room.

And that's it for the issues. Overall, I walked away satisfied and happy. There's a reason people love this character: he is the most relatable hero in fiction, and everyone can see themselves in him. The film captures that well. A hero audiences will show up for, dress up as, and be inspired by, both children and adults. Our friendly neighborhood Spider-Man.
author: MattyLuke-81663

title: Regret
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a huge disappointment for me. I went into the movie hoping for a fresh and exciting story, but I left feeling like the writing was the weakest part of the entire experience. The plot felt unfocused, with ideas that never came together in a satisfying way. Instead of building suspense or emotional depth, the story seemed to jump from one moment to another without giving enough time for the characters or the audience to connect with what was happening.

The dialogue also felt flat and forgettable. Many conversations lacked the emotion and charm that have made previous Spider-Man films so memorable. Some scenes that were clearly meant to be emotional or inspiring failed to have any real impact because the writing did not give the characters enough meaningful development. As a result, several important moments felt forced rather than earned.

Another major issue was the pacing. The movie struggled to balance action with storytelling, making some scenes feel rushed while others dragged on for too long. Even though the visuals and action sequences were entertaining at times, they could not make up for the weak script. A superhero movie can have amazing effects, but without a strong story, those moments lose much of their impact.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day did not live up to my expectations. I believe the writing lacked creativity, emotional depth, and a clear direction. While some viewers may enjoy it, I personally found it to be one of the weakest entries in the Spider-Man franchise. It had the potential to tell an exciting and meaningful story, but the screenplay never fully delivered on that promise. For me, the movie was more frustrating than enjoyable, and I hope future Spider-Man films return to the strong storytelling and character development that made the series so popular in the first place.

title: Everything I wanted it to be and more
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is everything I wanted it to be and somehow so much more! I genuinely don't remember the last time I left a Marvel movie this happy. It gave me the exact same high I had walking out of Superman last year-that overwhelming feeling where I just wanted to sit there and soak in how much I loved what I had just watched. THIS is why I fell in love with the MCU, and it's been so long since one of these movies made me feel this way. I am so unbelievably excited about where we go from here.

I cannot believe how much I loved this movie. This is why I love the MCU. This is why I love Spider-Man.

After three movies about Peter Parker becoming Spider-Man, Brand New Day finally asks what happens when Spider-Man is virtually all Peter has left.

Destin Daniel Cretton takes over from Jon Watts and brings a much more grounded, mature, back-to-basics approach to the character. In a lot of ways, it feels like he has done for Spider-Man what Matt Reeves did with The Batman: strip away so much of what we've come to associate with these massive superhero movies and refocus everything on the person underneath the mask. The result is simultaneously a fresh reset and a completely natural evolution of everything that came before it. This is still unmistakably the Spider-Man we've spent the last decade with, but he's older, more damaged, more independent, and struggling with problems that can't simply be webbed away.

And I absolutely LOVE how they handle the implications of the ending of No Way Home.

There are no easy outs. Peter's decision mattered. He didn't just lose MJ and Ned; he effectively severed himself from the people who made Peter Parker Peter Parker. Brand New Day lets us actually sit with the loneliness, grief, heartbreak, and emotional repression that followed. He's convinced himself that he can simply be Spider-Man-that losing Peter Parker is almost a necessary sacrifice if it keeps everyone else safe-but the movie understands that those two halves of him were never supposed to exist independently. Spider-Man needs Peter Parker just as much as Peter needs Spider-Man.

Watching him slowly confront that is beautiful.

It also gives Tom Holland easily his best material in the role. We've literally watched him grow up alongside this character, and Brand New Day takes full advantage of that. He can still effortlessly deliver the humour, physicality, awkwardness, and charm that have always made his Spider-Man work, but there's a sadness and maturity behind him now that feels completely earned after everything Peter has experienced. Holland gets to dig into the pain, anger, fear, and longing that Peter has been carrying since No Way Home, and some of his quieter moments hit me harder than I ever expected.

This movie made Tom Holland my favourite Spider-Man.

A huge part of that comes from the way Brand New Day refuses to forget what made the original trilogy work. As different as this movie feels tonally, Peter, MJ, and Ned remain its beating heart. We've known these characters for nearly a decade, and that history gives even the smallest interactions an enormous amount of weight. The movie doesn't need to constantly remind us what they meant to each other-we already know. Peter knows too. That's what hurts.

There's something incredibly relatable about watching these characters grow older, change, drift apart, and try to figure out who they are without the people and lives that once defined them. The Home trilogy had an innocence that fit Peter at that stage of his life; Brand New Day doesn't diminish that whatsoever. If anything, its maturity makes those movies more meaningful because this feels like the natural next stage of growing up.

For as emotionally heavy as all of that gets, though, Cretton also directs the absolute HELL out of this thing.

Spider-Man has rarely looked this good. The web-swinging, combat, choreography, cinematography, use of New York, and sheer physicality of Spider-Man's movement are phenomenal. There's an energy to the action that immediately reminded me why Shang-Chi was such an exciting showcase for Cretton as an action director, and one sequence here might genuinely be my favourite Spider-Man action scene ever. New York finally feels essential too-not simply a backdrop for Spider-Man to swing through, but a living city filled with people and stories happening whether Peter is there to see them or not.

Michael Giacchino's score deserves some love here too. I absolutely loved how he evolves the sound of this Spider-Man alongside Peter, while still maintaining the musical continuity of everything that came before. The familiar themes are still there, but they feel changed and matured with him-a perfect reflection of how Brand New Day can feel so different from the Home trilogy without ever losing its connection to it.

That extends to something else I absolutely adored: this might be the most naturally interconnected the MCU has ever felt. On paper, putting Spider-Man, Punisher, Hulk, and even more characters into the same movie sounds like exactly the kind of overstuffed crossover spectacle Marvel should probably be moving away from. Somehow, Cretton makes it feel like the complete opposite. Nobody is here just so the audience can point at the screen. These characters have their own lives, problems, and motivations, and they intersect with Peter because they all exist in the same world.

This is what I've always wanted the MCU to feel like.

It's a massive universe, but that doesn't mean every story within it needs to be massive. Hulk can exist somewhere in New York while Punisher is doing his thing a few streets away and Spider-Man is dealing with something completely different.

They don't overshadow Peter; they make his world feel bigger. The MCU hasn't felt this genuinely lived-in to me in a very long time, and Brand New Day somehow accomplishes that while remaining an incredibly focused, intimate Spider-Man story.

And the Spider-Man/Punisher dynamic is SO GOOD. Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal work ridiculously well together, giving the movie some of its funniest moments without ever undermining the much darker material surrounding them. It's exactly the balance of humour and seriousness that Spider-Man needs.

Then there's Sadie Sink. Without getting anywhere near spoilers, she completely steals this movie by the end. What initially feels like another piece of Peter's story gradually becomes something far more meaningful, and the way her character ties thematically into Peter's own journey is fantastic. Their dynamic adds another dimension to what the movie is saying about pain, isolation, and what we choose to do with the parts of ourselves we're afraid of. I desperately hope this is only the beginning of what they're doing with her.

And that's ultimately what makes Brand New Day so special to me. Beneath all the incredible action, web-swinging, humour, superheroes, and wider MCU implications, this is a surprisingly stripped-down character study about loneliness and human connection. It's about growing up and realizing you can't control every change happening around you. It's about losing people, losing pieces of yourself with them, and still having to wake up the next morning and keep going. It's about accepting that vulnerability and connection aren't weaknesses-that shutting everyone out isn't the same thing as protecting them.

It really does make Brand New Day, Thunderbolts, and Superman feel like this incredible unofficial thematic trilogy of superhero movies for me. All three approach loneliness, pain, connection, and hope from completely different directions, but they understand the same fundamental thing: these movies work best when the superheroes feel human. When saving somebody can mean extending a hand just as much as stopping the world from ending.

Brand New Day understands Spider-Man perhaps better than any of Tom Holland's movies before it. No Way Home is still the more purely fun movie for me, and the experience of seeing that for the first time is almost impossible to replicate, so right now I'd probably call them tied as my favourite Tom Holland Spider-Man films. But as a story? Emotionally? As an exploration of Peter Parker and everything that makes Spider-Man who he is? Brand New Day is better.

It might be one of my favourite Spider-Man movies, period.

This is the Spider-Man movie that has lived in my head for years-not necessarily beat-for-beat, but in spirit. A friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man living in a massive comic-book world, struggling to balance the person he is with the responsibility he's chosen to carry. A Peter Parker who has been knocked down over and over and still finds a reason to get back up.

It really is a brand new day for Peter Parker.

And holy crap, I cannot wait to see what tomorrow brings.

2) The decision to make Jean Grey the villain of this movie was terrible in my opinion. Firstly because it makes it obvious that she's going to turn good at the end. Secondly because I think Sadie Sink is a terrible casting choice for Jean Grey. author: DanLawson146

title: The street-level masterpiece we NEEDED! Easily Holland's best.
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is without a doubt Tom Holland's best Spider-Man movie to date, and easily the best Spider-Man film overall since Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2 (2004).

What makes this movie hit so hard is the emotional weight. Watching Peter deal with his actual personal life after No Way Home-completely forgotten by everyone he loved, starting from total scratch, and trying to build a life on his own-gives the film incredible depth.

A grounded, street-level Spider-Man story was exactly what this character needed. Stripped of high-tech gadgets and world-ending threats, it gets right back to the core of Peter Parker balancing personal sacrifice with being a neighborhood hero.

A few massive standouts: The Emotional Core: Holland delivers his finest performance yet, perfectly capturing Peter's resilience and loneliness as he navigates a world where no one remembers him.

The Web-Swinging: Absolute perfection. The director killed it with the kinetic camera work, momentum, and weight. Easily some of the best swinging scenes in the entire franchise.

The Costume: A complete 10/10. Classic, vibrant, and visually stunning against the city backdrop, specifically you can see peter's eyes through the lenses.

The Direction: Gritty, intimate, and wonderfully focused.

Brand New Day proves that Spidey doesn't need to save the universe to deliver a legendary film-he just needs a classic suit, a real city, and an authentic, personal story. A complete triumph for fans!

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
review: Homecoming was a great start, Long Way from Home was alright, and No Way Home was brilliant; this was the latest in the web-slinging adventures in the Marvel Cinematic Universe franchise, directed by Destin Daniel Cretton (Just Mercy, Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings). Basically, it has been four years since Dr. Stephen Strange's magic spell has made the world forget that Peter Parker (Tom Holland) exists, and that he is Spider-Man. Since then, Peter has chosen to protect his girlfriend Michelle "MJ" Jones-Watson (Zendaya) and best friend Ned Leeds (Jacob Batalon) by not reintroducing himself to them. Peter continues to anonymously protect the citizens of New York City as the masked hero, and crime has significantly dropped. He defeats major criminals including Ramrod (Billy Clements), Tarantula (Anton Miguel Rodriguez), Boomerang (Aidan Kennedy), crime boss Tombstone (Marvin Jones), and a group of ninjas called the Hand, earning the trust of NYPD (New York City Police Department) Detective Jean DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas). Parker regularly visits the grave of his aunt May (Marisa Tomei). Parker stops Frank Castle aka the Punisher (Jon Bernthal) from causing collateral damage whilst chasing a tank that crashes into a DODC (Department of Damage Control) prison. The driver is possessed by a telepath who body hops from person to person; the telepath attempts to enter Parker's mind but without success. The telepath helps Mac Gargan aka Scorpion (Michael Mando) escape. Yelena Belova aka Black Widow (Florence Pugh) informs Parker that multiple DODC facilities have been attacked by someone searching for "V-Max". Parker visits DODC director William 'Bill' Metzger (Tramell Tillman), who does not know "V-Max"; the Hand have sided with Metzger and become security personnel. Ned and MJ move back to New York after graduating from MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology). Peter follows MJ to a party and sees her kiss her new boyfriend, Paul Rabin (Eman Esfandi). Returning home in distress, he wakes up the next day with heightened senses and the ability to shoot webs from his wrists. When the telepath attacks another DODC facility, possessing Scorpion's body, Peter loses control of his new abilities and brutally beats Scorpion. DeWolff reprimands him for losing control after he inadvertently injures a police officer. Wanting to suppress his heightened senses, Peter visits Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo), who wears an inhibitor device that uses siRNA to suppress his super-powered alter ego the Hulk. With Stark Industries technology and AI assistant E. V. (Naomi Watts), he builds his own inhibitor. While he tests it, the telepath finds his apartment and reads a letter intended for MJ in which he reveals he is Spider-Man. Parker races to get MJ to safety. When they have a moment alone, MJ may be recalling memories of her time with Peter before her memory was wiped, and they share a kiss. But it turns out that the telepath has possessed her and almost kills her. After rescuing MJ from falling, using visual technology to identify nearby superhuman beings, the telepath is identified as Jean Grey (Sadie Sink). Parker takes MJ to Castle's hideout for protection, where she helps him with her knowledge of technology to complete his inhibitor and develop a universal inhibitor. Jean attacks the DODC's headquarters with a possessed Banner as the Hulk. Peter and Castle try to stop them, but Jean possesses Castle and uses him to open a vault hiding DODC agents. Peter stops the Hulk and plants the universal inhibitor on Jean to block her powers. He hears her mention "Sara", and Metzger claims he thought of this name while Jean was possessing him. Peter returns to MJ, who has found the letter. He apologises for not telling her and declares his love, but MJ does not remember him and cannot reciprocate. Despite this, she invites him into her apartment to meet Ned, who has been tracking Spider-Man using an app he created. MJ describes not remembering anything while possessed, and Parker realises that Metzger lied. He contacts Yelena, who learns from redacted DODC files that Sara (Olivia Booth-Ford) is Jean's sister, another telepath who was kidnapped by the DODC. Metzger experiments on Jean at a DODC facility on Roosevelt Island. Jean realises that "V-Max" was part of a label on the air vent in her cell, the last thing Sara saw and mentally communicated to Jean before she died. While Peter infiltrates the facility, an enraged Jean creates a psionic field that extends to the city, freezing everyone within a mile of the facility, except for Peter. Jean rebuffs his apologies and possesses the Hand to attack him. Feeling emotionally stronger and regaining control of his new abilities, Peter removes his inhibitor and defeats the Hand. Before Jean can kill Metzger, Peter allows Jean to enter his mind, where she experiences a memory of May saying she loves him for who he is. Peter and Jean acknowledge each other's losses, and he offers to be there for her. But before she can release Metzger, Peter senses Castle shooting at Jean from a distance and shields her. Jean drops the psionic field while Peter sustains a critical injury. Peter wakes up in a hospital with a remorseful Castle, who reveals that he was kept alive by Jean using her powers. Castle distracts the crowd outside, allowing Peter to walk out, while Jean leaves the city, Metzger disappears, and the DODC comes under investigation. At May's grave, Peter promises to stop trying to do everything alone, and later agrees to let DeWolff handle a robbery while he recovers. Seeing Ned again, Parker reintroduces himself with their old handshake. Also starring Zabryna Guevara as Mayor Sheila Rivera, and news anchor Pat Kiernan as himself, with the voice of Keith David as the Narrator of Spider Video. Holland is spirited and likeable as before, Zendaya does well as his long-lost love, Sink is well cast as the anti-villain, and there is great support from Batalon, Bernthal, Pugh, and Ruffalo. The story is well-scripted, with spectacular special effects, fast-paced fight and chase sequences, and moments of humour and emotion that work well; it is a most satisfying and impressive superhero fantasy action adventure. Very good!

author: The_Right-Brained_Reviewer

title: Spider Senses Working Overtime
review:
Although I've watched Tom Holland's three previous outings as Spider Man, I felt they weren't aimed at my demographic and didn't really hit home with me. Well, it is approaching 50 years since I was a teenager so perhaps that wasn't surprising as they were so obviously aimed at that market but I'm pleased to say that I was much more able to connect with the character in this, his latest adventure.

I'm also not fully au-fait with every aspect of the MCU so when the talk turns to the battle of New York and Spidey saving the Punisher's life, I'm pretty clueless but I still felt the movie worked well as a stand-alone feature, regardless of any other crossover events from the recent past.

As we recall from "No Way Home", Peter had to effectively delete his very existence from the whole world, including even his closest friends and so we initially find him living alone almost literally in a garret, but at least accepted as New York's favourite super-hero, where if nothing else, he has the ear and support of his friendly neighbourhood police captain as he goes about his crime-busting business.

It's not long however before a new threat comes to town, a seemingly invisible adversary with the abliity to body hop at will, jumping into the minds and controlling the actions of any one within 30 feet or so of them. The trail of this new, unnamed opponent will see Spider Man hook up with Mark Ruffalo's Hulk and Jon Bernthal's The Punisher before their surprising identity is revealed, while, as Peter Parker, our hero seeks to re-connect with his girl, Zendaya's MJ and best bud Ned, played by Jacob Batalon.

I found I enjoyed the unconventional storyline, lacking as it did a named super-villain from the established Rogues Gallery, although the Scorpion does get a brief look-in and the Hand are on hand (sorry) for a fair old scrap with a super-enhanced Spidey near the end. The human stuff worked well too as we see both hero and "villain" struggle with loss and loneliness before ultimately seeking and finding redemption in forming new / old relationships.

The fight sequences involving Spider Man and Scorpion, the Hand and especially Hulk were excellently rendered, plus I loved the depiction of the new enemy's mind-throwing ability. With a cleverly used Magoffin, funny, offbeat Ned-nerdy humour and some sensitive romantic interaction between the new Mr and Mrs Holland, if this is to be this cast's and Holland in particular's last go-round in the Spider-Verse (surely his baby-face must show signs of ageing sometime!), this was a pretty good way for them all to bow out.

title: A Fantastic Emotional Super Hero Film
review:
It has been five year since the excellent Spider-Man: No Way Home and we now have got our next Tom Holland led Spider-Man film with Brand New Day. I went into a packed cinema to watch it today and here is my review for the film. The premise of the film sees Peter Parker attempt to navigate adult life alone as he tries to balance being Spider-Man with the new things going on in his life.

Main Character I feel like every time there is a solo Spider-Man film led by Tom Holland, I always say that it is his best performance in the role and this is no different. He is excellent here and this is easily the darkest portrayal of the character that he has had to portray. There is so much going on with his character and Holland nails it and makes me really care about Peter and the struggles that he is in.

Supporting Characters Zendaya is back as MJ and I actually found her part in the film to be really well realised. Obviously, she can't remember who Peter is and I think that made the dynamic really different here and it felt like a natural progression for her character and their relationship.

I was nervous when Jon Bernthal was announced to be playing The Punisher here, that they would neuter him. But I am happy to report that they don't and it feels like a slightly toned down version of the great character we have. The chemistry between Holland & Bernthal is off the charts and for me is one of the aspects that carries the film.

Sadie Sink plays the villain here and I won't mention her role as it wasn't revealed before the films release. She was really good in the film, I think her character had a few issues but that doesn't take away the really good performance by Sink.

Smaller roles for Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner, Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova and Liz Colon-Zayas as DeWolff were fun characters and even though they weren't in the film that much, they added just about enough.

Story The story is good. I really liked the personal nature of Peter's story as he goes through these mental and physical issues that really change how he is seen as Spider-Man. I also liked Sadie Sink's characters overall story and arc throughout the last arc of the film. However, the film has way too much going on in it to really develop everything as much as it should. There are a few characters and story bits that could have been cut out of the film to give the major story beats a bit more depth and make it a really amazing story.

Script The script is great. As I mentioned above, this is probably the darkest Spider-Man film that has ever been made and the dialogue and writing really sells that and takes this usually light hearted character into some dark places. But it also knows when to have fun and the humour still works, making it an overall great experience.

Style The action scenes are superb. We had a change in director for this film and Destin Daniel Cretton who directed Shang-Chi shows his skill in directing action scenes and really adding some uniqueness to the character who has been on the big screen for over 25 years. The pacing is really good too, I was never bored and it kept me engaged throughout.

Overall Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a Fantastic Film that does the character justice. It keeps up the strong run of Tom Holland's Spider-Man films and is a really fun watch in the cinema. It is a truly great comic book film and definitely worth a watch.

Rating - 9/10.

title: Finally, a Spider-Man of His Own
review:
Feeling every swing through a 4DX seat certainly intensified the experience, but the joy I felt came from something much more important than the movement of the theater. For the first time in Tom Holland's Spider-Man films, Peter Parker truly feels like the owner of his own story. He is no longer waiting for an older hero to define him, guide him or carry the emotional weight of the film. He has people around him, but the decisions, failures and consequences finally belong to him. That change allows Spider-Man and Peter Parker to exist as equally important sides of the same person rather than as separate identities competing for screen time.

That independence also restores the personality I had been missing from this version of the character. His humor, awkwardness and physical energy now exist beside loneliness, exhaustion and a genuine understanding of responsibility. Watching him swing through New York felt exciting not only because of the movement, but because those scenes finally seemed connected to the person beneath the mask. The references to comic book covers and the confrontations with Scorpion understand the visual pleasure of seeing Spider-Man in motion without reducing the action to empty recognition. The 4DX experience made every swing feel physical, but the film itself gave those movements personality.

The suit immediately strengthens that feeling. It looks tangible, textured and connected to the body wearing it rather than digitally placed over an actor. Its colors and design take inspiration from previous versions without simply copying them, creating something familiar that still belongs to this Peter. Spider-Man's costume has always communicated something about the person inside it, and here it bends, wrinkles and occupies the frame like something he actually wears. New York receives the same care. The city feels populated, physical and alive rather than like a collection of digital backgrounds waiting for an action sequence, and every swing becomes part of Peter's relationship with the place he has chosen to protect.

Tom Holland gives his strongest performance in the role. I have always believed that he is an excellent actor, but the previous films rarely allowed him to explore everything he could bring to Peter. Watching The Odyssey earlier this year left me with a similar frustration, because I could see the quality of his work while still wishing he had been given more opportunities to demonstrate his full range. Here, the physical challenge is finally matched by an emotional one. He looks completely comfortable inside Spider-Man's movements while allowing Peter to appear vulnerable, uncomfortable, isolated and uncertain. The sincerity of the performance makes it clear that he understands the character deeply and has finally been given enough space to show what his version can become.

Zendaya remains essential to that emotional dimension. Their chemistry crosses the screen so naturally that even the quieter conversations carry a history much larger than the words being spoken. Jon Bernthal brings the intensity I expected from him, while Sadie Sink surprised me with how clearly she communicates the emotional condition of her character without making her feel like another addition included only to expand the universe. Liza Colón-Zayas, Tramell Tillman, Jacob Batalon and Michael Mando also help create a world that feels populated by actual people rather than recognizable faces waiting for their moment. The most important achievement is that none of them takes control of Peter's film.

That balance separates Brand New Day from the previous entries. Earlier stories often allowed another figure to become their center of gravity, whether it was Iron Man, Mysterio, Doctor Strange or the other Spider-Men. This film still embraces the fact that Spider-Man exists inside a much larger universe, but those connections feel like support rather than direction. Peter is surrounded by people, yet nobody decides the path for him. Even Hulk's appearance, already revealed in the trailer, works because it adds excitement without stealing ownership from the protagonist. That scene nearly made me jump from my seat and felt like one of the best uses of Hulk in years, but it never transformed the movie into someone else's story.

The film is not equally confident throughout. The third act suddenly loses momentum and begins to feel like several different conclusions placed beside one another. Each section contains emotional or thematic value, but together they stretch the ending beyond what it needs. The screenplay also explains its central message too often, with several supporting characters verbalizing lessons that Peter and the audience have already understood through his actions. Hearing the same idea repeated weakens discoveries that would have been more powerful through silence, gestures or consequences. The resolution becomes predictable not because the themes are weak, but because the film refuses to trust that it has already communicated them.

There are also practical details that the more grounded approach leaves strangely untouched. I would have appreciated a clearer sense of how Peter sustains his ordinary life and the technology surrounding him, even through one brief scene of work or daily responsibility. It is a minor absence, but it matters because this story is otherwise so committed to making his world feel physical and believable. The action, visual effects, music and photography all improve significantly, yet those ordinary details are part of what makes Peter Parker different from heroes whose resources never need explanation. Showing that side of his life would have made his independence feel even more complete.

Even with those weaknesses, this is easily my favorite film centered on this version of Spider-Man. It succeeds as a superhero story, but it becomes something more meaningful when it treats Peter Parker and Spider-Man as equally necessary parts of the protagonist. The hero does not erase the young man, and the young man does not exist only as a pause before the next action sequence. Someone behind me was crying uncontrollably during one of the final moments, and I could not blame them. Spider-Man has always represented the possibility that anyone could exist beneath the mask, not because everyone could possess his powers, but because everyone understands what it means to feel vulnerable, lonely and still responsible for doing what is right.

Brand New Day understands that responsibility is not a lesson Peter learns once and carries effortlessly forever. It is a choice he must make again every time he is hurt, afraid, uncomfortable or alone. He continues not because a more experienced hero tells him what to do, but because trying again has become part of who he is. That is what I had been waiting to see from this version of the character. The suit finally feels real, the city finally feels alive and the swinging finally carries the personality I remember from the comics, but the most important change exists beneath all of that. For the first time, this Spider-Man does not feel like he is searching for a place beside larger heroes. The story finally belongs to him.

title: A Stronger Peter Parker Story Hidden Inside a Very Crowded Marvel Movie
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day picks up four years after the devastating ending of No Way Home. Everyone still knows Spider-Man, but Doctor Strange's spell has erased Peter Parker from the memories of MJ, Ned and the rest of the world. Peter responds by devoting himself almost completely to crime-fighting, leaving very little ordinary life behind.

Tom Holland is the film's greatest strength. This is a more mature and tired Peter, and Holland handles that transition convincingly without losing the humour that made his version likeable in the first place.

The supporting cast is unusually large but mostly effective. Jon Bernthal's Punisher gives Peter a moral counterweight, Mark Ruffalo's Bruce Banner connects naturally with Peter's fear over his changing biology, and Florence Pugh steals her scenes as Yelena Belova, who apparently now conducts intelligence work from a bathhouse.

The biggest reveal is Sadie Sink as Jean Grey. Thankfully, she is more than an X-Men teaser. Jean's search for her missing sister gives her a personal motivation, while Tramell Tillman makes Damage Control director William Metzger a suitably calm and unpleasant human antagonist.

The film's main weakness is overcrowding. There are enough villains, heroes and MCU connections here for several films, and Peter's new organic webbing, heightened senses and disturbing physical mutation deserve more attention than they ultimately receive.

The unexplained history between Spider-Man and Punisher on Staten Island may also confuse viewers who assume it happened in another Marvel show. It did not; the film is deliberately referring to an off-screen incident.

Despite those issues, the ending lands. Peter's real journey is not about becoming a better Spider-Man. He already is one.

It is about becoming Peter Parker again.

A strong continuation, even if Marvel still has trouble leaving one good story alone without connecting six others to it.

title: The Street Level Spider Man We've Been Waiting For
review:
Compared with the pompous, tech driven Watts trilogy, this new installment from Destin Daniel Cretton feels far more grounded and true to the character's roots. The result is the best Holland Spider Man film to date, and perhaps the best since the Raimi era.

Cretton takes the trauma left behind by No Way Home and pairs it beautifully with the bustling New York City setting, showing just how easily loneliness can take root even in one of the world's largest cities. Of course, Peter Parker chooses this path to protect the people he loves, but he still needs a job, right?! The movie doesn't really bother explaining how Parker manages to pay his rent or afford his surveillance tech, but aside from that puzzling omission, it really captures the essence of the daily struggle to sustain a life with absolutely no balance.

Spider Man still knows a few people, though, including Bernthal's Punisher, and their interactions are hilarious while striking exactly the right note of New York tough love. I also loved the camaraderie between Spider Man and Liza Colón Zayas' NYPD detective, whose rapport with Peter adds another distinctly New York dynamic to the film. Several other Marvel characters are integrated just as naturally without overwhelming Peter's story.

I love Brand New Day's tonal shift and its more mature, street level take on Spider Man. It feels intimate, character driven, and refreshingly different, giving the superhero genre a much needed jolt at a time when it needs one most.

title: A new day has come. But is it too little, too late?
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the latest addition to the Marvel Cinematic Universe and follows the titular hero in an entertaining adventure of action, mystery, and pathos. And it is by far the most compellingly gripping and the strongest written of the four entries pertaining to the MCU, featuring a direction and tone the others really should have led with.

Up until Tom Holland's portrayal of Peter Parker and Spider-Man in his last solo outing, he has never really been asked to do much as an actor and has had too many opportunities come and go that would have otherwise established himself as the best on-screen actor playing the wall-crawling superhero to date, and this movie thankfully does the best job at demanding an emotionally resonate performance that Holland absolutely delivers on; the balance of Peter's depression and Spidey's quipy optimism sells you on his internal struggles as a lonely man. It is only unfortunate that now after three solo movies and several crossover appearances that the audience can finally live and connect with his portrayal of Peter, and that is not to say his prior appearances didn't have moments like that but that is also all they were, moments. Moreover, Peter being in the suit for a majority of his screentime is thematically relevant to the balance the iconic web-slinger needs, and this then connects directly to the villain's goals as well as their own sense of isolated loneliness. Additionally, the setting of New York City is given a much more lively spotlight in feeling intimately linked to its hero, with citizens being given throw away lines that helps the world feel more lived-in and worth protecting. But it is not just the regular folks either, as the additions of other pre-established heroes assists in the aforementioned lived-in aspect of this movie's depiction of New York, with the easy highlight being Jon Bernthal's Punisher who has shockingly great chemistry with Holland despite his inclusion adding more strain on the franchise's canon. The first hour or so is really solid at welcoming you back, catching you up, telling the detective-style plot, and establishing some other things such as the evolution of Peter's mutation. From more of a filmmaking perspective, the costumes are all colourful without being too vibrant for the plethora of the movie's villains, and Spider-Man's suit in particular may honestly be the best live-action suit to date if not purely for it being real fabric and such a faithful translation and fantastic enhancement of the source material's simplistic design. And director Destin Daniel Cretton's direction in the dynamic action is not only very well-choreographed but is also refreshingly fun to watch through the camera angles and movements that capture it all; the movie succeeds in grounding the digital effects by mostly sticking to practical tricks and real stunt work in flipping cars, hand-to-hand combat, and some less noticeable uses of real web-swinging that are combined with digitally exaggerated swings to sell the computer generated effects more convincingly.

However, despite the film's spectacular new takes on the old tropes, it does unfortunately fall short in a few areas that keep it from feeling truly amazing. The worst offending aspect is the story, which is although very compelling and conveys a meaningful message of allowing yourself to feel connection with others and embrace a healthy life balance, there are too many parts to make for a tightly efficient whole. Likewise, the film features naturally integrated and welcome surprise appearances (light spoilers ahead) that eventually bloat the runtime with overlong scenes of discussions that could have been shorter of the movie had Peter work out a few more clues by himself; the offenders in question are Yelena Belova and Bruce Banner, with the former being a fun short-lived performance from Florence Pugh that ultimately wastes time, whilst the latter contributes to the plot as he is being given a painfully phoned in performance from Mark Ruffalo. But cutting both of them would have been fine too, slimming down the runtime significantly by prioritising the NYPD and Damage Control factions with more focus and plot development. Similarly stale performances are Zendaya and Sadie Sink; although Zendaya gives a few effective moments of emotionality to MJ, she continues to treat the character with a disinterested dullness that is neither interesting nor fun to watch. Whereas the very talented Sink in her role on the other hand, holds great potential but the writing squanders it all by having her playing an unforgivably murderous snarky teen whom is responsible for countless deaths throughout the movie but suffers no remorse or backlash because she has a soft heart; her emotional core is strong but the movie refuses to acknowledge her murky moral compass. What is more frustrating is the secret primary antagonist, who is fine in serving a thematic purpose and establishing greater potential in the future, but is ultimately disappointing because they are given an emotional core yet also face a hollow moral dilemma that contrasts with their ruthlessness rather than blends with it. Furthermore, despite the plot carrying over the memory-wipe aspect that 'Spider-Man: No Way Home' had very sensitively, a lot of the rules and logic surrounding it can really creep into your mind; if Peter Parker does not exist, then what does he do for money? How does he register for an apartment? Is he erased only from memories or from physical records as well? And a few other minor nitpicks that do not affect the overall engagement with the movie include; the score feeling very by the numbers as far as scores for superhero movies go, which is a shame considering the popularity of the character in question; Michael Mando as Scorpion is wasted as an all too brief moment of payoff to his small yet significant scene in 'Spider-Man: Homecoming'; and no Marvel movie would be complete without at least one end-credits scene, with this one being a pointless waste that is simply not worth staying for.

It is getting harder and harder to discuss the crushing weight of context that is the grander Marvel Cinematic Universe. As the 56th MCU project, the 38th movie, and more specifically the 4th Holland-led Spider-Man outing, it holds a small population of pre-established characters that are hard to inexplicably accept into the overall plot, not to mention the new throwaway villains as well. Coming from such grounded beginnings to now being such a diversely populated world with costumes criminals all over the place makes for a strange moment of retrospect and how the franchise is nowhere near as clean-cut as it once was; there is no clear direction and the wild branches of creativity, or lack thereof, are straining audiences' memories as they stare and wonder if they are supposed to have seen prior entries for relevant context or if these movies now naturally bask in a care-free attitude towards exhibiting more comic-like random world-building behaviours. To be more effectively focused and blunt, an opening montage of unimportant villains is fun for kids but difficult for fans and general audiences to accept despite how accustomed they are to actors in spandex, given how detailed and developed this series' storytelling used to feel.

But in the end, Spider-Man: Brand New Day stands confidently as just an enjoyable and perfectly functional MCU movie. It is burdened and overcrowded, but is also simple, exciting, and highly entertaining.

title: The Spiderman We All Deserved.

And finally, when it comes to the villain, no one really knows who the true main villain is until the very end. All I can say is that if you haven't watched this movie yet, you should experience it in a cinema at least once. And if that's not possible, then wait for its OTT release.
