title: A hot mess that somehow works
review:
This is not a perfect movie, but it is a fun movie.

The good: Peter has lost most of his boyish immaturity - he's emotionally anguished and painfully lonely. From a writing perspective, it's a great way to tackle some serious themes and propel an aging Spiderman into adulthood. Tom Holland plays it well, and there are some tear-jerking moments to go along with the triumphs.

The bad: The portrayal of the antagonist is baffling. The limitations on her powers and the methodology she uses are in direct contradiction with everything we know about her, as well as basic common sense. The plot would have been better served by bringing in an alternate version of Kilgrave (Jessica Jones, S2), imho.

The ugly: Senseless cameos that somehow work. The Punisher, the Hulk, the Foot Clan, the New Black Widow (Yelena), Tombstone, Scorpion. Very little explanation or exposition as to how these characters came to be crossing paths with Peter Parker, just full-tilt fan service and plot device-ification. Somehow, it (mostly) works. The missing history, the time gap, the low-key mystery of what, exactly, Peter Parker has been up to - turns out that no explanation is SO much better than bad story-telling (for an example of over-explaining, see Captain America: Brand New Day).

This movie is not a 10, it's not winning an Oscar. It's just a fun way for a Marvel fan to spend 2 or 3 hours of their day. Have fun and enjoy!

title: Good but slightly underwhelming given the 5 year wait
review: This was a film I strongly anticipated since the day it was announced last year at CinemaCon, and although it is good to an extent, there are several factors that hinder it from being a "Masterpiece". I admired the approach Destin took with this film; however, it is somewhat lackluster in terms of the narrative pacing and included some filler content when it could've delivered more enjoyment. As for the positive aspects, the acting from this cast was phenomenal; Tom Holland's performance as Peter Parker/ Spider-Man was exceptional and I also cannot emphasize well enough how impactful and stellar Sadie Sink's portrayal of Jean Grey was. They both committed to their roles very well! The cinematography is surreal as well as the dialogue and direction. It is a grounded, mature street level film that is quite frankly a love letter to Spider-Man. What Peter goes through resonates so deeply with general audiences contributing to its profound themes of loneliness, darkness, and despair that amplifies itself which I and hopefully many others appreciate dearly as it simultaneously embraces his character and reassures the world they are not alone even when it appears that way. As for the nitpicks, I found Jean's backstory and motives to be particularly ambiguous as the first half was essentially her inhabiting multiple characters, including Scorpion, MJ, Punisher, and the Hulk, and it transitioned from that to Peter's relationship with MJ and Ned while Peter is insecure to confess his love to MJ due to the fear of her having no recollection of their past and not being able to convince her of that, which was extremely poignant and painful. Although Ned and MJ don't have that much screen time, their presence kind of lingers in the movie, ironically. Department of Damage Control (Bill Metzger) kept concealing information about Sarah from Peter and it was simply a long game of deception that inevitably resulted in Jean's outrage then Peter fights the Hand and reasons with her as she enters his mind, then sacrifices himself to save her life after suffering a bullet wound. Very naive of Peter as he suddenly has a change of heart and instantly forgives Jean for her unforgivable wrongdoings. I understand why he empathized with her but it felt impractical. Ending was satisfying as Peter earns the love and respect of all New Yorkers as he protects the city yet again. More of a fresh, new chapter of Peter Parker's life as Spider-Man and a reset of his character teasing more projects to come rather than an utter, complete film. Overall, great film. 8/10. Absolutely recommend it but could have been better given the hype.

title: Absolutely not as good as its predecessors

I went into Brand New Day with a neutral stance, and came out wondering if I would be watching another Spiderman movie with the same opinion coming into it.

The Bad: The movie felt too long, and after the first half of the movie ended, the movie started to lose its grip on me. Jean Gray was a very interesting antagonist until her identity got revealed and all of the mystique and wonder fell out from there. The second half of the movie fell from grace in my opinion, and noticeably slowed down.

The Ugly: The ending fight scene made absolutely no sense to me from a common sense standpoint, and this is what took the movie from a 7 down to a low 6 (Maybe 5 in a few weeks) in my books. I can never accept any solution to a problem that goes along the lines of "We both had shared trauma? Guess we wont keep fighting!" I understand that Jean got her heart touched by the late Aunt Mae but jeez, Jean JUST found out that her sister was dead, and the man who was controlling it was right next to her. It just didnt seem like enough, just felt like they needed to make Jean look like a okay person even though shes terrible. In my opinion, Sadie Sink saved the role with her acting, and most people would be agreeing with me if not for her.

Another part of the ugly is the casting, this goes away from the movie itself and is more of a personal pet peeve i have with marvel, which is only casting extremely well known actors as a safe route to garner public publicity and not take a riskier but much better route which would be to find a actor specifically suited for a role.

title: The Most Human Tom Holland Spider-Man So Far
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is, for me, the strongest Tom Holland Spider-Man film so far because it finally understands the human core of the character. The previous trilogy had bigger ideas, larger threats, and more spectacle, but it often depended too much on external conflicts, cameos, and stories that did not always feel deeply connected to Peter Parker.

This film feels different. It brings Spider-Man closer to what makes him work in the comics: a young man with problems, loneliness, grief, responsibility, financial pressure, and the constant need to keep helping others even when his own life is falling apart.

Destin Daniel Cretton's direction is a major improvement. The movie feels more personal, emotional, and focused than the previous films. The camera work is also stronger, especially the POV shots during swinging and action scenes. Those moments do not just show Spider-Man; they let us feel closer to his body, his fear, and his perspective.

Tom Holland gives his most convincing performance as Peter Parker and Spider-Man. He feels more mature, more vulnerable, and more real. Zendaya and Jacob Batalon return in a way that feels surprisingly organic, not forced. Their presence works because the film builds the emotional pain of Peter reconnecting with people who no longer remember him.

Sadie Sink is also very strong, bringing emotional weight and making her character a meaningful mirror to Peter's grief and loneliness. Jon Bernthal's Punisher works well as a contrast: two street-level vigilantes with very different ways of understanding justice. Mark Ruffalo's Hulk also feels more mature and aware than in earlier appearances.

The movie is not perfect. The score is forgettable and never becomes a real emotional force. Some soundtrack choices feel forced, especially when they seem designed more for viral impact than for narrative coherence. There are also realism issues: Peter is supposed to be broke and alone, but the film does not fully explain how he affords certain technology or how his daily life works.

Still, those issues do not ruin the experience. Brand New Day works because it understands that Spider-Man does not need to save the multiverse to feel important. Sometimes, watching Peter try to hold his own life together while still choosing to help others is more powerful.
author: PrimeraE

title: Tom Holland's Spider-Man Finally Has Teeth, Just not a True Villain to Use them On
review:
One Word: Grounded.

Highlights: Tom Holland, Jon Bernthal, Cinematography, Video Game Homages, Emotional Core.

Lowlights: Lingering MCU-isms, Minor Plot Holes, X-Men Set-up/Lack of True Villain.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the film Tom Holland's version of the character has been building toward for a decade, and it finally arrives. This is, without questions, his best outing as Peter Parker, and it's not particularly close.

A huge part of this comes down to how the film strips everything away from him. Losing his support system and watching the time jump play out is genuinely compelling, and it forces Holland into new territory as an actor; more isolated, more weathered, and all the better for it. He's an easy highlight in a film full of them. Jon Bernthal's Frank Castle never disappoints, and is another major standout. The Punisher steals every scene he is in, but more importantly, he gives the film a grounded, street-level weight that this genre has been missing for a while. The two's dynamic together is the backbone of much of the movie.

Visually, this might be the best-shot superhero film in recent memory. The New York City scenes are genuinely stunning, and the direction has a confidence and specificity that most Marvel projects don't bother reaching for. There is a clear sense that this is a superhero movie going back to the basics, street-level stakes, real consequences, a friendly neighborhood hero without the cosmic scale (for now I guess). The film is also emotionally moving, at least for true Spider-Man fans, in a way the character hasn't been on screen in quite some time. As a lifelong fan, the comic-accurate moments sprinkled throughout land as intended, and finishers pulled directly from the video games is a level of detail that shows genuine care for the character across mediums and an extremely high acknowledgement of the importance fan service can have on this genre.

It's not flawless. Marvel clearly knows what they have in Holland and they are going to lean on him hard going forward, and some of that corporate instinct shows through. Jean Grey is a great cheater and Sadie Sink is excellent in the role, but it's hard to feel that this didn't need to be the film that introduced her and starts reigniting interest in the X-Men. It pulls focus from what's an otherwise pure grounded Spider-Man story. The long standing critique of this incarnation never getting a real villain to go toe-to-toe with also holds up here, and it's the one thing keeping the film from greatness. I do have faith that this will be addressed in the next two installments to come, and if the quality continues to match what we see here, I am very excited about what is yet to come. A few plot holes crop up too, asking the audience to fill in gaps rather than answering them outright. None of this undoes what the film gets right though.

To me, Tom Holland is officially the best live-action Spider-Man, and Brand New Day is the movie that will prove it for a lot of viewers.

Overall: 9/10

title: A lonely spider finding his way forward
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a movie that understands the feeling of Spider-Man, even if it does not always deliver a story that feels completely new. Going into the film, I was in an interesting position: I was mostly walking in blind, but at the same time, I had a general idea of certain things that were going to happen. I knew about Sadie Sink's character and had an idea of who she might be, but I was more interested in seeing how the movie would introduce her and how she would fit into Peter Parker's story.

One of the biggest reasons I was excited for this movie was seeing what Tom Holland's Peter Parker would be dealing with after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home. That film left Peter in one of the most difficult places we have seen him in: completely alone, separated from the people he cares about, and forced to continue being Spider-Man without anyone knowing who he truly is. Brand New Day does a strong job exploring that emotional aftermath.

Peter's isolation feels realistic, both physically and emotionally. The loneliness, the frustration, and the feeling of wanting to reconnect with people around him all come across as genuine. There is a real sense of yearning in Peter's character that makes his journey easy to understand. The movie captures the feeling of someone who is trying to move forward while still carrying the weight of everything he lost.

Visually, the film is one of the strongest Spider-Man experiences in the franchise. The way New York is portrayed within the Marvel universe gives the city its own identity and makes it feel like a living part of Peter's world. The cinematography is incredible, with camera work that captures the movement, speed, and creativity that make Spider-Man unique. At times, the style reminded me of what The Amazing Spider-Man films with Andrew Garfield were trying to achieve, especially in how they focused on the feeling of being Spider-Man rather than just the superhero action.

The action sequences are another major strength. The fights provide just enough excitement while also showing Spider-Man's growth since his introduction in Captain America: Civil War. Instead of relying only on large-scale destruction, the movie highlights Peter's agility, intelligence, and ability to improvise during fights. It shows how much he has developed as both a hero and a fighter.

Another thing the movie does surprisingly well is handling its large cast of characters. With so many characters being introduced, there was always a risk that the film would feel overcrowded. Most of the characters feel like they have a purpose because they connect back to Peter Parker's development. Their roles feel tied to his journey rather than being included just for the sake of having more characters. Compared to many recent Marvel films, the additions feel more natural and less forced.

However, the movie does have weaknesses. The biggest issue is that some of its emotional themes feel familiar. Peter's struggles with anger, guilt, loneliness are important parts of who Spider-Man is, but they are also themes that have been explored many times before. While the movie handles these emotions well, it does not always feel like it is taking Peter into completely new territory.

The film also uses a Marvel formula that has become increasingly common: introducing a character who appears to be the villain before revealing that they are misunderstood or motivated by deeper reasons. While this idea can work when executed properly, it has become predictable after appearing in many Marvel projects. It makes some character reveals easier to anticipate and takes away some of the surprise.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a solid continuation of Peter Parker's story with incredible visuals, strong action, and a genuine understanding of his emotional struggles. Its biggest strengths come from how well it explores Peter's loneliness and how each character connects back to his development.

The movie succeeds because it understands where Peter Parker is after the events of No Way Home. It does not need to reinvent the character; instead, it focuses on showing how Peter continues forward after losing so much. While it may not be the most surprising Spider-Man story, it is still an enjoyable and meaningful chapter in Tom Holland's portrayal of the character.

7/10.

title: "And Lo, We Find What We Once Forsook, Ere Fate Doth Bid Us Part."
review:
I don't think I can properly explain how much this movie changed the way I see Tom Holland's Peter Parker.

Before today, I always carried a certain resistance toward Tom's Spider-Man. As someone who grew up loving Andrew's Peter - the loneliness, the brokenness, the weight he carried - I never quite accepted a Spider-Man who could be this funny, immature, and carefree. Maybe that version of Peter was simply never mine.

But today, something changed.

Yes, he is still immature. Still funny. Still Tom's Peter. But beneath all of that, I finally saw the man he has become-the maturity, the energy, the sacrifice, and especially the way he carried everyone when he could have simply walked away.

And what he did for Jean... I genuinely don't have the words. There was something so painfully beautiful about it. He has lost his MJ, yet somehow, for the first time, he isn't alone anymore.

And maybe that's where this story is heading - a peaceful, heartfelt, yet devastating farewell to the characters we have grown up with.

Today, they opened the door for the X-Men to return to the MCU through Jean. Peter found a new life, but somehow, we already know it may not last forever. Eventually, everyone will stand together against Doom.

We know they'll probably win.

But at what cost?

Whose sacrifice will break us? What will be left when the war is finally over?

Because somewhere deep inside, we already know the truth:

Secret Wars may not just be the end of a story. It may be the moment we lose everything we grew up with.

And after everything I felt today, I can say this without hesitation -

Whatever records this movie breaks, whatever the numbers become... for me, this is the greatest Spider-Man movie since The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014).

Not because it was perfect.

But because, for the first time, Tom's Peter finally felt like my Spider-Man too.

title: Different. More grounded. More serious but alsoLacks some of that MCU spark.
review:
It feels like half way through production, its direction changed.

Its pace is slower. More serious, more grounded. In some ways, an interesting take, in others, depressing.

There's a very solemn mood imposed onto the movie from around the half way point.

The inclusion of hulk, punisher and Yelena (Black Widow?) feel somewhat unnecessary. There's a lot of new characters but what value they add is somewhat negligible.

There's an odd ode to the previous Spider-man movies in some ways. For some scenes, the CG feels old school. Some, perhaps dated, and behind in "quality" but others as if they are deliberately trying to spark that nostalgia. But from a production point, too polished and studio esque. There are imperfections that occur IRL, like swinging through buildings that aren't apparent here, creating a sort of dissonance for me, making it difficult to connect with the movie.

The personal growth to villain problem balance is odd. It moves between the two, but the villain feels like the B-plot of it. While I appreciated the slower pacing and greater focus on characters, something about it didn't quite mash.

The performances of all actors felt great, it's the writing and directing which is in question for me. Some character moments felt synthetic. Like a perfume salesman trying to charm you with a "genuine moment". Minor tropes, but my biggest annoyance in the newest MCU movies is the "Humour is Oxygen" approach. Some scenes make the movie really feel like a product. "Insert funny moment here" with something like "Spider-man crashes into a wall and we all laugh".

Half the movie feels good and different, the other half feels like aura farming and "want would x do in this situation" and "what should we add here to please the audience" instead of writing a damn story people can genuinely connect to, because it's a story, and not a product calling to expand the universe and sell more merch.

Worth the watch. But a mixed end result imo. Glad for the experimentation but it feels like the MCU is at its end and we're at super hero fatigue, and the approach is aura farming hard instead of going back to genuine roots.

title: An Emotional Web Worth Swinging Into!
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New - A worthy and emotionally satisfying addition to the Spider-Man franchise!.

The movie delivers a well-written script, an impressive background score, and stunning visuals. Watching it in 3D is absolutely worth it, as the CGI and Spider-Man's action sequences look fantastic on the big screen.

One of the biggest strengths is seeing a more emotionally mature Spider-Man. The love story is beautifully written and cleverly becomes the movie's biggest twist, making the emotional moments hit even harder. The film balances emotion, action, and humor perfectly, with plenty of goosebumps moments and lots of laughs throughout.

Tom Holland and Zendaya once again deliver excellent performances. The addition of Punisher works surprisingly well, and his chemistry with Spider-Man is blended perfectly. I only wish the climax had a few more action sequences, but it still has enough wow moments to leave an impact.

The visuals are crisp, the VFX are clean, and the overall production quality is top-notch. Sadie Sink as Jean Grey gives a heartfelt performance, especially in the emotional scenes, and stands out whenever she's on screen.

The post-credit scene is decent-not mind-blowing, but it nicely sets up what's next.

Overall: A worthy sequel that continues Spider-Man's journey with heart, humor, and spectacular visuals. If you're a Spider-Man fan, this is one you definitely shouldn't miss!

title: High Emotional Impact Hurt by Over-Revealing Trailers
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day succeeds brilliantly as an emotional character study of Peter Parker, even if the surrounding story suffers from predictable writing and overly generous marketing.

The Good: Character Dynamics & Tone: The film captures Peter's lonely, heavy-hearted mental space exceptionally well before building toward an uplifting conclusion. His interactions with Ned and MJ bring great heart, and the moment Ned recognizes Peter after their handshake stands out as the absolute peak of the movie.

Surprising Highlights: Jon Bernthal's Frank Castle brings an unexpected comedic dynamic that completely shifts his typical portrayal. Sadie Sink delivers a compelling, multi-layered performance as Jean Grey-balancing genuine menace with a caring side driven by her sister. Plus, Mark Ruffalo's return as Savage Hulk is a welcome treat.

Visuals: The web-swinging and camera work look fantastic throughout.

The Bad: Predictable Plot: The narrative relies on familiar beats that are easy to guess in advance-casting an actor like Sadie Sink (the perfect casting choice) made her role obvious from the start.

Action & Spoilers: The action sequences felt far too brief. Worse, the official trailers robbed the film of its biggest surprises-moments like Spider-Man vs. Hulk and the Hand Ninja fight would have landed so much harder on the big screen had they been kept under wraps.

Verdict: Despite weak marketing ruining key reveals, the emotional core, visual polish, and standout character interactions make this a deeply moving and memorable chapter for Peter Parker.

title: This is the most human Spider-Man has felt in a long time.
review:
Tom Holland has been solid as Peter Parker from the start but this is easily his strongest turn yet. He feels older. Tired in a real way. The loneliness after everything that went down in No Way Home sits heavy on him and you can see it in every quiet moment. There are scenes where he barely says anything and still sells the whole emotional weight. I used to think Tobey had the lock on the more mature version of this character. Holland closes that gap here. Maybe even surpasses it in places.

Sadie Sink is a great addition. She brings this grounded intensity that the movie needed. Her scenes with Tom have real tension and neither of them overplays it. It feels honest.

The swinging looks better than it has in years. Destin Daniel Cretton actually lets Spidey move through the city with some freedom again. Those sequences have energy and weight. You feel the speed and the risk in a way the last few films sometimes missed.

The story leans into what it means for Peter to keep going when almost nobody remembers who he really is. It does not rush past that idea. Some parts drag a little in the middle but the emotional stuff lands hard enough that I did not mind.

Not every part is perfect. A few stretches in the middle feel a little padded. Still... the good stuff is strong enough that I walked out feeling like I had watched a real character grow instead of just another superhero outing.

title: No way back from No Way Home
review:
Who would've thought following the events of No Way Home that the most logical next step for another sequel was to scale everything back? I suppose there was no way back from No Way Home. I mean seriously, how do you top the simultaneous onscreen appearances of the holy trinity that is Tom Holland, Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield? You simply can't.

In some ways then, a scaled back, old-school outing centred more so around Peter Parker (and less so of his web-slinging alter ego) on paper at least, made for perfect sense. Really, in several ways Brand New Day is the better superhero film. This is actually a far more grounded take, surprisingly mature, with an emotionally vulnerable performance from Tom Holland. You really feel for his character who is left to navigate a world (or really, just New York) that has long forgotten him since the climactic events of NWH. Brand New Day shines in its quieter moments, with realistic scenes played out between Parker and MJ, none of which felt forced or a cop out as I originally predicted.

The action was solid (a fight with Hulk a particular standout) and there were plenty of slick and original camera shots. What I also really appreciated was the friendly neighbourhood tone more so akin to the original Spider Man and its 2004 sequel. It felt more comic accurate to see Holland's Spidey busting criminals and gangs rather than taking on big bad intergalactic foes. I also really enjoyed the chemistry and strained rivalry between Parker and Frank Castle, even if Castle's bigger than expected role was slightly jarring at times.

However, Brand New Day totally lacked any surprises. There was no suspense or anticipation, no revelations and no surprise cameos. Overall, this was a less unique cinematic experience than NWH. It was always obvious, despite the pointless secrecy, that Sadie Sink was going to be Jean Grey and her arrival in the MCU should've been a huge deal given the teasers for Doomsday. But in reality it all fell flat. Sadie Sink was perfectly fine as Grey, but she was letdown by the writing. There was no explanation for her powers, her origins, no mentioning of mutants, no context whatsoever for the organisation hunting her and perhaps most disappointingly, there was nothing that alluded to the imminent arrival of the X-Men in the MCU. Guess we'll have to wait for Doomsday.

title: This is what a Spider-Man movie should be!
review: To be honest, Tom Holland's Spider-Man never fully convinced me. His previous movies felt quite mediocre because they lacked depth, and the character was constantly dependent on others. Even his villains only had a few brief flashes of brilliance and not much else. Years later, we can finally admit that No Way Home relied heavily on nostalgia; it wasn't actually a great film on its own, even if it was enjoyable at the time. However, Brand New Day fixes absolutely everything. This movie gives us countless comic book references and features a mature Peter Parker with relatable struggles that truly make you connect with him-the scenes with Zendaya were incredibly tough to watch. It balances this emotional weight perfectly with exciting mini-fights and engaging cameos that keep the story entertaining throughout. There is also a fundamental reason why this movie succeeds so well: Sadie Sink. Beyond her undeniable beauty, she easily delivered the best performance in the entire cast. I'm not surprised since she was already my favorite in Stranger Things, but I'm thrilled to see her showcase her immense talent on the big screen. Furthermore, even though Jean Grey might seem like an odd match for Spider-Man at first, I loved their chemistry by the end. She becomes a great friend and mentor figure for him; they essentially saved each other, creating an unbreakable bond. title: A New Day, A Different Spider-Man
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day understands something important about Peter Parker.

Sometimes, starting again does not mean forgetting the past.

It means learning how to live with it.

Four years after the events of No Way Home, Peter is living alone, forgotten by the people who once knew him. He has chosen to become Spider-Man full-time, protecting a New York that no longer knows his name. But solitude has a price, and the pressure begins to affect him in ways he cannot simply punch away.

That is where the film becomes more interesting.

This is not simply another chapter in the Spider-Man saga. It feels like a transition. Peter is older now. More experienced. More isolated. And perhaps, for the first time, he has to discover who he is when there is nobody left to remind him.

Tom Holland brings a different weight to the character. There is still humor, still energy, still the Spider-Man we know. But underneath the mask there is something quieter.

Loss.

Responsibility.

And the need to keep moving.

The film also expands Peter's world with new threats and unexpected connections, while keeping the story grounded in the streets of New York. The result is a superhero movie that remembers that Spider-Man works best when the spectacular and the personal exist together.

Not everything works perfectly. Some elements feel designed to prepare the ground for what comes next, and the increasingly large Marvel universe can sometimes compete with Peter's own story.

But perhaps that is part of the point.

Brand New Day is not about returning to the beginning.

It is about continuing.

Peter Parker has lost almost everything.

And yet he is still there.

Still climbing.

Still protecting the city.

Still Spider-Man.

A new day does not erase what came before.

It simply gives you another chance to move forward.

title: The hardest battle is the battle against your memories.
review:
Every time the film opened a door for Peter to reconnect with his past, the audience burst into applause.

That was when I realized people were still there for Peter Parker himself-not Marvel's five-year plan.

Kiarash usually doesn't have much of a reaction to new superhero movies. He says most of them have become repetitive and worn out. So when he told me this Spider-Man was worth watching, I was surprised.

We went to see it, and he was right-though with one major caveat.

Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home. The world has forgotten Peter, and he has packed away his personal life in a cardboard box labelled "I'll deal with this later," dedicating himself full-time to cleaning up New York's criminals.

And this is exactly where the film comes alive.

When Spider-Man finally leaves the annual multiverse convention and returns to the streets of New York, we remember why we loved him in the first place.

He was supposed to be the friendly neighborhood Spider-Man-not the multiverse's PR representative, and certainly not some poor guy who steps out to buy milk only to run into three parallel universes and two supervillains along the way.

Tom Holland also delivers one of his most mature performances here. He doesn't need a five-minute speech to show us how broken Peter feels:

One look.

One pause.

One slumped shoulder.

That's all.

It feels as though he has spent years carrying rent, electricity bills, an identity crisis, loneliness, and the responsibility of saving New York-all at the same time.

But Marvel will always be Marvel. It simply cannot leave a good personal story alone and allow it to remain good.

Peter says, "I'm so lonely."

Marvel replies, "Perfect! Now take this mysterious case too. You'll find out what it means in 2029."

Whenever the film focuses on Peter Parker, it comes alive. Whenever it is forced to serve the future of the MCU, it struggles to breathe.

Overall, Brand New Day is not a revolution, but it is a return to the right path. It doesn't reinvent Spider-Man; it simply reminds us why we loved him in the first place.

A tired Peter.

A lonely Peter.

A defeated Peter.

But still Peter.

⭐ My rating: 7.5/10

Did I like it? Yes.

Did I fall in love with it? No.

Did I search for information about the sequel afterward? Unfortunately, yes.

So despite all my complaining, Marvel once again managed to do exactly what it wanted.

Which Spider-Man do you prefer: the friendly neighborhood Spider-Man, or the multiverse's PR representative?

title: A Brand-New Standard for Spider-Man
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is easily the best film of Tom Holland's Spider-Man run-and it may even be the best Spider-Man film across all three live-action actors.

The practical swinging sequences are incredible, drawing clear inspiration from Insomniac's Spider-Man games-some of my favorite Spider-Man media-as well as The Amazing Spider-Man 2. The dynamic between Spider-Man and the Punisher elevates the movie to another level, providing plenty of laughs while also delivering several meaningful emotional moments.

One of the film's greatest strengths is the attention it gives to Spider-Man's relationship with New York City. Whether through his connections with Detective DeWolff, the NYPD, the EMTs, or everyday New Yorkers, the movie understands that Spider-Man's bond with his community is an essential part of what makes him Spider-Man. Even the background characters with only a few lines make the most of their limited screen time and add life and personality to the city.

The dynamics between Peter, MJ, and Ned are also handled extremely well as they navigate the aftermath of Spider-Man: No Way Home. The film's themes-the importance of community, the dangers of isolation, and the need for vulnerability-are clear, impactful, and relatable. That relatability is especially important because it has always been at the heart of Spider-Man as a character.

The villain remains unpredictable throughout the movie and keeps the audience wondering what they will do next. The character also opens the door to some exciting possibilities for the future of the MCU. I especially appreciated how every major character served an important purpose in the story. In some previous Holland films, the additional MCU characters occasionally felt included simply for the sake of appearing, but everyone in this movie contributes meaningfully to the plot.

The soundtrack is exceptional-I enjoyed it so much that I took a picture of every song listed during the credits. The credits themselves also feature some amazing cinematography and are absolutely worth staying to watch.

My only real complaint is that characters such as Scorpion, Tombstone, Boomerang, Tarantula, and Ramrod are introduced or reintroduced only to appear briefly in a montage. I understand that their purpose is to provide a glimpse into the life Peter has been living since No Way Home, but I hope future projects give these street-level villains the opportunity to be developed further.

Overall, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an amazing Spider-Man movie that understands the character, his relationships, and his connection to New York City. I highly recommend seeing it for yourself-possibly more than once!

title: A New Day Has Come!
review:
First things first, congratulations to Marvel Studios and distributor Sony Pictures for achieving the highest opening weekend gross of all time in North America. Spider-Man: Brand New Day arrives with enormous expectations, and while it doesn't quite reach the heights of Spider-Man: No Way Home for me, it successfully gives Peter Parker something he desperately needs: a genuine new beginning.

This time, the director focuses on Peter Parker's bright side (his heart and humor) and his dark side (his inner demons), something I noticed in Spider-Man 2 when Sony re-released all the Spider-Man films in theaters back in 2024 for Columbia Pictures' 100th Anniversary. Like Spider-Man 2, the film understands that Peter's greatest battles aren't necessarily with supervillains. His personal struggles are what make him relatable. On a personal level, I experience tension headaches, so I loved seeing Peter Parker experiencing the same thing!

Next, the problem is that Hulk, Punisher, and other major Marvel characters occasionally make the film feel less like a Spider-Man story and more like an MCU crossover. Their appearances are entertaining, but they sometimes compete with Peter for the spotlight.

Unfortunately, the third act is where the film loses some of its momentum. Without getting into spoilers, the villain feels underdeveloped, and the motivations never become compelling enough to justify the threat. After spending so much time establishing Peter's personal journey, I wanted the antagonist to feel more closely connected to that journey.

What I appreciate most is that Brand New Day doesn't simply try to recreate the formula of the previous trilogy. It feels like a soft reboot, allowing Peter to move forward while still respecting everything he's experienced. And speaking of new beginnings, the MCU missed a golden opportunity by not including Celine Dion's "A New Day Has Come" The song practically writes itself!

Brand New Day may not surpass No Way Home for me, but it doesn't need to. Its greatest achievement is giving Peter Parker room to grow beyond the story we've already seen. Despite its uneven third act and occasionally distracting supporting characters, this feels like the beginning of a new chapter-and potentially a brand-new Spider-Man trilogy.

title: Best spider man movie yet
review:
I didn't watch any trailers or teasers going into this movie - even went as far as to block Sony and marvel accounts on my socials. I had absolutely no idea what to expect, and I'm so incredibly glad. From the moment this movie started, I didn't feel like I was watching yet another MCU multiverse story, I felt like I was watching spider man.

There were so many moments in this movie where my jaw dropped, so many references to the comics, I love that they took aspects of the spider man games and incorporated them into this movie, his suit was such a great homage to Tobey and Andrew's characters, and I'm so glad that Toms spider man has finally established himself as something other than a mini-Tony stark. It felt so refreshing to see him moving away from stark tech and actually being a more accurate version of spider man. On top of that, the storyline was incredible. Not a single scene felt wasted, the writing was impeccable, and they added just the right amount and the right type of humour.

When it comes to Tom Hollands acting, there's not a single fault. His ability to make acting seem natural and effortless is truly admirable, at not one point did I feel like I was watching "Tom playing spider man", I only felt like I was watching THE spider man. And you can truly feel not only his love for acting, but also his connection with his cast mates. Holland clearly has a drive to continue challenging himself through his roles, understanding exactly what the audience wants to see from spider man.

Jacob and Zendaya continue to steal the show with their talent and wit - Jacob's delivery of humour has always been incredible, and he just seems to keep getting better. As for Zendaya, as usual I never felt like I was watching Zendaya, only MJ, a skill which she carries across all of her roles. Her ability to put her own image and ego aside and fully embody different roles should be studied, and she is certainly an inspiration.

As for Sadie Sink, her acting skills were incredible. This is the first time I've really felt her acting presence, and for a first-time marvel appearance, she really has set the standard high and I'm so excited to see her in the future.

From the costume design to the writing, the acting and everything in between, I have absolutely no notes about this movie. The directors and writers have honed into exactly what a spider man movie is supposed to be. Cretton has once again absolutely blown audiences out of the water - you can certainly call me a fan.

title: The best MCU Spider-man movie
review:
It's refreshing seeing a a bit more grounded spider-man, one, who doesn't have multi-billion tech and costume and no weird magic. That's how the story of Peter Parker and Spider-man be told.

The cinematography also sticks out from the other movies, being more dynamic and innovative - the first person perspective, upside-down shots and more beginner/inexperienced swinging scenes. The battle scenes look very impressive, especially the Hulk battle.

The story is interesting and keeps you engaged, I didn't quite know where the movie was going throughout its runtime. The Punisher is a cool sidekick and the overall comedy in the movie is funny.

Jean's character has a heart-breaking backstory and it's cool seeing more nuanced "villains".

I like how Peter only uses one costume and not 5 like in the previous movies. Aunt May actually giving her nephew advice is also an improvement compared to the previous MCU movies, where she doesn't play that big of a role (except for No Way Home of course).

The movie is far from perfect though - the main villain doesn't seem to have any reason to why he exploits the people with superpowers. You could just say: "He just wants to have their power and become very strong and evil", but that's boring and lame.

As most Marvel movies connect to one another and are dependent one another and it feels like watching a long episode of a show. I am not saying that the ending is bad, it is actually very satisfying and sweet, but you don't feel a sense of completeness like other movies (like in No Way Home).

I wished the Scorpion played a bigger role and wasn't randomly left during the movie. Also after the incredible Hulk fight it just ends with the Hulk (or Bruce idk) remembering Peter, which is very anti-climactic.

It's weird how Peter is broke but also have highly advanced tech and relatively big apartment in NYC, that ruins the immersion a tiny bit.

All in all it is a descent movie, but typical Marvel problems don't allow it to become anything more that just a fun movie.

title: Does whatever a spider can...
review:
I'll put this right up there with the first Tom Holland Spider-Man. Following the events of the last movie, everyone that Peter Parker loved has completely erased him from existence, and we see that though his eyes as he peeks in on his best friends in the world moving on and without him. It is heartbreaking, but we know why he did it - to protect MJ and Ned and so many others following the huge mess he made in No Way Home.

After that bit of housekeeping, we are off to the races and see Spidey doing his part to keep the city safe from any number of nefarious characters. Some we've met before and others are there as a little nod to die-hard Spiderman fans. The action is fun, Spiderman seems to be having a good time with his little quips, and he's working closely with Detective Jean DeWolff to coordinate rounding up the "bad guys." But he's struggling. We see it. DeWolff sees it. The weight of his decision is pulling him to the brink, which is the catalyst for a major change in his core powers.

So, yeah, I'm not going to say anymore in the interest of NOT SPOILING anything. I knew very little going in, so when surprises popped up, I was pretty thrilled. Do whatever you can to shield yourself, because there are some great things sprinkled throughout.

The action sequences are amazing, the expression of superpowers is incredible, and there are some wonderful quieter moments between the characters which round them out and make them even more relatable.

All of that, and the score by Michael Giacchino is pitch perfect for this one. Not to mention the needle drops that fit nicely with the mood of living in New York as a young adult.

Not to put too fine a point on it, but when people post things like "The MCU is done" or "There's superhero fatigue," maybe keep this one in mind. It's rich, fun, and full of surprises.

title: It's actually 0 out 5.
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day

So this is Spider-Man: Brand New Day, 38th film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) produced alongside with Sony Pictures, 4th Spider-Man film in MCU, directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, starring Tom Holland as the titular character. The film follows Spider-Man fighting a faceless Villain, investigating a case without any clues or procedure apparently, while undergoing a dangerous mutation. He's alone, he's broken, he's everything we need from a Spider-Man. Just hearing that pitch, I'm in. This is all we've been wanting for from our Friendly Neighbourhood. The result, however, is empty, shallow and do you know what, this was the most unexpected outcome for me, it was really boring.

What a disappointment! My biggest issue was that I never understood what the film was actually trying to say. It lacks a clear thematic through line. The villain is the clearest example of this. There's very little that feels genuinely threatening or even particularly villainous about them, so the central conflict never carries any real weight. Instead, the film leans heavily into sentimental, overly cheesy emotional beats that really makes your eyes-roll. The lines are stiff and the emotional moments land with little-to-no impact.

On top of that, the film becomes a revolving door of superhero appearances. Characters constantly enter and exit the story, because why not?

I wasn't a fan of Spider-Man: No Way Home, but somehow this feels like a step down. I genuinely don't know what happened here. For me, this is one of the weakest Spider-Man films in recent memory.

Instead, here is what I recommend, watch the 2nd season of the 1994 animated Spider-Man. The entire season spins around this one problem and manages to swoop in all these characters. Neogenic Nightmare, the 2nd season, is split into 15 chapters, 15 episodes. It is one case. One problem. It has mutants. It has Punisher. And many more cameos. It actually essentially entails the same issue that Peter goes through in this film and yet it is so much more juicy. It is rich in emotional weight, it has fierce cameos and has set pieces that propels the story organically- it's relentless fun. Do yourself a favour, watch the 1994 Spider-Man and thank me later.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is more than another superhero movie!
review:
**Spider-Man: Brand New Day is more than another superhero movie-it is a powerful reminder of why Spider-Man continues to mean so much to generations of fans.**

The film carries the excitement, humor, heart, and emotional weight that define the best Spider-Man stories, while still feeling fresh and meaningful. It understands that beneath the suit, the spectacle, and the extraordinary abilities is a young man constantly choosing to stand up again, even when life gives him every reason to stay down.

Tom Holland once again proves that he was born to play Peter Parker. His performance is sincere, vulnerable, funny, and deeply human. He does not simply portray a superhero; he makes us feel the loneliness, courage, responsibility, and quiet hope of the person behind the mask.

Zendaya brings remarkable emotional depth and presence to every moment. She has the ability to communicate so much through the smallest expression, making her character feel authentic, intelligent, and unforgettable. Jacob Batalon remains one of the heartbeats of this world, bringing warmth, humor, and genuine humanity that make the relationships feel real rather than manufactured.

The Director (Destin Daniel Cretton) deserves enormous praise for balancing intimate character moments with the scale and energy expected from a Spider-Man film. The action is thrilling, but it never overshadows the story's emotional core. Every major sequence feels driven by character, purpose, and consequence-not spectacle for spectacle's sake.

My deepest appreciation also goes to the entire production team-the writers, cinematographers, editors, stunt performers, visual-effects artists, costume and production designers, composers, sound teams, and every person working behind the scenes. Their dedication can be felt throughout the film. Together, they created something that is not only entertaining, but also emotionally alive.

**Spider-Man: Brand New Day feels like a celebration of resilience-the courage to begin again when the future is uncertain. It is thrilling, heartfelt, beautifully performed, and made with genuine love for the character and the audience.**

Tom Holland, Zendaya, Jacob Batalon, the Director (Destin Daniel Cretton), and the entire production team have given us a Spider-Man story worthy of its name. This is not merely the beginning of a brand-new day for Peter Parker-it is a beautiful reminder that hope often begins after our darkest night.

**An unforgettable cinematic experience and a Spider-Man film I will carry with me for a very long time.**

title: A Promising New Chapter, But the Crown Still Belongs to No Way Home.
review:
Now, talking about the movie itself, I genuinely enjoyed it. Ever since it was announced, I had incredibly high expectations. I kept imagining where the story would go and how everything would come together in the end. While it didn't completely reach the sky-high expectations I had built in my mind, it was still a thoroughly enjoyable experience.

The performances were outstanding across the board, and the story was engaging from beginning to end. Yes, the film has a few minor flaws, but when you look at the bigger picture and what it was trying to accomplish, I think it succeeded. It delivers a solid and entertaining Spider-Man story that stays true to the character.

Tom Holland, without a doubt, is the heart of this movie. His performance was absolutely phenomenal and easily the strongest part of the film. He perfectly captured both Peter Parker's emotional struggles and Spider-Man's heroic spirit. He lived up to every expectation I had, and honestly, he's one of the biggest reasons I was so excited to watch this movie in the first place.

The movie also does a great job of keeping the audience invested with exciting moments, emotional beats, and surprises throughout. And finally, the introduction of a major new character-someone who could become one of the most powerful figures in the entire MCU-raises the stakes for the future in a huge way. That reveal alone has made me even more excited to see where the MCU goes next, and I genuinely can't wait to see what's coming next.

That said, Spider-Man: No Way Home still remains the best Spider-Man movie in the MCU, without a doubt. The emotional impact, the fan service, and the way it brought Peter Parker's journey full circle are still unmatched. Brand New Day is a strong and promising new chapter, but for me, No Way Home continues to hold the crown.

title: Amazing
review:
How can you be a Spider-Man fan and not love this movie?

On paper this story shouldn't work. You have many cameos, setup for future MCU projects and continuing the story of the previous trilogy while also telling a new one. I was actually a little surprised at how direct of a continuation it is. But somehow it all totally works. Every plot points ties very neatly with one another just like a web. The pacing is relentless, dare I say perfect.

Without a doubt, this is the best looking Tom Holland Spiderman movie. The picture is colourful and saturated and the cinematography matches the character perfectly. Seriously, the camerawork in this movie is amazing. As is the choreography of the fights. There are also a lot of dope swinging scenes which were missed in previous entries.

The Punisher is a standout. Surprisingly he works perfectly as a comedic character. This is without a doubt his second best MCU appearance right after Daredevil Season 2 (Netflix). To my surprise he works perfectly as a comedic character here. Jon Bernthal does a fantastic job.

Side tangent; I can't understand how you had a Daredevil season and a Punisher special this year, preceding this movie only by a few months, and NEITHER is connected in any way whatsoever. This is especially jarring with Spidey and Daredevil. WTF was Peter doing during the AVTF riots? How you mess up something so basic is beyond me. This is a big sign of what is wrong with Marvel these days and how it lost its way. All this is not a criticism of the movie, of course.

Probably my only complaint would be the villain. It's basically just a discount Millchick unfortunately.

This movie also makes a very interesting statement for the character, which is that he can't do this alone. Will this "choice" ultimately lead to another tragedy down the road? Personally I think this storyline is primed for the symbiote suit next.

title: Busterd frank
review:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day follows Peter Parker living a completely isolated life after Doctor Strange's spell makes the entire world forget who he is. Dedicated entirely to his superhero identity, Peter anonymously protects the streets of New York, battling street-level crime while coping with profound loneliness and the loss of Aunt May.

Soon, Peter's body undergoes a surprising and dangerous physical evolution: he develops organic web-shooters, extremely heightened spider-senses, and a growing, aggressive rage. Seeking a way to stabilize these changes, he visits Bruce Banner, who provides inspiration for a technological inhibitor device.

Complications arise when his former friends, MJ and Ned, return to New York from MIT. Though they do not remember him, Peter finds himself emotionally torn as he watches them from afar. Meanwhile, he is drawn into a dark conspiracy involving the Department of Damage Control (DODC) and a powerful young mutant named Jean, who possesses telepathic abilities and is searching for her captured sister.

After initial clashes, Peter and Jean form an alliance to expose the DODC's secret operations. Ultimately, Brand New Day transitions from a standard superhero action film into a deeply emotional coming-of-age story, focusing on grief, acceptance of change, and the inevitable journey into adulthood.

title: Four Beats Later
review:
Dynamic tonal choices and the trauma of loss sit cozily in this Spider-Man installment. The cast shares a bond that feels natural, while the action sequences offer some of the finest ballet in modern blockbuster filmmaking. Cameos from favorite characters elevate the story without overwhelming it.

No live-action Spider-Man had ever been given a fourth film. This one feels as though it were always meant to exist. Tom Holland's characterization of Spider-Man is given the opportunity to play through some dynamic shifts.

His Spider-Man began in high school and, four beats later, arrives at the fracture of self that follows trauma. The truly debilitating part of grief is the realization nothing could have been done to prevent the loss. Life continues even though the people worth living for are no longer a part of that life.

For a studio to allow its hero to evolve rather than sideline him in favor of his villains is a blessing. Pairing him with tried and true characters such as Jon Bernthal's Frank Castle offers something more meaningful than a cameo. It offers contrast.

Here is hoping we see a fifth chapter in the continuing growth of this Spider-Man and the friends who remain to grow alongside him.

title: My Review (No Spoilers).

The dark lighting alongside the colors gave a new twist to Spider-Man's world, which was surprisingly similar to Gotham City's theme. Tom Holland portrayed Spider-Man brilliantly in this film, showing how mature Peter has become. Sadie Sink's performance was convincing, but her trauma's writing weakened her character due to the lack of interpretation of her past. Bruce Banner and Frank Castle had a tremendous influence on this movie. Therefore, most characters' existences were meaningful in serving the events of the story. However, the lines were not the worst and also not the best. They were coherent enough to make you laugh, grasp, and cry.

The cinematography was fascinating, like Spider-Man: No Way Home. The ensemble's performance in this film was the best in comparison with most Spider-Man movies. The directing of this movie was quite balanced, as the director made the emotional phases solid by leaving touching flashbacks that reinforced the thesis.

The pacing of the events was convenient but went down at the end, as the conclusion felt hollow and surprisingly unclear about the characters' fates and futures. Many missing fragments could have been linked into this movie to make it a threshold before Avengers: Doomsday, like when Thunderbolts contributed its thesis to Marvel's future projects. In addition, this film lacks some bold decisions that could have jeopardized the characters' fates in the long run and kept the audience emotionally and spiritually captured about their futures in comparison with No Way Home.

Nevertheless, this is one of my favorite Spider-Man films, as it illustrated many mature emotions and the process of moving on through the hardships of life, which were delivered specifically for grown-ups.

My overall rating. 83%

title: Friendly Neighborhood Spiderman Done Right
review:
This isn't a movie trying to be the biggest, most universe shattering thing Marvel has ever made, and honestly that's exactly why it works.

Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal have genuinely great chemistry on screen. Their scenes together are easily some of the most enjoyable parts of the movie and you can tell there was real effort put into that dynamic. Jean Grey as the villain was fine, nothing more, nothing less. She does the job but doesn't leave a huge impression.

What I appreciated most is that the plot stays small in scope. It's a classic, typical Spiderman comic book story rather than another apocalyptic threat, and that choice pays off. The humor lands, the action sequences feel natural, and the character interactions never feel forced. The main plot itself isn't especially intricate or clever, it's a pretty basic story, but it's executed well enough that it doesn't matter.

The emotional beats are where the movie really shines. Peter reconnecting with his friends hits harder than expected, and Aunt May's monologue is a genuine highlight. There's a moment where Spiderman is just walking around inside government buildings that felt a little jarring given the tone of everything else, but it's easy enough to overlook.

On the downside, Hulk is completely wasted here. As a character and as a plot thread he adds almost nothing, and I'm hoping future movies give the secondary characters more to actually do. Also disappointed there were no hints or nuggets pointing toward Doomsday, which felt like a missed opportunity.

Overall it's nothing groundbreaking, just a solid, regular Marvel superhero movie where the comedy actually lands and the character work is strong. Worth a watch if you're not expecting a game changer.
author: yashbee

title: Spider-Man Groundhog Day
review:
I went into Spider-Man: Brand New Day with high expectations. I'd deliberately stayed away from most of the marketing, but the reviews had been overwhelmingly positive and, after a bit of a hiatus from Marvel, I was looking forward to diving back in.

Unfortunately, I came away feeling a little underwhelmed.

This is by no means a bad film. In fact, it's a perfectly competent superhero movie. The cinematography is polished, the action is well staged when it arrives, and the sound mix delivers the impact you'd expect from a blockbuster of this scale.

The biggest issue is the pacing. The film spends so much time trying to establish and rebuild relationships that it never quite finds its rhythm. Ironically, despite all that time, many of those relationships still don't feel as emotionally developed as they should. The result is a film that often lingers without giving the emotional payoff it seems to be aiming for.

I also found it surprisingly dependent on previous Marvel knowledge. Having taken a break from the franchise, I often felt as though I was expected to recognise characters, relationships and plot threads that the film made little effort to re-establish. While long-time fans may appreciate those connections, newcomers or more casual viewers could easily feel left behind.

There are flashes of what the film could have been. The action scenes are enjoyable, the performances are solid, and I can understand the decision to lower the stakes after years of increasingly universe-ending threats. In theory, bringing Spider-Man back to a more grounded story is a sensible direction.

It just never quite comes together.

Perhaps that's why I kept thinking about Superman while watching it. That film balanced spectacle with genuinely resonant themes and natural character development. Brand New Day has the technical polish but never finds the same emotional heartbeat.

Ultimately, this is a watchable, competently made Marvel film that does very little wrong, but very little that genuinely surprised or excited me either. It feels as though the franchise is following a familiar formula rather than finding a fresh direction.

title: Great Power, Slightly Fewer Consequences
review:
89/100

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is one of Tom Holland's strongest Spider-Man films. It is funny, emotional, visually polished and extremely entertaining, while still being accessible to children and younger viewers. It comes close to a 9/10 for me, but a safe ending, limited consequences and several familiar superhero clichés keep it at the very top of the 8/10 category.

There is plenty of Spider-Man humour, and I laughed several times, although the film knows when to become serious. There is also some obvious Tom Holland fan service for women. He somehow appears more muscular in every movie, and the film is fully aware of it. Having watched The Odyssey immediately beforehand, it was also amusing to see Holland return with such a similar haircut. It briefly felt as though he had left ancient Greece and put on the Spider-Man suit.

Holland is the film's greatest strength. He has always fitted the physical role extremely well and brings credibility to the action, but Brand New Day gives him more emotionally difficult material. He is especially convincing when Peter is depressed, emotionally unstable or fighting his own inner demons. Holland moves between humour, grief, anger, exhaustion and vulnerability naturally.

Those scenes made me think about whether he could carry the kind of dramatic role Timothée Chalamet played in Beautiful Boy. This performance suggests that he probably could. Holland does not merely play a sad superhero; he makes Peter feel like a person who is genuinely losing control of himself.

The emotional impact surprised me. My eyes teared up several times, more than they did during my first viewing of The Odyssey. The emotion in Nolan's film is connected to war, hospitality and civilisation, whereas this feels immediate and personal. You care about Peter, understand his pain and genuinely want him to find his way back.

The movie also has beautiful messages about accepting help, reconnecting with other people and refusing to let pain define you. Peter may reach a darker psychological place here than in any previous Spider-Man film I have seen. The film deserves praise for taking him that far.

Unfortunately, it does not go far enough. The story approaches something genuinely deep and then becomes cautious. Peter's struggle could have produced more lasting development and more difficult consequences, but the movie eventually falls back on familiar superhero solutions. There are too many tropes and clichés for a story that is otherwise trying to push the character into new emotional territory.

The relationship through which Peter begins to heal also feels rushed. The two characters help each other in a way that works emotionally in the moment, but the bond needed more time to feel completely earned. I am not a regular comic reader, so changing established comic relationships does not automatically bother me. However, I understand why readers may question a pairing between characters whose interactions have apparently been relatively rare. The movie can justify taking a different creative direction, but it still has to develop that relationship fully on screen.

The story is good and tied together better than I initially expected. It balances Peter's internal struggle, Ned and MJ, the increasingly fractured Spider-Man, the new threat and several characters with different loyalties. I did not predict exactly how those elements would connect.

The film also sets up future stories. Some fans may find that distracting, but I did not know about the setup while watching and did not find it especially noticeable. In hindsight, I can recognise moments that are clearly preparing later movies, yet they do not seriously weaken the experience for an average viewer.

The references to earlier Spider-Man films and the comics are also handled well. They feel connected to Peter's history rather than inserted merely to make the audience clap. The film understands that references are most effective when they support character and emotion.

The central trio play their roles very well, and the heroes, villains and morally uncertain characters are all convincing. Nobody in the supporting cast gives the kind of performance that completely takes over the movie, but nobody needs to. Tom Holland is clearly the standout, while the others support his story effectively.

The cinematography is good, and the movie is beautiful to look at. I did not watch it in IMAX, but the scale and visual polish make it a reasonable IMAX choice. The action is enjoyable throughout, although only one sequence made me think the choreography was genuinely exceptional. The rest is competent and entertaining rather than among the very best superhero action ever filmed.

The pacing is strong. The movie moves smoothly between humour, sadness, action and multiple storylines without becoming exhausting. It is consistently entertaining and rarely feels overloaded, even when it is managing several characters and preparing future stories.

The dialogue is good enough for what the film is trying to do, but its need to remain palatable to children and younger audiences places a ceiling on its depth. It has meaningful ideas and some effective emotional exchanges, but not enough truly exceptional dialogue to compete with the greatest dramas. The action is also not consistently extraordinary enough to compensate for that limitation.

The score works well and supports both the action and emotion. I would call it good rather than epic. It never damages a scene, but it is not one of the elements I expect to remember most clearly or listen to repeatedly on its own.

My largest criticism is the ending. An ending often determines how strongly a film remains with me, and this one could have been far more impactful. Without going into major spoilers, the conclusion needed greater consequences, fewer clichés and more courage.

This is one of those superhero films where you are genuinely rooting for the hero. I wanted Peter to succeed. But caring about a hero does not mean the story should protect everyone from lasting consequences. After taking Peter so far psychologically, the movie has an opportunity to complete his development through a genuinely difficult choice or loss. Instead, it pulls back. It feels as though very little ultimately changes for anyone.

A braver ending could have made Brand New Day a genuine 9/10. As it stands, the film offers an unusually emotional journey but stops short of fully committing to it.

Comparing this with The Odyssey is difficult because they have completely different ambitions. The Odyssey is far more technically demanding, historically and thematically expansive, and difficult to create. It is the greater filmmaking achievement. Brand New Day, however, feels more personal and immediately emotional. During my first viewing, it entertained me more consistently and made me tear up more often.

My ratings primarily reflect the experience a movie gives me, not simply the scale of the challenge behind it. That is why I can place Brand New Day one point above The Odyssey numerically, even while recognising that Nolan's film is the more impressive production. The difference is tiny, and both remain in the 8/10 category for different reasons.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is definitely one of the better superhero movies. It is funny without becoming disposable, emotional without forgetting to entertain and accessible to children without feeling entirely childish. Holland gives one of his best performances as Peter Parker and proves that he can handle far more dramatic material than the role usually requires.

It does not have the depth, dialogue, consequences or consistently exceptional action needed to join the greatest movies or reach a 9/10. But it is a really good film, and more importantly, it made me care.

title: Better than I Expected
review:
Spider Man Brand New Day, was a film I wasn't overly excited for. Not just because Marvel's track record over the past several years has been rather hit or miss, but because Tom Holland's Spider Man franchise has been very hit or miss for me. I liked him in Civil War and Infinity War. But, before this movie, No Way Home was the only Spider Man movie with him that I enjoyed. I don't like Homecoming or Far from Home much at all.

Is Brand New Day bad? No. Is it a masterpiece? No. Is it the best Spider Man movie ever? No. It's not even the best in Tom Holland's lineup. I still think No Way Home is overall better. But I like this movie. I thought it was alright. And I can see that opinion changing for the better on repeated viewings. There's a lot the movie does well, but there are also some really questionable story and character decisions made.

The movie succeeds in the most essential element, Spider Man himself, and his personal character arc. This is the first time Holland actually feels like Spider Man. That's one of my major complaints with the first two films in his run. He felt more like Iron Man Jr. Than Spider Man. I honestly found him rather whiny and unsympathetic in those films too. It wasn't until the end of No Way Home that he finally felt like the character he was supposed to be. Now, we finally get to see him actually be Spider Man, and for once I'm with him. I love his suit too. This might be my favorite Spidey suit I've seen Holland in. IU also like that we see him take down minor super villains in the movie. That's something we've never really seen in the movies yet.

The Punisher is also here. I thought he was just going to be a cameo, like Daredevil in No Way Home, but no. He's a major character, and him and Spider Man have good chemistry with each other. Another major issue with these Spiderman movies is I've never like Peter's supporting cast. I never cared for Zendaya's MJ, and I always found Ned annoying. But, because they're in the movie sporadically, I can deal with them much more.

The production value is great. All the action scenes are fun and well-shot. Like No Way Home, the film is very long, but doesn't feel, padded aside from a couple scenes.

Now we get to the things I didn't care much for. Hulk's inclusion is a bit strange. It's weird that they chose this movie to have him be in, and not Captain America 3, the one with all his villains in it. The Hulk is pretty much just here just to have a big fight with him. The fight itself is fun, there isn't much else to Hulk here. Also, Banner's relationship with Hulk in this feels at odds with everything we got in Endgame and the first Avengers movie regarding him. But, it's nice to see actual Hulk back in a movie after nearly ten years.

There was also this character that served as Peter's main confidant for the first half of the movie. She seemed like a major character, but then she just disappears for the entire second half. That was a bit strange.

The big thing is the villain of this movie. For most of the movie, the main villain is a character from the comics, who typically isn't a villain, but a hero. But here she definitely is a villain, and the worst kind of villain. The villain the narrative tries at the end to gaslight you into believing she was just misunderstood and not actually a bad person, despite doing many morally questionable if not heinous things throughout the film. The writers clearly don't want to make her a straight up villain, because she isn't supposed to be one, but many people either died or were injured because of her, be directly or indirectly. Bruce Banner was done very dirty by, but she never has to pay for any of that.

These next two things are very minor, but they irk me. One think that I always found irksome in this particular franchise is the lack of acknowledgement of Uncle Ben. It annoyed me more in this movie than the others. We see Peter constantly reference Aunt May and how much he misses her, but no acknowledgement of Uncle Ben at all. Also, I found it weird that J. Jonah Jameson isn't in this at all, especially given how prominent he was in the previous movie.

Overall, the movie was alright. I'd say go see, but given the box office, you probably have already.

title: Incredible action and web-swinging drag down a frustratingly messy street-level story
review:
While Spider-Man: Brand New Day features some of the best web-swinging, choreography, and visual set pieces in the entire MCU, it ultimately falls short due to forced crossovers and questionable handling of established street-level lore.

The Good: Spider-Man's Mutation Arc: The best part of the movie is watching Peter Parker's powers evolve and mutate. Seeing his physical transformation and heightened abilities pushed to the limit shows that Spider-Man can actually evolve into a stronger, more formidable superhero. Tom Holland nails the fear and raw intensity of losing control over his body.

Top-Tier Action & Web-Swinging: Destin Daniel Cretton's direction shines during the action sequences. The web-slinging feels fast, heavy, and visually stunning-easily some of the most dynamic swinging shots we've gotten on the big screen in years.

The Bad: Street-Level Lore Disrespect: If you loved the grounded storytelling of Netflix's Daredevil, The Defenders, or Daredevil: Born Again, this movie is going to frustrate you. Turning an ancient, terrifying mystic ninja syndicate like The Hand into glorified, brainwashed security guards for Damage Control completely strips them of their threat level.

Frank Castle as a Babysitter: Having Frank Castle save Peter multiple times and act like an off-screen buddy/mentor waters down the Punisher. Instead of the relentless vigilante from Daredevil Season 2, he feels shoved into Spidey's narrative just to bail Peter out.

Too Much MJ & Ned, Not Enough Villains: While I understand why the studio felt obligated to bring MJ and Ned back after No Way Home, they take up way too much screentime. Most fans bought a ticket to see Spider-Man fight terrifying villains, go all-out in combat, and stand on his own feet-not to spend half the movie re-treading relationship drama.

Verdict: It's not a complete waste-the mutation storyline is a fascinating direction for Spidey's future, and the visual spectacle is undeniable. But when compared to top-tier Marvel television like Daredevil, the shallow world-building and forced crowd-pleasing hold it back from being anything higher than a light 6/10.

title: Not as 'New' as You Might Think
review: When I watch a movie, I expect to be entertained, enlightened and/or informed (not necessarily in that order or all at once). But what I don't want is to be treated like a marketing prospect. And that, unfortunately, is one of the problems with many of the releases in the Marvel Universe, including this latest installment in the Spider-Man franchise. Given the studio's intricate web of properties (no pun intended) in this overlapping assortment of superhero franchises, there are considerable character and storyline cross-overs in virtually all of its film projects. Now, because of that, some cross-pollination of the narratives is bound to occur. But, when this practice becomes a key element in developing the plots of these offerings, it begins to feel more like marketing manipulation than bona fide storytelling, as is the case here. I don't particularly appreciate using existing efforts to purposely promote upcoming productions. It tends to make these movies somewhat formulaic and cookie-cutter in nature. And, even though that's not carried to an extreme in this release, it's present nevertheless, no matter how much director Destin Daniel Cretton may try to enliven whatever other distinguishing characteristics might have been incorporated into the script. In essence, the film continues the current Spider-Man mythology with protagonist Peter Parker (Tom Holland) working largely as a solo undercover crimefighter in New York going after bad guys in a world where he and his past accomplishments have been intentionally forgotten as part of a selfless protective initiative. Only he retains recollection of what came before, leaving him alone where this knowledge is concerned, since old colleagues, including his onetime love interest, M. J. (Zendaya), retain no personal memory of him. It causes him a certain sense of emotional weariness, but it's also something that he doesn't have the luxury of time to focus on, given his workload and the fact that he's going through transformations of his own while battling a menacing new nemesis (Sadie Sink). True, he secures some assistance from past superhero kindreds (Mark Ruffalo, Florence Pugh), but they don't remember him either, compromising their effectiveness. Can he overcome all of these challenges? That's a question as much for viewers as it is for Spidey himself, given that, in telling this story, multiple narrative threads are introduced (and not especially clearly), a problem that plagues the flow of the material in the opening half. This could potentially hamper viewer understanding until the picture's back end, when it finally finds a firmer footing to tell its tale (even if some of it isn't always adequately explained). Judicious editing may have helped here, but then that may have meant trimming some of the marketing material for future releases (and we can't have that now, can we?). In short, "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" is probably best seen as a mediocre Marvel offering that features some modestly entertaining enhanced character development but that nevertheless covers a lot of action-adventure ground we've already seen before in countless other studio releases and that could certainly use some shrewd pruning of its overlong 2:24:00 runtime, too. Diehard fans of the franchise will no doubt love this (or virtually anything else that Marvel chooses to put up on the screen) no matter what, but I can't help but take issue with that assessment. After all, there's quite an undeniable irony here in the bold wording of the film's title, which would seem to promise something new but doesn't follow through on that pledge as well as it might have.
